docs.text:
You now understand:

Singleton
Factory
Builder
Strategy
Observer
Decorator

These 6 patterns already cover ~70% of real-world backend architecture.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Adapter converts one interface into another interface that client code expects.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It helps integrate third-party APIs or legacy code without changing client code.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: An SMS adapter can wrap a third-party SMS provider and expose your application’s NotificationSender interface.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Adapter does not add new business behavior.
  • It translates interfaces.
  • Do not leak third-party API details into client code.
  • Too many adapters can signal poor boundaries.
  • Adapter is different from Facade.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Adapter sits between client code and an incompatible class. The client uses the expected interface, while the adapter translates calls to the adaptee. This keeps integration logic isolated.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Converts interface.
  • Useful for third-party APIs.
  • Keeps client code stable.
  • Wraps incompatible class.
  • Adapter translates calls.
  • Different from Facade.

docs.title: Adapter Pattern
docs.text:
It is used when:

Two incompatible interfaces must work together

Example from your projects:

WhatsApp API integration
SMS provider integration
Email provider integration

Each provider has different API structure, but your system wants one unified interface.

Before we go to Adapter Pattern, answer one quick thinking question:

Imagine you integrate:

Twilio SMS API
MSG91 SMS API
Gupshup WhatsApp API

Each API has different method signatures.

What design problem appears if your business logic directly calls those APIs everywhere?

It becomes hard to maintain and replace an existing API provider.

docs.title: Correct Reason
docs.text:
If business logic directly calls APIs like:

twilio.sendSMS(...)
msg91.sendSMS(...)
gupshup.sendMessage(...)

then these problems appear.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Tight Coupling
docs.text:
Your system becomes tightly coupled with specific providers:

Twilio
MSG91
Gupshup

If you want to switch provider:

Twilio → MSG91

you must modify many places in the code.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Hard to Replace Providers
docs.text:
Example:

Twilio API method
sendMessage(String number, String message)

MSG91 API method
sendSMS(String phone, String templateId)

Different signatures.

Your business logic must change everywhere.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Scattered Integration Logic
docs.text:
Provider-specific logic spreads across:

Controllers
Services
Jobs
Notification modules

Maintenance becomes difficult.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Hard to Test
docs.text: Testing becomes difficult because code depends on external APIs directly.

docs.title: Solution → Adapter Pattern
docs.text:
Adapter Pattern allows us to:

Convert one interface into another expected interface.

Meaning:

Your system interface
        ↓
Adapter
        ↓
Third-party API

docs.title: Adapter Pattern Definition
docs.text:
Adapter Pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface
that clients expect.

Simple meaning:

Make incompatible interfaces work together

docs.title: Real Life Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a power adapter 🔌

Your laptop charger:

3-pin plug

But the socket has:

2-pin outlet

Adapter converts:

3-pin → 2-pin

Same idea in software.

docs.title: Target Interface (Your System)
docs.text:
interface SmsService {
    void send(String number, String message);
}

Your business logic uses this interface only.

docs.title: Third-Party API (Different Interface)
docs.text:
Example Twilio:

class TwilioApi {

    public void sendMessage(String phone, String text) {
        System.out.println("Twilio sending SMS");
    }
}

docs.title: Adapter
docs.text:
class TwilioAdapter implements SmsService {

    private TwilioApi twilioApi;

    public TwilioAdapter(TwilioApi twilioApi) {
        this.twilioApi = twilioApi;
    }

    public void send(String number, String message) {
        twilioApi.sendMessage(number, message);
    }
}

Adapter converts your system call into Twilio API call.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        SmsService smsService =
            new TwilioAdapter(new TwilioApi());

        smsService.send("9999999999", "Diet reminder");
    }
}

Your business logic only knows:

SmsService

Not Twilio.

docs.title: Switching Provider Is Easy
docs.text:
Now if you use MSG91:

class Msg91Api {

    public void sendSMS(String mobile, String text) {
        System.out.println("MSG91 sending SMS");
    }
}

Create adapter:

class Msg91Adapter implements SmsService {

    private Msg91Api api;

    Msg91Adapter(Msg91Api api) {
        this.api = api;
    }

    public void send(String number, String message) {
        api.sendSMS(number, message);
    }
}

Now switch easily:

SmsService sms = new Msg91Adapter(new Msg91Api());

No business logic changes.

docs.title: Real Example From Your Projects
docs.text:
This pattern fits perfectly in your systems:

SMS providers
WhatsApp APIs
Email providers
Payment gateways
Analytics tools

Instead of writing provider logic everywhere, create adapters.

docs.title: Java Example
docs.text: Java uses Adapter Pattern here:

docs.title: Arrays.asList()
docs.text:
List<String> list = Arrays.asList(array);

This converts:

Array → List interface

That is Adapter Pattern.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Loose coupling
Easy provider replacement
Cleaner integration layer
Better maintainability

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
More classes
Extra abstraction layer

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is Adapter Pattern?

You can say:

Adapter Pattern is a structural design pattern that allows two incompatible interfaces to work together by converting the interface of one class into another interface expected by the client.

docs.title: Short Notes for Your Notes
docs.text:
Adapter Pattern

Purpose:
Make incompatible interfaces work together.

Structure:
Target interface
Adapter
Adaptee (third-party class)

Advantages:
Loose coupling
Easy provider switching
Cleaner integration

Examples:
API integrations
Payment gateways
SMS providers
Arrays.asList()

docs.text:
You now understand:

Singleton
Factory
Builder
Strategy
Observer
Decorator
Adapter

These 7 patterns already cover most real-world backend architecture.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Facade provides a simple interface over a complex subsystem.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It makes client code easier to use and hides internal workflow complexity.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A BookingFacade can coordinate payment, inventory, notification, and invoice services behind one method.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Facade should not become a giant service with all logic.
  • It simplifies access but does not replace subsystem classes.
  • Do not hide important errors.
  • Facade is not the same as Adapter.
  • Keep facade methods use-case focused.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Facade gives client code a clean entry point to a complex subsystem. It coordinates multiple internal classes and exposes a simpler API, while the subsystem can still exist independently.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Simple API over complex subsystem.
  • Improves readability.
  • Coordinates multiple services.
  • Does not change subsystem interfaces.
  • Different from Adapter.
  • Useful for use-case orchestration.

docs.title: Facade Pattern
docs.text:
It is used when:

Complex system
Many subsystems
Client needs simple interface

Example from your projects:

Send notification
→ SMS service
→ Email service
→ WhatsApp service
→ Logging
→ Retry
→ Analytics

Client just calls:

NotificationFacade.send()

and facade handles everything.

Before we start Facade Pattern, answer one quick thinking question:

docs.title: If a client must call 10 different services in sequence, what software design problem appears?
docs.text:
This creates tight coupling because concrete classes depend directly on other concrete classes.

Correct ✔️

But there are actually multiple problems in this situation.

docs.title: Problems When Client Calls Many Subsystems
docs.text:
Imagine client code like this:

SmsService sms = new SmsService();
EmailService email = new EmailService();
AnalyticsService analytics = new AnalyticsService();
RetryService retry = new RetryService();
Logger logger = new Logger();

sms.send();
email.send();
analytics.update();
retry.retry();
logger.log();

docs.title: 1️⃣ Tight Coupling
docs.text:
Client depends on many concrete classes:

SmsService
EmailService
AnalyticsService
RetryService
Logger

If any service changes → client must change.

docs.title: 2️⃣ High Complexity
docs.text:
Client must know:

Which services to call
In what order
What parameters to pass

This increases client complexity.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Hard to Maintain
docs.text:
If new steps appear:

Audit logging
Rate limiting
Security validation

Every client must update code.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Violates Principle of Least Knowledge
docs.text:
Also called:

Law of Demeter

Clients should not know too many subsystem details.

docs.title: Solution → Facade Pattern
docs.text:
Facade Pattern provides:

Simple interface
to a complex subsystem

So instead of client calling many services, it calls:

NotificationFacade.send()

docs.title: Facade Pattern Definition
docs.text:
Facade Pattern provides a simplified interface
to a complex system of classes, libraries, or frameworks.

Meaning:

Hide complexity behind a simple API

docs.title: Real-Life Analogy
docs.text:
Think of hotel reception desk.

Instead of contacting:

room service
laundry
restaurant
transport
maintenance

You just call:

Reception

Reception coordinates everything.

Reception = Facade

docs.title: Subsystems
docs.text:
class SmsService {
    void send(String msg) {
        System.out.println("SMS sent: " + msg);
    }
}

class EmailService {
    void send(String msg) {
        System.out.println("Email sent: " + msg);
    }
}

class AnalyticsService {
    void log(String msg) {
        System.out.println("Analytics logged");
    }
}

docs.title: Facade
docs.text:
class NotificationFacade {

    private SmsService sms = new SmsService();
    private EmailService email = new EmailService();
    private AnalyticsService analytics = new AnalyticsService();

    public void sendNotification(String msg) {

        sms.send(msg);
        email.send(msg);
        analytics.log(msg);
    }
}

docs.title: Client Code
docs.text:
Instead of calling many services:

NotificationFacade facade = new NotificationFacade();

facade.sendNotification("Diet reminder");

Simple and clean.

docs.title: Why This Is Powerful
docs.text:
Client only knows:

NotificationFacade

Not:

SmsService
EmailService
AnalyticsService

This reduces coupling.

docs.title: Real Example From Your Projects
docs.text:
Imagine your automation system:

Task assignment flow:

Update task database
Send notification
Update dashboard metrics
Log audit event
Trigger reminder

Without facade:

TaskService
NotificationService
MetricsService
AuditService
ReminderService

With facade:

TaskWorkflowFacade.assignTask()

Facade orchestrates everything.

docs.title: JDBC
docs.text:
You use:

DriverManager.getConnection()

Internally many classes work, but client sees simple interface.

docs.title: Spring Framework
docs.text:
Spring Boot hides complexity of:

Bean creation
Dependency injection
Lifecycle management
AOP

Spring acts like a large facade over many subsystems.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Reduces coupling
Simplifies complex systems
Improves readability
Centralizes workflow logic

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Facade can become a God class
May hide too much complexity

So use carefully.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is Facade Pattern?

You can say:

Facade Pattern is a structural design pattern that provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem. It hides the complexity of multiple interacting classes and exposes a single unified interface to the client.

docs.title: Short Notes for Your Pattern Notes
docs.text:
Facade Pattern

Purpose:
Provide simple interface to complex subsystem.

Problem solved:
Client interacting with too many subsystem classes.

Structure:
Facade class
Subsystem classes
Client

Advantages:
Reduces coupling
Simplifies usage
Centralizes workflow logic

Examples:
Spring Boot
JDBC
Notification workflow

docs.title: Your Pattern Progress
docs.text:
You now understand 8 very important patterns:

1 Singleton
2 Factory
3 Builder
4 Strategy
5 Observer
6 Decorator
7 Adapter
8 Facade

This already covers most patterns used in real backend systems.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Proxy controls access to another object by standing in front of it with the same interface.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It is important for Spring AOP, lazy loading, security checks, caching, and remote calls.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A service proxy can check permissions before calling the real service.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Proxy and Decorator look similar but intent is different.
  • Proxy controls access; Decorator adds behavior.
  • Spring often creates proxies around beans.
  • Self-invocation can bypass Spring proxy behavior.
  • Proxy should preserve expected behavior.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Proxy represents another object and controls access to it. It can add checks like security, caching, logging, lazy initialization, or remote communication before delegating to the real object.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Same interface as real object.
  • Controls access.
  • Used in Spring AOP.
  • Can support lazy loading.
  • Can add security/caching.
  • Intent differs from Decorator.

docs.title: Proxy Pattern
docs.text:
It is used for:

Security checks
Lazy loading
Caching
Remote calls
Access control

Examples in Java:

Hibernate lazy loading
Spring AOP proxies
Java dynamic proxies

Before we start Proxy Pattern, answer one quick thinking question:

Imagine a system where a file download service must:

check user authentication
check permission
log access
then download file

docs.title: Should these checks be inside FileDownloadService itself, or handled separately?
docs.text:
Explain why.

It should be handled separately, because FileDownloadService does not need to know about those other services.

docs.title: Why it should be handled separately
docs.text:
If FileDownloadService itself does:

  • authentication
  • authorization
  • logging
  • download logic

then these problems appear:

docs.title: 1. Single Responsibility Principle breaks
docs.text:
FileDownloadService should mainly handle:

file download

But now it is also doing:

security
permission validation
logging

So one class gets too many responsibilities.

docs.title: 2. Tight coupling increases
docs.text:
FileDownloadService will depend on:

  • AuthService
  • PermissionService
  • LoggerService

That makes the core service harder to maintain.

docs.title: 3. Reusability decreases
docs.text:
Suppose later you need same checks for:

  • image download
  • report download
  • invoice download

If checks are embedded in each service, code gets duplicated.

docs.title: This leads to Proxy Pattern
docs.text:
Proxy Pattern is useful when you want:

one object to control access to another object

So client calls proxy, and proxy decides:

  • authenticate
  • authorize
  • log
  • cache
  • lazy load
  • then call real service

docs.title: Proxy Pattern Definition
docs.text:
Proxy Pattern provides a placeholder or surrogate for another object
to control access to it.

Simple meaning:

middle layer before actual object

docs.title: Real-Life Analogy
docs.text:
Think of a VIP office receptionist.

You do not directly enter the CEO room.

First receptionist checks:

  • who you are
  • whether you have permission
  • whether appointment exists

Then access is granted.

Here:

  • Receptionist = Proxy
  • CEO = Real object

docs.title: Subject interface
docs.text:
interface FileService {
    void download(String fileName);
}

docs.title: Real service
docs.text:
class FileDownloadService implements FileService {

    public void download(String fileName) {
        System.out.println("Downloading file: " + fileName);
    }
}

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
class FileDownloadProxy implements FileService {

    private FileDownloadService realService = new FileDownloadService();

    public void download(String fileName) {

        System.out.println("Checking authentication");
        System.out.println("Checking permission");
        System.out.println("Logging access");

        realService.download(fileName);
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        FileService service = new FileDownloadProxy();
        service.download("report.pdf");
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Checking authentication
Checking permission
Logging access
Downloading file: report.pdf

docs.title: Why Proxy is useful
docs.text:
The client sees only:

FileService

And can call:

service.download(...)

But proxy adds extra control before delegating to real object.

docs.title: Types of Proxy Pattern
docs.text: Very important for interviews.

docs.title: 1. Protection Proxy
docs.text:
Controls access based on authorization.

Example:

admin can access
normal user cannot access

docs.title: 2. Virtual Proxy
docs.text:
Creates heavy object only when needed.

Example:

lazy loading image/file

docs.title: 3. Remote Proxy
docs.text:
Represents remote object.

Example:

RPC / network service / remote API

docs.title: 4. Caching Proxy
docs.text:
Stores results and avoids repeated expensive calls.

Example:

report download cache
API response cache

docs.title: 1. Spring AOP Proxies
docs.text:
Spring often creates proxies for:

  • transactions
  • security
  • logging
  • lazy beans

docs.title: 2. Hibernate Lazy Loading
docs.text:
Hibernate uses proxies for lazy-loaded entities.

Example: actual object loads only when needed.

docs.title: 3. Java Dynamic Proxy
docs.text: Java provides proxy support through reflection APIs.

docs.title: Real Example From Your Project Context
docs.text: This pattern fits your projects well.

docs.title: Example 1: Role-based dashboard access
docs.text:
Before opening candidate or admin dashboard:

  • check user role
  • check campaign access
  • log access

Then call real dashboard service.

docs.title: Example 2: API wrapper
docs.text:
Before calling sensitive API:

  • validate token
  • check permission
  • log request
  • then call actual API service

docs.title: Example 3: File/report download
docs.text:
Before exporting reports:

  • check whether user is admin
  • verify rate limit
  • log audit
  • then generate/download report

This is a perfect proxy use case.

docs.title: Proxy vs Decorator
docs.text:
Very common interview question.

They look similar because both wrap an object.

docs.title: Decorator
docs.text:
Adds behavior dynamically.

Example:

notification + logging + retry + encryption

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
Controls access to the real object.

Example:

auth check + permission + lazy loading + caching

Easy rule:

Decorator → enhance behavior
Proxy → control access

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Access control
Lazy loading
Logging and security outside main service
Better separation of concerns

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
Adds extra layer
Can increase complexity
Too many proxies may make flow harder to trace

docs.title: Interview-ready answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is Proxy Pattern?

You can say:

Proxy Pattern is a structural design pattern in which a proxy object controls access to a real object. It acts as an intermediary and can add features like security checks, logging, caching, lazy loading, or remote access without changing the real service implementation.

docs.title: Short notes for your separate notes
docs.text:
Proxy Pattern

Purpose:
Control access to a real object.

Problem solved:
Need security, logging, caching, lazy loading, or remote access before calling actual object.

Structure:
Subject interface
Real subject
Proxy class

Types:
Protection Proxy
Virtual Proxy
Remote Proxy
Caching Proxy

Examples:
Spring AOP proxies
Hibernate lazy loading
File access control
API security wrapper

Difference from Decorator:
Decorator adds behavior
Proxy controls access

docs.title: Small thinking question
docs.text:
Imagine an image gallery app.

Loading every full-size image immediately is expensive.

docs.title: Would Virtual Proxy be useful here?
docs.text: Answer yes or no and explain why.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: Yes, Virtual Proxy helps here.. Because it would provide lazy loading of images, It can create thumbnails and delay loading the full-size image until needed. Do some kind of sorting etc.

docs.title: Why Virtual Proxy is Useful Here
docs.text:
Your reasoning is correct.

A Virtual Proxy is used when:

Object creation is expensive
or
Object should be loaded lazily

Example:

High-resolution images
Large files
Remote resources
Database objects

Instead of loading everything immediately.

docs.title: Problem Without Proxy
docs.text:
Imagine a gallery with 1000 images.

If application loads all images:

1000 full-size images

Problems:

Huge memory usage
Slow UI loading
Poor performance

docs.title: Solution With Virtual Proxy
docs.text:
Instead of loading real images immediately:

Create lightweight proxy objects

Proxy loads the real image only when required.

Example:

Gallery shows thumbnails
↓
User clicks image
↓
Real image loads

This is lazy loading.

docs.title: Subject interface
docs.text:
interface Image {
    void display();
}

docs.title: Real object (heavy)
docs.text:
class RealImage implements Image {

    private String fileName;

    public RealImage(String fileName) {
        this.fileName = fileName;
        loadFromDisk();
    }

    private void loadFromDisk() {
        System.out.println("Loading image from disk: " + fileName);
    }

    public void display() {
        System.out.println("Displaying image: " + fileName);
    }
}

docs.title: Proxy
docs.text:
class ImageProxy implements Image {

    private RealImage realImage;
    private String fileName;

    public ImageProxy(String fileName) {
        this.fileName = fileName;
    }

    public void display() {

        if(realImage == null) {
            realImage = new RealImage(fileName);
        }

        realImage.display();
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Image image = new ImageProxy("photo.jpg");

        System.out.println("Gallery opened");

        image.display();   // real image loads here
    }
}

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
Gallery opened
↓
Proxy object created
↓
Real image NOT loaded yet
↓
display() called
↓
RealImage created
↓
Image loaded

docs.title: Output Example
docs.text:
Gallery opened
Loading image from disk: photo.jpg
Displaying image: photo.jpg

docs.title: 1️⃣ Hibernate Lazy Loading
docs.text:
Example:

User
   ↓
Orders

Orders may not load until accessed.

Proxy object represents database entity.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Image viewers
docs.text:
Used in:

photo gallery
video preview
document viewer

docs.title: 3️⃣ Remote service calls
docs.text: Proxy delays actual network call until needed.

docs.title: Real Example Related to Your Work
docs.text:
In systems like your automation or dashboard apps.

Example:

Large analytics report

Instead of generating full report immediately:

Dashboard shows summary
↓
User clicks report
↓
Proxy triggers full report generation

Same idea.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

When is Virtual Proxy useful?

You can answer:

Virtual Proxy is useful when an object is expensive to create or load. The proxy delays creation of the real object until it is actually needed, improving performance and memory usage.

docs.title: Short Notes for Your Pattern Notes
docs.text:
Virtual Proxy

Purpose:
Lazy loading of expensive objects.

Use cases:
Images
Database entities
Remote resources
Large reports

Key idea:
Create proxy object first
Real object created only when required

Examples:
Hibernate lazy loading
Image gallery systems
Large file viewers

docs.text:
You now understand 9 important patterns:

1 Singleton

These 9 patterns alone cover most real-world backend systems.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses customize specific steps.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It removes duplicate workflow code while allowing controlled variation.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A payment workflow can validate, process, and send receipt, while subclasses implement the processing step differently.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Base class controls the algorithm order.
  • Subclasses should customize steps, not rewrite the whole flow.
  • Too much inheritance can make design rigid.
  • Hooks should be clear.
  • Use Strategy if behavior should change through composition.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Template Method keeps the common algorithm in a parent class and delegates selected steps to subclasses. It is useful when many workflows have the same order but different implementation details.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Base class defines algorithm skeleton.
  • Subclasses implement steps.
  • Reduces workflow duplication.
  • Uses inheritance.
  • Good for fixed process order.
  • Compare with Strategy.

docs.title: Template Method Pattern
docs.text:
This pattern is used when:

Algorithm structure is fixed
but some steps vary

Examples:

Payment processing flow
Report generation flow
File import workflow
Data validation pipeline

Frameworks use this pattern heavily.

docs.title: Quick thinking question before Template Method
docs.text:
Imagine a payment processing workflow:

validate request
authorize payment
process payment
send receipt

For different payment types:

UPI
Credit Card
Net Banking

Some steps are same, some steps differ.

docs.title: Should we duplicate the whole workflow for each payment type? Why or why not?
Answer:
docs.text: No, we should not duplicate the workflow because it repeats business logic. If a new payment type is added, we would need to create another similar workflow again.

docs.title: Why duplication is a problem
docs.text:
If each payment type has its own full workflow:

  • UpiPaymentWorkflow
  • CardPaymentWorkflow
  • NetBankingWorkflow

and each one repeats:

  • validate request
  • process payment
  • send receipt

then these problems appear:

docs.title: 1. Code duplication
docs.text: Common steps are repeated in many classes.

docs.title: 2. Hard maintenance
docs.text: If one common step changes, you must update all workflows.

docs.title: 3. Inconsistent behavior
docs.text: One workflow may miss a step or implement it differently by mistake.

docs.title: Solution → Template Method Pattern
docs.text:
Template Method Pattern is useful when:

overall algorithm is fixed,
but some individual steps can vary

So we define:

  • common workflow once
  • variable steps in subclasses

docs.title: Template Method Pattern Definition
docs.text:
Template Method Pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and allows subclasses to override specific steps without changing the overall algorithm structure.

Simple meaning:

same flow, different step implementations

docs.title: Real-Life Analogy
docs.text:
Think of making tea and coffee.

Common flow:

  1. boil water
  2. prepare main ingredient
  3. pour into cup
  4. serve

But some steps differ:

  • tea leaves vs coffee powder
  • milk amount
  • extra flavor

So the template is same, but some steps vary.

docs.title: Abstract base class
docs.text:
abstract class PaymentProcessor {

    public final void processPayment() {
        validateRequest();
        authorizePayment();
        doPayment();
        sendReceipt();
    }

    void validateRequest() {
        System.out.println("Validating payment request");
    }

    abstract void authorizePayment();

    abstract void doPayment();

    void sendReceipt() {
        System.out.println("Sending payment receipt");
    }
}

class UpiPaymentProcessor extends PaymentProcessor {

    void authorizePayment() {
        System.out.println("Authorizing UPI payment");
    }

    void doPayment() {
        System.out.println("Processing UPI payment");

public class Test {

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
This method is the template:

public final void processPayment()

It defines the fixed workflow.

Subclasses change only these parts:

authorizePayment()
doPayment()

docs.title: Why final is important
docs.text:
Interview trap.

We often make the template method final:

public final void processPayment()

Why?

Because subclasses should not change the algorithm order.

They can customize steps, but not break the flow.

docs.title: Example idea in Java
docs.text: Abstract classes often define workflow methods and leave some steps abstract.

Removes duplication

Inheritance-based

docs.title: Strategy vs Template Method
docs.text: Very common interview question.

docs.title: Strategy
docs.text:
• changes behavior using composition
  • algorithm selected at runtime
  • object holds strategy reference

docs.title: Template Method
docs.text:
• changes steps using inheritance
  • workflow fixed in parent class
  • subclasses override selected steps

Easy rule:

Strategy → change whole behavior by plugging object
Template Method → keep workflow same, vary some steps

docs.title: Interview-ready answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is Template Method Pattern?

You can say:

Template Method Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and lets subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall algorithm structure.

docs.title: Short notes for your separate notes

Template Method Pattern

Purpose:
Define fixed workflow and allow some steps to vary.

Structure:
Abstract base class
Template method
Abstract/overridable steps
Concrete subclasses

Advantages:

Keeps flow consistent

Framework lifecycle hooks

docs.title: Small thinking question
docs.text:
Imagine a report export flow:

  • validate input
  • fetch data
  • format output
  • save/export file

CSV and PDF reports follow the same flow, but formatting differs.

docs.title: Would Template Method be a good choice here? Answer yes or no and explain why.
Answer
docs.text:
Yes, Template Method Pattern is a good choice here because the overall workflow of exporting reports is the same: validate input, fetch data, format the output, and save the file. Only some steps, such as formatting and saving, differ between CSV and PDF formats. We can define the common workflow in an abstract parent class and declare the varying steps as abstract methods. Then subclasses like CSVReportExporter and PDFReportExporter implement those steps with their specific logic.

That is a very strong design explanation.

docs.title: Abstract Template Class
docs.text:
abstract class ReportExporter {

    public final void exportReport() {
        validateInput();
        fetchData();
        formatOutput();
        saveFile();
    }

    void validateInput() {
        System.out.println("Validating input");
    }

    void fetchData() {
        System.out.println("Fetching data from database");
    }

    abstract void formatOutput();

    abstract void saveFile();
}

docs.title: CSV Implementation
docs.text:
class CsvReportExporter extends ReportExporter {

    void formatOutput() {
        System.out.println("Formatting report as CSV");
    }

    void saveFile() {
        System.out.println("Saving CSV file");
    }
}

docs.title: PDF Implementation
docs.text:
class PdfReportExporter extends ReportExporter {

    void formatOutput() {
        System.out.println("Formatting report as PDF");
    }

    void saveFile() {
        System.out.println("Saving PDF file");
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ReportExporter exporter = new CsvReportExporter();
        exporter.exportReport();

        System.out.println("-----");

        exporter = new PdfReportExporter();
        exporter.exportReport();
    }
}

Validating input
Fetching data from database
Formatting report as CSV
Saving CSV file
-----
Validating input
Fetching data from database
Formatting report as PDF
Saving PDF file

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Chain of Responsibility passes a request through a chain of handlers until one handles it or all handlers run.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It is useful for validation pipelines, filters, middleware, and approval flows.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A request can pass through authentication, authorization, validation, and rate-limit handlers.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Handler order matters.
  • A request may go unhandled.
  • Debugging can be harder in long chains.
  • Avoid hidden side effects between handlers.
  • Each handler should have one clear responsibility.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Chain of Responsibility decouples sender from receiver by passing a request through multiple handlers. Each handler decides whether to process the request, stop the chain, or pass it to the next handler.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Request moves through handlers.
  • Useful for filters and validators.
  • Order matters.
  • Handlers are decoupled.
  • Can stop or continue chain.
  • Servlet filters use this idea.

docs.title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern
docs.text:
Used for:

request pipelines
validation chains
middleware
filters
approval workflows

Real examples:

Spring Security filters
HTTP request filters
validation pipelines
logging pipelines

And it connects very well with your systems like:

request validation
role checks
audit logging
rate limiting

docs.title: Quick thinking question before we start
docs.text:
Imagine a request validation pipeline:

check authentication
check authorization
check input validation
check rate limit

docs.title: Should one class handle all validations, or should we split them into multiple handlers? Explain why.
docs.text: Use multiple handler here so everyone can handle its own responsibilities. If one handler completes its task, the next handler in the chain processes the request.

docs.title: Why multiple handlers are better
docs.text:
Your reasoning is correct.

If one class handles:

  • authentication
  • authorization
  • input validation
  • rate limiting

then that class becomes:

  • too large
  • hard to maintain
  • hard to test
  • hard to extend

So we split the work into multiple handlers, where each handler has one responsibility.

That is exactly the idea behind:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Chain of Responsibility Pattern passes a request through a chain of handlers, where each handler processes the request or forwards it to the next handler.

Simple meaning:

Request moves step by step through multiple handlers.

docs.title: Real-life analogy
docs.text:
Think of a company leave approval flow:

Team Lead
→ Manager
→ HR
→ Director

Each person checks the request and either:

  • handles it
  • approves it
  • passes it to the next person

That is Chain of Responsibility.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
There are usually 3 parts:

1. Handler interface / abstract class
2. Concrete handlers
3. Client

docs.title: Example: Request Validation Pipeline
docs.text:
Suppose request must pass:

Authentication
Authorization
Input validation
Rate limit

docs.title: Handler Base Class
docs.text:
abstract class Handler {

    protected Handler next;

    public Handler setNext(Handler next) {
        this.next = next;
        return next;
    }

    public abstract void handle(Request request);
}

docs.title: Request Class
docs.text:
class Request {
    boolean authenticated;
    boolean authorized;
    boolean validInput;
    boolean rateLimitOk;

    Request(boolean authenticated, boolean authorized, boolean validInput, boolean rateLimitOk) {
        this.authenticated = authenticated;
        this.authorized = authorized;
        this.validInput = validInput;
        this.rateLimitOk = rateLimitOk;
    }
}

docs.title: Authentication Handler
docs.text:
class AuthenticationHandler extends Handler {

    public void handle(Request request) {
        if (!request.authenticated) {
            System.out.println("Authentication failed");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Authentication passed");

        if (next != null) {
            next.handle(request);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Authorization Handler
docs.text:
class AuthorizationHandler extends Handler {

    public void handle(Request request) {
        if (!request.authorized) {
            System.out.println("Authorization failed");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Authorization passed");

        if (next != null) {
            next.handle(request);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Input Validation Handler
docs.text:
class InputValidationHandler extends Handler {

    public void handle(Request request) {
        if (!request.validInput) {
            System.out.println("Input validation failed");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Input validation passed");

        if (next != null) {
            next.handle(request);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Rate Limit Handler
docs.text:
class RateLimitHandler extends Handler {

    public void handle(Request request) {
        if (!request.rateLimitOk) {
            System.out.println("Rate limit failed");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Rate limit passed");
        System.out.println("Request processed successfully");
    }
}

docs.title: Client Code
docs.text:
public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Handler auth = new AuthenticationHandler();
        Handler permission = new AuthorizationHandler();
        Handler input = new InputValidationHandler();
        Handler rate = new RateLimitHandler();

        auth.setNext(permission).setNext(input).setNext(rate);

        Request request = new Request(true, true, true, true);

        auth.handle(request);
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Authentication passed
Authorization passed
Input validation passed
Rate limit passed
Request processed successfully

docs.title: If any handler fails
docs.text:
Example:

Request request = new Request(true, false, true, true);

Output:

Authentication passed
Authorization failed

Chain stops there.

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Each handler:

  • does its own work
  • decides whether to continue
  • forwards request to next handler

docs.title: 1. Single Responsibility
docs.text: Each handler manages only one concern.

docs.title: 2. Flexible order
docs.text: You can change chain order if needed.

docs.title: 3. Easy to add new checks
docs.text: Just add a new handler.

docs.title: 4. Cleaner code
docs.text: Avoids one giant validation class.

docs.title: Interview-ready answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is Chain of Responsibility Pattern?

Chain of Responsibility is a behavioral design pattern in which a request is passed through a sequence of handlers. Each handler processes the request or forwards it to the next handler in the chain. It is useful for validation pipelines, middleware, filters, and approval workflows.

docs.title: Small thinking question
docs.text:
Imagine a loan approval system:

check document completeness
check credit score
check income eligibility
final manager approval

docs.title: Would Chain of Responsibility be a good choice here? Answer yes or no and explain why.
Explanation (Interview-Ready Version)
docs.text:
Yes, Chain of Responsibility is a good choice here because loan approval consists of multiple sequential validations such as document verification, credit score checking, income eligibility, and final approval. Each step can be implemented as a separate handler. The request passes through the chain, and each handler performs its own responsibility before passing the request to the next handler.

This is exactly how interviewers expect you to explain it.

docs.title: Example Loan Approval Flow
docs.text:
Steps:

Document Check
↓
Credit Score Check
↓
Income Eligibility
↓
Manager Approval

Each step is a handler in the chain.

docs.title: Handler Base Class
docs.text:
abstract class LoanHandler {

    protected LoanHandler next;

    public LoanHandler setNext(LoanHandler next) {
        this.next = next;
        return next;
    }

    public abstract void process(LoanRequest request);
}

docs.title: Loan Request
docs.text:
class LoanRequest {

    boolean documentsValid;
    int creditScore;
    int income;

    LoanRequest(boolean docs, int creditScore, int income) {
        this.documentsValid = docs;
        this.creditScore = creditScore;
        this.income = income;
    }
}

docs.title: Document Handler
docs.text:
class DocumentCheckHandler extends LoanHandler {

    public void process(LoanRequest request) {

        if (!request.documentsValid) {
            System.out.println("Loan rejected: documents missing");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Documents verified");

        if (next != null)
            next.process(request);
    }
}

docs.title: Credit Score Handler
docs.text:
class CreditScoreHandler extends LoanHandler {

    public void process(LoanRequest request) {

        if (request.creditScore < 650) {
            System.out.println("Loan rejected: low credit score");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Credit score approved");

        if (next != null)
            next.process(request);
    }
}

docs.title: Income Handler
docs.text:
class IncomeHandler extends LoanHandler {

    public void process(LoanRequest request) {

        if (request.income < 30000) {
            System.out.println("Loan rejected: insufficient income");
            return;
        }

        System.out.println("Income verified");

        if (next != null)
            next.process(request);
    }
}

docs.title: Manager Approval
docs.text:
class ManagerApprovalHandler extends LoanHandler {

    public void process(LoanRequest request) {

        System.out.println("Loan approved by manager");
    }
}

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        LoanHandler doc = new DocumentCheckHandler();
        LoanHandler credit = new CreditScoreHandler();
        LoanHandler income = new IncomeHandler();
        LoanHandler manager = new ManagerApprovalHandler();

        doc.setNext(credit).setNext(income).setNext(manager);

        LoanRequest request = new LoanRequest(true, 700, 50000);

        doc.process(request);
    }
}

docs.text:
Documents verified
Credit score approved
Income verified
Loan approved by manager

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Command wraps a request or action as an object.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It is useful for queues, scheduling, undo/redo, logging actions, and decoupling callers from execution logic.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A scheduler can store EmailCommand, ReportCommand, and ApiCallCommand and execute them later.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Command is about representing an action.
  • It is different from Strategy, which represents interchangeable algorithms.
  • Commands can need context data.
  • Too many command classes can be heavy.
  • Undo needs extra state.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Command turns an operation into an object with an execute method. The caller does not need to know how the operation works. This allows actions to be queued, logged, retried, scheduled, or undone.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Action as object.
  • Usually has execute method.
  • Decouples caller and receiver.
  • Useful for queues and scheduling.
  • Supports undo/redo.
  • Runnable is command-like.

docs.title: Command Pattern
docs.text:
Used for:

task queues
job schedulers
undo/redo systems
request encapsulation
workflow engines

Real examples:

task execution systems
job queues
button actions
automation tools

And it actually fits extremely well with your automation project where tasks are scheduled and executed.

docs.title: Quick thinking question before Command Pattern
docs.text:
Imagine an automation system where you can schedule actions like:

Send email
Send SMS
Generate report
Trigger webhook

docs.title: Should the scheduler directly call these services, or should we encapsulate each action as an object? Explain why.
Answer:
docs.text: Encapsulate each action as an object. If the scheduler directly calls these services, the scheduler becomes overloaded with many responsibilities. Complex execution logic becomes mixed with scheduling logic. So it will decrease the maintainability

docs.title: Why Encapsulate Actions as Objects
docs.text:
If scheduler directly calls services like:

scheduler.sendEmail();
scheduler.sendSMS();
scheduler.generateReport();
scheduler.triggerWebhook();

then problems appear:

docs.title: 1. Scheduler becomes too complex
docs.text:
Scheduler must know:

  • email service
  • sms service
  • report service
  • webhook service

That violates Single Responsibility Principle.

docs.title: 2. Tight coupling
docs.text:
Scheduler depends on many services:

EmailService
SmsService
ReportService
WebhookService

Harder to extend.

docs.title: 3. Hard to add new actions
docs.text:
If new action appears:

ExportData
SendPushNotification
UpdateDashboard

Scheduler code must change again.

docs.title: Solution → Command Pattern
docs.text:
Command Pattern converts a request into an object.

Instead of:

scheduler → directly executes action

We do:

scheduler → executes command object
command → performs action

docs.title: Command Pattern Definition
docs.text:
Command Pattern encapsulates a request as an object, allowing you to parameterize clients with different requests and support operations like queuing, logging, and undo.

Simple meaning:

Turn actions into objects

docs.title: Real-life analogy
docs.text:
Think of a restaurant order.

Customer says:

Make pizza

But the waiter doesn't cook.

Instead:

Order slip (command)
↓
Chef executes it

Here:

Customer = client
Order slip = command
Chef = receiver

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Command pattern usually has:

Command interface
Concrete commands
Receiver
Invoker
Client

docs.title: Command interface
docs.text:
interface Command {
    void execute();
}

docs.title: Receiver Classes
docs.text:
class EmailService {
    void sendEmail() {
        System.out.println("Sending Email");
    }
}

class SmsService {
    void sendSMS() {
        System.out.println("Sending SMS");
    }
}

docs.title: Concrete Command
docs.text:
class SendEmailCommand implements Command {

    private EmailService emailService;

    SendEmailCommand(EmailService emailService) {
        this.emailService = emailService;
    }

    public void execute() {
        emailService.sendEmail();
    }
}

class SendSmsCommand implements Command {

    private SmsService smsService;

    SendSmsCommand(SmsService smsService) {
        this.smsService = smsService;
    }

    public void execute() {
        smsService.sendSMS();
    }
}

docs.title: Invoker (Scheduler)
docs.text:
class TaskScheduler {

    public void run(Command command) {
        command.execute();
    }
}

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        EmailService emailService = new EmailService();
        SmsService smsService = new SmsService();

        Command emailCommand = new SendEmailCommand(emailService);
        Command smsCommand = new SendSmsCommand(smsService);

        TaskScheduler scheduler = new TaskScheduler();

        scheduler.run(emailCommand);
        scheduler.run(smsCommand);
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Sending Email
Sending SMS

docs.title: Key idea
docs.text:
Scheduler only knows:

Command

Not:

EmailService
SmsService
ReportService

This reduces coupling.

docs.title: Why this pattern is powerful
docs.text:
Command pattern allows:

Task queues
Delayed execution
Retry mechanisms
Undo operations
Logging commands

Very useful for automation systems.

docs.title: Real examples related to your projects
docs.text:
Your automation tool scheduling tasks:

weight check call
birthday call
follow-up call
motivation call
feedback call

Each can be a Command object.

Scheduler simply executes:

command.execute()

Perfect Command Pattern scenario.

docs.title: Runnable in Java
docs.text:
new Thread(new Runnable() {
    public void run() {
        // task
    }
});

Runnable acts like a command object.

docs.text:

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
More classes
Extra abstraction

docs.title: Interview-ready answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is Command Pattern?

You can say:

Command Pattern encapsulates a request as an object so that it can be executed, queued, logged, or undone. It decouples the object that invokes the operation from the object that performs it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: State lets an object change behavior when its internal state changes.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It replaces complex state-based if-else logic with separate state classes.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: An order can behave differently in Created, Paid, Shipped, and Cancelled states.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• State is about object behavior changing by state.
  • Do not use it for a small simple enum switch.
  • State transitions should be controlled.
  • Too many states can add complexity.
  • State and Strategy look similar but have different intent.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: State pattern represents each state as a separate class. The context delegates behavior to the current state object. When state changes, the object behavior changes without large conditional blocks.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Behavior depends on state.
  • Each state is a class.
  • Context delegates to current state.
  • Reduces if-else chains.
  • Useful for workflows.
  • Different intent from Strategy.

docs.title: State Pattern
docs.text:
Used when an object's behavior changes based on its state.

Examples:

Order state
Payment state
Task workflow state
Campaign state
User account state

Very common in backend systems.

docs.title: Quick thinking question before State Pattern
docs.text:
Imagine an Order system:

CREATED
PAID
SHIPPED
DELIVERED
CANCELLED

Should we manage behavior using:

if (state == CREATED)
if (state == PAID)
if (state == SHIPPED)

or is there a better design approach? Explain why.

docs.title: Why if-else is bad for order states
docs.text:
Suppose you write:

if (state == CREATED) {
    // allow payment
}
else if (state == PAID) {
    // allow shipping
}
else if (state == SHIPPED) {
    // allow delivery
}
else if (state == CANCELLED) {
    // no action
}

As states grow, problems appear:

  • too many if-else conditions
  • behavior logic becomes scattered
  • hard to maintain
  • hard to add new state
  • state transition rules become messy

For example:

CREATED  -> can pay, can cancel
PAID     -> can ship, can refund
SHIPPED  -> can deliver
DELIVERED -> no more shipping
CANCELLED -> no more actions

Now every action needs state checks.

docs.title: Solution → State Pattern
docs.text:
State Pattern is used when:

an object's behavior changes depending on its current state

Instead of checking state with if-else, we move behavior into separate state classes.

docs.title: State Pattern Definition
docs.text:
State Pattern allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object appears to change its class.

Simple meaning:

Different state = different behavior

docs.title: Real-life analogy
docs.text:
Think of a traffic signal.

State can be:

  • Red
  • Yellow
  • Green

Behavior changes based on current state.

For example:

  • Red → stop
  • Green → go
  • Yellow → slow down

You do not want one huge if-else everywhere. Better to model each state separately.

docs.title: Order Example
docs.text:
States:

CreatedState
PaidState
ShippedState
DeliveredState
CancelledState

Each state decides:

  • what action is allowed
  • what next state should be

docs.title: Structure of State Pattern
docs.text:
Usually there are 3 parts:

State interface
Concrete state classes
Context object

docs.title: State interface
docs.text:
interface OrderState {
    void next(OrderContext context);
    void cancel(OrderContext context);
    String getStatus();
}

docs.title: Created state
docs.text:
class CreatedState implements OrderState {

    public void next(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Payment completed. Moving to PAID state.");
        context.setState(new PaidState());
    }

    public void cancel(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Order cancelled from CREATED state.");
        context.setState(new CancelledState());
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "CREATED";
    }
}

docs.title: Paid state
docs.text:
class PaidState implements OrderState {

    public void next(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Order shipped. Moving to SHIPPED state.");
        context.setState(new ShippedState());
    }

    public void cancel(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Order cancelled after payment.");
        context.setState(new CancelledState());
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "PAID";
    }
}

docs.title: Shipped state
docs.text:
class ShippedState implements OrderState {

    public void next(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Order delivered. Moving to DELIVERED state.");
        context.setState(new DeliveredState());
    }

    public void cancel(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Cannot cancel. Order already shipped.");
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "SHIPPED";
    }
}

docs.title: Delivered state
docs.text:
class DeliveredState implements OrderState {

    public void next(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Order already delivered.");
    }

    public void cancel(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Cannot cancel delivered order.");
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "DELIVERED";
    }
}

docs.title: Cancelled state
docs.text:
class CancelledState implements OrderState {

    public void next(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Cancelled order cannot move forward.");
    }

    public void cancel(OrderContext context) {
        System.out.println("Order already cancelled.");
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "CANCELLED";
    }
}

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
class OrderContext {

    private OrderState state;

    public OrderContext() {
        this.state = new CreatedState();
    }

    public void setState(OrderState state) {
        this.state = state;
    }

    public void next() {
        state.next(this);
    }

    public void cancel() {
        state.cancel(this);
    }

    public void printStatus() {
        System.out.println("Current state: " + state.getStatus());
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        OrderContext order = new OrderContext();

        order.printStatus();
        order.next();

        order.printStatus();
        order.next();

        order.printStatus();
        order.cancel();

        order.printStatus();
        order.next();

        order.printStatus();
    }
}

docs.title: What happens here
docs.text:
Flow:

CREATED
→ PAID
→ SHIPPED
→ cannot cancel
→ DELIVERED

Behavior changes automatically based on current state.

docs.title: 1. Cleaner code
docs.text: State-specific behavior lives in state classes.

docs.title: 2. Easy to add new state
docs.text:
Add new class like:

ReturnedState
RefundedState

docs.title: 3. Better maintainability
docs.text: No giant condition blocks.

docs.title: 4. Clear transition rules
docs.text: Each state controls valid next transitions.

docs.title: State vs Strategy
docs.text:
This is the important part.

You asked whether Strategy can solve it.

They look similar because both use composition + interface.

But the intention is different.

docs.title: Strategy Pattern
docs.text:
Used when:

we want to choose one algorithm among many

Example:

  • payment method
  • sorting algorithm
  • diet calculation algorithm

Client usually chooses strategy.

docs.title: State Pattern
docs.text:
Used when:

object behavior changes automatically based on internal state

Example:

  • order state
  • payment state
  • task workflow state

The object itself moves from one state to another.

docs.title: Easy rule to remember
docs.text:
Strategy → choose behavior
State → behavior changes because state changes

docs.title: Real examples from your projects
docs.text: This pattern fits your work very well.

docs.title: Example 1 — Task lifecycle
docs.text:
A task may be:

CREATED
ASSIGNED
IN_PROGRESS
COMPLETED
CANCELLED

Each state allows different actions.

docs.title: Example 2 — Import job flow
docs.text:
A job may be:

PENDING
PROCESSING
SUCCESS
FAILED
RETRYING

Very good State Pattern use case.

docs.title: Example 3 — Candidate / campaign workflow
docs.text:
A record may be:

NEW
CONTACTED
FOLLOWED_UP
CONVERTED
DROPPED

Again, behavior depends on state.

docs.title: Interview-ready answer
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is State Pattern?

You can say:

State Pattern is a behavioral design pattern used when an object's behavior changes depending on its internal state. Instead of using many conditional statements, each state is represented as a separate class, and the context delegates behavior to the current state object.

docs.title: Short notes for your separate notes
docs.text:
State Pattern

Purpose:
Change object behavior based on current state.

Structure:
State interface
Concrete state classes
Context class

Problem solved:
Too many if-else checks based on state.

Examples:
Order lifecycle
Task status flow
Payment status
Job processing state

Difference from Strategy:
Strategy = choose algorithm
State = behavior changes automatically due to current state

docs.title: Small thinking question
docs.text:
Imagine your automation task can be:

PENDING
ASSIGNED
IN_PROGRESS
COMPLETED
FAILED

Would State Pattern be a good choice here?

Answer yes or no and explain why.

docs.title: Explanation (Interview-Ready Version)
docs.text:
This is how you could answer in an interview:

State Pattern is suitable here because the behavior of the task depends on its current state. Each state allows different transitions. For example, a task in PENDING state may be assigned or cancelled, while a task in IN_PROGRESS state may be completed or marked as failed. Instead of using multiple if-else conditions, we can represent each state as a separate class that controls the allowed actions and state transitions.

That is a very strong design answer.

Already described a valid state machine.

PENDING
   ↓
ASSIGNED
   ↓
IN_PROGRESS
   ↓
COMPLETED

Other transitions:

PENDING → CANCELLED
ASSIGNED → REASSIGNED
IN_PROGRESS → FAILED
CANCELLED → RESCHEDULED

This is exactly how workflow engines work internally.

docs.title: State Interface
docs.text:
interface TaskState {
    void next(TaskContext context);
    void cancel(TaskContext context);
    String getStatus();
}

docs.title: Pending State
docs.text:
class PendingState implements TaskState {

    public void next(TaskContext context) {
        System.out.println("Task assigned");
        context.setState(new AssignedState());
    }

    public void cancel(TaskContext context) {
        System.out.println("Task cancelled");
        context.setState(new CancelledState());
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "PENDING";
    }
}

docs.title: Assigned State
docs.text:
class AssignedState implements TaskState {

    public void next(TaskContext context) {
        System.out.println("Task started");
        context.setState(new InProgressState());
    }

    public void cancel(TaskContext context) {
        System.out.println("Task cancelled after assignment");
        context.setState(new CancelledState());
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "ASSIGNED";
    }
}

docs.title: In Progress State
docs.text:
class InProgressState implements TaskState {

    public void next(TaskContext context) {
        System.out.println("Task completed");
        context.setState(new CompletedState());
    }

    public void cancel(TaskContext context) {
        System.out.println("Task failed");
        context.setState(new FailedState());
    }

    public String getStatus() {
        return "IN_PROGRESS";
    }
}

docs.title: Context Class
docs.text:
class TaskContext {

    private TaskState state;

    public TaskContext() {
        this.state = new PendingState();
    }

    public void setState(TaskState state) {
        this.state = state;
    }

    public void next() {
        state.next(this);
    }

    public void cancel() {
        state.cancel(this);
    }

    public void printStatus() {
        System.out.println("Current state: " + state.getStatus());
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        TaskContext task = new TaskContext();

        task.printStatus();

        task.next();
        task.printStatus();

        task.next();
        task.printStatus();

        task.next();
        task.printStatus();
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Current state: PENDING
Task assigned
Current state: ASSIGNED
Task started
Current state: IN_PROGRESS
Task completed
Current state: COMPLETED

docs.title: Why This Pattern Is Powerful
docs.text:
Without State Pattern:

if(state == PENDING)
if(state == ASSIGNED)
if(state == IN_PROGRESS)

Huge conditional blocks.

With State Pattern:

behavior belongs to state class

Much cleaner architecture.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) is the study of how to organize data and solve problems efficiently.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: DSA helps developers write code that scales. For interviews, it shows whether you can reason about time, memory, edge cases, and trade-offs instead of only writing code that works for small input.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Searching one value in an unsorted array takes O(n). Searching in a sorted array with binary search takes O(log n).

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Memorizing solutions without understanding patterns.
  • Ignoring input size.
  • Forgetting edge cases like empty input, duplicates, negative numbers, and overflow.
  • Using recursion without checking stack depth.
  • Choosing a data structure before understanding required operations.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: DSA is about choosing the right data structure and algorithm for a problem. A strong answer explains the approach, proves why it works, gives time and space complexity, handles edge cases, and writes clean code.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Learn complexity first.
  • Master arrays, strings, hashing, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and DP.
  • Practice patterns, not random problems.
  • Always explain time and space complexity.
  • Dry run with small examples.
  • Handle edge cases before final answer.

docs.title: Study Order
docs.text:
1. Complexity Analysis
  2. Arrays and Strings
  3. Linked Lists
  4. Stacks and Queues
  5. Hashing and Sets
  6. Trees and Binary Search Trees
  7. Heaps and Priority Queues
  8. Graphs
  9. Recursion and Backtracking
  10. Dynamic Programming
  11. Sorting and Searching
  12. Interview Problem Patterns

docs.title: Junior to Senior Progression
docs.text:
Junior developers should focus on correct implementation and basic complexity.

Mid-level developers should recognize patterns quickly and choose the right data structure.

Senior developers should explain trade-offs, constraints, failure cases, memory cost, and production alternatives.

docs.title: Interview Solving Framework
docs.text:
1. Restate the problem.
2. Clarify input size and constraints.
3. Discuss brute force.
4. Improve with a data structure or pattern.
5. Explain complexity.
6. Code cleanly.
7. Test edge cases.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Complexity analysis measures how an algorithm grows as input size grows.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Correct code can still fail if it is too slow or uses too much memory. Complexity helps you compare approaches before coding.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Looping through an array once is O(n). Two nested loops over the same array are usually O(n^2).

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Dropping important factors too early when input size is small.
  • Confusing O(log n) with O(n log n).
  • Forgetting space complexity.
  • Treating HashMap operations as always guaranteed O(1).
  • Ignoring recursion stack space.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Big O describes the upper growth rate of an algorithm. We usually keep the dominant term and ignore constants. Time complexity measures operations, while space complexity measures extra memory used by the algorithm.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• O(1): constant.
  • O(log n): divide input each step.
  • O(n): scan once.
  • O(n log n): many efficient sorts.
  • O(n^2): pair comparison or nested loops.
  • Recursion uses call stack space.

docs.title: Common Complexities
docs.text: Complexity Meaning Example O(1) Constant work Array index access O(log n) Input halves repeatedly Binary search O(n) Visit each item once Linear scan O(n log n) Split and process Merge sort O(n^2) Compare pairs Bubble sort O(2^n) Explore subsets Some recursion O(n!) Explore permutations Brute force permutations

docs.title: Time vs Space
docs.text:
Time complexity asks: how many operations grow with input?

Space complexity asks: how much extra memory grows with input?

Example:

Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
for (int x : nums) {
    seen.add(x);
}

Time: O(n) average.

Space: O(n).

docs.title: Recursion Complexity
docs.text:
For recursion, think about:

number of calls * work per call

Also include recursion stack.

Example:

int factorial(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 1;
    return n * factorial(n - 1);
}

Time: O(n).

Space: O(n) because of call stack.

docs.title: Senior Interview Notes
docs.text:
HashMap and HashSet operations are average O(1), but worst-case can degrade due to collisions. Java 8 improves heavy collision buckets by treeifying them, but you should still say average case when discussing hash tables.

When input size is small, simpler O(n^2) code may be acceptable. When input size is large, choose better complexity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An array stores elements in contiguous index-based positions. A string is a sequence of characters; in Java, String is immutable.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Arrays and strings are the base of many interview problems. They test indexing, two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, and careful edge-case handling.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Two Sum can be solved in O(n) using a HashMap instead of checking all pairs in O(n^2).

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Off-by-one errors.
  • Empty array or single-element array.
  • Confusing index and value.
  • Modifying a string repeatedly with + in loops.
  • Forgetting duplicate values.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: For array and string problems, first check if order matters. Then consider two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, hashing, sorting, or binary search depending on the constraints.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Array access is O(1).
  • Searching unsorted array is O(n).
  • Strings are immutable in Java.
  • Use StringBuilder for repeated changes.
  • Two pointers work well on sorted or paired movement problems.
  • Sliding window works for contiguous subarray or substring problems.

docs.title: Two Pointers
docs.text:
Use when two indexes move through the data.

Common cases:

  • Sorted pair sum.
  • Reverse array.
  • Remove duplicates.
  • Palindrome check.

Example:

boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = s.length() - 1;

    while (left < right) {
        if (s.charAt(left) != s.charAt(right)) return false;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
    return true;
}

Time: O(n).

Space: O(1).

docs.title: Sliding Window
docs.text:
Use for contiguous subarray or substring.

Examples:

  • Maximum sum subarray of size k.
  • Longest substring without repeating characters.
  • Minimum window substring.

Fixed-size window:

int maxSumOfSizeK(int[] nums, int k) {
    int window = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) window += nums[i];

    int best = window;
    for (int right = k; right < nums.length; right++) {
        window += nums[right];
        window -= nums[right - k];
        best = Math.max(best, window);
    }
    return best;
}

docs.title: Prefix Sum
docs.text:
Use when many range sum queries are needed.

int[] prefix = new int[nums.length + 1];
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i];
}

Range sum from l to r:

prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]

docs.title: String Notes for Java
docs.text:
Use StringBuilder for repeated string mutation.

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (String word : words) {
    sb.append(word);
}
return sb.toString();

docs.title: Senior-Level Questions
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Is input sorted?
  • Can I change the input array?
  • Are duplicates allowed?
  • Are negative values possible?
  • Is the answer a range, count, index, or actual values?

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A linked list stores elements as nodes where each node points to the next node.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Linked list problems test pointer handling, null checks, slow-fast pointer logic, and in-place manipulation.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: To reverse a linked list, keep prev, curr, and next pointers and change links one by one.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Losing the next node while changing links.
  • Not handling empty list.
  • Not handling one-node list.
  • Infinite loop in cycle problems.
  • Forgetting to update head after reversal.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Linked lists are useful when frequent insertions and deletions are needed and direct index access is not required. In interviews, linked list problems usually focus on pointer movement and edge cases.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Access by index is O(n).
  • Insert/delete after known node is O(1).
  • Use dummy node to simplify head changes.
  • Use slow-fast pointers for middle and cycle.
  • Reversal needs careful pointer updates.
  • Always check null before node.next.

docs.title: Node Structure
docs.text:
class ListNode {
    int val;
    ListNode next;

    ListNode(int val) {
        this.val = val;
    }
}

docs.title: Reverse Linked List
docs.text:
ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;
    ListNode curr = head;

    while (curr != null) {
        ListNode next = curr.next;
        curr.next = prev;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    return prev;
}

Time: O(n).

Space: O(1).

docs.title: Slow and Fast Pointer
docs.text:
Use for:

  • Find middle.
  • Detect cycle.
  • Find cycle start.

Cycle detection:

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head;
    ListNode fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

docs.title: Dummy Node Pattern
docs.text:
Use when head may change.

ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
dummy.next = head;

This makes delete/insert logic cleaner.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Linked lists are not cache-friendly because nodes are scattered in memory. In real Java code, ArrayList is often faster for iteration and random access. Linked lists are still important in interviews because they test pointer reasoning.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A stack follows Last In First Out (LIFO). A queue follows First In First Out (FIFO).

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Stacks and queues are used in parsing, BFS, monotonic problems, undo systems, scheduling, and expression evaluation.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Use a stack to check balanced parentheses. Push opening brackets and pop when a matching closing bracket appears.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Using legacy Stack instead of ArrayDeque.
  • Forgetting empty-stack checks.
  • Mixing queue and stack ordering.
  • Not recognizing monotonic stack problems.
  • Using recursion when an explicit stack is safer.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Stack is useful when the most recent item must be processed first. Queue is useful when the earliest item must be processed first. In Java, prefer ArrayDeque for stack and queue behavior unless a specific concurrent queue is needed.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Stack: LIFO.
  • Queue: FIFO.
  • Use ArrayDeque in Java.
  • BFS uses queue.
  • DFS can use stack.
  • Monotonic stack solves next greater/smaller problems.

docs.title: Java Choice
docs.text:
Prefer:

Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

Avoid old Stack for normal interview code.

docs.title: Balanced Parentheses
docs.text:
boolean isValid(String s) {
    Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (ch == '(' || ch == '[' || ch == '{') {
            stack.push(ch);
        } else {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) return false;
            char open = stack.pop();
            if (ch == ')' && open != '(') return false;
            if (ch == ']' && open != '[') return false;
            if (ch == '}' && open != '{') return false;
        }
    }
    return stack.isEmpty();
}

docs.title: Monotonic Stack
docs.text:
Use when you need next greater or next smaller element.

Example problem:

For each element, find the next greater element on the right.

Idea:

  • Keep a stack of unresolved indexes.
  • When current value is greater than stack top, resolve it.

docs.title: Queue for BFS
docs.text:
Queue<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer(root);

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    TreeNode node = queue.poll();
    if (node.left != null) queue.offer(node.left);
    if (node.right != null) queue.offer(node.right);
}

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Use BlockingQueue for thread coordination. Use PriorityQueue for ordered processing. Use ArrayDeque for normal stack/queue interview problems.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Hashing maps a key to an index or bucket. A set stores unique values.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Hashing is one of the most useful tools for improving brute-force solutions from O(n^2) to O(n).

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Two Sum can store visited values in a HashMap and find the complement in constant average time.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Forgetting duplicates.
  • Confusing HashMap keys and values.
  • Assuming HashMap is sorted.
  • Ignoring collision behavior.
  • Using mutable objects as keys without stable equals() and hashCode().

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: HashMap and HashSet provide average O(1) insert, lookup, and delete. They are useful when we need fast membership checks, frequency counting, duplicate detection, or key-value lookup.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• HashSet checks existence.
  • HashMap stores key-value pairs.
  • Average operations are O(1).
  • Worst case depends on collisions.
  • Keys need correct equals() and hashCode().
  • Not sorted by default.

docs.title: Frequency Map
docs.text:
Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
    freq.put(ch, freq.getOrDefault(ch, 0) + 1);
}

Use for:

  • Anagrams.
  • Counting occurrences.
  • Majority element variants.
  • First unique character.

docs.title: Two Sum
docs.text:
int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> indexByValue = new HashMap<>();

    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int need = target - nums[i];
        if (indexByValue.containsKey(need)) {
            return new int[] { indexByValue.get(need), i };
        }
        indexByValue.put(nums[i], i);
    }
    return new int[] { -1, -1 };
}

docs.title: Set for Duplicate Detection
docs.text:
boolean hasDuplicate(int[] nums) {
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (!seen.add(x)) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

docs.title: Hashing vs Sorting
docs.text:
Hashing:

  • Usually O(n) time.
  • Uses extra memory.
  • Does not preserve sorted order.

Sorting:

  • Usually O(n log n) time.
  • Can reduce extra memory.
  • Useful when order helps.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text:
In Java, custom HashMap keys must implement consistent equals() and hashCode().

If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode().

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A tree is a hierarchical data structure. A binary tree has at most two children per node. A binary search tree (BST) keeps left values smaller and right values larger.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Trees test recursion, traversal, divide-and-conquer thinking, and hierarchical data modeling.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Inorder traversal of a valid BST returns values in sorted order.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Confusing binary tree with BST.
  • Checking only parent-child relation instead of full BST range.
  • Forgetting null base case.
  • Ignoring recursion stack space.
  • Using BFS when DFS is simpler, or the reverse.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Trees are useful for hierarchical data. Common operations use DFS recursion or BFS queue traversal. For BST problems, always maintain valid min and max bounds, not only local parent comparison.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• DFS: preorder, inorder, postorder.
  • BFS: level order.
  • BST inorder gives sorted order.
  • Height affects performance.
  • Balanced BST operations are O(log n).
  • Skewed BST can become O(n).

docs.title: Tree Node
docs.text:
class TreeNode {
    int val;
    TreeNode left;
    TreeNode right;

    TreeNode(int val) {
        this.val = val;
    }
}

docs.title: DFS Traversals
docs.text:
Preorder:

root, left, right

Inorder:

left, root, right

Postorder:

left, right, root

docs.title: Recursive Inorder
docs.text:
void inorder(TreeNode root, List<Integer> result) {
    if (root == null) return;
    inorder(root.left, result);
    result.add(root.val);
    inorder(root.right, result);
}

docs.title: Level Order BFS
docs.text:
List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return result;

    Queue<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    queue.offer(root);

    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int size = queue.size();
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
