            TreeNode node = queue.poll();
            level.add(node.val);
            if (node.left != null) queue.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) queue.offer(node.right);
        }
        result.add(level);
    }
    return result;
}

docs.title: Validate BST
docs.text:
boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
    return valid(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
}

boolean valid(TreeNode node, long low, long high) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (node.val <= low || node.val >= high) return false;
    return valid(node.left, low, node.val)
        && valid(node.right, node.val, high);
}

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Balanced trees keep operations efficient. Java TreeMap and TreeSet are tree-based sorted collections with O(log n) operations.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A heap is a tree-based structure where the highest or lowest priority element can be accessed quickly. Java uses PriorityQueue for heap behavior.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Heaps are useful for top K problems, scheduling, merging sorted data, and shortest path algorithms.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: To find the k largest numbers, keep a min-heap of size k.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Java PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default.
  • Iterating a PriorityQueue does not produce sorted order.
  • Polling repeatedly gives priority order.
  • Top K can use min-heap or max-heap depending on direction.
  • Comparator mistakes can break ordering.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: A priority queue returns the smallest or highest-priority item first. In Java, PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default. It gives O(log n) insert and remove, and O(1) peek.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Min-heap gives smallest first.
  • Java PriorityQueue is min-heap.
  • Use comparator for max-heap.
  • offer is O(log n).
  • poll is O(log n).
  • peek is O(1).

docs.title: Java Min-Heap
docs.text: PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();

docs.title: Java Max-Heap
docs.text: PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());

docs.title: Top K Largest
docs.text:
List<Integer> topK(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();

    for (int x : nums) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) {
            heap.poll();
        }
    }

    return new ArrayList<>(heap);
}

Time: O(n log k).

Space: O(k).

docs.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
docs.text:
Use a min-heap containing the current node from each list.

This gives:

O(n log k)

where n is total nodes and k is number of lists.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text:
Use heaps when you only need the next best item, not a fully sorted list.

If you need all items sorted, sorting may be simpler. If you need repeated priority extraction, a heap is better.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Graphs model networks, dependencies, routes, permissions, recommendations, and many system design problems.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Use BFS to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Forgetting visited set.
  • Infinite loops in cyclic graphs.
  • Confusing directed and undirected edges.
  • Using DFS for shortest path in unweighted graph when BFS is needed.
  • Not handling disconnected components.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Graph problems usually need a representation, traversal, and visited tracking. Use BFS for shortest path in unweighted graphs, DFS for connected components and cycle exploration, topological sort for dependencies, and Dijkstra for weighted shortest paths with non-negative weights.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Graph has vertices and edges.
  • Use adjacency list for most problems.
  • BFS uses queue.
  • DFS uses recursion or stack.
  • Topological sort works on DAG.
  • Dijkstra needs non-negative weights.

docs.title: Graph Representation
docs.text:
Adjacency list:

Map<Integer, List<Integer>> graph = new HashMap<>();

Build undirected graph:

graph.computeIfAbsent(a, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(b);
graph.computeIfAbsent(b, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(a);

docs.title: BFS
docs.text:
void bfs(int start, Map<Integer, List<Integer>> graph) {
    Set<Integer> visited = new HashSet<>();
    Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

    visited.add(start);
    queue.offer(start);

    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int node = queue.poll();
        for (int next : graph.getOrDefault(node, List.of())) {
            if (visited.add(next)) {
                queue.offer(next);
            }
        }
    }
}

docs.title: DFS
docs.text:
void dfs(int node, Map<Integer, List<Integer>> graph, Set<Integer> visited) {
    if (!visited.add(node)) return;

    for (int next : graph.getOrDefault(node, List.of())) {
        dfs(next, graph, visited);
    }
}

docs.title: Topological Sort
docs.text:
Use for dependency order.

Examples:

  • Course schedule.
  • Build order.
  • Task dependencies.

Kahn algorithm:

1. Count indegree for every node.
2. Push nodes with indegree 0 into queue.
3. Remove node, reduce neighbors indegree.
4. If all nodes processed, no cycle.

docs.title: Dijkstra
docs.text:
Use when:

  • Graph has weights.
  • Weights are non-negative.
  • Need shortest path.

Uses priority queue.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: For large graphs, recursion may overflow the stack. Use iterative DFS or BFS. In production, graph traversal also needs limits, timeouts, and memory awareness.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Recursion is a function calling itself. Backtracking is recursion with choices, exploration, and undoing choices.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Many tree, graph, subset, permutation, and search problems are naturally recursive.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Generating all subsets means deciding for each element: include it or skip it.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Missing base case.
  • Infinite recursion.
  • Forgetting to undo a choice.
  • Sharing mutable lists incorrectly.
  • Ignoring recursion stack space.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Recursion solves a problem by reducing it into smaller versions of itself. Backtracking uses recursion to explore possible choices and undo choices when returning. It is useful when we need all combinations, permutations, subsets, or valid configurations.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Base case stops recursion.
  • Recursive case reduces problem.
  • Backtracking makes a choice, explores, then undoes.
  • Recursion stack uses memory.
  • Use copies when storing current path.
  • Prune invalid paths early.

docs.title: Recursion Template
docs.text:
void solve(state) {
    if (baseCase) {
        recordAnswer();
        return;
    }

    for (choice : choices) {
        makeChoice(choice);
        solve(nextState);
        undoChoice(choice);
    }
}

docs.title: Subsets
docs.text:
List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums) {
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    backtrack(nums, 0, new ArrayList<>(), result);
    return result;
}

void backtrack(int[] nums, int index, List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> result) {
    if (index == nums.length) {
        result.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
        return;
    }

    backtrack(nums, index + 1, path, result);

    path.add(nums[index]);
    backtrack(nums, index + 1, path, result);
    path.remove(path.size() - 1);
}

docs.title: Permutations
docs.text:
Use:

  • used[] array.
  • Current path.
  • Add answer when path size equals input size.

docs.title: Backtracking vs DFS
docs.text:
DFS is traversal.

Backtracking is DFS with state changes and undo logic.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text:
Backtracking often has exponential complexity. Mention pruning when possible.

Examples:

  • Stop when partial sum exceeds target.
  • Sort input to skip duplicates.
  • Validate partial board early in Sudoku/N-Queens.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Dynamic Programming (DP) solves problems by reusing results of overlapping subproblems.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: DP is a senior-level interview filter because it tests pattern recognition, state design, recurrence, and optimization.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Fibonacci can be improved from exponential recursion to O(n) by storing previous results.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Starting with table before defining state.
  • Wrong base cases.
  • Confusing index meaning.
  • Forgetting overlapping subproblems.
  • Not explaining recurrence clearly.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Use DP when the problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Define the state, write the recurrence, set base cases, choose top-down or bottom-up, then optimize space if possible.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• DP needs repeated subproblems.
  • Define state first.
  • Recurrence explains transition.
  • Base cases stop or initialize.
  • Memoization is top-down.
  • Tabulation is bottom-up.

docs.title: DP Thinking Process
docs.text:
1. What does dp[i] mean?
2. What smaller answers are needed?
3. What is the recurrence?
4. What are base cases?
5. What is final answer?
6. Can space be optimized?

docs.title: Fibonacci
docs.text:
int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;

    int prev2 = 0;
    int prev1 = 1;

    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        int curr = prev1 + prev2;
        prev2 = prev1;
        prev1 = curr;
    }
    return prev1;
}

Time: O(n).

Space: O(1).

docs.title: 1D DP
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Climbing stairs.
  • House robber.
  • Decode ways.

docs.title: 2D DP
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Grid paths.
  • Longest common subsequence.
  • Edit distance.

docs.title: Knapsack
docs.text:
Examples:

  • 0/1 knapsack.
  • Subset sum.
  • Partition equal subset sum.

docs.title: Interval DP
docs.text:
Examples:

  • Matrix chain multiplication.
  • Burst balloons.

docs.title: Top-Down vs Bottom-Up
docs.text:
Top-down:

  • Easier to write from recursion.
  • Uses memo map/table.

Bottom-up:

  • Often faster.
  • Iterative.
  • Space optimization is clearer.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: In interviews, DP is won by explaining state clearly. A correct recurrence with clean base cases matters more than jumping directly into code.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Sorting arranges data in order. Searching finds a target or position in data.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Sorting and searching are core tools for optimization. Many problems become easier after sorting or by using binary search.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Binary search finds a target in a sorted array in O(log n).

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Binary search overflow with (low + high) / 2.
  • Infinite loop from wrong boundary update.
  • Sorting changes original order.
  • Comparator mistakes.
  • Assuming binary search only works on arrays.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Sorting is useful when order helps simplify comparisons, grouping, or duplicate handling. Binary search is useful when the search space is sorted or monotonic. The key is to define the condition that tells us which half to discard.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Merge sort: O(n log n).
  • Quick sort: average O(n log n).
  • Binary search: O(log n).
  • Java Arrays.sort for primitives is optimized.
  • Comparator controls object sorting.
  • Binary search works on monotonic answer spaces too.

docs.title: Binary Search Template
docs.text:
int binarySearch(int[] nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.length - 1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (nums[mid] < target) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

docs.title: Binary Search on Answer
docs.text:
Use when:

  • You can check if an answer is possible.
  • If answer x works, all larger or smaller answers also work.

Examples:

  • Minimum capacity to ship packages.
  • Koko eating bananas.
  • Allocate books.

docs.title: Sorting in Java
docs.text:
Arrays.sort(nums);

For objects:

people.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::age));

docs.title: Comparator Trap
docs.text:
Avoid subtraction comparator when overflow is possible:

(a, b) -> a - b

Prefer:

Integer.compare(a, b)

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Sorting can simplify a problem but costs O(n log n). If hashing solves the same problem in O(n) and order is not needed, hashing may be better.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Interview patterns are reusable ways to recognize and solve groups of DSA problems.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Strong developers do not memorize thousands of problems. They identify the pattern, explain the trade-off, and adapt it to constraints.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: If a problem asks for the longest contiguous substring with a condition, sliding window is often a strong candidate.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Forcing a pattern without checking constraints.
  • Ignoring edge cases.
  • Not explaining why the pattern fits.
  • Jumping to optimized code without brute force.
  • Memorizing code but failing to adapt it.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: I first classify the problem by input structure and required output. Then I check common patterns like two pointers, sliding window, hashing, stack, BFS/DFS, heap, binary search, backtracking, or DP. I choose the pattern that matches the constraints and explain complexity.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Contiguous range: sliding window or prefix sum.
  • Sorted pair: two pointers.
  • Fast lookup: hashing.
  • Nested matching: stack.
  • Shortest unweighted path: BFS.
  • All possibilities: backtracking.
  • Overlapping subproblems: DP.

docs.title: Pattern Map
docs.text: Problem Signal Likely Pattern Sorted array, pair needed Two pointers Longest/shortest contiguous range Sliding window Range sum queries Prefix sum Fast existence/count lookup HashMap/HashSet Matching brackets or next greater Stack Level order or shortest unweighted path BFS Connected components or path existence DFS Top K or repeated best item Heap Monotonic answer space Binary search on answer All subsets/permutations Backtracking Repeated subproblems Dynamic programming

docs.title: Interview Communication Template
docs.text:
Brute force:
  Explain simplest correct approach.

Optimization:
  Identify repeated work or expensive operation.

Data structure:
  Choose array, map, set, stack, queue, heap, tree, or graph.

Complexity:
  State time and space clearly.

Edge cases:
  Empty input, duplicates, negative values, overflow, null.

docs.title: Senior-Level Trade-Offs
docs.text:
Hashing improves lookup but uses extra memory.

Sorting simplifies order-based logic but costs O(n log n).

Recursion is clean but can overflow stack.

DP is powerful but can use large memory.

Heaps are good for top K but not for full sorting.

docs.title: Practice Plan
docs.text:
1. Solve 5 problems per pattern.
  2. Write brute force first in notes.
  3. Write optimized version.
  4. Explain why optimization works.
  5. Re-solve after one week without looking.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A variable is a named storage location. A data type tells Java what kind of value the variable can hold.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This is the base for understanding memory, primitives, references, default values, constants, and type safety.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: int age = 25; stores an integer value. String name = "Java"; stores a reference to a String object.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Local variables do not get default values.
  • Instance variables get default values.
  • String is not a primitive type.
  • final variables are not always compile-time constants.
  • Primitive variables and reference variables behave differently.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Variables store values used by a Java program. Primitive variables store simple values like int, double, and boolean. Reference variables store references to objects like String or custom classes. Java uses data types to provide compile-time safety and decide what operations are valid.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Primitive types store simple values.
  • Reference variables point to objects.
  • Local variables must be initialized.
  • Instance variables get default values.
  • String is a class.
  • Data types give type safety.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Basic Definition (Interview Style – 2 Lines)
docs.text: A variable is a named memory location used to store data. A data type defines what kind of data a variable can store and how much memory it occupies.

docs.title: 2️⃣ What Happens Internally (Deep Understanding)
docs.text:
When you write:

int age = 25;

docs.title: What JVM Does:
docs.text:
1. int → tells JVM to allocate 4 bytes
  2. age → variable name
  3. 25 → literal value

  4. Memory allocated in:

  5. Stack (if local variable)

  6. Heap (inside object) if instance variable

docs.title: 3️⃣ Types of Data Types in Java
docs.text: Java has 2 main categories

docs.title: 1️⃣ Primitive Data Types (Store actual value)
docs.text:
Type Size Default Example byte 1 byte 0 byte b = 10; short 2 bytes 0 short s = 100; int 4 bytes 0 int x = 5; long 8 bytes 0L long l = 100L; float 4 bytes 0.0f float f = 5.5f; double 8 bytes 0.0 double d = 10.5; char 2 bytes '\u0000' char c = 'A'; boolean JVM dependent false boolean flag = true;

👉 Primitive variables store actual value directly in memory.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Non-Primitive (Reference Types)
docs.text:
Examples:

  • String
  • Arrays
  • Objects
  • Interfaces

Example:

String name = "Vishu";

Here:

  • name → stored in stack
  • "Vishu" object → stored in heap (String Pool area)

👉 Reference variables store memory address, not actual object.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Local Variable
docs.text:
Declared inside method.

void test() {
    int x = 10;
}
  • Stored in stack
  • No default value
  • Must initialize before use

docs.title: 2️⃣ Instance Variable
docs.text:
Declared inside class but outside method.

class Person {
    int age;
}
  • Stored in heap (inside object)
  • Gets default value

docs.title: 3️⃣ Static Variable
docs.text:
Belongs to class.

static int count;
  • Stored in method area (before Java 8) / metaspace
  • One copy for entire class

docs.title: 🔹 Q1: Where are variables stored?
docs.text:
Answer:

  • Local → Stack
  • Instance → Heap
  • Static → Method Area / Metaspace

docs.title: 🔹 Q2: Why local variables don’t have default values?
docs.text: Because JVM does not initialize stack memory automatically for performance reasons.

docs.title: 🔹 Q3: Difference between primitive and reference type?
docs.text:
Primitive:

  • Stores value
  • Fixed size
  • Faster
  • No methods

Reference:

  • Stores address
  • Dynamic size
  • Stored in heap
  • Has methods

docs.title: 🔹 Q4: What is default value of int instance variable?
docs.text: 0

docs.title: 🔹 Q5: What happens if you don’t initialize local variable?
docs.text:
Compilation error:

variable might not have been initialized

docs.title: ❌ Trap 1
docs.text:
int x;
System.out.println(x);

❌ Compile-time error

docs.title: ❌ Trap 2
docs.text:
long l = 10000000000;

❌ Error Correct:

long l = 10000000000L;

docs.title: ❌ Trap 3
docs.text:
float f = 5.5;

❌ Error Correct:

float f = 5.5f;

docs.title: ❌ Trap 4
docs.text:
char size confusion

char is 2 bytes, not 1 byte (Unicode support).

docs.title: 7️⃣ How To Answer in Interview (Confident Way)
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

👉 “Explain variables in Java.”

You answer:

In Java, a variable is a named memory location used to store data. Each variable must be declared with a data type, which defines the size and type of data it can store. Variables in Java are categorized as local, instance, and static based on their scope and memory location.

Then continue with stack vs heap explanation if they ask deeper.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Real-Life Analogy
docs.text:
Primitive → like storing money in your pocket Reference → like storing a house address in your pocket

You hold address, but actual house is somewhere else.

docs.title: ✅ 1️⃣ Why is boolean size JVM dependent?
✅ Correct Explanation:
docs.text:
Java specification does NOT define exact size of boolean.

Why?

Because boolean only stores:

  • true
  • false

It logically needs just 1 bit.

But:

  • JVM does not allocate memory bit-by-bit.
  • Most CPUs work with 1 byte minimum.
  • In arrays, JVM may use 1 byte per boolean.
  • Internally, implementation may vary.

👉 That’s why Java says: “boolean size is JVM dependent.”

docs.title: Interview Answer:
docs.text: The Java specification does not define exact size of boolean because it only represents true or false. Internally JVM may use 1 byte or optimize differently depending on implementation.

docs.title: Why String is NOT primitive?
docs.text:
Primitive types:

  • Store value directly
  • Fixed memory size
  • No methods
  • Not objects

String:

  • Is an object
  • Stored in heap
  • Has methods
  • Immutable
  • Supports pooling

So real reason:

Because String has object behavior (methods, immutability, pooling, dynamic memory allocation), it cannot be primitive.

Also:

If String were primitive:

  • It would not support methods like .length(), .substring()
  • No immutability concept
  • No String pool optimization

docs.title: Before Java 8:
docs.text:
• Class metadata → Method Area (PermGen)
  • Static variables → Method Area

docs.title: After Java 8 (including Java 17):
docs.text:
• Class metadata → Metaspace
  • Static variables → Heap

⚠ Important: Metaspace stores class metadata, NOT static variable values.

Static variables are stored: 👉 In heap 👉 Inside the Class object

docs.title: Deep Explanation:
docs.text:
When class loads:

  • JVM creates a Class object in heap.
  • Static variables become part of that Class object.
  • Only one copy exists.

So correct interview answer:

In modern Java (Java 8+), static variables are stored in heap memory as part of the Class object. Metaspace stores only class metadata.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Trap Here
docs.text:
Many candidates say: “Static variables are stored in Metaspace.”

❌ Wrong.

Metaspace = Class metadata Heap = Objects + Static variables

docs.title: ✅ 1️⃣ Where is static final int x = 10; stored?
docs.text:
Correct answer (deep + interview):

  • x is a static field, so it belongs to the Class (not object instances).
  • In Java 8+ (including Java 17), static fields live on the Heap as part of the class’s runtime data (associated with the Class<?> object / class representation).
  • The value 10 is a primitive constant; it doesn’t create any object.

Extra interview point (trap):

  • For static final primitives, the compiler may inline the value into bytecode of other classes if it’s a compile-time constant. So sometimes you don’t even “read it” at runtime from the field (depends on usage / compilation).

One-line interview answer:

Static fields are stored on the heap with the class’s runtime representation; static final int may also be compile-time inlined.

docs.title: ✅ 2️⃣ Where is static final String s = "Vishu"; stored?
docs.text:
Correct, with precision:

  • s (the static reference variable) → stored in heap with class data.
  • "Vishu" (the String object) → stored in the String Pool, which is in the heap.
  • s points to that pooled "Vishu".

Interview-ready:

The reference s is a static field (heap). The String literal "Vishu" is in the String pool (also heap). s points to the pooled object.

docs.title: ✅ 3️⃣ Why local variables don’t get default values but instance variables do?
docs.text:
Polished answer:

  • Local variables are on the stack and JVM does not auto-initialize them because:

  • it avoids extra work (performance)

  • it prevents using garbage/unknown values accidentally (compiler forces initialization)

  • Instance variables are part of an object on the heap.

  • When JVM allocates memory for an object, it zero-initializes it first (0, false, null)

  • then constructor runs and assigns real values.

Interview answer:

Local variables must be initialized because stack memory isn’t automatically set. Instance fields get defaults because object memory is zeroed during allocation before the constructor executes.

docs.title: Static fields (Java 8+)
docs.text:
• Stored: Heap (with class runtime data)
  • Metaspace: only class metadata (methods/constant pool/type info), not field values

docs.title: String literal
docs.text: • Stored in String Pool (inside heap)

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
• Local: no default, must initialize
  • Instance/static: default values exist

docs.title: Given:
docs.text:
static final int A = 10;
static final Integer B = 10;

docs.title: ✅ 1️⃣ Is A compile-time constant?
docs.text:
✔ YES.

Because:

  • static
  • final
  • primitive type
  • assigned with constant expression (10)

So compiler treats A as compile-time constant.

It gets stored in the constant pool of the class file.

docs.title: ✅ 2️⃣ Is B compile-time constant?
docs.text:
✔ NO.

Even though:

  • It is static
  • It is final
  • Value looks constant

But:

Integer is an object, not primitive.

So:

Integer B = 10;

Actually becomes:

Integer B = Integer.valueOf(10);

That means:

  • Object creation / method call
  • Not a pure constant expression

So it is not compile-time constant.

docs.title: ✅ 3️⃣ Which one gets inlined into other classes?
docs.text:
👉 Only A gets inlined.

Example:

Class1:

static final int A = 10;

Class2:

System.out.println(Class1.A);

Compiler replaces it with:

System.out.println(10);

So Class2 does not even access Class1 at runtime.

But for:

static final Integer B = 10;

Class2 must access Class1 at runtime to get B.

No inlining.

docs.title: 🔥 VERY IMPORTANT INTERVIEW TRAP
docs.text:
Suppose:

Class1:

static final int A = 10;

Class2:

System.out.println(Class1.A);

Now you change A to 20 in Class1 and recompile only Class1.

What happens?

👉 Class2 will still print 10 Because 10 was already inlined in its bytecode.

This is a famous interview trap.

docs.title: Compile-time constant must be:
docs.text:
• static
  • final
  • primitive or String
  • assigned with constant expression

docs.title: Given:
docs.text: static final String S = "Hello";

docs.title: ✅ 1️⃣ Is this compile-time constant?
docs.text:
✔ YES.

Because:

  • static ✔
  • final ✔
  • String ✔
  • assigned with literal ✔

Java treats String literals as compile-time constants.

docs.title: ✅ 2️⃣ Will it be inlined?
docs.text:
✔ YES.

If another class uses:

System.out.println(Class1.S);

The compiler replaces it with:

System.out.println("Hello");

No runtime lookup required.

docs.title: ✅ 3️⃣ Why is String allowed but Integer not?
docs.text: Your idea was close, but let’s refine it properly.

docs.title: The Real Reason:
docs.text:
Java Language Specification defines:

A compile-time constant must be:

  • primitive OR
  • String literal
  • assigned using constant expression

Important:

String is special because:

  • String literals are stored in constant pool
  • String is immutable
  • String literal expressions are resolved at compile time

But:

static final Integer B = 10;

This is NOT constant because:

  • It requires a method call: Integer.valueOf(10)
  • It creates/returns an object
  • Object creation cannot happen at compile time
  • It’s resolved at runtime

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
This works:

static final String S1 = "Hello";
static final String S2 = "Hel" + "lo";

Because "Hel" + "lo" is resolved at compile time.

But this:

static final String S3 = new String("Hello");

❌ Not compile-time constant Because new forces runtime object creation.

docs.title: 📘 Notebook Summary
docs.text:
Compile-time constant:

  • static
  • final
  • primitive or String
  • constant expression only
  • no method calls
  • no new keyword

docs.title: Given:
docs.text:
static final String A = "Hello";
static final String B = A + "World";

docs.title: ✅ Is B compile-time constant?
docs.text:
✔ YES.

Because:

  • A is compile-time constant
  • "World" is literal
  • + operation between compile-time constants
  • No method call
  • No new
  • No runtime variable

So compiler resolves this as:

static final String B = "HelloWorld";

Before bytecode generation.

docs.title: 🔥 Why this works?
docs.text:
Because Java compiler performs constant folding.

It evaluates constant expressions at compile time.

docs.title: Case 1
docs.text:
static final String A = getValue();
static final String B = A + "World";

docs.title: Why NOT compile-time?
docs.text:
Because getValue() is a method call → value known only at runtime.

So A is not a compile-time constant, and therefore B cannot be either.

✅ What happens internally:

  • Compiler generates bytecode that will do concatenation at runtime (typically via StringBuilder or invokedynamic depending on Java version).

docs.title: Case 2
docs.text:
static final String A = "Hello";
static final String B = A + new String("World");

docs.title: Why NOT compile-time?
docs.text:
Because new String("World") creates an object at runtime.

Even though "World" literal is constant, the expression includes new, so the whole expression is not a constant expression.

✅ Runtime behavior:

  • "World" literal exists in String pool
  • new String("World") creates a new heap object (different reference)
  • concatenation happens at runtime

docs.title: 📘 Notebook: Rule (One line)
docs.text: ✅ Only expressions made purely of compile-time constants (primitives/String literals/constant folding) are compile-time constants. ❌ Any method call, new, non-final variable, or runtime value breaks it.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
String a = "Hello";
String b = "Hel" + "lo";
String c = a + "World";
String d = "Hello" + "World";
String e = a + "lo";

System.out.println(a == b);   // ?
System.out.println(c == "HelloWorld"); // ?
System.out.println(d == "HelloWorld"); // ?
System.out.println(e == "Hello"); // ?

docs.title: ✅ Correct outputs
docs.text:
1. a == b → true ✅ (you were right)

  2. "Hel" + "lo" is compile-time constant folding

  3. so b becomes "Hello" in the pool

  4. both refer to same pooled literal

  5. c == "HelloWorld" → false ❌ (you said true)

  6. c = a + "World" → a is a variable, so concatenation happens at runtime

  7. result is a new String object on heap (not automatically pooled)
  8. "HelloWorld" on the right is a pooled literal

  9. different references → false

  10. d == "HelloWorld" → true ✅ (you were right)

  11. "Hello" + "World" is compile-time constant folding

  12. d points to pooled "HelloWorld"

  13. e == "Hello" → false ✅ (you were right)

  14. e = a + "lo" is runtime concatenation (because a is variable)

  15. creates new heap String "Hellolo" actually? Wait carefully:

  16. a is "Hello"

  17. "Hello" + "lo" becomes "Hellolo" (not "Hello") So it’s false for two reasons:
  18. content differs ("Hellolo" vs "Hello")
  19. and reference differs anyway

✅ Final answers (4 lines):

  • true
  • false
  • true
  • false

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Tip (1-liner you should remember)
docs.text: ✅ == compares references, not content. Compile-time concatenation → pooled; runtime concatenation → new object (unless you call .intern()).

docs.title: 🔎 Given:
docs.text:
String a = "Hello";
String x = a + "World";
System.out.println(x.intern() == "HelloWorld");

docs.title: 1️⃣ "Hello"
docs.text: Stored in String Pool

docs.title: 2️⃣ a + "World"
docs.text:
Since a is a variable → runtime concatenation JVM creates a new String object in heap (not in pool)

So now:

  • x → heap object "HelloWorld"
  • "HelloWorld" literal → in String Pool

They are different references.

docs.title: 3️⃣ x.intern()
docs.text:
What does .intern() do?

👉 It checks:

  • If an equal string exists in the String Pool

  • return reference of pooled string

  • Otherwise:

  • add it to pool and return that reference

In our case:

  • "HelloWorld" already exists in pool
  • So intern() returns pooled reference

Now comparison becomes:

pooled "HelloWorld" == pooled "HelloWorld"

✔ true

docs.title: 🧠 Interview-Level Definition of intern()
docs.text: The intern() method ensures that a string is stored in the String Pool and returns the pooled reference. If the string already exists in the pool, it returns the existing reference instead of creating a new one.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
String s1 = new String("ABC");
String s2 = s1.intern();

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

✅ Correct — it prints false (in the normal/common case).

docs.title: 1️⃣ "ABC" literal
docs.text: • When the class is loaded (or when this line executes), the literal "ABC" is in the String Pool.

docs.title: 2️⃣ new String("ABC")
docs.text:
• Creates a new String object on the heap (separate from the pooled one).
  • s1 points to this heap object.

So now:

  • pool has "ABC" (pooled ref)
  • heap has another "ABC" (s1 ref)

docs.title: 3️⃣ s1.intern()
docs.text:
• JVM checks String Pool for "ABC"
  • It already exists, so it returns the pooled "ABC" reference.
  • s2 points to pooled string.

docs.title: 4️⃣ s1 == s2
docs.text: • heap object reference vs pool reference → different → false

docs.title: ⚠️ Interview Note (extra sharp)
docs.text: In some specific scenarios (especially older Java versions / particular ordering), results around intern() can look surprising. But for this exact code in typical modern JVM behavior, the correct expected answer is false, and interviewers want this explanation.

docs.title: ✅ Your Notes Summary (String Pool + intern traps)
docs.text:
• == checks reference (address), not content.
  • String literal → goes to String Pool.
  • new String("X") → always makes a new heap object.
  • intern() → returns pooled reference (existing or newly added).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Type conversion changes a value from one data type to another. Casting is explicit conversion written by the programmer.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Conversion rules explain compile errors, data loss, numeric promotion, and safe assignment in Java.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: int x = 10; long y = x; is widening. long a = 10; int b = (int) a; is narrowing.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Widening is automatic.
  • Narrowing needs explicit cast.
  • Narrowing can lose data.
  • Arithmetic with smaller integer types promotes to int.
  • Casting does not make an invalid object type valid.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Java supports widening and narrowing conversion. Widening moves a smaller type to a larger compatible type and happens automatically. Narrowing moves a larger type to a smaller type and requires an explicit cast because data loss is possible.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Widening is automatic.
  • Narrowing needs cast.
  • Narrowing can lose data.
  • byte/short/char arithmetic promotes to int.
  • Object casts need compatible runtime type.
  • Casting can fail with ClassCastException.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Basic Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text:
Type conversion is the process of converting one data type into another. In Java, it happens in two ways:

  • Implicit (Widening)
  • Explicit (Narrowing / Casting)

docs.title: 2️⃣ Implicit Type Conversion (Widening)
docs.text:
Also called: Automatic Casting

When:

  • Smaller type → Larger type
  • No data loss

Example:

int x = 10;
long y = x;   // automatic

docs.title: Why allowed?
docs.text:
Because:

  • long (8 bytes) can hold int (4 bytes)
  • No information lost

docs.title: Primitive Widening Order (Very Important)
docs.text:
byte → short → int → long → float → double
           char ↗

⚠ boolean cannot be converted to any other type.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
byte b = 10;
int i = b;      // OK
double d = i;   // OK

docs.title: 3️⃣ Explicit Type Conversion (Narrowing)
docs.text:
When:

  • Larger type → Smaller type
  • Possible data loss
  • Must use casting operator

Example:

double d = 10.5;
int x = (int) d;

Output:

10

Decimal part removed (not rounded).

docs.title: ⚠️ Data Loss Example
docs.text:
int x = 130;
byte b = (byte) x;
System.out.println(b);

Output:

-126

Why?

Because:

  • byte range: -128 to 127
  • 130 exceeds range
  • Overflow happens
  • Binary truncation

This is very common interview trap.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 1: Arithmetic Promotion
docs.text:
byte a = 10;
byte b = 20;
byte c = a + b;  // ERROR

Why error?

Because:

  • a + b automatically promoted to int
  • So result is int
  • Cannot assign int to byte without casting

Correct:

byte c = (byte)(a + b);

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 2: Char + Int
docs.text:
char c = 'A';
int x = c;   // OK

Output:

65

Because char stores Unicode value.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 3: Final Keyword Trick
docs.text:
final int x = 10;
byte b = x;   // OK

Why?

Because x is compile-time constant within range of byte.

But:

int x = 10;
byte b = x;   // ERROR

Even though value same.

Interviewers love this.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Reference Type Casting
docs.text: There are two:

docs.title: Upcasting (Automatic)
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();

Child → Parent Safe No cast needed

docs.title: Downcasting (Explicit)
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();
Dog d = (Dog) a;

Parent → Child Needs cast May cause ClassCastException

docs.title: ⚠️ Dangerous Trap
docs.text:
Animal a = new Animal();
Dog d = (Dog) a;  // Compiles but runtime exception

docs.title: 6️⃣ How to Answer in Interview
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

👉 “Explain type casting in Java.”

Answer:

In Java, type conversion happens either automatically (widening) when converting smaller types to larger types, or explicitly (narrowing) when converting larger types to smaller types which may cause data loss. Java also supports reference type casting through upcasting and downcasting.

docs.title: 📘 Notes Summary
docs.text:
• Widening → safe → automatic
  • Narrowing → data loss → manual cast
  • Arithmetic → smaller types become int
  • boolean → no conversion
  • Object casting → runtime type matters

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
int x = 5;
double y = x / 2;
System.out.println(y);

docs.title: Step-by-step:
docs.text:
• x is int (5)
  • 2 is int
  • So x / 2 → integer division
  • 5 / 2 = 2 (decimal part discarded)

Then:

  • double y = 2;
  • int 2 is widened to double → 2.0

docs.title: ✅ Output:
docs.text:
2.0

✔ It is integer division (fraction part removed)

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
double y = 5 / 2;
System.out.println(y);
  • 5 is int
  • 2 is int
  • division happens BEFORE assignment

So result?

👉 It is still integer division.

So:

5 / 2 = 2 Then 2 → converted to double → 2.0

docs.title: ✅ Output:
docs.text:
2.0

Many beginners say 2.5. That is wrong.

docs.title: If you want 2.5
docs.text:
You must make one operand double:

double y = 5 / 2.0;

or

double y = (double)5 / 2;

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Why does Java promote byte/short to int in arithmetic?

This is important.

docs.title: Reason:
docs.text:
CPU works efficiently with at least 32-bit integers.

So Java promotes:

  • byte
  • short
  • char

to int before arithmetic operations.

This is called Integer Promotion Rule.

Example:

byte a = 10;
byte b = 20;
int c = a + b;   // promoted to int

Even though both are byte, addition happens in int.

System.out.println(5 / 2.0);
  • 2.0 is double
  • int 5 is promoted to double
  • double division → 2.5
System.out.println(5.0 / 2);
  • 5.0 is double
  • int 2 promoted to double
  • double division → 2.5
System.out.println(5.0 / 2.0);
  • both double
  • double division → 2.5

docs.title: 🔥 Golden Rule (Write in your notes)
docs.text:
If any one operand is double, the entire expression becomes double.

If both operands are int → integer division.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
System.out.println(5 / 2 * 1.0);
System.out.println(5 * 1.0 / 2);

docs.title: 1️⃣ 5 / 2 * 1.0
docs.text:
Operator precedence:

  • / and * have same precedence
  • evaluated left to right

So:

Step 1:

5 / 2

Both int → integer division → 2

Step 2:

2 * 1.0

Now one operand is double → result becomes double → 2.0

✅ Output:

2.0

docs.title: 2️⃣ 5 * 1.0 / 2
docs.text:
Step 1:

5 * 1.0

int promoted to double → 5.0

Step 2:

5.0 / 2

double division → 2.5

✅ Output:

2.5

docs.title: 🔥 What Interviewer Tests Here
docs.text:
They test:

  • Order of evaluation
  • Type promotion
  • Integer division behavior
  • Expression evaluation left to right

docs.title: 📘 Write This Rule in Notes
docs.text: Arithmetic operators evaluate left to right. Type promotion happens at the time of operation, not at assignment.

docs.title: ✅ Why It Does NOT Compile
docs.text:
byte b = 100;
b = b + 1;

docs.title: Step-by-step:
docs.text:
• b is byte
  • 1 is int (default literal type)
  • In arithmetic, byte is promoted to int
  • So b + 1 becomes int
  • Cannot assign int to byte without casting

So compiler error:

possible lossy conversion from int to byte

docs.title: ✅ Correct Version
docs.text:
b = (byte) (b + 1);

Now it compiles.

docs.title: 🔥 Why Does This Compile?
docs.text:
byte b = 100;
b += 1;  // ✅ compiles!

Even though b = b + 1; does NOT compile, this b += 1; version DOES compile.

docs.title: ✅ Reason:
docs.text:
Java applies implicit cast in compound assignment (+=, -=, *=, etc.)

The compiler automatically inserts a cast, like:

b = (byte)(b + 1);

So:

"compiler resolves b += 1 as b = (byte)(b + 1);" ✅

docs.title: ⚠ Why Does This Rule Exist?
docs.text:
To make code cleaner:

  • Compound operators (+=, -=) were designed to allow implicit narrowing cast
  • But direct assignment (b = b + 1;) does not allow implicit cast
  • This is how Java maintains strict typing and convenient shorthand at the same time

docs.title: 📘 Write in Your Notes
docs.text:
byte b = 100;
b = b + 1;       // ❌ Compilation error (int → byte)
b += 1;          // ✅ Compiles (implicit cast)

Same applies to:

short s = 10;
s = s * 2;      // ❌
s *= 2;         // ✅

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Operators are symbols that perform operations on values or variables.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Operators appear in output questions, precedence traps, boolean logic, increments, comparisons, and bit-level interview questions.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: a + b adds values, a == b compares primitive values or object references, and a && b performs short-circuit boolean logic.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• == compares object references for objects.
  • && short-circuits but & evaluates both sides for booleans.
  • Post-increment and pre-increment behave differently.
  • Operator precedence can change output.
  • Integer division drops decimal part.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Java operators perform arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, bitwise, and unary operations. In interviews, the important parts are precedence, short-circuit behavior, increment behavior, and the difference between reference comparison and logical equality.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Arithmetic operators calculate values.
  • Relational operators compare values.
  • == checks references for objects.
  • && and || short-circuit.
  • Pre/post increment changes timing.
  • Use parentheses for clarity.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
We will cover:

  1. Increment / Decrement (++, --)
  2. Short-circuit operators (&&, ||)
  3. Ternary operator (?:)
  4. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>, >>>)

Step by step. No confusion.

docs.title: Two Types
docs.text:
• Pre-increment → ++x
  • Post-increment → x++

docs.title: Post-increment
docs.text:
int x = 5;
int y = x++;

Step-by-step:

  • y = 5
  • then x becomes 6

Final:

x = 6
y = 5

docs.title: Pre-increment
docs.text:
int x = 5;
int y = ++x;

Step-by-step:

  • x becomes 6
  • y = 6

Final:

x = 6
y = 6

docs.title: 🔥 Dangerous Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict:

int x = 5;
System.out.println(x++ + ++x);

Solve carefully.

Step-by-step:

  1. x++ → 5 (then x becomes 6)
  2. ++x → x becomes 7, value 7
  3. 5 + 7 = 12

Final x = 7

Output:

12

⚠ Interview tip: Avoid writing such confusing code in real projects.

docs.title: Logical AND
docs.text:
if (a > 5 && b > 10)

If first condition is false → second NOT evaluated.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
int x = 5;
if (x > 10 && ++x > 6) {
}
System.out.println(x);

Since x > 10 is false → ++x never executes.

Output:

5

docs.title: Difference Between && and &
docs.text:
&& → short-circuit & → evaluates both sides always

Same for:

|| vs |

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap
docs.text:
int x = 0;
if (true || ++x > 0) {
}
System.out.println(x);

Output?

true || anything → second not evaluated

Output:

0

docs.title: 3️⃣ Ternary Operator (?:)
docs.text:
Syntax:

condition ? value1 : value2;

Example:

int x = 10;
String result = (x > 5) ? "Big" : "Small";

docs.title: 🔥 Trap
docs.text:
int x = 10;
System.out.println(x > 5 ? x++ : x--);
System.out.println(x);

Step-by-step:

  • condition true
  • prints 10 (post-increment)
  • x becomes 11

Final output:

10
11

docs.title: 4️⃣ Bitwise Operators
docs.text: Used at binary level.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
System.out.println(5 & 3);

Binary:

5 = 0101
3 = 0011
--------------
    0001 = 1

Output:

1

docs.title: Left Shift
docs.text:
System.out.println(5 << 1);

Binary:

0101 << 1 = 1010

Result:

10

Means: 5 * 2

docs.title: Right Shift
docs.text:
System.out.println(8 >> 1);

Binary:

1000 >> 1 = 0100

Result:

4

Means: 8 / 2

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
int x = 10;
int y = x++ + ++x + x++;
System.out.println(y);
System.out.println(x);

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution (Left → Right Evaluation)
docs.text:
Java evaluates operands left to right.

Initial:

x = 10

docs.title: 1️⃣ First term → x++
docs.text:
Post-increment:

  • Use current value → 10
  • Then increment

After this:

Value used = 10
x = 11

docs.title: 2️⃣ Second term → ++x
docs.text:
Pre-increment:

  • Increment first → x = 12
  • Then use value → 12

After this:

Value used = 12
x = 12

docs.title: 3️⃣ Third term → x++
docs.text:
Post-increment:

  • Use current value → 12
  • Then increment

After this:

Value used = 12
x = 13

docs.title: Final Calculation
docs.text:
y = 10 + 12 + 12
y = 34

Final:

x = 13

docs.title: ✅ Output
docs.text:
34
13

docs.title: ⚠ Interview Insight
docs.text:
Interviewers use this to test:

  • Pre vs post increment understanding
  • Left-to-right evaluation
  • Side effects in expressions

And important:

👉 In real projects, never write such code. It reduces readability and increases bugs.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
int x = 5;
int y = x++ + x++ + ++x;
System.out.println(y);
System.out.println(x);

docs.title: Step-by-step (Left → Right)
docs.text:
Initial:

x = 5

docs.title: 1️⃣ First term → x++
docs.text:
• Use value → 5
  • Then increment → x becomes 6

Used value = 5 x = 6

docs.title: 2️⃣ Second term → x++
docs.text:
• Use value → 6
  • Then increment → x becomes 7

Used value = 6 x = 7

docs.title: 3️⃣ Third term → ++x
docs.text:
• Increment first → x becomes 8
  • Use value → 8

Used value = 8 x = 8

docs.title: Final Calculation
docs.text:
y = 5 + 6 + 8
y = 19

Final:

x = 8

docs.title: ✅ Output
docs.text:
19
8

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Insight
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

What is rule for expression evaluation in Java?

Answer:

Java evaluates expressions strictly from left to right. Side effects like post and pre-increment happen during evaluation in that order.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
int x = 5;
System.out.println(x++ + x++ + x++);
System.out.println(x);

docs.title: Step-by-step (Left → Right)
docs.text:
Initial:

x = 5

docs.title: 1️⃣ First x++
docs.text:
• Use 5
  • Then x becomes 6

Used = 5 x = 6

docs.title: 2️⃣ Second x++
docs.text:
• Use 6
  • Then x becomes 7

Used = 6 x = 7

docs.title: 3️⃣ Third x++
docs.text:
• Use 7
  • Then x becomes 8

Used = 7 x = 8

docs.title: Final Calculation
docs.text:
5 + 6 + 7 = 18

Final:

x = 8

docs.title: ✅ Output
docs.text:
18
8

docs.title: 🧠 Important Interview Note
docs.text:
Java guarantees:

  • Left-to-right operand evaluation.
  • Post-increment returns old value, then increments.

This is defined behavior (unlike C/C++ where this can be undefined).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
int x = 1;
int y = 1;

if (x++ == 1 && ++y == 2) {
    x++;
}

System.out.println(x);
System.out.println(y);

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution
docs.text:
Initial:

x = 1
y = 1

docs.title: 1️⃣ Evaluate: x++ == 1
docs.text:
• x++ → use 1
  • then x becomes 2
  • 1 == 1 → true

Now:

x = 2
y = 1

Since first condition is true, second condition will be evaluated (&& needs both true).

docs.title: 2️⃣ Evaluate: ++y == 2
docs.text:
• ++y → y becomes 2
  • 2 == 2 → true

Now:

x = 2
y = 2

Both conditions true → enter if block.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Inside if:
docs.text:
x++;
  • Use 2
  • x becomes 3

Now:

x = 3
y = 2

docs.title: ✅ Final Output
docs.text:
3
2

docs.title: 🧠 What Interviewer Tests Here
docs.text:
• Post vs pre increment
  • Short-circuit &&
  • Evaluation order (left → right)
  • Side effects inside condition

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
```java id="zky2lk" int x = 1; int y = 1;

if (x++ == 2 && ++y == 2) { x++; }

System.out.println(x); System.out.println(y); 

---

#### Step-by-step

Initial:

* x = 1
* y = 1

##### 1️⃣ Evaluate `x++ == 2`

* `x++` uses 1, then x becomes 2
* `1 == 2` → **false**

Now:

* x = 2
* y = 1

##### 2️⃣ Short-circuit happens

Because first part of `&&` is false, Java **will not evaluate** `++y == 2`.

So:

* y stays 1
* `if` block not executed

✅ Final output:

* 2
* 1

---

### Code

```java
int x = 10;
int y = 20;

int z = (x > y) ? x++ : y++;
System.out.println(z);
System.out.println(x);
System.out.println(y);

docs.title: Condition:
docs.text:
x > y

10 > 20 → false

So ternary chooses the false branch:

y++

docs.title: Evaluate y++
docs.text:
• Use current value → 20
  • Then increment → y becomes 21

So:

z = 20
y = 21

x was never touched.

docs.title: ✅ Final State
docs.text:
z = 20
x = 10
y = 21

docs.title: 🧠 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
In ternary operator:

👉 Only ONE branch executes. 👉 The other branch is completely ignored.

Unlike if statements where confusion sometimes happens with side effects, ternary is strictly one branch execution.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
int x = 5;
int y = 10;

System.out.println(x > y ? x++ : ++y);
System.out.println(x);
System.out.println(y);

docs.title: Step 1: Evaluate condition
docs.text:
x > y
5 > 10 → false

So ternary chooses false branch:

++y

docs.title: Step 2: Evaluate ++y
docs.text:
Pre-increment:

  • y becomes 11
  • value used = 11

So first print:

11

Now:

x = 5
y = 11

docs.title: Step 3: Print x and y
docs.text:
5
11

docs.title: ✅ Final Output
docs.text:
11
5
11

docs.title: 🧠 What Interviewer Is Testing
docs.text:
• Only one branch executes
  • Pre-increment changes value before usage
  • Order of evaluation

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
int x = 3;
int y = 4;

if ((x & 1) == 1 && (y++ > 3)) {
    x++;
}

System.out.println(x);
System.out.println(y);

docs.title: 1️⃣ Evaluate (x & 1) == 1
docs.text:
• x = 3 → binary 0011
  • 1 → binary 0001
  • 3 & 1 → 0001 → 1

So:

(x & 1) == 1  →  true

Meaning: x is odd (common trick to check odd/even).

docs.title: 2️⃣ Because first part is true, evaluate second part
docs.text:
(y++ > 3)

  • y++ uses current value 4
  • checks 4 > 3 → true
  • then y becomes 5

So the full && becomes:

true && true → true

So if block runs.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Inside if: x++;
docs.text:
x becomes 4.

Final:

  • x = 4
  • y = 5

✅ Output:

4
5

docs.title: 📘 Notes (Important Interview Lines)
docs.text:
• x & 1 checks odd/even:

  • 1 → odd

  • 0 → even
  • && short-circuits, but here it didn’t short-circuit because first condition was true.
  • y++ changes y even if condition is true/false depending on whether that side executes.
int x = 0;
int y = 0;

if (x++ == 0 & y++ == 0) { }
System.out.println(x);
System.out.println(y);

docs.title: Key point: & is NOT short-circuit
docs.text: Even in boolean expressions, single & evaluates both sides.

docs.title: Left side: x++ == 0
docs.text:
• uses x=0 → true
  • then x becomes 1

docs.title: Right side: y++ == 0
docs.text:
• still evaluated because &
  • uses y=0 → true
  • then y becomes 1

So:

  • x = 1
  • y = 1

docs.title: 📘 Notes line (important)
docs.text:
• && short-circuit: may skip right side
  • & evaluates both sides always (even in boolean)

docs.title: 1️⃣ What they do (Interview style)
docs.text:
• << Left shift: shifts bits left, fills right with 0
  • >> Signed right shift: shifts bits right, fills left with sign bit (0 for +, 1 for -)
  • >>> Unsigned right shift: shifts bits right, fills left with 0 always

docs.title: For positive numbers:
docs.text: • >> and >>> behave the same (both fill with 0)

docs.title: For negative numbers:
docs.text:
• >> keeps negative sign (fills 1 on left)
  • >>> makes it “look positive” (fills 0 on left)

docs.title: 5 << 1
docs.text:
5 in binary (8-bit view): 00000101 Shift left 1 → 00001010 = 10

So:

5 << 1  => 10

docs.title: 8 >> 1
docs.text:
8: 00001000 Right shift 1 → 00000100 = 4

So:

8 >> 1  => 4

docs.title: 4️⃣ The BIG Interview Trap: negative numbers
Example: -4 >> 1
docs.text:
Two’s complement (conceptually):

  • -4 ends with bits ...11111100

Signed right shift >> 1 fills with 1 (sign bit):

  • result becomes ...11111110 which is -2

✅ So:

-4 >> 1   => -2

docs.title: Example: -4 >>> 1
docs.text:
Unsigned right shift fills with 0:

  • left side becomes 0-filled
  • result becomes a large positive int

✅ So:

-4 >>> 1  => 2147483646

Why that number?

  • For int (32-bit), -4 is 0xFFFFFFFC
  • >>> 1 → 0x7FFFFFFE = 2147483646

docs.title: 5️⃣ Another common trap: shift count masking
docs.text:
Java masks the shift distance:

  • For int: only lower 5 bits used → n & 31 (0–31)
  • For long: only lower 6 bits used → n & 63 (0–63)

So:

1 << 32   // same as 1 << (32 & 31) = 1 << 0 = 1

This surprises many people.

docs.title: 6️⃣ When shifts act like multiply/divide
docs.text:
• x << 1 ≈ x * 2
  • x >> 1 ≈ x / 2 (for positives)

⚠ For negatives, >> is like divide-by-2 with rounding toward negative infinity behavior depending on bits. Safer to say: “it shifts bits; division equivalence is not always safe for negatives.”

docs.title: ✅ Bitwise shift “How to answer in interview”
docs.text: << shifts left and fills zeros. >> shifts right and preserves the sign bit (arithmetic shift). >>> shifts right and fills zeros (logical shift), so for negative numbers it produces a large positive value.

docs.title: 📘 Operator Precedence Table (Interview-focused)
docs.text:
Highest → Lowest (common ones)

  1. Postfix: expr++ expr-- () [] .
  2. Unary: ++expr --expr + - ! ~ (type)
  3. Multiplicative: * / %
  4. Additive: + -
  5. Shift: << >> >>>
  6. Relational: < <= > >= instanceof
  7. Equality: == !=
  8. Bitwise AND: &
  9. Bitwise XOR: ^
  10. Bitwise OR: |
  11. Logical AND: &&
  12. Logical OR: ||
  13. Ternary: ?:
  14. Assignment: = += -= *= /= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>=

docs.title: Golden note:
docs.text: • Same precedence operators evaluate left to right (except assignments are right to left)

docs.title: Trap 1: + vs <<
docs.text:
System.out.println(1 << 2 + 1);

+ happens before << So it becomes 1 << 3 = 8

docs.title: Trap 2: & vs ==
docs.text:
System.out.println(1 & 2 == 0);

== happens before &? Actually: & has lower precedence than ==, so 2 == 0 evaluated first? Wait carefully:

  • Precedence: Equality (==) is higher than bitwise AND (&) ✅ So expression becomes:
1 & (2 == 0)  // invalid: int & boolean

➡️ This does NOT compile.

Correct way:

System.out.println((1 & 2) == 0); // true

docs.title: ✅ Your Notes Snapshot (copy-paste)
docs.text:
• >> keeps sign bit, >>> fills 0
  • -4 >> 1 = -2
  • -4 >>> 1 = 2147483646
  • int shift distance masked by & 31

docs.title: ✅ Question 1
docs.text:
System.out.println(1 << 2 + 1);

You answered 8 ✔ Correct.

Because:

  • 2 + 1 = 3
  • 1 << 3 = 8

docs.title: ✅ Question 2
docs.text:
System.out.println(-1 >>> 1);

Let me explain quickly and finish this topic cleanly.

  • -1 in 32-bit binary = all 1s
11111111 11111111 11111111 11111111
  • >>> 1 shifts right and fills left with 0

So result becomes:

01111111 11111111 11111111 11111111

That equals:

2147483647

So answer is:

2147483647

docs.title: ✅ Operators Topic – Completed
docs.text:
You now clearly understand:

  • Pre vs Post increment
  • Short-circuit vs &
  • Ternary
  • Bitwise basics
  • Shift traps
  • Precedence basics

That’s strong.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Control flow decides the order in which Java statements execute.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Control flow is needed for conditions, loops, branching, and reading output-based interview questions.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: if chooses a branch, for repeats a block, and break exits a loop or switch.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• break exits the nearest loop or switch.
  • continue skips to the next loop iteration.
  • Loop conditions are checked at specific times.
  • Nested loops can make break/continue confusing.
  • Unreachable code can cause compile errors.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Control flow statements control execution order. Java uses decision statements like if and switch, loops like for, while, and do-while, and jump statements like break, continue, and return to control how code runs.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• if/else chooses branches.
  • switch selects matching case.
  • for/while repeat code.
  • break exits.
  • continue skips current iteration.
  • return exits method.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
We’ll cover:

1️⃣ if / else 2️⃣ switch 3️⃣ Loops (for, while, do-while) 4️⃣ break, continue 5️⃣ Common Interview Traps

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
if (condition) {
   // code
}

Condition must be boolean.

⚠ Java does NOT allow:

if (1)   // ❌ Not allowed (C allows this)

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap 1
docs.text:
int x = 5;
if (x = 10) { }  // ❌

Why error?

Because:

  • x = 10 returns int
  • if expects boolean

In C it works. In Java it doesn’t.

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap 2: No Braces
docs.text:
int x = 5;
if (x > 3)
    System.out.println("Hi");
    System.out.println("Hello");

Output:

Hi
Hello

Because only first statement is inside if.

Always use {} in real projects.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
int x = 2;

switch(x) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("One");
        break;
    case 2:
        System.out.println("Two");
        break;
}

docs.title: 🔥 Trap: Fall-through
docs.text:
int x = 1;

switch(x) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("One");
    case 2:
        System.out.println("Two");
}

Output:

One
Two

Because no break.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap: Valid Types
docs.text:
Switch supports:

  • byte
  • short
  • char
  • int
  • String
  • enum

❌ Not allowed:

  • long
  • float
  • double
  • boolean

docs.title: 🔥 Trap: Duplicate case
docs.text:
final int x = 1;
switch(1) {
    case x:  // allowed (compile-time constant)
}

But:

int x = 1;
case x;  // ❌ not constant

docs.title: FOR Loop
docs.text:
for(int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
   System.out.println(i);
}

docs.title: 🔥 Trap
docs.text:
for(;;) {
   System.out.println("Hi");
}

Infinite loop.

All 3 parts optional.

docs.title: WHILE
docs.text:
while(condition) {
}

docs.title: DO-WHILE
docs.text:
Runs at least once.

do {
   System.out.println("Hi");
} while(false);

Output:

Hi

docs.title: Break
docs.text: Stops loop.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text: Skips current iteration.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap
docs.text:
for(int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    if(i == 2) continue;
    System.out.print(i);
}

Output:

0134

docs.title: 5️⃣ Labelled Break (Interview Trap)
docs.text:
outer:
for(int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for(int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        break outer;
    }
}

Exits both loops.

docs.title: ✅ Question 1 – Dangling Else
docs.text:
int x = 0;
if (x > 0)
    if (x < 10)
        System.out.println("A");
    else
        System.out.println("B");

docs.title: Rule:
docs.text:
👉 In Java, else always matches the nearest unmatched if.

So else belongs to:

if (x < 10)

This is called the Dangling Else Problem.

In real code → always use braces {}.

docs.title: ✅ Question 2 – While with Semicolon
docs.text:
int x = 0;
while(x++ < 3);
System.out.println(x);

Notice:

while(x++ < 3);   // <-- semicolon

This is an empty loop.

Step-by-step:

  • x=0 → 0<3 → true → x=1
  • x=1 → 1<3 → true → x=2
  • x=2 → 2<3 → true → x=3
  • x=3 → 3<3 → false → x=4 (because post-increment happens)

Loop exits.

Final x = 4

Correct answer: 4

docs.title: ✅ Question 3 – For Loop with Print in Update
docs.text:
for(int i = 0; i < 3; System.out.print(i++));

Execution order in for:

Initialization
Condition
Body
Update

But body is empty because of semicolon.

So:

  • i=0 → condition true → update prints 0 (i becomes 1)
  • i=1 → condition true → update prints 1 (i becomes 2)
  • i=2 → condition true → update prints 2 (i becomes 3)
  • i=3 → condition false → stop

Output:

012

Correct.

docs.title: 🧠 You Are Strong in Control Flow
docs.text:
You are thinking clearly about:

  • Semicolon traps
  • Post increment behavior
  • Loop evaluation order
  • Dangling else

This is very good sign.

docs.title: ✅ Question 4 – Dangling Else
docs.text:
int x = 0;
if (x > 0)
    if (x < 10)
        System.out.println("A");
    else
        System.out.println("B");

docs.title: Rule:
docs.text:
👉 In Java, else always matches the nearest unmatched if.

So else belongs to:

if (x < 10)

This is called the Dangling Else Problem.

In real code → always use braces {}.

docs.title: ✅ Question 5 – While with Semicolon
docs.text:
int x = 0;
while(x++ < 3);
System.out.println(x);

Notice:

while(x++ < 3);   // <-- semicolon

This is an empty loop.

Step-by-step:

  • x=0 → 0<3 → true → x=1
  • x=1 → 1<3 → true → x=2
  • x=2 → 2<3 → true → x=3
  • x=3 → 3<3 → false → x=4 (because post-increment happens)

Loop exits.

Final x = 4

Correct answer: 4

docs.title: ✅ Question 6 – For Loop with Print in Update
docs.text:
for(int i = 0; i < 3; System.out.print(i++));

Execution order in for:

Initialization
Condition
Body
Update

But body is empty because of semicolon.

So:

  • i=0 → condition true → update prints 0 (i becomes 1)
  • i=1 → condition true → update prints 1 (i becomes 2)
  • i=2 → condition true → update prints 2 (i becomes 3)
  • i=3 → condition false → stop

Output:

012

Correct.

docs.title: 🧠 You Are Strong in Control Flow
docs.text:
You are thinking clearly about:

  • Semicolon traps
  • Post increment behavior
  • Loop evaluation order
  • Dangling else

This is very good sign.

docs.title: ✅ Next: Nested Loops (Very Important)
docs.text:
Interviewers use nested loops to test:

  • Understanding of iteration
  • Dry run ability
  • Time complexity thinking
  • Pattern logic

docs.title: 📘 1️⃣ Basic Nested Loop
docs.text:
for(int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for(int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");
    }
}

docs.title: 📘 2️⃣ Classic Pattern Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

for(int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for(int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {
        System.out.print("*");
    }
    System.out.println();
}

Think step-by-step.

docs.title: 📘 3️⃣ Time Complexity Insight
docs.text:
Nested loops like:

for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for(int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
    }
}

Time complexity = O(n²)

But this:

for(int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for(int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
    }
}

Time complexity = 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²) (still quadratic)

Interviewers love asking this.

Now let’s quickly verify like interview dry-run style.

docs.title: ✅ Pattern 1
docs.text:
for(int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for(int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {
        System.out.print("*");
    }
    System.out.println();
}

i = 1 → print 1 star i = 2 → print 2 stars i = 3 → print 3 stars

So:

*
**
***

Correct.

docs.title: ✅ Pattern 2
docs.text:
for(int i = 3; i >= 1; i--) {
    for(int j = 1; j <= i; j++) {
        System.out.print(j);
    }
    System.out.println();
}

i = 3 → 1 2 3 i = 2 → 1 2 i = 1 → 1

So:

123
12
1

Correct.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Insight
docs.text:
Nested loops are testing:

  • Control of outer loop
  • Resetting inner loop each iteration
  • Understanding loop boundaries

docs.title: Let’s Confirm (Interview Dry Run)
docs.text:
for(int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for(int j = i; j <= 3; j++) {
        System.out.print(j);
    }
    System.out.println();
}

docs.title: i = 1
docs.text:
j starts at 1 → prints 1 2 3

123

docs.title: i = 2
docs.text:
j starts at 2 → prints 2 3

23

docs.title: i = 3
docs.text:
j starts at 3 → prints 3

3

docs.title: 🧠 Why This Is Important
docs.text:
Interviewers use this to test:

  • Inner loop start value depends on outer loop
  • Changing bounds changes pattern
  • Understanding triangular iteration (used in DSA often)

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
for(int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for(int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) {
        if(i == j)
            break;
        System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");
    }
}

docs.title: i = 1
docs.text: • j = 1 → i == j → break (no print)

docs.title: i = 2
docs.text:
• j = 1 → i != j → print 21
  • j = 2 → i == j → break

docs.title: i = 3
docs.text:
• j = 1 → print 31
  • j = 2 → print 32
  • j = 3 → break

✅ Output:

21 31 32

docs.title: Let’s Dry Run (Interview Style)
docs.text:
for(int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    for(int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) {
        if(i == j)
            continue;
        System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");
    }
}

docs.title: i = 1
docs.text:
• j = 1 → skip (continue)
  • j = 2 → print 12
  • j = 3 → print 13

docs.title: i = 2
docs.text:
• j = 1 → print 21
  • j = 2 → skip
  • j = 3 → print 23

docs.title: i = 3
docs.text:
• j = 1 → print 31
  • j = 2 → print 32
  • j = 3 → skip

✅ Final Output:

12 13 21 23 31 32

docs.title: 🧠 Key Difference (Interview Gold)
docs.text: break continue exits loop skips current iteration stops inner loop completely moves to next iteration

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Modern switch is the newer Java switch syntax that supports arrow labels and switch expressions.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It reduces boilerplate, avoids many fall-through bugs, and is common in newer Java codebases.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: String result = switch (day) { case MONDAY -> "Start"; default -> "Other"; }; returns a value from switch.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Old switch can fall through without break.
  • Switch expressions must produce a value.
  • yield can return a value from a block case.
  • Arrow switch labels do not fall through.
  • Exhaustiveness matters for switch expressions.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Modern switch improves old switch by using arrow syntax and allowing switch to be used as an expression. It reduces accidental fall-through and can return a value directly. For block cases, Java uses yield to provide the result.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Arrow cases avoid fall-through.
  • Switch can be an expression.
  • Use yield in block cases.
  • Old switch may need break.
  • Modern switch is cleaner.
  • Good for enum and fixed-value branching.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Now we move to Switch Advanced + Modern Switch (Java 14+)

This topic is important for interviews because many candidates only know old switch.

docs.title: 📘 1️⃣ Traditional Switch (Old Style)
docs.text:
Basic syntax:

switch(expression) {
    case value1:
        // code
        break;
    case value2:
        // code
        break;
    default:
        // code
}

docs.title: 1️⃣ Expression Type Must Be:
docs.text:
Allowed:

  • byte
  • short
  • char
  • int
  • String
  • enum

❌ Not allowed:

  • long
  • float
  • double
  • boolean

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 1: Fall-Through
docs.text:
int x = 2;

switch(x) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("One");
    case 2:
        System.out.println("Two");
    case 3:
        System.out.println("Three");
}

docs.title: Output:
docs.text:
Two
Three

Because no break.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 2: Order of Cases
docs.text:
Cases can be in any order.

switch(x) {
    case 5:
    case 1:
    case 3:
}

Valid.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 3: Case Must Be Compile-Time Constant
docs.text:
int a = 5;
switch(5) {
    case a:   // ❌ ERROR
}

But:

final int a = 5;
case a:   // ✅ allowed

Because final primitive constant is compile-time constant.

docs.title: 📘 2️⃣ Switch with String
docs.text:
String day = "MON";

switch(day) {
    case "MON":
        System.out.println("Start");
        break;
}

Internally, Java uses hashcode comparison.

docs.title: 📘 3️⃣ Modern Switch (Java 14+)
docs.text: This is very important for modern interviews.

docs.title: ✅ Switch Expression (Arrow Style)
docs.text:
int day = 2;

String result = switch(day) {
    case 1 -> "Monday";
    case 2 -> "Tuesday";
    default -> "Other";
};

System.out.println(result);

No break needed.

docs.title: 🔥 Key Difference
docs.text:
Old switch:

  • statement
  • needs break
  • fall-through possible

New switch:

  • expression
  • no fall-through
  • returns value
  • cleaner syntax

docs.title: 📘 4️⃣ Multiple Cases in One Line (Modern)
docs.text:
int day = 2;

String result = switch(day) {
    case 1, 2, 3 -> "Weekday";
    case 6, 7 -> "Weekend";
    default -> "Other";
};

docs.title: 📘 5️⃣ Block Style in Modern Switch
docs.text:
int day = 2;

String result = switch(day) {
    case 2 -> {
        System.out.println("Processing...");
        yield "Tuesday";
    }
    default -> "Other";
};

yield is required when using block.

docs.title: ✅ Question 1
docs.text:
int x = 1;

switch(x) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("A");
    default:
        System.out.println("B");
    case 2:
        System.out.println("C");
}

docs.title: Execution:
docs.text:
• x = 1 → case 1 matches
  • Print A
  • No break → fall through
  • default → print B
  • case 2 → print C

✅ Output:

A
B
C

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
int x = 1;

String result = switch(x) {
    case 1 -> "A";
    case 2 -> "B";
};

System.out.println(result);

docs.title: The Real Reason
docs.text:
Modern switch (switch expression) must be exhaustive.

That means:

  • It must cover all possible values
  • Or have a default

Since int can be many values (not just 1 and 2), compiler says:

"Switch expression does not cover all possible input values"

So it does NOT compile.

docs.title: Correct Version
docs.text:
String result = switch(x) {
    case 1 -> "A";
    case 2 -> "B";
    default -> "Other";
};

Now it compiles.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Insight
docs.text:
Old switch:

  • default optional

New switch expression:

  • must be exhaustive
  • especially for int

BUT:

If switching on enum and covering all enum constants, default is not required.

Example:

enum Day { MON, TUE }

String result = switch(day) {
    case MON -> "Start";
    case TUE -> "Next";
};

This compiles because enum values are fully covered.

docs.title: 🧠 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
Modern switch:

  • Multiple values per case allowed (case 1, 2)
  • No fall-through
  • Must be exhaustive
  • Cleaner and safer than old switch

docs.title: ✅ Control Flow Topic Status
docs.text:
You now understand:

  • if / else (dangling else)
  • loops (semicolon traps)
  • nested loops
  • break vs continue
  • traditional switch
  • modern switch expression
  • exhaustiveness rule

That is strong foundation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A method is a reusable block of code. A stack frame is the runtime memory created for one method call.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This explains local variables, method calls, recursion, stack memory, and StackOverflowError.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When main() calls add(), the JVM creates a new stack frame for add() and removes it when the method returns.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Each method call gets a new stack frame.
  • Local variables live in the stack frame.
  • Objects created inside methods usually live in heap.
  • Recursion can create many stack frames.
  • Returning from a method removes its frame.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: When a method is called, the JVM creates a stack frame for that call. The frame stores local variables, operand stack data, and return information. When the method finishes, its frame is removed. This is why deep recursion can cause StackOverflowError.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Method call creates stack frame.
  • Method return removes stack frame.
  • Local variables are stored in frames.
  • Objects usually live in heap.
  • Each thread has its own stack.
  • Deep recursion can overflow stack.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
We will cover:

1️⃣ What happens when a method is called 2️⃣ Stack memory structure 3️⃣ Stack Frame creation 4️⃣ Pass-by-value (big confusion area) 5️⃣ Recursion stack behavior 6️⃣ Interview traps

docs.title: 1️⃣ What Happens When a Method is Called?
docs.text:
Example:

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int x = 5;
        int result = add(x);
        System.out.println(result);
    }

    static int add(int num) {
        return num + 10;
    }
}

docs.title: 🧠 Step 1: Program starts
docs.text:
• JVM creates main thread
  • Stack created for main thread
  • main() stack frame pushed

docs.title: 🧠 Step 2: x = 5
docs.text:
main()
  x = 5

docs.title: 🧠 Step 3: add(x) is called
docs.text:
• New stack frame created for add()
  • Parameter num receives copy of x

Important: 👉 Java is pass-by-value 👉 num gets copy of 5

docs.title: 🧠 Step 4: return num + 10
docs.text:
• 15 returned
  • add() frame destroyed (popped)

docs.title: 🧠 Step 5: Print result
docs.text:
Output:

15

docs.title: 2️⃣ What is a Stack Frame?
docs.text:
Every method call creates:

  • Local variables
  • Parameters
  • Return address
  • Operand stack

Stored inside a stack frame.

When method finishes: 👉 Frame is popped 👉 Memory automatically cleaned

docs.title: 3️⃣ Important Rule
docs.text:
Each thread has:

  • Its own stack
  • Multiple stack frames

Stack is LIFO (Last In First Out).

docs.title: 4️⃣ Big Interview Question: Is Java Pass-by-Reference?
docs.text:
Answer:

❌ NO ✔ Java is always pass-by-value

Even for objects.

Example:

static void change(int x) {
    x = 100;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int a = 10;
    change(a);
    System.out.println(a);
}

Output:

10

Because:

  • Copy of 10 passed
  • Original not changed

docs.title: 5️⃣ Object Pass-by-Value Trap
docs.text:
class Person {
    int age;
}

static void change(Person p) {
    p.age = 50;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Person obj = new Person();
    obj.age = 20;
    change(obj);
    System.out.println(obj.age);
}

Output:

50

Why?

Because:

  • Copy of reference passed
  • Both point to same object
  • Object modified

But if:

static void change(Person p) {
    p = new Person();
    p.age = 100;
}

Then output:

20

Because:

  • Only local copy changed
  • Original reference unchanged

docs.title: 🔥 Now I Test Your Understanding
docs.text:
Predict output:

static void modify(int a) {
    a = a + 5;
}

static void modifyArray(int[] arr) {
    arr[0] = 100;
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int x = 10;
    modify(x);
    System.out.println(x);

    int[] nums = {1, 2, 3};
    modifyArray(nums);
    System.out.println(nums[0]);
}

✅ Output:

10
100

Now the interview-level explanation (short but deep):

docs.title: 1️⃣ modify(x)
docs.text:
• x is a primitive (int)
  • Java passes a copy of the value (10) into a
  • Inside method, a becomes 15, but that’s only the local copy
  • x in main stays 10

So first print: 10

docs.title: 2️⃣ modifyArray(nums)
docs.text:
• nums is a reference variable
  • Java passes a copy of the reference
  • Both arr (inside method) and nums (in main) point to the same array object in heap
  • Changing arr[0] changes the same heap array

So second print: 100

docs.title: 📘 Notes Line (Most Important)
docs.text:
✅ Java is pass-by-value always.

  • For primitives: value copy
  • For objects/arrays: reference copy (so object can be mutated)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Person p = new Person(20);

changeRef(p);
System.out.println(p.age);

changeObj(p);
System.out.println(p.age);

docs.title: 1️⃣ changeRef(p)
docs.text:
static void changeRef(Person p) {
    p = new Person(99);
}

docs.title: What happens?
docs.text:
• A copy of reference is passed
  • Inside method, p now points to a NEW object
  • But original reference in main still points to old object

So after method:

main → p → Person(age=20)

Output:

20

docs.title: 2️⃣ changeObj(p)
docs.text:
static void changeObj(Person p) {
    p.age = 99;
}

docs.title: What happens?
docs.text:
• Copy of reference passed
  • Both references point to SAME object
  • Modifying p.age modifies heap object

So:

main → p → Person(age=99)

Output:

99

docs.title: 🧠 Interview-Level Explanation (Memorize This)
docs.text:
Java is strictly pass-by-value. When passing objects, the value passed is a copy of the reference. Therefore, methods can modify the object’s state but cannot change the original reference.

This line alone can impress interviewers.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Stack Frame Deep Test
docs.text:
Predict output:

static void fun(int x) {
    x = x + 1;
    System.out.println(x);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    int x = 5;
    fun(x);
    System.out.println(x);
}

✅ Correct Output:

6
5

docs.title: Why (quick stack-frame reasoning)
docs.text:
• fun(x) receives a copy of x (5)
  • inside fun, local x becomes 6 → prints 6
  • main’s x stays 5 → prints 5

docs.title: 📘 Stack Frames + Recursion (Next)
docs.text: Now we move to recursion because it’s the clearest way to see stack frames.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
static void f(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return;
    System.out.print(n + " ");
    f(n - 1);
    System.out.print(n + " ");
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    f(3);
}

✅ Correct Output:

3 2 1 1 2 3

Now let’s make it crystal clear with stack-frame thinking (this is what interviewers love).

docs.title: Why this output happens
docs.text:
f(3):
 print 3
  f(2):
   print 2
    f(1):
     print 1
      f(0): return
     print 1   // after returning
   print 2
 print 3

So:

  • First half prints while going down the recursion: 3 2 1
  • Second half prints while coming back up: 1 2 3

docs.title: 📘 Notes (One line)
docs.text:
Recursion has two phases:

  • Forward (call) phase
  • Backtracking (return) phase

docs.title: 🔥 Next Recursion + Stack Frame Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

static int g(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return n + g(n - 1);
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(g(3));
}

✅ Correct Output.

6

g(3) computes:

  • g(3) = 3 + g(2)
  • g(2) = 2 + g(1)
  • g(1) = 1 + g(0)
  • g(0) = 0

So total = 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6.

docs.title: 🔥 Next: Stack Overflow + Recursion Depth (Interview)
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

“Why does recursion cause StackOverflowError?”

You answer:

Each recursive call creates a new stack frame. If recursion is too deep (or has no base case), the call stack grows until it exceeds the stack memory limit, causing StackOverflowError.

docs.title: Final Method + Stack Frame Trap (Super Common)
docs.text:
Predict output:

static void h(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return;
    h(n - 1);
    System.out.print(n + " ");
}

public static void main(String[] args) {
    h(3);
}
