✅ Correct Output:

1 2 3

Reason (quick, interview-style):

  • h(3) calls h(2) calls h(1) calls h(0) return
  • Printing happens after the recursive call returns, so it prints in reverse order while the stack unwinds: 1 2 3

docs.title: ✅ Methods & Stack Frames Notes — Completed Core
docs.text:
You now fully understand:

  • Stack vs stack frame
  • Method call frame creation & pop
  • Pass-by-value (primitive + reference)
  • Recursion call stack (forward + backward phase)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Overloading means same method name with different parameters. Overriding means a child class changes inherited method behavior.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This is a core polymorphism topic and a common source of compile-time vs runtime binding questions.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: print(int x) and print(String s) are overloaded. Dog.sound() overriding Animal.sound() is overriding.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Overloading is resolved at compile time.
  • Overriding is resolved at runtime.
  • Return type alone cannot overload a method.
  • Static methods are hidden, not overridden.
  • Private methods are not overridden.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Method overloading happens in the same class or inheritance hierarchy when methods have the same name but different parameter lists. It is compile-time polymorphism. Method overriding happens when a subclass provides a new implementation of a parent instance method. It is runtime polymorphism.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Overloading: same name, different parameters.
  • Overriding: child changes parent method.
  • Overloading is compile-time.
  • Overriding is runtime.
  • Return type alone is not enough for overload.
  • Static methods are hidden.

docs.title: Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text: Method overloading means defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class MathUtil {
    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    double add(double a, double b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

Same method name → different parameters.

docs.title: Rules for Overloading
docs.text:
Must differ by:

  • Number of parameters
  • Type of parameters
  • Order of parameters

❌ Return type alone cannot differentiate.

Wrong:

int add(int a, int b) { }
double add(int a, int b) { }  // ❌ compile error

docs.title: When Does Overloading Get Resolved?
docs.text:
👉 At compile time

This is called:

Compile-time polymorphism

docs.title: 🔥 Overloading Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    void show(int a) {
        System.out.println("int");
    }

    void show(long a) {
        System.out.println("long");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test t = new Test();
        t.show(10);
    }
}

What prints?

Answer: int

Because:

  • 10 is int literal
  • Exact match preferred

docs.title: Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text: Method overriding occurs when a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method already defined in its parent class.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    @Override
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barks");
    }
}

docs.title: When Is Overriding Resolved?
docs.text:
👉 At runtime

This is called:

Runtime polymorphism Dynamic method dispatch

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();
a.sound();

Output:

Dog barks

Because:

  • Method call decided at runtime
  • Based on object type (Dog)

docs.title: 🔥 Overriding Rules
docs.text:
• Method signature must be same
  • Cannot reduce access modifier
  • Return type must be same or covariant
  • Cannot override static method
  • Cannot override final method
  • Private methods are not overridden

docs.title: 🔥 Very Common Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    static void show() {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static void show() {
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Parent p = new Child();
        p.show();
    }
}

✅ Output:

Parent

Now let’s deeply understand why — this is a very common interview trap.

docs.title: Why It Prints "Parent"
docs.text:
Parent p = new Child();
p.show();

Key point:

👉 show() is static

Static methods:

  • Belong to the class
  • Not to the object
  • Are resolved at compile time
  • Are not overridden — they are hidden

This is called:

Method Hiding

docs.title: What happens internally?
docs.text:
Compiler looks at:

Parent p

Since reference type is Parent, compiler binds method call to:

Parent.show();

It does NOT check the object type (new Child()).

So output:

Parent

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Answer Line
docs.text:
Static methods are not overridden. They are hidden. Method call is resolved at compile time based on reference type.

That one sentence can impress interviewer.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Slightly Harder Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Parent p = new Child();
        p.show();
    }
}

✅ Correct.

Child

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because this time show() is not static.

Parent p = new Child();
p.show();

For non-static methods:

  • Java uses dynamic method dispatch
  • Method is chosen at runtime
  • Based on the actual object type
  • Not the reference type

Here:

  • Reference type → Parent
  • Object type → Child

So JVM calls:

Child.show()

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Comparison (Very Important Table)
docs.text: Feature Overloading Overriding Class Same class Parent → Child Signature Must differ Must be same Return type Can differ (but not alone) Same or covariant Access modifier Any Cannot reduce visibility Resolution time Compile-time Runtime Static methods Can overload Cannot override (hidden)

docs.title: 🔥 Final Boss Trap (Most Asked)
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Parent show");
    }

    void display() {
        System.out.println("Parent display");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    @Override
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Child show");
    }

    void display(int x) {
        System.out.println("Child display");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Parent p = new Child();
        p.show();
        p.display();
    }
}

✅ Correct.

Child show
Parent display

Now let’s break it down like an interviewer expects.

docs.title: Code Summary
docs.text:
Parent p = new Child();
p.show();
p.display();

docs.title: 1️⃣ p.show()
docs.text:
• show() is overridden in Child
  • Non-static method
  • Runtime polymorphism applies
  • Object type is Child

So JVM calls:

Child show

docs.title: 2️⃣ p.display()
docs.text:
Now look carefully:

In Parent:

void display()

In Child:

void display(int x)

That is NOT overriding.

That is overloading.

The method signature is different.

So for:

p.display();

Compiler checks reference type (Parent).

Only method available is:

Parent.display()

So it prints:

Parent display

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Insight
docs.text:
This tests:

  • Overriding vs overloading difference
  • Method resolution based on reference type vs object type
  • Signature matching rule

docs.title: 🚀 Ultra Important Final Trap (Real Interview Favorite)
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    Parent() {
        System.out.println("Parent constructor");
    }

    void show() {
        System.out.println("Parent show");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    Child() {
        System.out.println("Child constructor");
    }

    @Override
    void show() {
        System.out.println("Child show");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Parent p = new Child();
        p.show();
    }
}

✅ Output (in order):

Parent constructor
Child constructor
Child show

docs.title: Why (quick but interview-strong)
docs.text:
• new Child() triggers constructor chaining:

  • Parent() runs first via implicit super()

  • then Child() runs
  • After object creation, p.show() is a virtual (overridden) method, so it calls Child.show() at runtime.

docs.title: Notebook lines (copy-paste)
docs.text:
• Constructors are not overridden; they run in parent → child order.
  • Overridden methods are resolved at runtime based on object type.

docs.title: Next trap (last one, very common): Overloading with null
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }
    void print(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test t = new Test();
        t.print(null);
    }
}

✅ Output — it prints:

String

docs.title: Why (interview-ready)
docs.text: null can match both String and Object, but Java chooses the most specific overload. String is more specific than Object, so print(String) is selected at compile time.

docs.title: 🔥 Extra trap (very common follow-up)
docs.text:
What happens here?

class Test {
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }
    void print(Integer i) { System.out.println("Integer"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test().print(null);
    }
}

Does it compile? If yes, what prints? If not, why?

It does not compile because the compiler finds the method call ambiguous.

docs.title: Why It Fails
docs.text:
void print(String s)
void print(Integer i)

new Test().print(null);

null can match:

  • String
  • Integer

But now:

  • Neither String is subclass of Integer
  • Nor Integer is subclass of String

So compiler cannot decide which is more specific.

Result:

reference to print is ambiguous

Compilation error.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Insight (Very Important Rule)
docs.text:
When overloading:

  1. Compiler chooses method at compile time
  2. It looks for the most specific match
  3. If two methods are equally specific → ambiguity error

docs.title: 🔥 Final Overloading Trap (Hard Level)
docs.text:
Predict:

class Test {

    void print(Object o) { System.out.println("Object"); }
    void print(String s) { System.out.println("String"); }
    void print(StringBuilder sb) { System.out.println("StringBuilder"); }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test().print(null);
    }
}

Does it compile? If yes, what prints? If not, why?

It does not compile because the compiler finds the method call ambiguous.

docs.title: Why it does NOT compile
docs.text:
We have overloads:

print(Object)
print(String)
print(StringBuilder)

Calling:

print(null)

null can match all reference types, so candidates are:

  • String
  • StringBuilder
  • Object

Java picks the most specific method.

  • Object is least specific → eliminated

  • Now between String and StringBuilder:

  • They are siblings (both extend Object, neither extends the other)

So neither is more specific → compiler cannot choose → ambiguous.

✅ Compile-time error similar to:

reference to print is ambiguous

docs.title: Notes (1-liner for interviews)
docs.text: print(null) chooses the most specific overload; if multiple unrelated reference types are equally specific (like String and StringBuilder), the call is ambiguous and won’t compile.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A constructor is a special block used to initialize a new object.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Constructors explain object initialization, constructor chaining, default constructors, and common output traps.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: new Person("Asha") allocates an object and then calls the matching constructor to initialize it.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Constructor name must match class name.
  • Constructors do not have return types.
  • Constructor does not allocate memory by itself.
  • If no constructor is written, Java adds a default constructor.
  • this() or super() must be first statement if used.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: A constructor initializes an object after memory is allocated. It has the same name as the class and no return type. Java provides a default no-argument constructor only when no constructor is defined. Constructors can be overloaded and can call other constructors using this() or parent constructors using super().

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Constructor initializes object.
  • No return type.
  • Same name as class.
  • Can be overloaded.
  • Default constructor exists only if none is written.
  • this()/super() must be first.

docs.title: Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text: A constructor is a special method used to initialize objects. It has the same name as the class and has no return type.

docs.title: Basic Example
docs.text:
class Person {
    int age;

    Person(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }
}

When you write:

Person p = new Person(20);

JVM does:

  1. Allocate memory in heap
  2. Set default values
  3. Call constructor
  4. Assign provided values

docs.title: 📘 2️⃣ Execution Order in Inheritance (VERY IMPORTANT)
docs.text:
Consider:

class Parent {
    Parent() {
        System.out.println("Parent constructor");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    Child() {
        System.out.println("Child constructor");
    }
}

When you write:

new Child();

docs.title: Output:
docs.text:
Parent constructor
Child constructor

Why?

Because:

👉 super() is automatically inserted as first line in child constructor.

docs.title: Rule (Memorize)
docs.text:
• this() calls another constructor in same class
  • super() calls parent constructor
  • Must be first line
  • Cannot use both together

docs.title: Example of this()
docs.text:
class Test {
    Test() {
        this(10);
        System.out.println("Default");
    }

    Test(int x) {
        System.out.println("Parameterized");
    }
}

When:

new Test();

Output:

Parameterized
Default

docs.title: 📘 4️⃣ Initialization Blocks
docs.text: There are two types:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Instance Initialization Block
docs.text:
{
   System.out.println("Instance block");
}

Runs: 👉 Every time object is created 👉 Before constructor body

docs.title: 2️⃣ Static Initialization Block
docs.text:
static {
   System.out.println("Static block");
}

Runs: 👉 Only once 👉 When class is loaded

docs.title: 🔥 Execution Order (VERY IMPORTANT)
docs.text:
When object is created:

  1. Static variables
  2. Static blocks
  3. Instance variables
  4. Instance blocks
  5. Constructor

In inheritance:

Parent static Child static Parent instance Parent constructor Child instance Child constructor

docs.title: 🔥 Interview-Level Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("Parent static");
    }

    {
        System.out.println("Parent instance");
    }

    Parent() {
        System.out.println("Parent constructor");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("Child static");
    }

    {
        System.out.println("Child instance");
    }

    Child() {
        System.out.println("Child constructor");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Child();
    }
}

✅ Output:

Parent static
Child static
Parent instance
Parent constructor
Child instance
Child constructor

docs.title: ✅ Why This Order Happens (Interview-Level Explanation)
docs.text: When new Child() runs:

docs.title: 🔹 Step 1: Class Loading Phase (Only once)
docs.text:
1️⃣ Parent static block 2️⃣ Child static block

Static blocks run:

  • Once
  • When class is loaded
  • Parent loads before child

docs.title: 🔹 Step 2: Object Creation Phase
docs.text: Now instance-level execution begins.

docs.title: Order in inheritance:
docs.text: 3️⃣ Parent instance block 4️⃣ Parent constructor 5️⃣ Child instance block 6️⃣ Child constructor

docs.title: 🧠 Golden Rule (Memorize This)
docs.text:
When creating child object:

Parent static
Child static
Parent instance
Parent constructor
Child instance
Child constructor

docs.title: 🚨 Now Harder Trap (Very Common)
docs.text:
Predict output:

class A {
    A() {
        System.out.println("A constructor");
        show();
    }

    void show() {
        System.out.println("A show");
    }
}

class B extends A {
    int x = 10;

    B() {
        System.out.println("B constructor");
    }

    @Override
    void show() {
        System.out.println("B show " + x);
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new B();
    }
}

⚠ This is a famous interview trap.

docs.title: ✅ Correct Output (in order)
docs.text:
A constructor
B show 0
B constructor

docs.title: Key rule:
docs.text: ✅ Overridden methods are virtual, even inside constructors. So when A() calls show(), it actually calls B.show() because the real object is new B().

docs.title: 1️⃣ new B() starts
docs.text:
Before B constructor body runs, Java must run:

👉 super() → calls A() first

docs.title: 2️⃣ Inside A() constructor
docs.text:
System.out.println("A constructor");   // prints
show();                                // calls overridden method!

So it prints:

A constructor

Now show() call:

Because actual object is B, it calls:

@Override
void show() {
    System.out.println("B show " + x);
}

docs.title: 🚨 Trap: What is x at this moment?
docs.text:
x = 10 is an instance field initializer in class B. But B’s instance fields are initialized only after super() finishes.

So during A() execution:

  • x is still at its default value → 0

So it prints:

B show 0

docs.title: 3️⃣ A() finishes
docs.text:
Now Java initializes B instance fields:

  • x = 10

Then B() constructor body runs:

B constructor

docs.title: ✅ Final Output
docs.text:
A constructor
B show 0
B constructor

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Answer (One line)
docs.text: Calling overridable methods from constructors is dangerous because subclass fields may not be initialized yet, so the overridden method can see default values.

docs.title: 🔥 Quick check (one question)
docs.text:
If I make int x = 10; into static int x = 10; then what would show() print during A() constructor?

✅ Correct — it would print 10.

docs.title: Why (quick, interview-ready)
docs.text: static variables are initialized at class loading time, before any object is created. So when A() constructor calls show(), B.show() reads static x which is already initialized to 10.

docs.title: Notes line (very important)
docs.text:
• Instance fields may still be default (0/null) during super() execution.
  • Static fields are ready earlier (class-load phase).

docs.title: 🔥 Next constructor trap: this() vs super() rule
docs.text:
Does this compile? If not, why?

class A {
    A() { }
}

class B extends A {
    B() {
        this(10);
        super();
    }

    B(int x) { }
}

Answer: compile / not compile + reason (1–2 lines).

✅ Ouput — it does not compile.

It does not compile because a constructor must call either this() or super() as the first statement, and you cannot have both.

docs.title: Why Exactly It Fails
docs.text:
class B extends A {
    B() {
        this(10);
        super();   // ❌ compile error
    }
}

docs.title: Java Rule:
docs.text:
• If you write this(), it must be the first line
  • If you write super(), it must also be the first line
  • You cannot call both
  • You cannot place super() after this()

So compiler error:

Constructor call must be the first statement in constructor

docs.title: Important Clarification
docs.text:
When you write:

B() {
    this(10);
}

Then inside B(int x), Java automatically inserts:

super();

So the actual call chain becomes:

B() → B(int x) → super() → A()

Java ensures parent constructor runs first, but through the chained constructor.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Rule (Memorize)
docs.text:
• Constructor can call either this() or super()
  • It must be the first statement
  • If not written, compiler inserts super() automatically

docs.title: 🔥 Final Constructor Trap (Very Common)
docs.text:
Predict output:

class A {
    A() {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

class B extends A {
    B() {
        System.out.println("B");
    }

    B(int x) {
        this();
        System.out.println("C");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new B(10);
    }
}

Write exact output in order.

✅ Ouput:

A
B
C

Now let’s break it down clearly (interview style).

docs.title: Code
docs.text: new B(10);

docs.title: Step 1️⃣ → B(int x) constructor runs
docs.text:
B(int x) {
    this();          // calls B()
    System.out.println("C");
}

So first it calls:

docs.title: Step 2️⃣ → B() constructor
docs.text:
B() {
    System.out.println("B");
}

But before B() runs, Java automatically inserts:

super();

So it calls:

docs.title: Step 3️⃣ → A() constructor
docs.text:
A() {
    System.out.println("A");
}

Prints:

A

docs.title: Step 4️⃣ → Back to B()
docs.text:
Prints:

B

docs.title: Step 5️⃣ → Back to B(int x)
docs.text:
Prints:

C

docs.title: 🧠 Final Execution Chain
docs.text:
B(int) → this() → B() → super() → A()

And printing order:

A
B
C

docs.title: 🔥 You Now Fully Understand
docs.text:
• Constructor chaining
  • this() vs super()
  • Execution order
  • Static vs instance blocks
  • Method call inside constructor trap

That is strong OOP foundation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Static members belong to the class. Instance members belong to each object.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This topic explains shared data, object-specific data, static methods, class loading, and common access mistakes.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: static int count is shared by all objects, while String name is separate for each object.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Static methods cannot directly access instance members.
  • Static variables are shared.
  • Instance variables belong to objects.
  • Static is not inheritance-based object polymorphism.
  • Too much static state can make code hard to test.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Static members are associated with the class and are shared across all instances. Instance members are associated with a specific object. Static methods can be called using the class name, while instance methods need an object because they work with object state.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Static belongs to class.
  • Instance belongs to object.
  • Static variables are shared.
  • Instance variables are per object.
  • Static methods cannot use this.
  • Use class name for static access.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is an Instance Member?
docs.text:
Instance members:

  • Belong to an object
  • Stored in heap (inside object)
  • Each object gets its own copy

Example:

```java id="i1gk2s" class Person { int age; // instance variable } 

If you create:

```java id="z3w8tm"
Person p1 = new Person();
Person p2 = new Person();

Memory:

```id="q9a4lf" Heap: p1 → { age } p2 → { age } 

Each object has its own `age`.

---

### 2️⃣ What is a Static Member?

Static members:

* Belong to the class
* Only ONE copy exists
* Shared among all objects
* Loaded when class loads

Example:

```java id="u7dn23"
class Person {
    static int count;
}

No matter how many objects:

```java id="t4dk1x" new Person(); new Person(); 

There is only ONE `count`.

---

### 3️⃣ Memory Location (Important for Interviews)

Modern JVM (Java 8+):

* Instance variables → Heap (inside object)
* Static variables → Heap (inside Class metadata structure)
* Static methods → Method area (metadata)
* Stack → Local variables & method calls

---

### 4️⃣ Static Method vs Instance Method

#### Static Method

```java id="s8v34k"
static void show() { }

  • Belongs to class
  • Cannot access instance variables directly
  • Cannot use this
  • Cannot call non-static method directly

docs.title: Instance Method
docs.text:
```java id="f1y27d" void show() { } 

* Belongs to object
* Can access both static & instance members

---

### ✅ Trap 1 — Deep Explanation

```java
class Test {
    static int x = 0;
    int y = 0;

    Test() {
        x++;
        y++;
    }
}

docs.title: After Test t1 = new Test();
docs.text:
• x = 1
  • t1.y = 1

docs.title: After Test t2 = new Test();
docs.text:
• x = 2
  • t2.y = 1

Because:

  • x is static → shared
  • y is instance → each object has separate copy

docs.title: So output:
docs.text:
2 1
2 1

docs.title: ✅ Trap 2 — Why It Does Not Compile
docs.text:
static void show() {
    System.out.println(this);
}

Why error?

Because:

  • Static method belongs to class
  • No object context
  • this refers to current object
  • Static method may be called without object

So compiler error:

non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Static members belong to the class and do not have access to instance context, therefore they cannot use this.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Slightly Harder Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static int x = 10;

    static {
        x = x + 5;
    }

    {
        x = x + 2;
    }

    Test() {
        x = x + 3;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test();
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

✅ Correct — final value is 20.

Here’s the clean dry run (interview style):

docs.title: Code flow
docs.text:
Initial:

  • static int x = 10

docs.title: 1️⃣ Static block (runs once when class loads)
docs.text:
static { x = x + 5; }

So:

  • x = 15

docs.title: 2️⃣ new Test() starts object creation
docs.text:
Instance block runs before constructor:

{ x = x + 2; }

So:

  • x = 17

docs.title: 3️⃣ Constructor runs
docs.text:
Test() { x = x + 3; }

So:

  • x = 20

docs.title: Print:
docs.text: 20

docs.title: 🧠 Notes line
docs.text: Order: static fields → static blocks → instance blocks → constructor

docs.title: 🔥 Next trap: Static method “overriding” (actually hiding)
docs.text:
Predict output:

class A {
    static void m() { System.out.println("A"); }
}
class B extends A {
    static void m() { System.out.println("B"); }
}
public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        A a = new B();
        a.m();
    }
}

✅ Correct — output is A.

Reason (interview one-liner):

Static methods are hidden, not overridden. The call is resolved at compile time based on the reference type (A), so it calls A.m().

docs.title: 📘 Static vs Instance: Final Notes Snapshot
docs.text:
• Instance members: per-object, heap, accessed via object, support runtime polymorphism (overriding).
  • Static members: per-class (one copy), available without object, no this, no overriding (only hiding), resolved at compile time.

docs.title: Next mini-trap (last for Static vs Instance)
docs.text:
Does this compile? If yes, what prints?

class Test {
    static int x = 10;
    int x = 20;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Answer: compile / not compile + reason.

✅ Correct Output: — it does not compile.

It does not compile because a class cannot have two fields with the same name, even if one is static and the other is instance.

docs.title: Why Exactly?
docs.text:
static int x = 10;
int x = 20;

Even though:

  • One is static
  • One is instance

They are still fields of the same class, and Java does not allow duplicate field names in the same class scope.

You’ll get compile-time error like:

variable x is already defined in class Test

docs.title: 🧠 Important Clarification
docs.text:
You can have same variable name in:

  • Different classes
  • Parent & child class (field hiding)

Example:

class A {
    int x = 10;
}

class B extends A {
    int x = 20;
}

This compiles.

But in same class → not allowed.

docs.title: 🔥 Final Static vs Instance Master Question
docs.text:
Predict output:

class A {
    int x = 10;
}

class B extends A {
    int x = 20;

    void print() {
        System.out.println(x);
        System.out.println(super.x);
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        B b = new B();
        b.print();
    }
}

✅ Output:

20
10

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
class A {
    int x = 10;
}

class B extends A {
    int x = 20;
}

This is field hiding, not overriding.

Important difference:

  • Methods → can be overridden (runtime polymorphism)
  • Fields → are resolved at compile time based on reference type

docs.title: Inside print() method
docs.text:
System.out.println(x);        // refers to B.x
System.out.println(super.x);  // refers to A.x

So:

  • x → 20
  • super.x → 10

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Insight
docs.text:
Fields are not polymorphic. They are accessed based on reference type at compile time.

Example trap:

A obj = new B();
System.out.println(obj.x);

What prints?

👉 10 (because reference type is A)

Even though object is B.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: final restricts modification: final variables cannot be reassigned, final methods cannot be overridden, and final classes cannot be extended.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Final is common in immutability, constants, inheritance control, and interview traps around references.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: final List<String> names means the reference cannot point to another list, but the list object may still be mutable.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Final reference does not always mean immutable object.
  • Final variables must be initialized once.
  • Final methods cannot be overridden.
  • Final classes cannot be inherited.
  • Compile-time constants have special behavior.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: final means the target cannot be changed in a specific way. A final variable cannot be reassigned after initialization. A final method cannot be overridden by subclasses. A final class cannot be extended. For object references, final protects the reference, not necessarily the object contents.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Final variable: no reassignment.
  • Final method: no overriding.
  • Final class: no inheritance.
  • Final reference can point to mutable object.
  • Final fields need initialization.
  • Useful for constants and design safety.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
final can be used with:

1️⃣ Variables 2️⃣ Methods 3️⃣ Classes

Each has different meaning.

docs.title: Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text: A final variable cannot be reassigned once initialized.

docs.title: Example (Primitive)
docs.text:
final int x = 10;
x = 20;   // ❌ compile error

Because final means constant.

docs.title: 🔥 Important: final Reference Variable
docs.text:
final Person p = new Person();
p = new Person();  // ❌ error

But:

p.age = 30;   // ✅ allowed

⚠ Important rule:

final reference means reference cannot change, but object state can change.

This is a big interview trap.

docs.title: 2️⃣ final Method
docs.text:
class A {
    final void show() { }
}

class B extends A {
    void show() { }   // ❌ compile error
}

final method:

  • Cannot be overridden
  • But can be overloaded

docs.title: 3️⃣ final Class
docs.text:
final class A { }

class B extends A { }   // ❌ error

final class:

  • Cannot be inherited

Example:

String

String is final.

docs.title: 🔥 Important: Blank Final Variable
docs.text:
class Test {
    final int x;

    Test(int value) {
        x = value;
    }
}

Allowed because:

  • final variable initialized once
  • Inside constructor

But:

final int x;  // ❌ must initialize

docs.title: 🔥 Static Blank Final
docs.text:
class Test {
    static final int x;

    static {
        x = 10;
    }
}

Allowed.

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap 1
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    final int x = 10;

    void change() {
        // x = 20;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test t = new Test();
        System.out.println(t.x);
    }
}

Output?

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap 2
docs.text:
Does this compile?

class Test {
    final int x;

    Test() {
        x = 10;
    }

    Test(int y) {
        // no initialization of x
    }
}

If not, why?

docs.title: ✅ Trap 1
docs.text:
final int x = 10;

Since x is initialized at declaration and never changed:

Output:

10

Simple.

docs.title: ✅ Trap 2
docs.text:
final int x;

Test() {
    x = 10;
}

Test(int y) {
    // x not initialized
}

Rule:

A blank final instance variable must be initialized in every constructor.

Since Test(int y) does not assign value to x, compilation fails.

Compiler error:

variable x might not have been initialized

docs.title: 🧠 Important Rule
docs.text:
For blank final instance variable:

  • Must be assigned exactly once
  • Must be initialized in all constructors

docs.title: 🔥 Now Slightly Harder Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    final int x;

    Test() {
        x = 10;
        x = 20;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test();
    }
}

Compile or not? Why?

“Once a final variable is initialized, it cannot be reassigned.”

docs.title: Why it does NOT compile
docs.text:
final int x;

Test() {
    x = 10;
    x = 20;  // ❌ second assignment
}

A final variable can be assigned exactly once.

So compiler error like:

cannot assign a value to final variable x

docs.title: 🔥 Next final Trap (very common)
docs.text:
Predict output:

import java.util.*;

class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        final List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
        list.add(1);
        list.add(2);
        System.out.println(list);

        // list = new ArrayList<>();  // ?
    }
}
  1. What prints?
  2. Does list = new ArrayList<>(); compile? Why?
  1. It prints [1, 2]
  2. No, it does not compile.

docs.title: ✅ 1️⃣ What prints?
docs.text:
final List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(1);
list.add(2);
System.out.println(list);

Output:

[1, 2]

Because:

  • list is a final reference
  • The reference cannot change
  • But the object it points to can change

So modifying list contents is allowed.

docs.title: ❌ 2️⃣ Does this compile?
docs.text:
list = new ArrayList<>();

No.

Because:

  • list is declared as final
  • A final reference cannot be reassigned
  • So this gives compile-time error

Error like:

cannot assign a value to final variable list

docs.title: 🧠 Important Interview Line
docs.text:
final reference means you cannot change the reference, but you can change the object's state.

This is extremely common interview question.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Slightly Deeper final Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    final int x;

    {
        x = 10;
    }

    Test() {
        System.out.println(x);
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test();
    }
}

What prints?

✅ Output — it prints 10.

docs.title: Why (interview-ready explanation)
docs.text:
Order during object creation:

  1. Memory allocated
  2. Instance fields get default values
  3. Instance initialization blocks run
  4. Constructor body runs

Here:

final int x;

{
    x = 10;   // instance block initializes x
}

So x is assigned in the instance initialization block, which runs before the constructor body. By the time constructor executes, x is already 10.

Then constructor prints:

10

docs.title: 🧠 Important Rule
docs.text:
A blank final instance variable can be initialized in:

  • Field declaration
  • Instance initialization block
  • Constructor (but must be initialized exactly once)

docs.title: 🔥 Final final Boss Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static final int x;

    static {
        x = 5;
    }

    static {
        x = 10;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Compile or not? If not, why?

✅ Output: “It does not compile because you cannot assign to a static final variable more than once.”

docs.title: Why it fails
docs.text:
static final int x;

static { x = 5; }
static { x = 10; }  // ❌ second assignment

static final (blank final) must be assigned exactly once during class initialization.

After x = 5, it’s already initialized, so x = 10 is illegal.

Compiler error like:

cannot assign a value to final variable x

docs.title: ✅ Final Notes Snapshot for your notebook
docs.text:
• final variable: cannot be reassigned
  • final reference: reference fixed, object mutable
  • blank final instance var: must be assigned once in every constructor OR init block
  • final method: cannot override
  • final class: cannot extend
  • static final blank var: initialize once in static block

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Access modifiers control where classes, fields, methods, and constructors can be accessed from.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: They are important for encapsulation, API design, package structure, and inheritance behavior.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: private fields can be accessed only inside the same class. public methods can be accessed from anywhere.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Default access means package-private.
  • Protected is not simply public to subclasses everywhere.
  • Top-level classes can be public or package-private only.
  • Private members are not inherited as accessible members.
  • Access level cannot be reduced when overriding.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Java access modifiers define visibility. private is only inside the class. Default or package-private is inside the same package. protected is available in the same package and through inheritance rules. public is available everywhere.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• private: same class.
  • default: same package.
  • protected: same package plus subclass rules.
  • public: everywhere.
  • Top-level class cannot be private/protected.
  • Overriding cannot reduce visibility.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Java has 4 access levels:

1️⃣ private 2️⃣ default (no modifier) 3️⃣ protected 4️⃣ public

docs.title: 1️⃣ private
docs.text:
Accessible only inside the same class.

class Test {
    private int x = 10;
}

❌ Not accessible outside class.

docs.title: 2️⃣ default (package-private)
docs.text:
If you don’t write any modifier:

class Test {
    int x = 10;   // default
}

Accessible:

  • Inside same class
  • Same package

❌ Not accessible from different package

docs.title: 3️⃣ protected
docs.text:
Accessible:

  • Same class
  • Same package
  • Subclass (even in different package)

docs.title: 4️⃣ public
docs.text: Accessible everywhere.

docs.title: 📘 Visibility Table (Very Important)
docs.text:
Modifier Same Class Same Package Subclass (diff pkg) Other Package private ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ default ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌ protected ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ public ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

Memorize this table.

docs.title: 🔥 Important: protected in Different Package (Common Trap)
docs.text:
If subclass is in different package:

package p1;
public class A {
    protected int x = 10;
}

package p2;
import p1.A;

class B extends A {
    void show() {
        System.out.println(x);  // ✅ allowed
    }
}

But:

A obj = new A();
System.out.println(obj.x);  // ❌ not allowed

Important rule:

In different package, protected members are accessible only through inheritance, not through object reference.

Very common interview trap.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Test Your Understanding
docs.text:
Assume:

Package p1:

package p1;

public class A {
    protected int x = 10;
}

Package p2:

package p2;
import p1.A;

class B extends A {
    void test() {
        A obj = new A();
        System.out.println(obj.x);   // Line 1
        System.out.println(this.x);  // Line 2
    }
}

Question:

Does Line 1 compile? Does Line 2 compile?

docs.title: ✅ Line 1
docs.text:
A obj = new A();
System.out.println(obj.x);   // Line 1

❌ Does not compile.

Reason:

  • x is protected
  • B is in a different package (p2)
  • In different package, protected access is allowed only via inheritance, not via an object of the parent class.

So obj.x is not accessible.

docs.title: ✅ Line 2
docs.text:
System.out.println(this.x);  // Line 2

✅ Compiles.

Reason:

  • B extends A, so B inherits x
  • Accessing via this.x uses inherited member (inheritance path), which is allowed even across packages.

docs.title: ✅ About super.x
docs.text:
In this exact case, super.x also compiles.

Because:

  • super.x means “access the inherited x from parent”
  • That’s still inheritance-based access (allowed)

So inside B (subclass), both are valid:

System.out.println(this.x);
System.out.println(super.x);

docs.title: 🧠 Interview one-liner to remember
docs.text: In a different package, protected members are accessible only through the subclass instance (this/super), not through a parent-class reference (new A()).

docs.title: 🔥 Next Access Modifier Trap (very common)
docs.text:
Assume:

  • p1.A has protected int x
  • p2.B extends A

Now inside B, what about this?

B b = new B();
System.out.println(b.x);

Does this compile? Why?

It DOES compile.

docs.title: Let’s Analyze
docs.text:
We are inside class B (subpackage p2), which extends A (package p1).

B b = new B();
System.out.println(b.x);

docs.title: Why this compiles:
docs.text:
• x is protected
  • B extends A
  • b is a B object
  • We are inside subclass context

Access is happening through: ✔ subclass ✔ subclass object

So this is allowed.

docs.title: Important Rule (Precise Version)
docs.text:
In different package:

Protected member is accessible only:

✔ Inside subclass ✔ Through subclass type reference

Not allowed:

A obj = new A();
System.out.println(obj.x);  // ❌

Because:

  • That is parent-type reference
  • Not inheritance access path

docs.title: 🧠 Final Clear Rule
docs.text: Case Different Package Allowed? obj.x (where obj is A) ❌ No this.x ✅ Yes super.x ✅ Yes b.x (b is subclass object) ✅ Yes

docs.title: 🔥 Now Ultimate Protected Trap
docs.text:
Inside B, what about this?

A obj = new B();
System.out.println(obj.x);

Compile or not? Why?

This one is NOT compile ❌

docs.title: Why A obj = new B(); obj.x does NOT compile
docs.text:
A obj = new B();
System.out.println(obj.x);

Even though the object is B, the reference type is A.

In a different package, Java’s protected access check is based on where you are (subclass) and the type of the reference used to access the member.

✅ Allowed access across packages must be through a reference that is:

  • this / super, or
  • a reference whose compile-time type is the subclass (like B b)

Here, access is through an A reference (obj), so it fails.

So compiler error (conceptually):

x has protected access in A

docs.title: ✅ What compiles instead
docs.text:
B b = new B();
System.out.println(b.x);   // ✅

or

System.out.println(this.x);  // ✅

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: In a different package, protected members are accessible in a subclass only via subclass instance (this, super, or a reference typed as the subclass), not via a parent-typed reference even if it points to a subclass object.

docs.title: Quick check (final for access modifiers)
docs.text:
If x was default (no modifier) in A instead of protected, would this.x inside B compile across packages?

✅ Correct — it would not compile.

Reason (interview-style, one line):

Default (package-private) access is only within the same package, so a subclass in a different package cannot access it—even through inheritance (this.x).

docs.title: 📘 Notes Snapshot: Access Modifiers (copy-paste)
docs.text:
• private: only same class
  • default (package-private): same package only
  • protected: same package + subclass (even different package), but cross-package access must be via subclass instance (this/super or subclass-typed reference)
  • public: everywhere

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An abstract class is a partial class that can hold state and behavior. An interface defines a contract that classes can implement.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This helps decide between inheritance-based reuse and capability-based design in Java applications.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Vehicle can be an abstract class with shared fields, while Payable can be an interface implemented by different unrelated classes.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• A class can extend only one class but implement multiple interfaces.
  • Interfaces can have default and static methods.
  • Abstract classes can have constructors.
  • Use interface for capability or contract.
  • Use abstract class for shared base state or behavior.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Use an interface when you want to define a contract or capability that many unrelated classes can implement. Use an abstract class when classes share common state or base behavior and have a natural parent-child relationship. Java allows multiple interfaces but only one direct class inheritance.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Interface defines contract.
  • Abstract class can share state.
  • Class can implement many interfaces.
  • Class can extend one class.
  • Abstract class can have constructor.
  • Prefer interface for flexible design.

docs.title: Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text: An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated and may contain abstract and concrete methods.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
abstract class Animal {
    abstract void sound();   // abstract method

    void eat() {             // concrete method
        System.out.println("Eating");
    }
}

Subclass must implement abstract methods:

class Dog extends Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

docs.title: Definition (Interview Style)
docs.text: An interface defines a contract that a class must implement.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
interface Animal {
    void sound();   // abstract by default
}

Implementation:

class Dog implements Animal {
    public void sound() {
        System.out.println("Bark");
    }
}

docs.title: 🔥 Major Differences (Very Important Table)
docs.text: Feature Abstract Class Interface Instantiation ❌ Cannot create object ❌ Cannot create object Methods Abstract + Concrete Abstract (default & static allowed since Java 8) Variables Can have instance variables Only public static final Constructors ✅ Yes ❌ No Access modifiers Any Methods are public by default Inheritance Single inheritance Multiple interfaces allowed

docs.title: 📘 3️⃣ Important Modern Java Facts (Java 8+)
docs.text:
Interface can now have:

  • default methods
  • static methods
  • private methods (Java 9+)

Example:

interface Test {
    default void show() {
        System.out.println("Default method");
    }

    static void display() {
        System.out.println("Static method");
    }
}

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap 1
docs.text:
Does this compile?

interface Test {
    int x = 10;
}

class Demo implements Test {
    void change() {
        x = 20;
    }
}

Why?

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap 2
docs.text:
Does this compile?

abstract class A {
    abstract void show();
}

class B extends A {
}

If not, why?

docs.title: ✅ Trap 1
docs.text:
interface Test {
    int x = 10;
}

All interface variables are:

public static final

So this is actually:

public static final int x = 10;

In class:

x = 20;   // ❌

You cannot modify a final variable.

Correct reasoning.

docs.title: ✅ Trap 2
docs.text:
abstract class A {
    abstract void show();
}

class B extends A {
}

B must either:

  • Implement show() OR
  • Be declared abstract

Correct fix:

class B extends A {
    void show() { }
}

OR

abstract class B extends A { }

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liners
docs.text:
• Interface variables are always public static final.
  • A subclass must implement all abstract methods unless it is also abstract.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Slightly Harder Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

interface A {
    default void show() {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

interface B {
    default void show() {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

class Test implements A, B {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test().show();
    }
}

Compile or not? If not, why?

It does not compile because there is a conflict between default methods show() from interfaces A and B.

docs.title: Why It Fails
docs.text:
class Test implements A, B

Both interfaces provide:

default void show()

Java does not know which one to use:

  • A.show() ?
  • B.show() ?

So compiler error like:

class Test inherits unrelated defaults for show() from types A and B

docs.title: How To Fix It
docs.text:
You must override show() in Test:

class Test implements A, B {
    @Override
    public void show() {
        A.super.show();   // or B.super.show();
    }
}

Now it compiles.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Rule
docs.text: If a class implements two interfaces that contain the same default method, the class must override that method to resolve ambiguity.

docs.title: 🔥 Next Important Concept
docs.text:
What happens here?

interface A {
    default void show() {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

class B {
    void show() {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

class Test extends B implements A {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test().show();
    }
}

docs.title: ✅ Does it compile? What prints?
docs.text:
✅ Yes, it compiles. ✅ It prints:

B

docs.title: Why? (Most important rule)
docs.text:
When there is a conflict between:

  • a class method (from superclass), and
  • an interface default method

👉 Class wins.

This is called:

Class wins over interface default method (or “classes take precedence”).

So in:

class Test extends B implements A

B.show() is chosen over A’s default show().

docs.title: Interview one-liner (memorize)
docs.text: If a superclass provides a method implementation, it overrides/conflicts-resolves any interface default method with the same signature. Class method always wins.

docs.title: Quick follow-up (1 line)
docs.text:
If B.show() was private, would Test still print B or A?

it will compile, and it will print:

A

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
If B.show() is private, like:

class B {
    private void show() {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

Important rule:

👉 Private methods are not inherited.

So from Test's perspective:

  • There is NO accessible show() from class B
  • But interface A provides a default show()

So Java uses:

A.show()

And output becomes:

A

docs.title: 🔥 Critical Rule (Interview Gold)
docs.text:
Priority order when resolving methods:

1️⃣ Class methods (public/protected/package-private) 2️⃣ Interface default methods 3️⃣ If conflict between interfaces → must override

But:

  • Private superclass methods are not inherited, so they do NOT block interface defaults.

docs.title: 🧠 One-liner to remember
docs.text:
Class wins over interface — unless the class method is private (not inherited).

🔥 You are now understanding deep OOP resolution rules.

docs.title: Final quick check
docs.text:
If B.show() was static, what would happen?

Compile or not? If compile, what prints?

docs.title: Case: If B.show() is static
docs.text:
interface A {
    default void show() {
        System.out.println("A");
    }
}

class B {
    static void show() {
        System.out.println("B");
    }
}

class Test extends B implements A {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Test().show();
    }
}

docs.title: ❌ Does it compile?
docs.text: No. It does NOT compile.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Important rules:

  • Interface A provides:
default void show()

→ instance method

  • Class B provides:
static void show()

→ static method

Now Java sees conflict:

You cannot:

  • Override an instance method with static
  • Or inherit both static + default method with same signature

Compiler error like:

show() in B cannot implement show() in A
overriding method is static

docs.title: 🔥 Core Rule
docs.text:
A static method cannot override or hide an instance method.

And here:

  • Interface default method = instance method
  • Superclass method = static method

That is illegal conflict.

docs.title: 🧠 Final Method Resolution Priority (Memorize)
docs.text:
When calling a method:

1️⃣ Class instance method 2️⃣ Interface default method 3️⃣ Must override if multiple defaults 4️⃣ Static methods are not part of polymorphism

You’ve now covered:

  • Default method conflicts
  • Class vs interface resolution
  • Private method inheritance
  • Static method conflict

This is already strong OOP level.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: String is immutable. StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronized. StringBuffer is mutable and synchronized.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This topic explains string pool behavior, performance, immutability, and thread-safety trade-offs.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Use StringBuilder when building a string inside a loop in single-threaded code.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• String concatenation can create many objects.
  • String is immutable.
  • StringBuilder is not thread-safe.
  • StringBuffer is synchronized but usually slower.
  • == compares references, not string content.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: String represents immutable text, so every modification creates a new string. StringBuilder is mutable and efficient for repeated modifications in single-threaded code. StringBuffer is also mutable, but its methods are synchronized, so it is safer for shared multi-threaded use but usually slower.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• String is immutable.
  • String literals use string pool.
  • StringBuilder is mutable.
  • StringBuilder is not synchronized.
  • StringBuffer is synchronized.
  • Use equals for content comparison.

docs.title: 1) What is String?
docs.text: String is a reference type (class) that represents immutable text.

docs.title: Most important property
docs.text:
✅ Immutability: once created, the characters inside a String never change.

When you “modify” a String, Java creates a new String object.

docs.title: 2) Why String is immutable (interview depth)
docs.text:
Main reasons:

  1. Security: Strings are used in class loading, file paths, DB URLs, tokens, etc. If mutable, a reference shared somewhere could be altered.
  2. String Pool optimization: immutability makes pooling safe.
  3. Hashing: Strings are keys in HashMap/HashSet. If content changed after hashing, map breaks.
  4. Thread safety: immutable objects are inherently thread-safe.

Interview one-liner:

String is immutable for security, pooling, caching of hashcode, and safe use as map keys.

docs.title: Where it is
docs.text: ✅ String Pool is in the heap (Java 7+). (In older Java it was in PermGen.)

docs.title: What goes into pool
docs.text:
• String literals: "Vishu"
  • Compile-time constant concatenations: "Hel" + "lo"
  • Strings added by calling .intern()

docs.title: What does NOT automatically go to pool
docs.text:
• new String("X") (creates a new heap object)
  • runtime concatenation like a + "World" (usually creates a new heap string)

docs.title: 4) == vs .equals() (must be perfect)
docs.text:
• == compares references (same object?)
  • .equals() compares content (same characters?)

Examples:

String a = "Hello";
String b = "Hello";
System.out.println(a == b);      // true (same pooled literal)
System.out.println(a.equals(b)); // true

String c = new String("Hello");
System.out.println(a == c);      // false (different object)
System.out.println(a.equals(c)); // true

docs.title: 5) What happens in concatenation (+)
docs.text: This is a huge interview area.

docs.title: Case A: compile-time concat
docs.text:
String s = "Hel" + "lo";

✅ compiler folds it into "Hello" → pooled.

docs.title: Case B: runtime concat
docs.text:
String a = "Hel";
String s = a + "lo";

✅ happens at runtime → typically uses StringBuilder under the hood → result is a new String (not pooled unless interned).

In modern Java, concatenation may use invokedynamic, but conceptually:

runtime concatenation creates new objects.

docs.title: 6) intern() (pool control)
docs.text:
intern() returns pooled reference:

  • if exists, returns existing pooled one
  • else adds to pool and returns it
String x = new String("ABC");  // heap
String y = x.intern();         // pool ref
System.out.println(x == y);    // false

docs.title: 1) What is StringBuilder?
docs.text:
A mutable sequence of characters. Used to build strings efficiently.

Key properties:

  • mutable
  • not thread-safe
  • faster than StringBuffer in single-thread

Example:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hi");
sb.append(" Vishu");
System.out.println(sb.toString());

docs.title: 2) Why it’s faster than String in loops
docs.text:
String is immutable → every + can create new objects.

Bad:

String s = "";
for (...) s = s + i; // creates many objects

Good:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (...) sb.append(i);
String s = sb.toString();

docs.title: 3) Capacity growth (interview)
docs.text:
StringBuilder has:

  • length = number of characters currently stored
  • capacity = internal allocated buffer size

Default capacity is typically 16 (empty builder), and growth often follows:

newCapacity = oldCapacity * 2 + 2

You can set initial capacity to avoid resizing:

new StringBuilder(1000)

docs.title: 1) What is StringBuffer?
docs.text:
Same concept as StringBuilder but: ✅ thread-safe (methods are synchronized) ❌ slower than StringBuilder in single-thread

When to say in interview:

  • Single-thread code → prefer StringBuilder
  • Multi-thread shared mutable text → StringBuffer (or better: avoid sharing mutable state)

docs.title: The Core Comparison Table (Interview)
docs.text: Feature String StringBuilder StringBuffer Mutability Immutable Mutable Mutable Thread-safe Yes (immutable) No Yes (synchronized) Performance Slow in heavy concat Fastest Slower than SB Typical use constants, keys, text values loops, building output shared mutable text (rare)

docs.title: Trap 1: String + loop
docs.text: O(n²) style behavior due to repeated allocations.

docs.title: Trap 2: == works sometimes
docs.text: Because of pooling, == may return true for literals, but it’s not content comparison.

docs.title: Trap 3: new String("X")
docs.text: Creates a new object even though "X" already exists in pool.

docs.title: Trap 4: final StringBuilder
docs.text: final stops reassignment, but you can still append (object is mutable).

docs.title: How to Answer in Interview (ready answer)
docs.text:
If interviewer asks: “String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?”

You answer:

String is immutable and safe for constants and keys. For frequent modifications or concatenation, use StringBuilder because it’s mutable and fast but not thread-safe. StringBuffer is also mutable but synchronized, so it’s thread-safe but slower.

docs.title: Quick depth test (to confirm nothing missed)
docs.text:
Answer these (just outputs):

1.

String a = "Hello";
String b = "Hel" + "lo";
System.out.println(a == b);

2.

String a = "Hel";
String b = a + "lo";
System.out.println(b == "Hello");

3.

String x = new String("Hi");
System.out.println(x == "Hi");
System.out.println(x.intern() == "Hi");

✅ Output(ordered):

1. true
2. false
3.
false
true

docs.title: 🔎 Why Each Answer Is Correct (JVM-Level Thinking)
1️⃣
docs.text:
String a = "Hello";
String b = "Hel" + "lo";
System.out.println(a == b);

docs.title: What happens?
docs.text:
"Hel" + "lo" is compile-time constant expression.

Compiler converts it to:

String b = "Hello";

So both a and b point to same pooled object.

✔ Output: true

docs.title: 2️⃣
docs.text:
String a = "Hel";
String b = a + "lo";
System.out.println(b == "Hello");

Now this is runtime concatenation.

Because a is a variable.

Internally something like:

new StringBuilder().append(a).append("lo").toString();

So:

  • "Hello" literal → pool
  • b → new heap object

References different → false

✔ Output: false

docs.title: 3️⃣
docs.text:
String x = new String("Hi");
System.out.println(x == "Hi");
System.out.println(x.intern() == "Hi");

Step-by-step:

  • "Hi" literal → pool
  • new String("Hi") → new heap object

So:

x == "Hi" → false

Then:

x.intern() → returns pooled reference

So:

x.intern() == "Hi" → true

✔ Output:

false
true

docs.title: 🔥 Question: Where exactly does String store characters?
docs.text:
Before Java 9:

  • internally stored in char[]

After Java 9:

  • uses byte[]
  • plus a coder flag (LATIN1 or UTF16)

This reduces memory usage for ASCII strings.

Interview bonus answer:

Since Java 9, String uses a byte array with a coder flag to optimize memory.

docs.title: 🔥 String Immutability Deep Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s = "Java";
s.concat("8");
System.out.println(s);

✅ Ouput:

Java

docs.title: Why? (Deep Understanding)
docs.text:
String s = "Java";
s.concat("8");
System.out.println(s);

Important:

  • String is immutable.
  • concat() does not modify the existing object.
  • It returns a new String.

So internally:

String temp = s.concat("8");  // creates "Java8"

But you ignored the returned value.

So s still points to:

"Java"

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: String methods like concat(), replace(), substring() return a new object. They do not modify the original string.

docs.title: 🔥 If You Change This
docs.text:
String s = "Java";
s = s.concat("8");
System.out.println(s);

Now output:

Java8

Because now s points to new object.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Going Deeper: StringBuilder Internal Behavior
1️⃣ Capacity vs Length (Very Important)
docs.text:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();

Default:

  • capacity = 16
  • length = 0

If you do:

sb.append("Hello");
  • length = 5
  • capacity still 16

If you exceed capacity, it resizes.

docs.title: 🔥 Resizing Formula (Interview Favorite)
docs.text:
When capacity exceeded:

newCapacity = (oldCapacity * 2) + 2

Example:

  • 16 → 34
  • 34 → 70

You can avoid resizing by:

new StringBuilder(1000);

docs.title: 🔥 Performance Comparison (Very Important)
docs.text:
In loops:

❌ Bad:

String s = "";
for(int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)
    s += i;

Creates thousands of objects.

✔ Good:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for(int i = 0; i < 10000; i++)
    sb.append(i);

docs.title: 🔥 Now Advanced Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder("Hello");
StringBuilder sb2 = sb1;

sb1.append(" World");

System.out.println(sb2);

✅ Ouput:

Hello World

docs.title: Why? (Deep Understanding)
docs.text:
StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder("Hello");
StringBuilder sb2 = sb1;

Important:

  • sb1 and sb2 point to the same object
  • No new object created in second line

Memory:

Heap:
[StringBuilder object: "Hello"]

Stack:
sb1 → (ref)
sb2 → (same ref)

Then:

sb1.append(" World");

Since StringBuilder is mutable, the same object is modified.

So printing sb2 shows:

Hello World

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Rule
docs.text: StringBuilder is mutable. If two references point to the same object, changes through one reference are visible through the other.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Slightly Tricky Comparison
docs.text:
Predict output:

StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder("Hi");
StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder("Hi");

System.out.println(sb1 == sb2);
System.out.println(sb1.equals(sb2));

✅ Ouput:

false
false

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder("Hi");
StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder("Hi");

These are two different objects in heap.

docs.title: 1️⃣ sb1 == sb2
docs.text:
== compares references.

Different objects → different references → ✔ false

docs.title: 2️⃣ sb1.equals(sb2)
docs.text:
Here is the important part:

StringBuilder does NOT override equals().

So it inherits Object.equals() which is basically:

return this == obj;

So it again compares references.

Therefore:

✔ false

docs.title: 🔥 Very Important Interview Insight
docs.text: String overrides equals() → compares content StringBuilder does NOT override equals() → compares reference

docs.title: 🔥 Now If You Do This
docs.text:
System.out.println(sb1.toString().equals(sb2.toString()));

Now output would be:

true

Because now you are comparing two String objects with content comparison.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: StringBuilder does not override equals(), so equals() behaves like == (reference comparison).

docs.title: Question:
docs.text:
What is the output?

String s1 = "abc";
String s2 = s1.replace('a', 'z');

System.out.println(s1);
System.out.println(s2);

✅ Output:

abc
zbc

docs.title: Why (deep but crisp)
docs.text:
• String is immutable
  • replace() returns a new String
  • s1 still points to "abc"
  • s2 points to "zbc"

docs.title: Now we go deeper: StringBuilder vs StringBuffer (Thread safety + performance)
1) StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
docs.text:
Both are mutable, but:

  • StringBuilder: not synchronized → faster → use in single-thread
  • StringBuffer: synchronized → thread-safe → slower

Interview one-liner:

Use StringBuilder in single-threaded code; use StringBuffer only when multiple threads mutate the same instance.

docs.title: Very important: StringBuilder method chaining
docs.text:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append("A").append("B").append(10);
System.out.println(sb); // AB10

Because append returns this.

docs.title: 🔥 Next Interview Trap: StringBuilder reverse
docs.text:
Predict output:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("abc");
String s = sb.reverse().toString();
System.out.println(sb);
System.out.println(s);

✅ output:

cba
cba

docs.title: Why? (Deep Understanding)
docs.text:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("abc");
String s = sb.reverse().toString();

Important:

  • reverse() modifies the same StringBuilder object
  • It does NOT create a new one
  • It returns this

So after:

sb.reverse();

The internal buffer becomes:

"cba"

Then:

s = sb.toString();

Now s is a new String object containing "cba".

docs.title: Final State
docs.text:
• sb → mutable object → "cba"
  • s → immutable String → "cba"

So both print:

cba
cba

docs.title: 🔥 Very Important Difference
docs.text:
If this was String:

String s = "abc";
s.reverse();  // ❌ no such method

Because String is immutable and does not provide reverse.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Rule
docs.text: StringBuilder methods like append(), insert(), reverse() modify the same object and return this.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Next Deep Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";
String s3 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);
System.out.println(s1 == s3);
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3));

✅ Output:

true
false
true

Now let’s lock this deeply in your brain (interview depth).

docs.title: 🔎 Why Each Line Prints That
docs.text:
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";

Both are string literals.

  • JVM checks String Pool
  • "Java" already exists
  • s1 and s2 point to same pooled object

So:

s1 == s2  → true

String s3 = new String("Java");

This creates:

  1. "Java" in pool (if not already there)
  2. A new object in heap

So:

s1 == s3  → false

Different objects.

s1.equals(s3) → true

Because .equals() compares content, not reference.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: == checks reference. .equals() checks content. String literals are pooled, but new String() always creates a new object.

docs.title: 🚀 Now We Go Even Deeper (Compile-Time Constant Trap)
docs.text:
Predict output:

final String s1 = "Hello";
String s2 = "Hello";
String s3 = s1 + "World";
String s4 = "HelloWorld";

System.out.println(s3 == s4);

✅ output:

true

Now let’s understand why (this is important interview depth).

docs.title: Why true?
docs.text:
final String s1 = "Hello";
String s3 = s1 + "World";

Because s1 is:

  • final
  • initialized with a compile-time constant

The compiler treats s1 as a constant.

So this:

s1 + "World"

Is converted at compile time into:

"HelloWorld"

So effectively:

String s3 = "HelloWorld";

Now:

String s4 = "HelloWorld";

Both s3 and s4 refer to the same pooled literal.

So:

s3 == s4 → true

docs.title: 🔥 Now Change Slightly
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s1 = "Hello";   // not final
String s3 = s1 + "World";
String s4 = "HelloWorld";

System.out.println(s3 == s4);

✅ Output is false.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
String s1 = "Hello";   // not final
String s3 = s1 + "World";

Because s1 is not final, the compiler cannot treat s1 as a compile-time constant.

So s1 + "World" becomes runtime concatenation, producing a new String object (on heap).

Meanwhile:

String s4 = "HelloWorld";

is a pooled literal.

So references are different:

  • s3 → heap string "HelloWorld" (created at runtime)
  • s4 → pooled "HelloWorld"

Therefore:

false

docs.title: ✅ Deep Notes Summary for String / StringBuilder / StringBuffer
String
docs.text:
• Immutable
  • Pooling of literals
  • == vs .equals()
  • intern() returns pooled reference
  • Runtime concat creates new objects

docs.title: StringBuilder
docs.text:
• Mutable
  • Not thread-safe
  • Best for loops / heavy concatenation
  • equals() is reference-based (not content)

docs.title: StringBuffer
docs.text:
• Mutable + synchronized (thread-safe)
  • Slower than StringBuilder
  • Rarely needed unless shared across threads

docs.title: Final high-value interview question
docs.text:
Why is String immutable but StringBuilder mutable? Answer in 3–4 lines (interview style).

because in java string is frequently used in map, json, constants. so making it immutable give best performance to handle it inside string pool. String builder is mutable because it separate class than string. it specially designed to handle heavy concat nations during runtime. it avoid rapidly instant creations when heavily concat nation happen.

docs.title: ✅ Perfect Interview Answer
docs.text:
String is immutable to ensure security, enable safe string pooling, allow caching of hash codes, and make it thread-safe. Since Strings are widely used as keys in HashMap, file paths, class names, and constants, immutability prevents unexpected modification.

StringBuilder, on the other hand, is mutable and designed for efficient string manipulation during runtime, especially for heavy concatenation, to avoid frequent object creation and improve performance.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Let’s Go EVEN Deeper (Senior-Level Depth)
1️⃣ String as HashMap Key (VERY IMPORTANT)
docs.text:
Because String is immutable:

Map<String, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("key", "value");

When String is used as key:

  • hashCode is computed once
  • It can be cached
  • Since content never changes → hashCode stays stable

If String were mutable:

  • Changing content after putting into map
  • hashCode changes
  • Map breaks

This is a huge reason for immutability.

docs.title: 2️⃣ HashCode Caching (Deep JVM Insight)
docs.text:
Inside String class:

private int hash;

When hashCode() is first called:

  • It computes and stores in hash
  • Next time it returns cached value

This is possible only because String is immutable.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Security Reason (Important)
docs.text:
Imagine:

String path = "/secure/path";

If String was mutable:

  • Another thread could modify path
  • Security hole

Immutability prevents that.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Performance Misconception (Important)
docs.text:
Many think:

String is immutable for performance.

Actually:

  • String immutability enables pooling
  • Pooling improves memory usage
  • But heavy concatenation with String is slow

So for performance:

  • Use StringBuilder for runtime modification
  • Use String for constant values

docs.title: 🔥 Now Final Advanced Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s1 = "abc";
String s2 = new String("abc");
String s3 = s2.intern();

System.out.println(s1 == s3);

✅ Output:

true

docs.title: Why? (Deep JVM-Level Explanation)
docs.text:
String s1 = "abc";
  • "abc" literal goes into the String Pool.
  • s1 points to pooled object.
String s2 = new String("abc");
  • "abc" literal already exists in pool.
  • new String("abc") creates a new heap object.
  • s2 points to heap object.
String s3 = s2.intern();

What intern() does:

  • If the string already exists in pool → return pooled reference.
  • If not → add to pool and return it.

Since "abc" already exists in pool:

s3 → pooled "abc"

So:

s1 == s3 → true

docs.title: Important behavior difference (Java 6 vs Java 7+)
docs.text:
Before Java 7:

  • Pool was in PermGen.
  • intern() sometimes copied strings into pool.

After Java 7:

  • Pool is in heap.
  • intern() may reuse existing object instead of copying.

You don’t need extreme JVM internals for interviews, but knowing this gives extra confidence.

docs.title: 🧠 Now One Slightly Tricky Variant
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s1 = new String("abc");
String s2 = s1.intern();
String s3 = "abc";

System.out.println(s2 == s3);

✅ Output — it prints true.

docs.title: Why (short but deep)
docs.text:
• s1 is a new heap String.
  • s2 = s1.intern() returns the pooled "abc" reference.
  • s3 = "abc" is also the pooled "abc" reference. So s2 and s3 point to the same pooled object → true.

docs.title: ✅ We’ve Finished String / StringBuilder / StringBuffer in Depth
docs.text: To make sure no point is missed, here is the complete checklist we covered (and you can use this as notes):

docs.title: String
docs.text:
• Immutable and reasons (security, pooling, hash caching, thread safety)
  • String pool behavior (literals, compile-time constants, intern)
  • == vs .equals()
  • runtime concat vs compile-time concat
  • new String("x") behavior
  • Java 9+ compact strings concept (byte[] + coder)

docs.title: StringBuilder
docs.text:
• Mutable, append/insert/reverse modify same object
  • Capacity vs length + resizing idea
  • Why faster in loops
  • equals() not overridden (reference comparison)

docs.title: StringBuffer
docs.text:
• Thread-safe via synchronization
  • Slower than StringBuilder
  • When to use (rare)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Collections Framework Part 2 covers advanced collection behavior, utilities, immutability, concurrent options, and deeper interview comparisons.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: These topics help answer practical backend questions about choosing safe, efficient, and readable collection APIs.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Use immutable collections when data should not change after creation, and use concurrent collections when data is shared across threads.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Immutable collection and unmodifiable view are not always the same idea.
  • Thread-safe collection choices affect performance.
  • Legacy classes like Vector and Hashtable are usually not preferred.
  • Fail-fast behavior is not guaranteed thread safety.
  • Collection utility methods can return views.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Advanced collection topics focus on safe and appropriate API choices. We compare legacy and modern classes, mutable and immutable collections, fail-fast behavior, utility methods, and thread-safe alternatives. The right collection depends on access pattern, ordering, mutation, and concurrency needs.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Prefer modern collections over legacy classes.
  • Know mutable vs immutable behavior.
  • Use concurrent collections for shared data.
  • Utility methods can wrap or transform collections.
  • Fail-fast detects unsafe modification.
  • Choose collections by behavior and complexity.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Following topics we will conver in this part:

1️⃣ Time Complexity Master Table (Complete Revision Map) 2️⃣ Red-Black Tree Basics (for TreeMap understanding) 3️⃣ ConcurrentHashMap Internals (Deep concurrency insight) 4️⃣ Generics Deep Dive (PECS, Wildcards, Type Erasure)

We start with Phase 1.

docs.title: 🔥 PHASE 1 — MASTER TIME COMPLEXITY TABLE (Interview Gold)
docs.text: You must know this without thinking.

docs.title: 1️⃣ List Implementations
docs.text:
Operation ArrayList LinkedList add(e) O(1)* O(1) add(index, e) O(n) O(n) get(index) O(1) O(n) remove(index) O(n) O(n) removeFirst() O(n) O(1) removeLast() O(1) O(1) contains() O(n) O(n) Iteration O(n) O(n)
  • O(1) amortized.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Set Implementations
docs.text:
Operation HashSet LinkedHashSet TreeSet add() O(1)* O(1)* O(log n) remove() O(1)* O(1)* O(log n) contains() O(1)* O(1)* O(log n) Ordering No Insertion Sorted Null allowed Yes Yes No (if using natural ordering)
  • average case.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Map Implementations
docs.text: Operation HashMap LinkedHashMap TreeMap ConcurrentHashMap put() O(1)* O(1)* O(log n) O(1)* get() O(1)* O(1)* O(log n) O(1)* remove() O(1)* O(1)* O(log n) O(1)* Ordering No Insertion Sorted No Thread-safe No No No Yes Null key 1 1 No No

docs.title: 4️⃣ Worst Case Summary
docs.text: Structure Worst Case HashMap (pre-Java 8) O(n) HashMap (Java 8+) O(log n) TreeMap O(log n) ArrayList add O(n) (resize) LinkedList get O(n)

docs.title: 🔥 Important Pattern Recognition
docs.text:
Hash-based structures:

  • Fast average
  • Depend on hashCode quality

Tree-based structures:

  • Always O(log n)
  • Ordered

Array-based structures:

  • Fast random access
  • Expensive shifting

Linked structures:

  • Fast head/tail ops
  • Slow random access

docs.title: 🚀 Now Small Rapid-Fire Test
docs.text:
Answer without thinking too much:

1️⃣ Fastest for search? (Average case) 2️⃣ Best for sorted data? 3️⃣ Best for LRU cache base? 4️⃣ Best for concurrent high-read workload? 5️⃣ Best for frequent head insertions?

Answer 1 line each.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Fastest for search (average case)?
docs.text: ✔ Hash-based structures (HashMap / HashSet) Because average time complexity is O(1).

docs.title: 2️⃣ Best for sorted data?
docs.text: ✔ TreeMap / TreeSet Because they maintain sorted order using Red-Black Tree.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Best for LRU cache base?
docs.text:
You said: “Maybe HashBased” → ❌ Not precise.

✔ Correct answer: LinkedHashMap

Why?

LinkedHashMap:

  • Maintains insertion order
  • Can maintain access order
  • Supports overriding:
protected boolean removeEldestEntry()

Used internally to build LRU cache.

Interview one-liner:

LinkedHashMap is best for implementing LRU cache because it maintains access order.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Best for concurrent high-read workload?
docs.text:
✔ ConcurrentHashMap

Because:

  • Thread-safe
  • Allows high concurrency
  • Uses fine-grained locking / CAS

docs.title: 5️⃣ Best for frequent head insertions?
docs.text:
✔ LinkedList

Because:

  • O(1) insertion at head
  • No shifting

docs.title: 🔥 Summary: You’re thinking in correct direction.
docs.text:
Only LRU needed correction.

Now we go deeper.

docs.title: 🚀 PHASE 2 — RED-BLACK TREE BASICS
docs.text:
This is important for:

  • TreeMap
  • TreeSet
  • HashMap treeification

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is Red-Black Tree?
docs.text:
It is a:

Self-balancing Binary Search Tree

Guarantees:

Height ≈ log n

So operations:

insert → O(log n)
delete → O(log n)
search → O(log n)

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why Not Normal BST?
docs.text:
Normal BST can become:

1
 \
  2
   \
    3
     \
      4

Height becomes n Operations become O(n)

Red-Black Tree prevents that.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Core Red-Black Rules (Memorize)
docs.text:
1️⃣ Every node is either RED or BLACK 2️⃣ Root is always BLACK 3️⃣ No two RED nodes adjacent 4️⃣ Every path from node to null has same number of BLACK nodes 5️⃣ Null leaves are BLACK

These rules maintain balance.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Why TreeMap Uses Red-Black Tree?
docs.text:
Because:

  • Predictable O(log n)
  • Self-balancing
  • Efficient for sorted maps

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Insight
docs.text:
When HashMap bucket size ≥ 8:

  • LinkedList → converted to Red-Black Tree
  • Improves from O(n) → O(log n)
