docs.title: ✅ Which is faster for small data size?
docs.text: ✔ HashMap

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Average time complexity = O(1)
  • No tree balancing overhead
  • Lower constant factors

TreeMap:

  • Always O(log n)
  • Has Red-Black Tree rotations
  • More pointer operations

So for small and unsorted data:

HashMap is generally faster.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Insight
docs.text:
Even though HashMap worst-case is O(log n) (Java 8+), TreeMap always remains O(log n).

So unless you need sorted order:

Prefer HashMap.

docs.title: 🚀 Now PHASE 3 — ConcurrentHashMap Deep Internals
docs.text: This is advanced and very important for backend interviews.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Why Not Just Use HashMap in Multi-thread?
docs.text:
If multiple threads modify HashMap:

  • Data corruption
  • Lost updates
  • Infinite loop during resize (pre-Java 8)
  • Race conditions

So not safe.

docs.title: 2️⃣ How Hashtable Solves It?
docs.text:
• Entire methods synchronized

Example:

public synchronized V put(K key, V value)

Problem:

  • Only one thread at a time
  • Low performance

docs.title: Java 7 approach:
docs.text:
• Segmented locking
  • Divides map into segments
  • Lock only segment

docs.title: Java 8+ approach:
docs.text:
• No segments

  • Uses:

  • CAS (Compare-And-Swap)

  • synchronized only on bucket level

So:

  • Multiple threads can operate on different buckets simultaneously

docs.title: 🔥 Important Differences
docs.text: Feature HashMap ConcurrentHashMap Thread-safe No Yes Locking None Fine-grained Null allowed Yes No Resize safe No Yes

docs.title: 🔥 Key Concept: CAS
docs.text:
CAS = Compare And Swap

Used for:

  • Lock-free updates
  • High concurrency

docs.title: 🚀 Interview-Level Question
docs.text:
Is ConcurrentHashMap completely lock-free?

✅ Answer — No, ConcurrentHashMap is not completely lock-free.

Now let’s explain properly at interview level.

docs.title: 🔥 Is ConcurrentHashMap completely lock-free?
docs.text:
👉 No.

It uses a combination of:

  • CAS (Compare-And-Swap) for some operations
  • Synchronized blocks (on bins/buckets) for others

So it is:

Partially lock-free, but not fully lock-free.

docs.title: 🔍 What is Lock-Free Here?
docs.text:
For example:

  • When inserting into an empty bucket
  • It uses CAS to set the value

No lock needed.

docs.title: 🔒 When Does It Use Lock?
docs.text:
If:

  • Bucket already contains elements
  • Collision happens
  • Tree bin modification

Then it uses:

synchronized (bucketNode) {
   // modify bucket
}

But only that specific bucket is locked, not whole map.

docs.title: 🔥 Why This Is Powerful?
docs.text:
Because:

  • Different threads can modify different buckets simultaneously.
  • Very high concurrency compared to Hashtable.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap is not fully lock-free. It uses CAS for simple operations and synchronized blocks at bucket level for collision handling, providing high concurrency without full map locking.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Important Question
docs.text:
Does ConcurrentHashMap allow:

1️⃣ Concurrent reads without locking? 2️⃣ Concurrent writes on different buckets?

docs.title: 1️⃣ Concurrent reads without locking?
docs.text:
✔ Yes

ConcurrentHashMap allows:

  • Multiple threads to read simultaneously
  • No locking required for read operations (in most cases)

Why?

  • It uses volatile variables
  • Proper memory visibility guarantees
  • Reads do not block writes

docs.title: 2️⃣ Concurrent writes on different buckets?
docs.text:
✔ Yes

Because:

  • Locking happens at bucket level (Java 8+)
  • Different threads modifying different buckets
  • No interference

This gives high concurrency.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Clarification
docs.text:
If two threads modify the same bucket:

  • Then synchronization happens
  • Only one thread modifies that bucket at a time

But other buckets remain free.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads and concurrent writes on different buckets using fine-grained locking and CAS, improving performance over Hashtable.

docs.title: 🚀 Now PHASE 4 — GENERICS (Deep + Senior-Level)
docs.text: This is extremely important.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Why Generics?
docs.text:
Before Java 5:

```java id="zpmv0t" List list = new ArrayList(); list.add("A"); list.add(10); 

Problem:

* No type safety
* ClassCastException at runtime

Generics introduced:

* Compile-time type safety
* No casting needed

---

### 2️⃣ Basic Syntax

```java id="1k0msp"
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();

Now:

  • Only String allowed
  • Compile-time safety

docs.title: 3️⃣ What is Type Erasure?
docs.text:
Generics exist only at compile-time.

At runtime:

```java id="h5bivv" List 

Becomes:

```java id="cjj3cn"
List

Type information erased.

So:

List<String>.class

Does NOT exist.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Consequence
docs.text:
You cannot do:

```java id="xok5qq" if (obj instanceof List) 

Because generics erased at runtime.

---

### 🚀 Now Important Question

Can you create:

```java id="sdntm1"
List<int> list = new ArrayList<>();

Why or why not?

✅ Answer: No, we can not create using primitive types.

> Generics work only with reference types because of type erasure. Primitive types like int must be wrapped in their corresponding wrapper classes like Integer.

Small correction:

  • Wrapper classes like Integer do not extend Object directly, they extend Number, and Number extends Object.

Now let’s give the perfect answer.

docs.title: ✅ Why List<int> is Not Allowed?
docs.text:
List<int> list = new ArrayList<>(); ❌

Because:

1️⃣ Generics work only with reference types 2️⃣ int is a primitive type, not a reference type 3️⃣ Generics use type erasure, and primitives cannot be used in type parameters

So you must use:

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

Java automatically handles autoboxing:

list.add(10);   // int → Integer

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
Why generics don’t support primitives?

Because internally after type erasure:

List<Integer>

Becomes:

List

And everything is treated as Object.

But primitive types are not objects.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Generics work only with reference types because of type erasure. Primitive types like int must be wrapped in their corresponding wrapper classes like Integer.

docs.title: 🚀 Now We Go Deeper — Wildcards
docs.text:
Explain the difference between:

List<?>
List<Object>
List<? extends Number>
List<? super Integer>

We go step-by-step.

docs.title: ✅ What is List<?> ?
docs.text:
Correct meaning:

List<?> means a list of unknown type.

It does NOT mean “any reference item allowed to add”.

It means:

  • It could be List<String>
  • Or List<Integer>
  • Or List<Person>
  • We don’t know which.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Rule
docs.text:
With List<?>:

✔ You can read elements as Object ❌ You cannot add elements (except null)

Example:

List<?> list = new ArrayList<String>();

Object obj = list.get(0);   // allowed

list.add("Hello");  // ❌ Compile error
list.add(null);     // ✅ allowed

docs.title: Why can’t we add?
docs.text:
Because compiler does not know actual type.

If:

List<?> list = new ArrayList<Integer>();

Then:

list.add("Hello");  // would break type safety

So Java blocks all additions (except null).

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: List<?> represents a list of unknown type. You can read elements as Object, but you cannot add elements except null.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Next Level
docs.text:
What is the difference between:

List<Object>

and

List<?>

Think carefully. This is very important.

List<?> it define list is any kind of similar type. So basically you don't know the type here. SO you cannot add elements here because type safety.
But List<Object> is define list is object type. It contains object which may or may not similar types.
It will allow add method. Here get method return element as object

Let me refine it into a perfect interview-level explanation.

docs.title: 1️⃣ List<Object>
docs.text:
List<Object> list = new ArrayList<>();

Meaning:

  • This list can store any object type
  • Because everything in Java extends Object

You can:

list.add("Hello");
list.add(10);
list.add(new Person());

✔ You can add elements ✔ get() returns Object

Important:

List<String> is NOT a subtype of List<Object>

This is very important.

List<String> strList = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objList = strList;  // ❌ Compile error

Generics are invariant.

docs.title: 2️⃣ List<?>
docs.text:
List<?> list = new ArrayList<String>();

Meaning:

  • A list of unknown type
  • Could be List
  • Could be List
  • Compiler does not know

    • So:

    ✔ You can read as Object ❌ You cannot add elements (except null)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The Java Collections Framework is a set of interfaces and classes used to store, access, search, sort, and process groups of objects.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Collections are used in almost every Java backend application. Interviewers expect clear understanding of interfaces, implementations, performance, and trade-offs.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Use List when order matters and duplicates are allowed. Use Set when duplicates should not be allowed. Use Map when data is stored as key-value pairs.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Map is part of the Collections Framework but does not extend Collection.
  • Collection and Collections are different.
  • Choosing an implementation matters for performance.
  • Generics give compile-time type safety.
  • Iteration behavior can change between implementations.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: The Collections Framework provides common data structures through interfaces like List, Set, Queue, and Map. These interfaces have implementations such as ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet, HashMap, and TreeMap. We choose the implementation based on ordering, duplicates, lookup speed, insertion cost, and thread-safety needs.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Collection is an interface hierarchy.
  • Collections is a utility class.
  • List allows duplicates and keeps order.
  • Set avoids duplicates.
  • Map stores key-value pairs.
  • Implementation choice affects performance.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: We will cover in this order:

docs.title: Phase 1 – Foundation
docs.text:
1. What is Collections Framework?
  2. Core Interfaces hierarchy
  3. Iterable vs Collection vs Map
  4. Why Map is not a Collection

docs.title: Phase 2 – List Internals
docs.text:
1. ArrayList (internal working, resizing, complexity)
  2. LinkedList (doubly linked list internals)
  3. Vector (legacy + synchronization)
  4. Stack (legacy vs modern)

docs.title: Phase 3 – Set Internals
docs.text:
1. HashSet (uses HashMap internally)
  2. LinkedHashSet (ordering logic)
  3. TreeSet (Red-Black Tree internals)
  4. Comparable vs Comparator

docs.title: Phase 4 – Map Internals (Most Important)
docs.text:
1. HashMap internal working (bucket, hashing, collisions)
  2. equals() & hashCode() contract
  3. Load factor & resizing
  4. Java 8 treeification (LinkedList → Tree)
  5. LinkedHashMap
  6. TreeMap (Red-Black Tree)
  7. Hashtable vs HashMap
  8. ConcurrentHashMap (basic intro)

docs.title: Phase 5 – Advanced
docs.text:
1. Fail-fast vs Fail-safe
  2. ConcurrentModificationException
  3. Collections utility class
  4. Immutable collections
  5. Time complexity table

We go step-by-step. Today we start Phase 1.

docs.title: 🔹 1️⃣ What is Collections Framework?
docs.text:
It is a unified architecture for storing and manipulating groups of objects.

Before Java 1.2:

  • Arrays
  • Vector
  • Hashtable

After Java 1.2:

  • Unified framework introduced

docs.title: 🔹 2️⃣ Core Interface Hierarchy (VERY IMPORTANT)
docs.text:
Iterable
                    |
                Collection
               /    |     \
            List   Set    Queue
                             |
                           Deque

Map (separate hierarchy)

Important: 👉 Map does NOT extend Collection.

docs.title: Iterable
docs.text:
Contains only:

Iterator<T> iterator();

Allows:

for (T item : collection)

docs.title: Collection
docs.text:
Adds:

  • add()
  • remove()
  • size()
  • contains()
  • clear()

Collection is parent of:

  • List
  • Set
  • Queue

docs.title: 🔥 Why Map is NOT part of Collection?
docs.text:
Collection stores:

  • Single elements

Map stores:

  • Key-value pairs

Map does NOT extend Collection.

Interview question:

Why Map is not a subtype of Collection?

Answer:

Because Collection represents a group of individual elements, whereas Map represents key-value mappings.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Deep Question
docs.text:
Which of these allow duplicates?

  1. List
  2. Set
  3. Map keys
  4. Map values

Answer carefully.

Answer carefully:

Which allow duplicates?

1️⃣ List → ✅ Yes 2️⃣ Set → ❌ No 3️⃣ Map keys → ❌ No 4️⃣ Map values → ✅ Yes

docs.title: 1️⃣ List
docs.text:
• Maintains insertion order
  • Allows duplicate elements

Example:

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(10);
list.add(10);   // allowed

docs.title: 2️⃣ Set
docs.text:
• No duplicate elements allowed
  • Uses equals() to determine duplicates

docs.title: 3️⃣ Map Keys
docs.text:
• Keys must be unique
  • Internally uses hashCode() + equals()

If duplicate key inserted:

  • Old value gets replaced

docs.title: 4️⃣ Map Values
docs.text:
• Values can be duplicate
  • No restriction

Example:

Map<Integer, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put(1, "A");
map.put(2, "A");   // allowed

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("A", 1);
map.put("A", 2);

System.out.println(map.size());
System.out.println(map.get("A"));

👍 Output:

size: 1
get: 2

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
map.put("A", 1);
map.put("A", 2);

HashMap rule:

  • Keys must be unique.
  • If same key inserted again → value is replaced.
  • No new entry created.

So internally:

  • First put → adds entry ("A",1)
  • Second put → finds existing key using hashCode + equals
  • Replaces value 1 with 2

Final map:

"A" → 2

docs.title: Therefore:
docs.text:
map.size() → 1
map.get("A") → 2

docs.title: 🔥 Very Important Concept (Deep)
docs.text:
When inserting into HashMap:

Steps:

  1. Calculate hashCode() of key
  2. Find bucket index
  3. If bucket empty → insert

  4. If bucket not empty:

  5. Compare keys using equals()

  6. If equal → replace value
  7. Else → collision handling

We will go deep into this next.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: ArrayList is a resizable array implementation of the List interface.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: ArrayList is very common in Java code, and interviews often ask about capacity, resizing, random access, and time complexity.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When an ArrayList becomes full, it creates a larger internal array and copies existing elements into it.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Size and capacity are different.
  • Default capacity is not the same as current size.
  • Adding is amortized O(1), not always O(1).
  • Insertion in the middle can be O(n).
  • Removing from the middle shifts elements.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: ArrayList stores elements in an internal array. It gives fast random access because indexing is direct. When the internal array becomes full, ArrayList grows by creating a larger array and copying old elements. This makes normal append operations amortized O(1), while insertions or removals in the middle are O(n).

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Backed by an array.
  • Fast random access.
  • Maintains insertion order.
  • Allows duplicates.
  • Resizes when capacity is full.
  • Middle insert/remove can shift elements.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: This is very important.

docs.title: 🔹 What is ArrayList?
docs.text:
ArrayList is:

  • Resizable array implementation
  • Maintains insertion order
  • Allows duplicates
  • Allows null
  • Not synchronized

docs.title: 🔥 Internal Structure
docs.text:
Internally:

transient Object[] elementData;
int size;

It uses:

  • A dynamic array

docs.title: 🔥 Default Capacity
docs.text:
In Java 8+:

new ArrayList<>();

Initially:

  • elementData is empty array (size 0)
  • First add → capacity becomes 10

Old Java versions:

  • Initial capacity 10 immediately

docs.title: 🔥 Resizing Formula
docs.text:
When capacity exceeded:

newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)

That means:

  • 10 → 15
  • 15 → 22
  • 22 → 33 (1.5x growth)

docs.title: 🔥 Time Complexity
docs.text: Operation Time get(index) O(1) add() at end O(1) amortized add(index) O(n) remove(index) O(n) contains() O(n)

docs.title: 🔥 Now Deep Interview Question
docs.text:
Why is add() amortized O(1) and not O(1) always?

> When the array becomes full, a new array is created with larger capacity and elements are copied. That is the reason.

Now let’s refine this into a perfect interview answer.

docs.title: ✅ Why is add() amortized O(1)?
docs.text:
ArrayList uses a dynamic array.

Most of the time:

list.add(element);
  • Just places element at elementData[size]
  • Increments size
  • Takes O(1)

But when the internal array is full:

1️⃣ A new larger array is created 2️⃣ All existing elements are copied 3️⃣ Then the new element is added

Copying takes O(n) time.

docs.title: 🧠 Why still called amortized O(1)?
docs.text:
Because resizing does not happen on every insert.

Example growth:

10 → 15 → 22 → 33 → ...

Resizing happens rarely.

If you insert 1000 elements:

  • Only ~log(n) resizes
  • Most inserts are O(1)

So average per insertion cost becomes constant.

That is called:

Amortized O(1)

docs.title: 🔥 Deep Insight (Senior-Level)
docs.text:
Total cost of inserting n elements:

O(1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... + n) ≈ O(n)

Divide by n operations → average = O(1)

docs.title: 🔥 Now Important Trap
docs.text:
Predict behavior:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(2);
list.add(1);
list.add(2);
list.add(3);

System.out.println(list.size());

What prints?

Also: What was the capacity after adding 3rd element?

docs.title: 1️⃣ Size
docs.text:
System.out.println(list.size());

You added 3 elements.

So:

3

Correct.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Capacity After Adding 3rd Element
docs.text:
Initial:

new ArrayList<>(2);

So:

  • capacity = 2

After:

  • add(1) → size = 1
  • add(2) → size = 2 (full now)

When you add 3rd element:

Capacity growth formula in Java 8+:

newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)

For capacity = 2:

oldCapacity = 2
oldCapacity >> 1 = 1
newCapacity = 2 + 1 = 3

So new capacity becomes:

3

But here is the important part:

⚠ In some older explanations people assume doubling (like 2 → 4). But Java uses 1.5x growth, not 2x.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
ArrayList growth:

newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)

Which is:

≈ 1.5 times growth

docs.title: 🚀 Now Slightly Harder Question
docs.text:
Suppose:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

You add first element.

What is capacity after first add?

Is it:

  1. 0
  2. 1
  3. 10
  4. 16

Think carefully — this is version-dependent but important for interviews.

✅ Answer — the answer is 10 (for Java 8+).

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

In Java 8+:

  • Initially, elementData is an empty array (DEFAULTCAPACITY_EMPTY_ELEMENTDATA)
  • Capacity is 0
  • No memory allocated for 10 elements yet

When you add the first element:

list.add(1);

Then Java expands capacity to:

DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 10

So after first add:

  • size = 1
  • capacity = 10

docs.title: Important Deep Detail (Interview Bonus)
docs.text:
In older Java versions (before Java 8):

  • new ArrayList<>() immediately created array of size 10.

In Java 8+:

  • It lazily allocates capacity 10 only when first element is added.

This was done to save memory.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Harder Question
docs.text:
What happens here?

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(0);
list.add(1);

After adding first element:

  • What is capacity?

Correct answer:

👉 Capacity becomes 1, not 10.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
When you do:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(0);

This is different from:

new ArrayList<>();

In this case:

  • You explicitly set initial capacity to 0
  • So elementData is created as an array of size 0

Now when you add first element:

list.add(1);

Growth logic runs:

Growth formula:

newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)

But oldCapacity = 0

So Java ensures minimum growth to 1

So capacity becomes:

1

docs.title: 🔥 Important Difference
docs.text:
Constructor After first add Capacity new ArrayList<>() 10 10 new ArrayList<>(0) 1 1

This is a favorite interview trap.

docs.title: 🧠 Why Java behaves like this?
docs.text:
Because:

  • Default constructor uses special empty array marker
  • Capacity 10 is applied lazily only for default constructor
  • But when user explicitly sets capacity (even 0), Java respects that

docs.title: 🚀 Now Next Deep Question
docs.text:
Predict:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(1);
list.add(1);
list.add(2);

What is capacity after adding second element?

Correct answer: 2

But wait — let’s analyze properly and very precisely.

docs.title: Step-by-step
docs.text:
ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(1);

Initial:

  • capacity = 1
  • size = 0

docs.title: After list.add(1);
docs.text:
• size = 1
  • capacity = 1 (full now)

docs.title: Now list.add(2);
docs.text:
Capacity is full → resize needed.

Growth formula (Java 8+):

newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1)

For oldCapacity = 1:

1 >> 1 = 0
newCapacity = 1 + 0 = 1

But capacity cannot remain 1 because we need space for 2 elements.

So Java ensures minimum required capacity.

It calculates:

minCapacity = size + 1 = 2

Since computed newCapacity (1) < minCapacity (2),

It sets:

newCapacity = minCapacity

So final capacity becomes:

2

docs.title: Final Answer
docs.text: Capacity = 2

docs.title: 🔥 Important Insight
docs.text:
For small capacities like 0 or 1:

Java ensures minimum required capacity.

So growth sometimes behaves like:

0 → 1
1 → 2

After that, normal 1.5x growth applies.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Harder
docs.text:
Predict capacity after this:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(2);
list.add(1);
list.add(2);
list.add(3);
list.add(4);

What is capacity after adding 4th element?

Here’s the exact dry run:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(2); // capacity = 2
list.add(1); // size=1 cap=2
list.add(2); // size=2 cap=2 (full)
list.add(3); // resize: old=2 → new=2+(2>>1)=2+1=3  => cap=3, size=3
list.add(4); // full again, resize: old=3 → new=3+(3>>1)=3+1=4 => cap=4, size=4

✅ Capacity after adding 4th element = 4

Next (quick): if capacity is 4 and you add 5th element, what will capacity become?

✅ Correct — capacity becomes 6.

Because when oldCapacity = 4:

  • growth: 4 + (4 >> 1) = 4 + 2 = 6

So adding 5th element triggers resize from 4 → 6.

docs.title: ✅ ArrayList Internals Summary (deep, interview-ready)
docs.text:
• Backed by Object[] elementData
  • size tracks actual elements
  • Default constructor: capacity becomes 10 on first add (Java 8+ lazy)
  • Growth: 1.5x → old + old/2
  • add() is amortized O(1), worst O(n) during resize
  • Insert/remove in middle is O(n) due to shifting

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Fail-fast iterators detect structural modification during iteration. TreeMap stores sorted keys. Comparable and Comparator define sorting rules.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: These topics test practical collection usage: safe iteration, sorted maps, and custom object sorting.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A TreeMap can keep employee IDs sorted, while a Comparator can sort employees by salary instead of natural order.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Fail-fast behavior is not a thread-safety feature.
  • Removing directly from a collection during iteration can cause ConcurrentModificationException.
  • TreeMap lookup is O(log n), not O(1).
  • Comparable defines natural ordering.
  • Comparator defines external/custom ordering.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException when a collection is structurally modified outside the iterator during iteration. TreeMap stores entries sorted by key using a red-black tree, so operations are O(log n). Comparable gives a class its natural order, while Comparator lets us define separate custom ordering rules.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Fail-fast detects unsafe structural modification.
  • Use iterator remove or safe alternatives.
  • TreeMap keeps keys sorted.
  • TreeMap operations are O(log n).
  • Comparable is natural ordering.
  • Comparator is custom ordering.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: Map Type Thread-Safe Null Key Null Value HashMap ❌ No ✅ 1 ✅ Yes Hashtable ✅ Yes ❌ No ❌ No ConcurrentHashMap ✅ Yes ❌ No ❌ No

docs.title: 🚀 Now Important Concept: Fail-Fast
docs.text:
What happens if you modify an ArrayList while iterating using for-each loop?

Example:

ArrayList<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(1);
list.add(2);
list.add(3);

for (Integer i : list) {
    list.remove(i);
}

What happens?

✅ Answer: — it throws:

ConcurrentModificationException

Now let’s go deep and make it interview-ready.

docs.title: Why ConcurrentModificationException Happens?
docs.text:
When you iterate using:

for (Integer i : list)

Internally it uses an Iterator:

Iterator<Integer> it = list.iterator();

ArrayList maintains:

modCount

Every structural modification:

  • add()
  • remove()
  • clear()

Increments modCount.

docs.title: What Iterator Stores
docs.text:
Iterator stores:

expectedModCount

During iteration:

if (modCount != expectedModCount)
    throw ConcurrentModificationException;

So when you modify list directly:

list.remove(i);

modCount changes But iterator’s expectedModCount does not → mismatch → exception thrown

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Concept
docs.text:
This is called:

Fail-Fast behavior

Fail-fast means:

  • Detects structural modification
  • Fails immediately
  • Does not allow unpredictable behavior

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ArrayList iterators are fail-fast. If the collection is structurally modified after the iterator is created (except through iterator.remove()), it throws ConcurrentModificationException.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Question
docs.text: How can you safely remove elements while iterating?

docs.title: ✅ Correct & Recommended Approach (Interview Answer)
docs.text:
Use Iterator.remove()

Iterator<Integer> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    Integer val = it.next();
    if (val % 2 == 0) {
        it.remove();  // SAFE
    }
}

Why safe?

Because:

  • it.remove() updates both

  • modCount

  • expectedModCount
  • So no mismatch

docs.title: 🔥 Java 8+ Best Way
docs.text:
Use:

list.removeIf(val -> val % 2 == 0);

Internally safe.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: To safely remove elements while iterating, use Iterator.remove() or removeIf(). Modifying the collection directly during iteration causes ConcurrentModificationException.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Important Question
docs.text:
Are HashMap iterators fail-fast?

Example:

for (String key : map.keySet()) {
    map.remove(key);
}

Will this throw exception?

✅ Yes, it will throw ConcurrentModificationException (in normal HashMap).

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
HashMap iterators are also fail-fast, just like ArrayList.

When you iterate:

for (String key : map.keySet())

Internally it uses an iterator over the keySet view, and HashMap also maintains a modification count (modCount).

If you do:

map.remove(key);

That’s a structural modification while iterating → modCount changes → iterator detects mismatch → throws ConcurrentModificationException.

docs.title: ✅ Correct ways to remove while iterating a HashMap
1️⃣ Use iterator.remove()
docs.text:
Iterator<String> it = map.keySet().iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String key = it.next();
    if (/* condition */) {
        it.remove(); // safe
    }
}

docs.title: 2️⃣ Use removeIf on entrySet (Java 8+)
docs.text: map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> /* condition */);

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: HashMap iterators are fail-fast. Modifying the map structurally during iteration (except via iterator.remove()) causes ConcurrentModificationException.

docs.title: 🔥 Next: TreeSet / TreeMap Core Concept
docs.text:
Before we move there, answer this:

What is the difference between HashMap and TreeMap in terms of ordering and internal data structure? (2–3 lines)

HashMap not maintain sorting order but TreeMap does. Tree map maintains sorted order (based on natural ordering or Comparator). May be HashMap internally use arrays to store bucket and TreeMap use tree data structure.

Now let’s make it interview-perfect.

docs.title: HashMap
docs.text:
• Does NOT maintain insertion order
  • Does NOT maintain sorted order
  • Order is unpredictable

docs.title: TreeMap
docs.text:
• Maintains sorted order

  • Sorting based on:

  • Natural ordering (Comparable)

  • OR custom Comparator

docs.title: HashMap
docs.text:
• Uses:

  • Array of buckets

  • LinkedList (before Java 8)
  • Red-Black Tree (if bucket size ≥ 8)

So it's primarily hash-based.

docs.title: TreeMap
docs.text:
• Uses Red-Black Tree
  • Self-balancing binary search tree
  • All operations O(log n)

docs.title: 🔥 Time Complexity Comparison
docs.text: Operation HashMap TreeMap get() O(1) average O(log n) put() O(1) average O(log n) remove() O(1) average O(log n) Ordering No Sorted

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: HashMap is hash-based and provides O(1) average time complexity without ordering guarantees. TreeMap is a Red-Black Tree that maintains sorted order with O(log n) operations.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Important Concept
docs.text:
TreeMap requires keys to be:

1️⃣ Comparable OR 2️⃣ Provided with Comparator

Why?

What happens if keys are not comparable?

Correct answer:

👉 It will throw ClassCastException at runtime.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
TreeMap uses a Red-Black Tree.

To insert a key, it must compare keys:

Either using:

Comparable.compareTo()

OR

Comparator.compare()

If keys are not comparable, TreeMap cannot determine:

  • left child
  • right child

So it fails during insertion.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Person {
    int id;
}

TreeMap<Person, String> map = new TreeMap<>();
map.put(new Person(), "A");

This will throw:

java.lang.ClassCastException

Because Person does not implement Comparable and no Comparator provided.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: TreeMap requires keys to be comparable. If keys are not comparable and no Comparator is provided, it throws ClassCastException at runtime.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Deep Question
docs.text:
What is difference between:

1️⃣ Comparable 2️⃣ Comparator

Explain in 3–4 lines. This is very common interview question.

Comparable: It is a interface provide a compare method to decide natural sort order.
Comparator you can use explicity to sort the collection.

Now let’s make it interview-perfect + deeper.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Comparable
docs.text:
• Package: java.lang
  • Method:
int compareTo(T o);
  • Defines natural ordering
  • Class itself implements it
  • Only one natural order possible

Example:

class Person implements Comparable<Person> {
    int age;

    public int compareTo(Person p) {
        return this.age - p.age;
    }
}

Now:

Collections.sort(list);

Uses compareTo()

docs.title: 2️⃣ Comparator
docs.text:
• Package: java.util
  • Method:
int compare(T o1, T o2);
  • Used for custom ordering
  • Separate class or lambda
  • Multiple sorting strategies possible

Example:

Comparator<Person> byName = (p1, p2) -> p1.name.compareTo(p2.name);
Collections.sort(list, byName);

docs.title: 🔥 Key Differences Table
docs.text: Feature Comparable Comparator Package java.lang java.util Method compareTo() compare() Defined in Same class Separate class Natural order Yes No Multiple sorting ❌ Only one ✅ Multiple

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Comparable defines the natural ordering of objects within the class, while Comparator defines custom ordering externally and allows multiple sorting strategies.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Important Edge Case
docs.text:
If compareTo() returns 0, what does that mean in:

1️⃣ TreeSet 2️⃣ TreeMap

Think carefully — this is important.

Correct answer:

If compareTo() returns 0, it means:

The two objects are considered equal in terms of ordering.

And in TreeSet / TreeMap, that means:

👉 The second element will NOT be inserted.

docs.title: 🔥 Why?
docs.text:
TreeSet and TreeMap use:

  • compareTo() (or Comparator)
  • NOT equals() to determine uniqueness

So if:

obj1.compareTo(obj2) == 0

TreeSet treats them as duplicates — even if equals() returns false.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Person implements Comparable<Person> {
    int age;
    String name;

    public int compareTo(Person p) {
        return this.age - p.age;  // only age considered
    }
}

Now:

TreeSet<Person> set = new TreeSet<>();

set.add(new Person(25, "A"));
set.add(new Person(25, "B"));

Since compareTo returns 0 (same age):

Second object is NOT added.

Even though names differ.

docs.title: 🧠 Critical Interview Rule
docs.text: In TreeSet and TreeMap, uniqueness is determined by compareTo() (or Comparator), not equals().

docs.title: 🚀 Now Deep Question
docs.text:
If equals() says two objects are equal, but compareTo() does NOT return 0,

what happens in TreeSet?

✅ Answer:

If:

  • equals() returns true
  • but compareTo() does NOT return 0

👉 Both objects will be inserted into TreeSet.

docs.title: 🔥 Why?
docs.text:
Because:

TreeSet uses:

compareTo() OR Comparator

to determine:

  • Order
  • Uniqueness

It does NOT use equals() to prevent duplicates.

So if:

obj1.equals(obj2) == true

But:

obj1.compareTo(obj2) != 0

TreeSet thinks they are different.

docs.title: 🚨 Important Rule (Very Important for Interviews)
docs.text:
For sorted collections:

compareTo() returning 0 defines equality, not equals().

docs.title: 🔥 Why This Is Dangerous?
docs.text:
Because this violates the general contract:

Java recommends:

if a.equals(b) == true
then a.compareTo(b) should return 0

If not:

  • You may get inconsistent behavior
  • Collections behave unexpectedly

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: In TreeSet and TreeMap, equality is determined by compareTo() or Comparator. If compareTo() is inconsistent with equals(), it may allow logical duplicates.

docs.title: 🚀 We Have Covered:
docs.text:
• ArrayList internals
  • LinkedList internals
  • HashSet internals
  • HashMap internals
  • Resize logic
  • Treeification
  • Fail-fast
  • Null behavior
  • TreeMap internals
  • Comparable vs Comparator
  • Uniqueness rules

You are now at strong intermediate-to-senior level on Collections.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: HashMap stores key-value pairs using hashing, buckets, and collision handling.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: HashMap is one of the most asked Java interview topics because it connects hashing, equality, resizing, null handling, and performance.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When map.put(key, value) runs, HashMap calculates the key hash, chooses a bucket, and stores or updates the entry.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values.
  • HashMap is not thread-safe.
  • Resize changes bucket distribution.
  • Hash collisions are handled inside buckets.
  • Poor hashCode can hurt performance.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: HashMap stores entries in an internal table of buckets. It uses the key hash to choose a bucket. If multiple keys land in the same bucket, HashMap compares keys using equals(). In Java 8+, a long collision chain can become a tree for better lookup performance. HashMap resizes when the load factor threshold is crossed.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Stores key-value pairs.
  • Uses hashCode and equals.
  • Allows one null key.
  • Not thread-safe.
  • Resizes based on load factor.
  • Java 8 can treeify heavy collision buckets.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: We are now entering the most important data structure in Java interviews.

docs.title: 🔹 HashMap Internal Structure (Java 8+)
docs.text:
Internally:

Node<K,V>[] table;

Each bucket contains:

static class Node<K,V> {
    final int hash;
    final K key;
    V value;
    Node<K,V> next;
}

So structure is:

Array of buckets
Each bucket → LinkedList OR Tree

docs.title: 🔥 Step-by-Step: What Happens When You Do
docs.text: map.put(key, value);

docs.title: Step 1️⃣ Compute hash
docs.text: int hash = hash(key);

docs.title: Step 2️⃣ Find index
docs.text:
index = (n - 1) & hash;

(n = table length)

docs.title: Step 3️⃣ Check bucket
docs.text:
Case A: bucket empty → Insert new node.

Case B: bucket not empty → Traverse:

  • If key equal → replace value
  • Else → collision → add node

docs.title: Step 4️⃣ Resize Check
docs.text:
If:

size > capacity * loadFactor

Default:

  • capacity = 16
  • loadFactor = 0.75

Resize occurs.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Question
docs.text:
If initial capacity = 16 loadFactor = 0.75

At what size does resize occur?

Correct answer: Resize happens when size becomes 13 (i.e., after inserting the 13th element).

Let’s calculate properly 👇

docs.title: Given
docs.text:
• Initial capacity = 16
  • Load factor = 0.75

Resize threshold formula:

threshold = capacity × loadFactor

So:

16 × 0.75 = 12

Threshold = 12

docs.title: When Does Resize Actually Trigger?
docs.text:
Resize happens when:

size > threshold

So:

  • After inserting 12 elements → size = 12 → OK
  • When inserting 13th element → size becomes 13 → 13 > 12 → resize

docs.title: ✅ Final Answer
docs.text: Threshold = 12 Resize happens when size becomes 13

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Detail
docs.text:
Many people say:

Resize happens at 12.

That is incorrect.

Correct statement:

Resize happens when inserting the 13th element.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Slightly Harder
docs.text:
After resize, what will be new capacity?

Initial capacity was 16.

Answer?

✅ Answer — correct instinct. It becomes double.

docs.title: 🔥 After Resize
docs.text:
Initial:

  • Capacity = 16
  • Threshold = 12

When inserting 13th element → resize triggered.

New capacity:

newCapacity = oldCapacity * 2

So:

16 → 32

docs.title: 🔥 What about new threshold?
docs.text:
Threshold = capacity × loadFactor

32 × 0.75 = 24

So after resize:

  • Capacity = 32
  • Threshold = 24

Resize will happen again when size becomes 25.

docs.title: 🧠 Important Difference from ArrayList
docs.text:
Structure Resize Factor ArrayList 1.5x HashMap 2x

HashMap doubles capacity to reduce collisions.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Concept (Senior-Level)
docs.text:
When HashMap resizes, does it:

A) Just copy buckets to new array B) Recalculate hash and redistribute entries

✅ Answer — it redistributes entries (rehashes to new buckets). But small refinement: it usually doesn’t “recalculate hashCode()” of the key again; it recomputes bucket index using the stored hash and the new table size.

docs.title: What really happens on HashMap resize (deep)
docs.text:
When capacity doubles (e.g., 16 → 32):

  • HashMap creates a new Node[] table of size 32
  • For each existing entry, it decides the new bucket using:
newIndex = hash & (newCapacity - 1)

Since newCapacity changed, bucket index changes, so entries move.

docs.title: Java 8 optimization (interview bonus)
docs.text:
During resize, Java 8 doesn’t fully recompute everything expensively. It uses a smart trick:

When capacity doubles, each entry either:

  • stays in the same index, or
  • moves to index + oldCapacity

Based on one bit:

(hash & oldCapacity) == 0  → stay
(hash & oldCapacity) != 0  → move to index + oldCapacity

This makes resizing faster.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview one-liner
docs.text: On resize, HashMap redistributes nodes into a larger table because bucket index depends on capacity. In Java 8, entries either stay or move by oldCapacity based on one hash bit.

docs.title: 🔥 Next Critical Question (Collision handling)
docs.text:
In Java 8+, when many keys collide into the same bucket, HashMap may convert the bucket from a LinkedList into a Tree.

  1. What is this conversion called?
  2. After how many nodes (default) does it happen?

docs.title: 1️⃣ Conversion Name
docs.text:
✔ Treeification

When a bucket (collision chain) becomes too long, LinkedList → converted to Red-Black Tree

docs.title: 2️⃣ When does it happen?
docs.text:
✔ When bucket size becomes ≥ 8

More precisely:

  • If bucket size > TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8)
  • AND table size ≥ 64

Only then treeification happens.

docs.title: 🔥 Important Condition (Many Miss This)
docs.text:
Treeification happens only if:

bucket size ≥ 8
AND
table capacity ≥ 64

If capacity < 64:

  • HashMap will resize instead of treeify.

This avoids unnecessary tree creation.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: In Java 8+, if a bucket contains more than 8 nodes and table size is at least 64, it is converted into a Red-Black Tree to improve lookup from O(n) to O(log n).

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Question
docs.text:
What is the time complexity of:

1️⃣ HashMap get() normally 2️⃣ HashMap get() in worst case (before Java 8) 3️⃣ HashMap get() in worst case (after treeification)

✅ Answers:

docs.title: HashMap get() Complexity (Interview-Ready)
docs.text:
1️⃣ Normal average case: O(1)

  • Good hash distribution, small bucket size.

2️⃣ Worst case before Java 8: O(n)

  • All keys collide → one long linked list bucket → linear search.

3️⃣ Worst case after treeification (Java 8+): O(log n)

  • Long bucket becomes Red-Black Tree → log-time lookup.

docs.title: 🔥 Ultra Important Interview Trap: null in HashMap
docs.text:
Answer these:

  1. Does HashMap allow null key?
  2. Does HashMap allow multiple null keys?
  3. How many null keys allowed?
  4. Does HashMap allow null values?

Now let’s go deep because this is a very common interview trap.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Does HashMap allow null key?
docs.text:
✔ Yes

HashMap allows one null key.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Does HashMap allow multiple null keys?
docs.text:
❌ No

Because:

  • Keys must be unique
  • Only one null key allowed

If you insert:

map.put(null, 10);
map.put(null, 20);

Second one replaces the first.

docs.title: 3️⃣ How many null keys allowed?
docs.text: ✔ Only 1

docs.title: 4️⃣ Does HashMap allow null values?
docs.text:
✔ Yes

Multiple null values allowed.

Example:

map.put("A", null);
map.put("B", null);

Perfectly valid.

docs.title: 🔥 Now the Important Internal Question
docs.text:
Where does HashMap store null key internally?

Think carefully.

Since null has no hashCode, what bucket is used?

✅ Answer — it is stored in the first bucket (index 0).

Now let’s explain properly and deeply.

docs.title: 🔥 How HashMap Handles null Key Internally
docs.text:
When you do:

map.put(null, "value");

HashMap logic:

if (key == null)
    return putForNullKey(value);

It does NOT call hashCode().

Instead:

  • It directly inserts into bucket index 0

Why?

Because:

hash(null) = 0
index = (n - 1) & 0 = 0

So null key always goes to bucket 0.

docs.title: 🧠 Important Interview Insight
docs.text: HashMap allows one null key and stores it in bucket 0.

docs.title: 🔥 Now Hard Question (Very Important)
docs.text: Why does HashMap allow null key but Hashtable does NOT?

docs.title: 🔥 Why HashMap allows null but Hashtable does NOT
1️⃣ Design Difference
docs.text:
HashMap

  • Introduced in Java 1.2
  • Not synchronized
  • More flexible
  • Allows 1 null key and multiple null values

Hashtable

  • Legacy class (Java 1.0)
  • Fully synchronized
  • Does NOT allow null key or null value

docs.title: 🔥 The Real Reason (Important)
docs.text:
Hashtable methods are synchronized and older design assumed:

value = table[index];
if (value == null)
    // means key not present

If null values were allowed:

  • Cannot distinguish between:

  • Key not present

  • Key present but value = null

So to avoid ambiguity:

Hashtable does not allow null key or null value.

docs.title: 🔥 Why HashMap allows null then?
docs.text:
HashMap is more modern and internally handles null carefully:

  • Special handling for null key (bucket 0)
  • Null values allowed
  • Uses containsKey() to differentiate

Example:

map.put("A", null);

map.get("A") → null
map.containsKey("A") → true

So HashMap can differentiate.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Hashtable does not allow null keys or values to avoid ambiguity and because of its legacy synchronized design, while HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Question
docs.text:
Which is thread-safe?

1️⃣ HashMap 2️⃣ Hashtable 3️⃣ ConcurrentHashMap

Correct answer:

docs.title: 3️⃣ ConcurrentHashMap → ✅ Thread-safe (better design)
docs.text: Now let’s explain properly.

docs.title: 🔥 1️⃣ HashMap
docs.text:
• Not synchronized
  • If multiple threads modify it → data corruption possible
  • Can even cause infinite loop during resize (older Java versions)

So:

HashMap → NOT thread-safe

docs.title: 🔥 2️⃣ Hashtable
docs.text:
• All methods are synchronized
  • Only one thread can access at a time
  • Safe but slow

Example:

public synchronized V put(K key, V value)

So:

Hashtable → Thread-safe but inefficient

docs.title: 🔥 3️⃣ ConcurrentHashMap (Most Important)
docs.text:
• Designed for concurrency
  • Not fully synchronized
  • Uses fine-grained locking
  • Allows multiple threads to read/write safely
  • Much faster than Hashtable

So:

ConcurrentHashMap → Thread-safe and efficient

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: HashMap is not thread-safe. Hashtable is thread-safe but fully synchronized and slow. ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe with better performance using segmented locking (Java 7) or CAS + synchronized bins (Java 8+).

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Question
docs.text:
Does ConcurrentHashMap allow null key or null value?

Think carefully. This is tricky.

✅ Answer — ConcurrentHashMap does NOT allow null key or null value.

Now let’s understand why (very important for interviews).

docs.title: 🔥 Why ConcurrentHashMap does NOT allow null?
docs.text:
In concurrent environment:

If this was allowed:

map.put("A", null);

Now if another thread does:

map.get("A");

It returns null.

Now ambiguity:

  • Is key not present?
  • Or key present but value is null?

In single-threaded HashMap, you can call:

map.containsKey("A");

But in concurrent environment:

Between get() and containsKey():

  • Another thread may remove or modify entry.
  • So result becomes inconsistent.

To avoid this ambiguity:

ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values because in concurrent environments null creates ambiguity between “key absent” and “value null”.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: HashSet is a Set implementation that stores unique elements using a backing HashMap.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: HashSet is a common interview topic because duplicate prevention depends on hashCode() and equals().

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When you add an object to HashSet, Java uses its hash code to find a bucket, then uses equals() to check duplicates in that bucket.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• HashSet does not guarantee insertion order.
  • Duplicate detection needs both hashCode() and equals().
  • If equals() is overridden, hashCode() should also be overridden.
  • Hash collisions are possible.
  • Mutable fields used in hashCode can break set behavior.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: HashSet stores unique elements by using a HashMap internally. The element becomes the key, and a dummy object is stored as the value. Java first uses hashCode() to find the bucket, then uses equals() to check whether an equal element already exists.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Stores unique elements.
  • Backed by HashMap.
  • No guaranteed order.
  • Uses hashCode for bucket selection.
  • Uses equals for duplicate check.
  • hashCode and equals contract is critical.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Very important concept:

HashSet internally uses HashMap.

docs.title: 🔥 Question (Very Important)
docs.text:
How does HashSet prevent duplicates?

Explain in 3–4 steps.

Think about:

  • hashCode()
  • equals()
  • bucket
  • internal structure

Answer in your own words.

Hash set use hash map internally to store the value. for each value calculate hash code, use equals to find the bucket if bucket is empty then add the value as key.

Small correction:

docs.title: ✅ Correct Deep Explanation — How HashSet Prevents Duplicates
docs.text:
Internally:

public class HashSet<E> {
    private transient HashMap<E,Object> map;
    private static final Object PRESENT = new Object();
}

So when you do:

set.add("A");

Internally it does:

map.put("A", PRESENT);

docs.title: Step 1️⃣ Calculate hashCode()
docs.text:
When you insert element:

set.add(element);

HashSet calls:

element.hashCode()

docs.title: Step 2️⃣ Find Bucket
docs.text:
Using hashCode, it calculates bucket index:

index = hash & (n - 1)

(where n is table length)

docs.title: Step 3️⃣ Check Existing Elements in Bucket
docs.text: Now two possibilities:

docs.title: Case A: Bucket empty
docs.text: → Insert new node.

docs.title: Case B: Bucket not empty
docs.text:
→ It compares keys using:

equals()

If equals() returns true: → Duplicate found → Do NOT insert → Return false

If equals() returns false: → Collision → Insert in bucket chain

docs.title: 🔥 Very Important Concept
docs.text:
HashSet depends on:

  • hashCode()
  • equals()

If you override one but not the other → HashSet breaks.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview Perfect Answer
docs.text: HashSet internally uses a HashMap. When adding an element, it computes hashCode to determine the bucket. If another element exists in the same bucket, it uses equals() to check equality. If equals returns true, it prevents duplicate insertion.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Deep Question (Critical Interview Level)
docs.text:
What happens if:

  • Two objects have same hashCode
  • But equals() returns false

Will HashSet store both?

✅ Answer — it will store both.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
Two objects:

  • Same hashCode()
  • But equals() returns false

Example:

class Person {
    int id;

    public int hashCode() {
        return 1;   // same hash for all
    }

    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return false;   // always different
    }
}

docs.title: Step 1️⃣ Same hashCode
docs.text: Both objects go to same bucket.

docs.title: Step 2️⃣ equals() check
docs.text:
Since equals returns false:

  • They are considered different
  • So both are stored

docs.title: Internal Structure
docs.text:
Before Java 8:

  • Bucket stored as LinkedList

After Java 8:

  • If bucket size > 8
  • And table size ≥ 64 → Bucket converted to Red-Black Tree

This is called:

Treeification

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
HashMap handles collisions by:

  • LinkedList (small bucket)
  • Red-Black Tree (large bucket, Java 8+)

docs.title: 🧠 Final Answer Style (Interview Ready)
docs.text: If two objects have the same hashCode but are not equal according to equals(), they will be stored in the same bucket but as separate entries. HashMap handles this collision using a linked list or tree structure internally.

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Question
docs.text:
What happens if:

  • Two objects have different hashCode
  • But equals() returns true

Will HashSet store both?

✅ Answer: it will not store both — but only if the objects end up in the same bucket, which normally requires the same hash.

Now let’s explain the full rule clearly (this is a very important interview point).

docs.title: If equals() is true, then hashCode() must be same.
docs.text:
So this situation:

  • different hashCode
  • equals true

👉 violates the contract.

docs.title: What actually happens in HashSet?
docs.text:
HashSet/HashMap works like this:

  1. It first uses hashCode() to choose the bucket
  2. It only calls equals() on elements inside that bucket

So if two objects have:

  • different hashCode → they go to different buckets
  • HashSet won’t even compare them with equals()

✅ Result: Both will be stored (duplicates happen!) Even though equals() says they are equal.

So the correct practical behavior is:

HashSet may store both, because different hashCodes lead to different buckets, and equals is not checked across buckets.

docs.title: ✅ Final Correct Answer (Interview-ready)
docs.text: If two objects have different hashCode but equals() returns true, it breaks the equals-hashCode contract. HashSet may store both objects in different buckets, causing duplicates.

docs.title: 🔥 Super Important Interview One-Liner
docs.text: HashSet uniqueness is guaranteed only when equals() and hashCode() follow the contract.

docs.title: Quick check (yes/no)
docs.text: If you override equals() in a custom class, must you override hashCode() also? Why?

docs.title: ✅ Correct Interview Answer
docs.text: Yes. Whenever we override equals(), we must also override hashCode(). Because HashSet and HashMap use hashCode() to determine the bucket and equals() to check equality within that bucket. If we override only equals() and not hashCode(), equal objects may go into different buckets, breaking uniqueness and causing inconsistent behavior.

docs.title: 🔥 Why This Is Critical (Deep Understanding)
docs.text:
HashMap insertion steps:

1️⃣ Calculate hashCode() 2️⃣ Find bucket index 3️⃣ Compare with existing elements using equals()

If two objects are logically equal but have different hash codes:

  • They go into different buckets
  • equals() never gets called
  • Both objects get stored
  • HashSet allows duplicates

docs.title: 🔥 Official Contract (Must Memorize)
docs.text:
If:

a.equals(b) == true

Then:

a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()

Must be true.

But reverse is not required:

  • Same hashCode does NOT mean equals() must be true.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: LinkedList is a doubly linked list implementation of List and Deque.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: LinkedList questions test whether you understand node-based storage, traversal cost, and when linked structures are useful.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Each node stores data plus links to the previous and next nodes.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• LinkedList is not faster for every insertion.
  • get(index) is O(n).
  • It uses more memory because each node stores links.
  • ArrayList is usually better for random access.
  • Iteration over LinkedList can still be efficient, but indexing is not.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: LinkedList stores elements as nodes connected with previous and next references. It is efficient for adding or removing at the beginning or end when the node position is known. But random access is slow because Java must traverse nodes from the start or end.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Doubly linked list.
  • Implements List and Deque.
  • Slow random access.
  • Good for frequent add/remove at ends.
  • Uses extra memory for links.
  • ArrayList is usually better for index-based access.

docs.title: What is LinkedList?
docs.text:
• Doubly linked list implementation
  • Implements: List + Deque
  • Good for frequent add/remove at ends
  • Poor for random access

docs.title: Internal Structure (concept)
docs.text:
Each node stores:

  • item
  • prev reference
  • next reference

Operations:

  • addFirst, addLast → O(1)
  • removeFirst, removeLast → O(1)
  • get(index) → O(n)

docs.title: 🔥 First LinkedList Trap
docs.text:
Which is faster and why?

  1. ArrayList.get(i)
  2. LinkedList.get(i)

Answer in 2 lines.

✅ Correct — ArrayList.get(i) is faster.

Now let’s make this answer interview-strong.

docs.title: 🔹 ArrayList
docs.text:
• Internally backed by Object[]
  • Direct index access:
return elementData[index];
  • Time complexity: O(1) (constant time)
  • Because memory is contiguous and index-based

docs.title: 🔹 LinkedList
docs.text:
Internally:

Node {
    prev
    item
    next
}

To get element at index i:

  • It must traverse nodes
  • Either from head or tail (whichever closer)

Time complexity: O(n)

Because it must walk through the list.

docs.title: 🔥 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ArrayList provides O(1) random access because it uses an array, while LinkedList requires traversal, so get(i) is O(n).

docs.title: 🚀 Now Important LinkedList Trap
docs.text:
Which is faster and why?

  1. ArrayList.add(0, element)
  2. LinkedList.addFirst(element)

Answer carefully with reasoning.

LinkedList.addFirst(element) is faster because adding first element in linked list mean just changing root node of list.
ArrayList.add(0, element) required O(n) time complexity to add element because its shift all element to right

✅ Perfect. That’s exactly the right reasoning.

Small correction:

  • “root node” → “head pointer / first node reference”
  • “shift all element” → “shift all elements”

docs.title: 1️⃣ LinkedList.addFirst(element) → O(1)
docs.text:
A doubly-linked list just updates pointers:

  • newNode.next = oldFirst
  • oldFirst.prev = newNode
  • head = newNode

No shifting.

docs.title: 2️⃣ ArrayList.add(0, element) → O(n)
docs.text:
ArrayList is backed by an array. Inserting at index 0 requires:

  • shift existing elements right by 1
  • possible resize too

So it’s linear.

docs.title: ✅ Next: LinkedList internal working details (Deep)
docs.text:
LinkedList implements both:

  • List (index-based operations)
  • Deque (queue/stack operations)

So it supports:

  • addFirst/removeFirst (stack/queue)
  • addLast/removeLast

docs.title: 🔥 Now Common Interview Trap
docs.text:
What is time complexity of:

  1. LinkedList.addLast(x)
  2. LinkedList.removeLast()
  3. LinkedList.add(index, x)

Assume Java’s LinkedList keeps references to both first and last.

Answer with Big-O for each.

👍 Correct answers:

1️⃣ LinkedList.addLast(x) → O(1) 2️⃣ LinkedList.removeLast() → O(1) 3️⃣ LinkedList.add(index, x) → O(n)

docs.title: 1️⃣ addLast(x) → O(1)
docs.text:
LinkedList maintains:

first
last

To add at end:

  • Create new node
  • last.next = newNode
  • newNode.prev = last
  • last = newNode

No traversal needed.

docs.title: 2️⃣ removeLast() → O(1)
docs.text:
Because:

  • It already has reference to last
  • Just update last = last.prev
  • Adjust pointers

No traversal.

docs.title: 3️⃣ add(index, x) → O(n) ❌
docs.text:
This is the important correction.

To add at index:

  • Must first find the node at that index
  • LinkedList does NOT have random access

  • It traverses from:

  • head (if index < size/2)

  • tail (if index > size/2)

Traversal takes O(n)

After finding position:

  • Insert node in O(1)

But total complexity = O(n)

docs.title: 🔥 Interview Trick
docs.text:
People often think:

LinkedList insertion is always O(1)

That is only true if:

  • You already have reference to the node
  • Or adding/removing at head/tail

Index-based operations are O(n).

docs.title: 🚀 Now Very Important Question
docs.text:
Which is better for:

1️⃣ Frequent random access 2️⃣ Frequent insertions at beginning 3️⃣ Iterating through all elements 4️⃣ Memory efficiency

Answer each with:

  • ArrayList or LinkedList
  • 1 line reason.

docs.title: ✅ 1️⃣ Frequent random access
docs.text:
✔ ArrayList

Reason:

  • Backed by array
  • get(index) is O(1)
  • Direct memory access

Your answer correct.

docs.title: ✅ 2️⃣ Frequent insertions at beginning
docs.text:
✔ LinkedList

Reason:

  • Just update head pointer
  • O(1)
  • No shifting required

Correct again.

docs.title: ⚠ 3️⃣ Iterating through all elements
docs.text:
You said: “I think both”

Correct answer: ✔ ArrayList is generally faster

Reason:

  • ArrayList stores elements in contiguous memory
  • Better CPU cache locality
  • Less pointer chasing

LinkedList:

  • Each node separate object
  • Pointer traversal
  • Poor cache locality
  • More GC pressure

So although both are O(n), 👉 ArrayList performs better in real-world iteration.

This is important.

docs.title: ⚠ 4️⃣ Memory efficiency
docs.text:
You said both are not good — good intuition.

Correct detailed answer:

✔ ArrayList is more memory efficient

Why?

ArrayList:

  • Just stores Object[] references

LinkedList: Each node stores:

item
prev pointer
next pointer

So for every element:

  • Extra 2 references
  • Plus node object overhead

LinkedList uses much more memory per element.

docs.title: 🔥 Final Comparison Table (Interview Ready)
docs.text: Scenario Best Choice Why Random access ArrayList O(1) index access Insert/remove at head LinkedList O(1) pointer update Iteration ArrayList Better cache locality Memory usage ArrayList No extra node overhead Heavy mid insertions LinkedList No shifting Frequent resizing Pre-size ArrayList Avoid growth cost

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Exception handling is Java’s mechanism for handling runtime problems without crashing the normal program flow immediately.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It helps you write reliable code and explain checked exceptions, unchecked exceptions, error handling flow, and exception hierarchy in interviews.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: If file reading fails, Java can throw an exception and the program can handle it with try and catch.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Exception and Error are different.
  • Checked exceptions must be handled or declared.
  • Unchecked exceptions are not checked at compile time.
  • Catching very broad exceptions can hide bugs.
  • An exception object contains type, message, and stack trace.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Exception handling lets Java separate normal logic from error handling logic. Code that may fail is placed in try, problems are caught in catch, and cleanup can happen in finally or try-with-resources. Checked exceptions are verified by the compiler, while unchecked exceptions usually represent programming or runtime problems.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Throwable is the root type.
  • Exception is for recoverable problems.
  • Error is for serious JVM/system problems.
  • Checked exceptions need handling or throws.
  • Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException.
  • Use specific catch blocks when possible.

docs.title: Exception Topic Roadmap (We Will Cover Everything)
docs.text:
We will go deep step-by-step like we did with multithreading.

1. What is an Exception
2. Exception hierarchy
3. Checked vs Unchecked exceptions
4. try-catch-finally
5. throw vs throws
6. Custom exceptions
7. try-with-resources
8. Multiple catch blocks
9. Exception propagation
10. Suppressed exceptions
11. Best practices
12. Interview traps

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An exception is an event that occurs during program execution and disrupts the normal flow of the program.

Example:

int a = 10;
int b = 0;

int c = a / b;

Output:

java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero

Program crashes.

docs.title: Why Exceptions Exist
docs.text:
Without exception handling:

Program crashes immediately
No recovery
Bad user experience

With exception handling:

Detect error
Handle it properly
Continue program

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
try {
    int x = 10 / 0;
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Cannot divide by zero");
}

Output:

Cannot divide by zero

Program continues.

docs.title: Exception Handling Flow
docs.text:
Error occurs
      ↓
Exception object created
      ↓
JVM searches for matching catch block
      ↓
If found → handle
If not found → program terminates

docs.title: Java Exception Hierarchy
docs.text:
Very important for interviews.

Throwable
   |
   +-- Error
   |
   +-- Exception
          |
          +-- RuntimeException

Explanation:

Error → serious JVM problems
Exception → application errors
RuntimeException → programming mistakes

docs.title: Error
docs.text:
OutOfMemoryError
StackOverflowError

Usually cannot recover.

docs.title: Checked Exception
docs.text:
IOException
SQLException
FileNotFoundException

Compiler forces handling.

docs.title: Unchecked Exception
docs.text:
NullPointerException
ArithmeticException
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

Occurs due to programming mistakes.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: An exception is an object representing an abnormal condition that disrupts the normal flow of program execution.

docs.title: First Check Question
docs.text:
Which of these are checked exceptions?

A) IOException
B) NullPointerException
C) SQLException
D) ArithmeticException

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
✅ — A and C are checked exceptions.

“IOException and SQLException are checked exceptions because the compiler forces the programmer to handle or declare them.”

docs.title: Checked Exceptions
docs.text:
These are exceptions that the compiler forces you to handle.

Example:

FileReader file = new FileReader("data.txt");

Compiler error:

Unhandled exception: FileNotFoundException

You must handle it:

try {
    FileReader file = new FileReader("data.txt");
} catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
}

or declare it:

public void readFile() throws FileNotFoundException

docs.title: Examples of Checked Exceptions
docs.text:
IOException
SQLException
FileNotFoundException
ClassNotFoundException
InterruptedException

docs.title: Unchecked Exceptions
docs.text:
These are not checked by compiler.

Examples:

NullPointerException
ArithmeticException
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
IllegalArgumentException

These usually indicate programming mistakes.

Example:

String s = null;
s.length();   // NullPointerException

Compiler does not force handling.

docs.title: Key Interview Rule
docs.text:
Checked Exception → compile-time checking
Unchecked Exception → runtime error

docs.title: Very Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
Which of these is NOT a checked exception?

A) IOException
B) SQLException
C) RuntimeException
D) ClassNotFoundException

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked exceptions, meaning the compiler does not require them to be caught or declared.

docs.title: Why RuntimeException is Unchecked
docs.text:
Example:

int a = 10 / 0;

Compiler allows it.

But at runtime:

ArithmeticException: / by zero

Program crashes.

Compiler does not force handling.

docs.title: RuntimeException Hierarchy
docs.text:
Throwable
   |
   +-- Exception
          |
          +-- RuntimeException
                 |
                 +-- NullPointerException
                 +-- ArithmeticException
                 +-- IndexOutOfBoundsException
                 +-- IllegalArgumentException

All of these are unchecked exceptions.

docs.title: Checked Exception Hierarchy
docs.text:
Throwable
   |
   +-- Exception
          |
          +-- IOException
          +-- SQLException
          +-- ClassNotFoundException

These must be handled or declared.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: RuntimeException and its subclasses are unchecked exceptions, meaning the compiler does not require them to be caught or declared.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: catch handles exceptions and finally runs cleanup code after try/catch flow, usually whether an exception occurs or not.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This topic has many interview traps around catch order, return statements, finally execution, and exception overriding.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A finally block can close a resource even if an exception is thrown in the try block.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Catch child exceptions before parent exceptions.
  • finally usually runs even when there is a return.
  • finally may not run if JVM exits.
  • A return in finally can hide an exception or earlier return.
  • Catch order matters at compile time.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: catch blocks handle matching exception types. More specific exceptions must be caught before broader parent exceptions. finally is used for cleanup and normally runs after try/catch, even if an exception or return happens. But writing return statements in finally is dangerous because it can suppress earlier results or exceptions.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Specific catch before generic catch.
  • finally is for cleanup.
  • finally usually runs.
  • System.exit() can stop finally.
  • Avoid return inside finally.
  • Catch only what you can handle.

docs.title: Multi-catch and catch order
docs.text:
Question:

Will this compile?

try {
    int x = 10 / 0;
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Exception");
}
catch(ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Arithmetic");
}

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: It does not compile because the parent exception is caught before the subclass exception, making the second catch block unreachable.

docs.title: Why This Does Not Compile
docs.text:
Code:

try {
    int x = 10 / 0;
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Exception");
}
catch(ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Arithmetic");
}

Hierarchy:

Exception
   ↑
ArithmeticException

So:

catch(Exception e)

already catches ALL exceptions, including:

ArithmeticException
NullPointerException
IOException
etc.

Therefore the next block:

catch(ArithmeticException e)

will never execute.

Compiler error:

Unreachable catch block

docs.title: Correct Order
docs.text:
Always catch more specific exceptions first.

try {
    int x = 10 / 0;
}
catch(ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Arithmetic");
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Exception");
}

Now it works.

docs.title: Rule for Catch Blocks
docs.text:
Child exception → first
Parent exception → later

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: In multiple catch blocks, more specific exceptions must be caught before their parent exceptions to avoid unreachable code.

docs.title: Very Famous Java Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

try {
    System.out.println("A");
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("B");
}
finally {
    System.out.println("C");
}

What will be printed?

docs.title: Output will be:
docs.text:
A
C

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
Code:

try {
    System.out.println("A");
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("B");
}
finally {
    System.out.println("C");
}

docs.title: Execution flow
docs.text:
1️⃣ try block runs

print "A"

2️⃣ No exception occurs So catch block is skipped

3️⃣ finally always executes

print "C"

docs.title: Final Output
docs.text:
A
C

docs.title: Important Rule
docs.text:
If no exception → try → finally
If exception → try → catch → finally

docs.title: Another Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

try {
    System.out.println("A");
    return;
}
finally {
    System.out.println("B");
}

What will be printed?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: “The try block prints A, then the return statement is prepared. Before returning, the JVM executes the finally block, which prints B.”

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A
B

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
Code:

try {
    System.out.println("A");
    return;
}
finally {
    System.out.println("B");
}

Step-by-step:

1️⃣ try block executes

print A

2️⃣ return encountered

But before the method exits:

finally block executes

3️⃣ finally prints:

B

4️⃣ Method returns.

docs.title: Important JVM Rule
docs.text:
finally always executes
even if try contains return

Except rare cases:

System.exit()
JVM crash
Power failure

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Even if a return statement exists in the try block, the finally block executes before the method returns.

docs.title: Super Famous Java Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

public static int test() {

    try {
        return 10;
    }
    finally {
        return 20;
    }

}

What will this method return?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: ✅ — the method returns 20.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Code:

public static int test() {
    try {
        return 10;
    } finally {
        return 20;
    }
}

Execution flow:

  1. try executes → return 10 is prepared (value saved).
  2. Before the method actually returns, the finally block runs.
  3. finally has its own return, which overrides the previous return.

So the final result becomes:

20

docs.title: Key Rule
docs.text: A return in finally overrides any return from try or catch.

docs.title: Important Interview Note ⚠
docs.text:
This is considered bad practice, because it can:

  • hide exceptions
  • override earlier return values
  • make debugging difficult

Example problem:

try {
    throw new RuntimeException();
} finally {
    return 10;   // hides the exception!
}

The exception is lost.

✅ Interview one-liner

A return statement inside finally overrides any previous return from try or catch, which is why using return in finally is discouraged.

If you're okay, the next very important exception topic (often asked in interviews) is:

try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions.

It explains how Java automatically closes resources like files, streams, and database connections.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A custom exception is an application-specific exception class created to represent a meaningful business or domain error.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Custom exceptions make error handling clearer and help express domain-specific problems in service and backend code.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: InsufficientBalanceException is clearer than throwing a generic Exception in a banking flow.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Do not create custom exceptions for every small error.
  • Use checked exceptions only when callers can reasonably recover.
  • Use unchecked exceptions for programming or business rule violations when compile-time handling is not useful.
  • Preserve the original cause when wrapping exceptions.
  • Name exceptions clearly.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Custom exceptions represent application-specific error cases. We create them by extending Exception for checked exceptions or RuntimeException for unchecked exceptions. They improve readability when the exception name clearly explains the failure, such as InvalidOrderStateException or InsufficientBalanceException.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Extend Exception for checked custom exceptions.
  • Extend RuntimeException for unchecked custom exceptions.
  • Use meaningful names.
  • Include useful messages.
  • Preserve root cause when wrapping.
  • Do not overuse custom exceptions.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: One more concept remains in exceptions:

docs.title: Custom Exceptions
docs.text:
Example:

if(age < 18) {
    throw new InvalidAgeException();
}

Before I explain:

docs.title: Quick question
docs.text:
Custom exceptions should usually extend:

A) Throwable
B) Exception
C) Error
D) Object

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
✅ — B) Exception is the typical choice.

“Custom exceptions usually extend Exception when we want a checked exception, or RuntimeException when we want an unchecked exception.”

docs.title: Custom Exceptions in Java
docs.text:
Custom exceptions allow you to create application-specific errors.

Example cases:

InvalidAgeException
InsufficientBalanceException
UserNotFoundException
OrderLimitExceededException

docs.title: 1️⃣ Checked Custom Exception
docs.text:
Extend:

Exception

Example:

class InvalidAgeException extends Exception {

    public InvalidAgeException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }

}

Usage:

public void vote(int age) throws InvalidAgeException {

    if(age < 18) {
        throw new InvalidAgeException("Age must be >= 18");
    }

}

Compiler forces handling.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Unchecked Custom Exception
docs.text:
Extend:

RuntimeException

Example:

class InvalidAgeException extends RuntimeException {

    public InvalidAgeException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }

}

Now compiler does not force handling.

docs.title: When to Use Which?
docs.text: Type Use Case Checked Exception recoverable conditions RuntimeException programming errors

docs.title: Real Example (Bank System)
docs.text:
class InsufficientBalanceException extends Exception {
    public InsufficientBalanceException(String msg){
        super(msg);
    }
}

Usage:

if(balance < withdrawAmount) {
    throw new InsufficientBalanceException("Balance too low");
}

docs.title: Best Practice for Custom Exceptions
docs.text:
Always include:

constructor with message
constructor with cause

Example:

public class MyException extends Exception {

    public MyException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }

    public MyException(String message, Throwable cause) {
        super(message, cause);
    }

}

docs.title: Interview One-liner
docs.text:
Custom exceptions are user-defined exception classes that extend Exception or RuntimeException to represent application-specific errors.

Before we move forward, one last classic interview trap:

What happens here?

try {
    throw new Exception("Error");
}
catch(RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("Runtime");
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Exception");
}

What will be printed?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: It will print Exception

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution
docs.text:
Code:

try {
    throw new Exception("Error");
}
catch(RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println("Runtime");
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("Exception");
}

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Exception thrown:

Exception

Type:

java.lang.Exception

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
JVM checks catch blocks from top to bottom.

First catch:

catch(RuntimeException e)

But:

Exception ≠ RuntimeException

So this block does not match.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Next catch:

catch(Exception e)

This matches because:

Exception → same type

So it executes.

Output:

Exception

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Catch blocks are checked:

top → bottom
first matching catch executes

docs.title: Exception Hierarchy Here
docs.text:
Throwable
   |
   +-- Exception
          |
          +-- RuntimeException

Since RuntimeException is a subclass, it cannot catch a parent exception.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: The JVM checks catch blocks sequentially from top to bottom and executes the first matching exception handler.

docs.title: Exception Handling Topic Complete 🎯
docs.text:
Exception hierarchy
Checked vs Unchecked
try/catch/finally
throw vs throws
Propagation
Multiple catch
finally behavior
try-with-resources
Suppressed exceptions
Custom exceptions

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: throw actually throws an exception object. throws declares that a method may pass an exception to its caller. Propagation means the exception moves up the call stack.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: These keywords are often confused. They are central to checked exception handling and method API design.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A method can throw new IOException() and declare throws IOException so callers know they must handle or declare it.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• throw and throws are not the same.
  • throw is used inside method body.
  • throws is used in method signature.
  • Checked exceptions must be handled or declared.
  • Unchecked exceptions can propagate without declaration.

docs.title: Interview Answer
