docs.text: throw is used to create and throw a specific exception from code. throws is written in a method signature to tell callers that the method may pass that exception upward. If an exception is not handled in the current method, it propagates to the caller until it is caught or the program terminates.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• throw: action.
  • throws: declaration.
  • Propagation moves exception up the stack.
  • Checked exceptions need handling or declaration.
  • Unchecked exceptions do not require throws.
  • Use throws when caller should decide handling.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: Now we move to a very common interview question:

docs.title: throw vs throws
docs.text:
Example:

throw new IOException();

vs

public void readFile() throws IOException

docs.title: Quick Question
docs.text:
Which keyword is used to declare that a method may throw an exception?

A) throw
B) throws

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: “The throws keyword declares that a method may throw a specified exception.”

docs.title: throw vs throws
docs.text: This is a very common Java interview question, so you should know it clearly.

docs.title: 1️⃣ throws (Declaration)
docs.text:
throws is used in the method signature to declare that the method may throw an exception.

Example:

public void readFile() throws IOException {
    FileReader file = new FileReader("data.txt");
}

Meaning:

This method might throw IOException
Caller must handle it

So responsibility goes to the caller method.

docs.title: 2️⃣ throw (Actual Exception)
docs.text:
throw is used inside the method to actually create and throw an exception.

Example:

throw new ArithmeticException("Division by zero");

Example:

public void divide(int a, int b) {
    if(b == 0) {
        throw new ArithmeticException("Cannot divide by zero");
    }
}

docs.title: Key Difference
docs.text: Feature throw throws Purpose throw an exception declare exception Location inside method method signature Number allowed one exception multiple exceptions Used with exception object exception class

docs.title: Example Combining Both
docs.text:
public void readFile() throws IOException {

    if(fileNotFound) {
        throw new IOException("File missing");
    }

}

Here:

throws → declaration
throw → actual exception

docs.title: Interview One-liner
docs.text: throw is used to explicitly throw an exception, while throws is used in the method signature to declare possible exceptions.

docs.title: Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
What will happen here?

public static void main(String[] args) {

    throw new IOException("Error");

}

Will it:

A) Compile
B) Not compile
C) Compile but crash at runtime

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: “It will not compile because IOException is a checked exception, and the compiler forces us to handle or declare it.”

docs.title: What Happens in This Code
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {

    throw new IOException("Error");

}

Compilation error:

Unhandled exception: IOException

Because:

IOException → checked exception

Java requires either:

Handle it with try-catch
OR
Declare it with throws

docs.title: Correct Version 1 — Try/Catch
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {

    try {
        throw new IOException("Error");
    } catch(IOException e) {
        System.out.println("Handled");
    }

}

docs.title: Correct Version 2 — throws
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {

    throw new IOException("Error");

}

Here:

main() declares the exception

JVM handles it.

Program will compile but crash at runtime.

docs.title: Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
Even main() can declare exceptions:

public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception

This is very common.

docs.title: Next Important Topic
docs.text:
Now we should understand Exception Propagation.

Example:

method3()
  ↓
method2()
  ↓
method1()
  ↓
main()

If method3() throws an exception and no catch block exists, where does the exception go?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Exception propagation is the process where an exception moves up the call stack until it is handled by a catch block.

“It will go to method2.” “If method2 does not handle it, it goes to the next caller method.”

docs.title: Exception Propagation
docs.text:
Exception propagation means:

Exception moves up the call stack
until a catch block handles it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
public class Test {

    static void method3() {
        int a = 10 / 0;
    }

    static void method2() {
        method3();
    }

    static void method1() {
        method2();
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        method1();
    }
}

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
main()
   ↓
method1()
   ↓
method2()
   ↓
method3()
   ↓
Exception occurs

Exception type:

ArithmeticException

docs.title: Propagation Path
docs.text:
method3 → method2 → method1 → main → JVM

If none handle it:

Program crashes
Stack trace printed

Example output:

Exception in thread "main"
java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero

docs.title: Important Rule
docs.text:
Propagation happens only if there is no catch block.

Example:

static void method2() {
    try {
        method3();
    } catch(Exception e) {
        System.out.println("Handled");
    }
}

Now the exception stops at method2.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Exception propagation is the process where an exception moves up the call stack until it is handled by a catch block.

docs.title: Very Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

try {
    return 10;
}
finally {
    return 20;
}

What will be the output?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: 20 will be returned because finally executes even if try has a return.

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text:
Code:

try {
    return 10;
}
finally {
    return 20;
}

Execution flow:

try block executes
return 10 prepared
before returning → finally executes
finally returns 20

So the finally return overrides the try return.

docs.title: Step-by-Step JVM Behavior
docs.text:
1 try executes
2 JVM stores return value (10)
3 finally executes
4 finally returns 20
5 final result = 20

docs.title: Very Important Rule
docs.text:
finally block always executes
even if try contains return

Except in rare cases:

System.exit()
JVM crash

docs.title: Interview Warning ⚠
docs.text:
This is considered bad coding practice.

Example:

try {
    return value;
}
finally {
    cleanup();
}

Good.

But this is bad:

finally {
    return something;
}

Because it hides exceptions and return values.

docs.title: Another Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
What will be printed?

try {
    System.out.println("A");
    throw new RuntimeException();
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("B");
}
finally {
    System.out.println("C");
}

What do you think the output is?

docs.title: ✅ the output is:
docs.text:
A
B
C

“First A is printed, then the exception is caught so B is printed, and finally the finally block prints C.”

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution
docs.text:
Code:

try {
    System.out.println("A");
    throw new RuntimeException();
}
catch(Exception e) {
    System.out.println("B");
}
finally {
    System.out.println("C");
}

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
try block starts

Prints:

A

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Exception occurs:

RuntimeException

So execution jumps to the catch block.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Catch block executes:

B

Printed.

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text:
Finally block always executes.

Prints:

C

docs.title: Final Output
docs.text:
A
B
C

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Execution order:

try → catch → finally

If exception occurs:

try → catch → finally

If no exception:

try → finally

docs.title: Very Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

try {
    System.out.println("A");
    throw new RuntimeException();
}
finally {
    System.out.println("B");
}

Will the program:

A) print A B and terminate
B) print A B then crash
C) print only A

What do you think?

Correct ✅ — B) print A, then B, then crash.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
A
B
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.RuntimeException

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• try prints A
  • exception is thrown
  • there is no catch
  • finally still runs and prints B
  • then exception propagates upward and program terminates

docs.title: Key rule
docs.text: finally executes even when an exception is not caught.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: try-with-resources automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable after the try block finishes.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It prevents resource leaks and makes cleanup simpler for files, streams, database connections, and similar resources.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A FileInputStream opened in try-with-resources is closed automatically when the block ends.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• The resource must implement AutoCloseable.
  • Resources close in reverse order of creation.
  • Suppressed exceptions can exist when close also fails.
  • try-with-resources is better than manual finally cleanup for closeable resources.
  • Closing can also throw an exception.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: try-with-resources is a Java feature that automatically closes resources declared in the try header. The resource must implement AutoCloseable or Closeable. It reduces boilerplate and handles cleanup reliably, including suppressed exceptions when both the try block and close operation fail.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Introduced in Java 7.
  • Works with AutoCloseable.
  • Closes resources automatically.
  • Closes in reverse order.
  • Can record suppressed exceptions.
  • Use it for files, streams, sockets, and database resources.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Java introduced try-with-resources in Java 7 to automatically close resources like:

File
Stream
Socket
Database Connection
Scanner

This prevents resource leaks.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Problem Before Java 7
docs.text:
Old code:

FileInputStream file = null;

try {
    file = new FileInputStream("data.txt");
}
catch(IOException e) {
}
finally {
    if(file != null) {
        file.close();
    }
}

Problems:

verbose code
easy to forget closing
resource leak risk

docs.title: 2️⃣ try-with-resources Solution
docs.text:
Java allows declaring resources inside try().

Example:

try(FileInputStream file =
        new FileInputStream("data.txt")) {

    // use file

}

JVM automatically calls:

file.close()

after the block finishes.

docs.title: 3️⃣ How It Works Internally
docs.text:
The resource must implement:

AutoCloseable

or

Closeable

Example hierarchy:

AutoCloseable
      ↑
   Closeable
      ↑
FileInputStream
BufferedReader
Scanner

Because these implement close().

docs.title: 4️⃣ Example
docs.text:
try(Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)) {

    int x = sc.nextInt();
    System.out.println(x);

}

After execution:

sc.close()

is called automatically.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Multiple Resources
docs.text:
You can declare multiple resources.

try(
    FileInputStream f = new FileInputStream("a.txt");
    BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(f))
) {

}

Close order:

br.close()
f.close()

Reverse order.

docs.title: Suppressed Exceptions
docs.text:
Suppose this happens:

Exception in try block
Exception in close()

Example:

try(Resource r = new Resource()) {
    throw new RuntimeException("try error");
}

and

close() throws another exception

Now Java must decide which exception to show.

Rule:

Primary exception → try block exception
Suppressed exception → close() exception

Java keeps suppressed exceptions inside the main exception.

Example output:

Exception in try
Suppressed: exception in close()

docs.title: 7️⃣ Access Suppressed Exceptions
docs.text: e.getSuppressed();

docs.title: Interview One-liner
docs.text: try-with-resources automatically closes resources that implement AutoCloseable, preventing resource leaks.

docs.title: Very Common Interview Question
docs.text:
Which interface must a resource implement to be used in try-with-resources?

A) Serializable
B) AutoCloseable
C) Runnable
D) Cloneable

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: “AutoClosable interface resource mush implement to try with resources so auto close the resource.” → “A resource must implement the AutoCloseable interface to be used in try-with-resources so that it can be automatically closed.”

docs.title: Correct Answer
docs.text: B) AutoCloseable

docs.title: Why AutoCloseable?
docs.text:
Any resource used in:

try (resource) { }

must implement:

AutoCloseable

Because Java will automatically call:

close()

when the block finishes.

docs.title: AutoCloseable Interface
docs.text:
Definition:

public interface AutoCloseable {
    void close() throws Exception;
}

So when the try block ends:

resource.close()

is executed automatically.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
try(Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in)) {
    int x = sc.nextInt();
}

After execution:

sc.close()

runs automatically.

docs.title: Many Java Classes Implement AutoCloseable
docs.text:
Examples:

Scanner
FileInputStream
BufferedReader
Connection (JDBC)
Statement
ResultSet
Socket

This is why try-with-resources is used heavily in database and file operations.

docs.title: Example (Database)
docs.text:
try(
    Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url);
    Statement st = con.createStatement();
    ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM user")
) {

}

All of these will automatically close:

rs.close()
st.close()
con.close()

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: A resource must implement AutoCloseable to be used in try-with-resources, allowing Java to automatically call close() when the block finishes.

docs.title: Vishwambhar — Important
docs.text:
You have now covered almost the entire Exception Handling topic:

Exception hierarchy
Checked vs Unchecked
try / catch / finally
throw vs throws
Exception propagation
Multiple catch blocks
try-with-resources
Suppressed exceptions

This is strong interview preparation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The JVM is the runtime that loads Java bytecode, verifies it, manages memory, and executes the program on the machine.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: JVM internals explain why Java is platform independent, how objects are created, how memory is managed, and why performance issues happen.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When you run java Main, the JVM loads classes, creates the main thread, creates stack frames, allocates objects in heap, and executes bytecode.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Java source code is not executed directly.
  • javac creates bytecode, not native machine code.
  • The JVM loads classes when they are needed.
  • Object references and objects are not stored in the same place.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: The JVM runs Java bytecode. First, javac compiles .java files into .class files. Then the JVM loads required classes, verifies bytecode, prepares memory, starts the main thread, creates stack frames, allocates objects in heap, and executes the program using the execution engine.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• .java becomes .class bytecode.
  • Bytecode is platform independent.
  • JVM loads classes lazily.
  • Each thread has its own stack.
  • Objects live in heap.
  • Method calls create stack frames.

docs.title: Roadmap we will follow
docs.text:
1. What happens when you run a Java program
  2. JDK vs JRE vs JVM
  3. ClassLoader System
  4. JVM Memory Structure
  5. Heap Memory Deep Dive
  6. Stack Memory & Stack Frames
  7. String Pool Internals
  8. Object Creation in JVM
  9. Garbage Collection
  10. Execution Engine
  11. JIT Compiler
  12. Common Interview Traps

docs.title: What Happens When You Run a Java Program
docs.text:
Suppose we have this program.

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Person p = new Person("Vishu");
        p.sayHello();
    }
}

class Person {
    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    void sayHello() {
        System.out.println("Hello " + name);
    }
}

docs.title: Step 1 — Compilation
docs.text:
You run

javac Main.java

Java compiler converts .java → .class

Main.class
Person.class

These .class files contain bytecode.

Important:

Java does NOT compile to machine code.

It compiles to bytecode.

Example bytecode instruction:

aload_0
invokespecial
getfield
invokevirtual

This bytecode is platform independent.

docs.title: Step 2 — JVM Starts
docs.text:
When you run

java Main

JVM starts.

Now JVM performs these steps.

1 Load class
2 Verify bytecode
3 Prepare memory
4 Initialize static variables
5 Execute main method

docs.title: Step 3 — ClassLoader loads classes
docs.text:
JVM loads:

Main.class
Person.class
System.class
String.class

Important:

Java loads classes on demand (lazy loading).

docs.title: Step 4 — JVM Creates Main Thread
docs.text:
JVM starts main thread.

Then it creates stack memory for that thread.

Main Thread
   |
   |--- Stack

docs.title: Step 5 — main() Stack Frame Created
docs.text:
Inside stack a stack frame is created.

Stack

| main() frame |

Stack frame contains:

Local variables
Operand stack
Method data

docs.title: Step 6 — Object Creation
docs.text:
This line executes:

Person p = new Person("Vishu");

JVM does:

1 Allocate memory in Heap 2 Create object 3 Call constructor 4 Store reference in stack

Memory becomes:

Stack                        Heap
-----                        -----
p  ----------->        Person Object
                       name = "Vishu"

docs.title: Step 7 — Method Call
docs.text:
This line executes:

p.sayHello();

New stack frame created.

Stack

| sayHello() frame |
| main() frame     |

docs.title: Step 8 — Output
docs.text: Hello Vishu

docs.title: Step 9 — Method Ends
docs.text:
sayHello() frame removed.

Stack

| main() frame |

docs.title: Step 10 — Program Ends
docs.text:
Main frame removed.

Stack becomes empty.

docs.title: PART 2 — JDK vs JRE vs JVM
docs.text: This question comes in almost every Java interview.

docs.title: JDK
docs.text:
Java Development Kit

Used for development.

Contains:

JDK
 ├── JRE
 ├── javac compiler
 ├── debugger
 ├── tools

Example tools:

javac
javadoc
jar
jdb

docs.title: JRE
docs.text:
Java Runtime Environment

Used to run Java programs.

Contains:

JRE
 ├── JVM
 └── Java libraries

docs.title: JVM
docs.text:
Java Virtual Machine.

It runs Java bytecode.

Responsibilities:

Load classes
Verify bytecode
Manage memory
Execute bytecode
Garbage collection

docs.title: Diagram (Important for Interview)
docs.text:
Developer
   |
   v
 Java Code (.java)
   |
   v
 Compiler (javac)
   |
   v
 Bytecode (.class)
   |
   v
 JRE
   |
   v
 JVM
   |
   v
 OS / Hardware

docs.title: Why Java is platform independent?
docs.text:
Because:

Java → Bytecode
Bytecode → JVM → Machine Code

Each OS has its own JVM.

So same .class file runs everywhere.

docs.title: Is JVM platform independent?
docs.text:
Answer:

No

JVM is platform dependent.

Each OS has its own JVM.

But Java bytecode is platform independent.

docs.title: Trap 1
docs.text:
Does Java compile to machine code?

No.

It compiles to bytecode.

docs.title: Trap 2
docs.text:
Does JRE contain JVM?

Yes.

JDK → JRE → JVM

docs.title: Trap 3
docs.text:
Can we run Java program without JDK?

Yes.

If JRE is installed.

docs.title: Very Important Concept
docs.text: Next we will study the most asked JVM interview topic:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The ClassLoader subsystem loads .class files into JVM memory when a class is needed.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: ClassLoader questions test whether you understand lazy loading, parent delegation, class initialization, and static block execution.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When Main uses Person, the JVM asks the ClassLoader to load Person.class. Core Java classes like String are loaded by higher-level parent class loaders.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Creating a reference as Test t = null does not initialize the class.
  • Accessing a compile-time constant may not trigger class initialization.
  • Parent delegation checks parent loaders before child loaders.
  • Loading and initialization are not the same step.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: The ClassLoader loads class bytecode into JVM memory. Java mainly uses Bootstrap, Extension or Platform, and Application class loaders. They follow the parent delegation model, where a loader asks its parent first. After loading, the JVM links and initializes the class when active use requires it.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Class loading happens on demand.
  • Bootstrap loads core Java classes.
  • Application loader loads application classes.
  • Parent delegation protects core classes.
  • Class lifecycle: loading, linking, initialization.
  • Static blocks run during class initialization.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
This is very commonly asked in backend interviews.

Many candidates know memory but fail ClassLoader questions.

docs.title: What is ClassLoader?
docs.text:
ClassLoader is responsible for:

Loading .class files into JVM memory

Example:

Main.class
Person.class
String.class
System.class

When JVM needs a class, the ClassLoader loads it into memory.

docs.title: ClassLoader Types
docs.text:
There are 3 main ClassLoaders.

1 Bootstrap ClassLoader
2 Extension ClassLoader
3 Application ClassLoader

Diagram:

           Bootstrap ClassLoader
                 ↑
           Extension ClassLoader
                 ↑
          Application ClassLoader

This is called Parent Delegation Model.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Bootstrap ClassLoader
docs.text:
This is the root classloader.

Loads core Java classes.

Examples:

java.lang.String
java.lang.Object
java.lang.System
java.util.*

Location:

<JAVA_HOME>/lib

Important:

Bootstrap is written in native code (C/C++), not Java.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Extension ClassLoader
docs.text:
Loads Java extension libraries.

Location:

<JAVA_HOME>/lib/ext

Examples:

security extensions
crypto libraries

docs.title: 3️⃣ Application ClassLoader
docs.text:
Loads your application classes.

Example:

Main.class
Person.class
Demo.class

These are loaded from:

CLASSPATH

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
When JVM runs:

java Main

Application ClassLoader loads:

Main.class
Person.class

docs.title: Parent Delegation Model
docs.text:
This is very important interview concept.

Suppose JVM needs to load:

java.lang.String

Steps:

Application ClassLoader
   ↓
asks parent

Extension ClassLoader
   ↓
asks parent

Bootstrap ClassLoader

Bootstrap loads the class.

docs.title: Why Parent Delegation Exists
docs.text:
Security.

Imagine if Application ClassLoader loaded java.lang.String.

Someone could write a fake String class like:

package java.lang;

public class String {
}

Parent delegation prevents this.

Core classes must come from Bootstrap ClassLoader.

docs.title: Who loads java.lang.String?
docs.text:
Answer:

Bootstrap ClassLoader

docs.title: Can we override java.lang.String?
docs.text:
Answer:

No

Because parent delegation loads it first.

docs.title: Class Loading Phases
docs.text:
When JVM loads a class, there are 3 major phases.

1 Loading
2 Linking
3 Initialization

docs.title: 1️⃣ Loading
docs.text: ClassLoader reads .class file and loads it into memory.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Linking
docs.text:
Linking has 3 steps.

Verification
Preparation
Resolution

You already saw this earlier.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Initialization
docs.text:
Static variables get actual values.

Static blocks run.

Example:

class Test {
    static int x = 10;

    static {
        System.out.println("Loaded");
    }
}

When class loads:

Loaded

prints.

docs.title: Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test t = null;
    }
}

docs.title: Will "Static Block" print?
docs.text:
Think carefully.

This question checks when class initialization happens, which is a very famous JVM interview trap.

correct answer is actually NO ❌.

docs.title: Output:
docs.text:
(no output)

The static block will NOT execute.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because class initialization does not happen here.

Important rule:

Loading ≠ Initialization

JVM may load the class, but the static block runs only when the class is initialized.

docs.title: When Does Class Initialization Happen?
docs.text:
Class initialization happens only when JVM detects active use of the class.

Examples of active use:

1️⃣ Creating an object

Test t = new Test();

2️⃣ Accessing a static variable

System.out.println(Test.x);

3️⃣ Calling a static method

Test.method();

4️⃣ Reflection

5️⃣ Main class loading

docs.title: Why Test t = null Does Not Trigger Initialization
docs.text:
This line:

Test t = null;

does not create an object.

It only creates a reference variable.

Memory:

Stack
-----
t → null

No object, no static access → no class initialization.

So:

Static block not executed

docs.title: Correct Example Where Static Block Runs
docs.text:
class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test t = new Test();
    }
}

Output:

Static Block

Because object creation triggers initialization.

docs.title: Another Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }

    static int x = 10;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Test.x);
    }
}

Output:

Static Block
10

Because accessing static field initializes the class.

docs.title: Very Famous JVM Interview Question
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("Child");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Child c = new Child();
    }
}

Output:

Parent
Child

Reason:

Superclass initializes before subclass

docs.title: One More Trap (Very Important)
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Class.forName("Test");
    }
}

Output:

Static Block

Because:

Class.forName() triggers class initialization

docs.title: Summary Rule
docs.text: Static block executes when class initialization occurs, not just when class is loaded.

docs.title: What will be the output?
docs.text:
class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }

    static int x = 10;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Test.x);
        System.out.println(Test.x);
    }
}

Will "Static Block" print once or twice? Explain why.

It prints once because the class is initialized only one time. If the class is already initialized, the static block does not run again.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Static Block
10
10

Static block runs only once.

docs.title: Important Clarification
docs.text:
You said:

class loading happen one time

But the correct JVM concept is:

Static block runs during CLASS INITIALIZATION

Not during class loading.

docs.title: JVM Class Lifecycle
docs.text:
When JVM deals with a class, it goes through three main phases:

1 Loading
2 Linking
3 Initialization

Static blocks run during:

Initialization

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
When JVM reaches:

System.out.println(Test.x);

JVM sees that class Test is not initialized yet.

So it performs initialization:

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Static block executes:

Static Block

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Static variable initialized:

x = 10

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Now Test.x is accessed.

10

docs.title: Second Access
docs.text:
Now JVM executes:

System.out.println(Test.x);

But the class is already initialized.

So:

Static block does NOT run again

Only prints:

10

docs.title: Key Interview Rule
docs.text:
Class initialization happens only once per classloader

That’s why static block executes only once.

docs.title: Another Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }

    static int x = 10;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test t1 = new Test();
        Test t2 = new Test();
    }
}

What will print?

Correct answer:

Static Block

Only once.

Because:

Class initialization happens only once

Even if multiple objects are created.

docs.title: Another Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Test[] arr = new Test[10];
    }
}

Will the static block run?

Think carefully.

This question checks whether array creation triggers class initialization, which is a very tricky JVM interview concept.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
The static block will NOT execute.

Output:

(no output)

docs.title: Why Static Block Does NOT Run
docs.text:
This line:

Test[] arr = new Test[10];

creates an array of references, not objects.

Memory looks like:

Stack
-----
arr  → reference

Heap
-----
Array[10]
   null
   null
   null
   null
   null
   null
   null
   null
   null
   null

Important:

No Test objects are created

Therefore:

Test class is not initialized

So the static block does not execute.

docs.title: Important JVM Rule
docs.text:
Array creation does not trigger class initialization

Only active use of a class triggers initialization.

docs.title: Example Where Static Block WILL Run
docs.text:
Test[] arr = new Test[10];
arr[0] = new Test();

Now output:

Static Block

Because:

new Test()

creates an object → class initialization happens.

docs.title: Another Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }

    static final int x = 10;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Test.x);
    }
}

docs.title: What will print?
docs.text: Will "Static Block" print or not?

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
10

There is no Static Block.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because:

static final int x = 10;

is a compile-time constant.

So the compiler replaces:

System.out.println(Test.x);

with something like:

System.out.println(10);

That means JVM does not need to initialize Test class to get x.

So:

  • class initialization does not happen
  • static block does not run

docs.title: Important JVM Rule
docs.text:
Accessing a static field usually triggers class initialization, but not when the field is a compile-time constant.

Examples of compile-time constants:

static final int x = 10;
static final String s = "Java";
static final boolean flag = true;

docs.title: But See This
docs.text:
class Test {
    static {
        System.out.println("Static Block");
    }

    static final Integer x = 10;
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Test.x);
    }
}

Now the output is:

Static Block
10

docs.title: Why this time?
docs.text:
Because:

static final Integer x = 10;

is not a compile-time constant in the same way as primitive int.

Integer is an object reference, so JVM must initialize the class.

docs.title: Static block will NOT run
docs.text:
static final int x = 10;
System.out.println(Test.x);

Because x is a compile-time constant.

docs.title: Static block WILL run
docs.text:
static int x = 10;
System.out.println(Test.x);

or

static final Integer x = 10;
System.out.println(Test.x);

Because class initialization is required.

docs.title: Easy Rule for Interview
docs.text:
If it is:

  • static final
  • primitive or String
  • value known at compile time

then it may be inlined by compiler and class initialization may not happen.

docs.title: Now you are entering real JVM interview depth.
docs.text: Before moving to GC, let’s finish this class-loading trap section with one more famous question.

docs.title: Predict output
docs.text:
class Parent {
    static int x = 10;

    static {
        System.out.println("Parent Static");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("Child Static");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Child.x);
    }
}

docs.title: Will it print:
docs.text:
1. only 10
  2. Parent Static then 10
  3. Parent Static, Child Static, then 10

Answer this:

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Parent Static
10

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
This line executes:

System.out.println(Child.x);

But x is not declared in Child.

It is declared in:

Parent

So JVM rule:

Accessing a static field triggers initialization
of the class that actually declares that field

Since x belongs to Parent, JVM initializes Parent only.

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
Step 1

JVM accesses:

Child.x

Step 2

JVM finds x in Parent class.

Step 3

JVM initializes Parent class.

Parent Static

Step 4

JVM reads x = 10.

10

docs.title: Why Child Static Block Does NOT Run
docs.text:
Because:

Child class is not initialized

We only accessed Parent’s static field.

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Referencing a static field initializes
only the class that declares the field

Not the subclass.

docs.title: Visual Flow
docs.text:
Child.x
   ↓
x belongs to Parent
   ↓
Initialize Parent
   ↓
Print Parent Static
   ↓
Return x
   ↓
Print 10

docs.title: Interview Trap Example
docs.text:
Now predict this:

class Parent {
    static {
        System.out.println("Parent Static");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    static int x = 10;

    static {
        System.out.println("Child Static");
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(Child.x);
    }
}

docs.title: What will print?
docs.text: 1️⃣ Child Static 10 2️⃣ Parent Static Child Static 10 3️⃣ Parent Static 10

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Parent Static
Child Static
10

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Now x is declared inside Child:

static int x = 10;

So when JVM accesses:

Child.x

it must initialize Child class.

But before a subclass is initialized:

Superclass must be initialized first

So JVM flow is:

Initialize Parent
→ print Parent Static

Initialize Child
→ assign x = 10
→ print Child Static

Access x
→ print 10

docs.title: If static member belongs to parent:
docs.text: Only parent initializes.

docs.title: If static member belongs to child:
docs.text:
Parent initializes first, then child initializes.

Excellent. Now let’s move to the next big JVM interview topic:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Escape Analysis is a JIT optimization that checks whether an object is used only inside a method or escapes outside it.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Escape Analysis helps explain why the JVM may optimize object allocation, remove unnecessary locks, and improve performance without changing Java code behavior.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: If a StringBuilder is created inside a method and never returned, stored globally, or passed somewhere unsafe, the JVM may optimize its allocation.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Java source code still uses normal object creation syntax.
  • Escape Analysis is an optimization, not a language guarantee.
  • The JVM may optimize allocation, but you should not depend on it for correctness.
  • An object escapes if it becomes reachable outside the method or thread.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Escape Analysis checks whether an object escapes the current method or thread. If it does not escape, the JIT compiler may apply optimizations like scalar replacement, stack allocation-like behavior, or lock elimination. These optimizations improve performance but do not change program output.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Escape means accessible outside the method or thread.
  • Non-escaping objects are easier to optimize.
  • JIT performs Escape Analysis.
  • Possible optimizations include scalar replacement and lock elimination.
  • It is not guaranteed by Java syntax.
  • Use it as a performance concept, not a coding rule.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Example:

public void method() {
    Person p = new Person();
}

If object p does not escape the method:

JVM may allocate it on stack instead of heap

This improves performance.

docs.title: Final Interview Question for You
docs.text:
Look at this code:

public void test() {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    sb.append("Java");
}

Do you think StringBuilder must always be allocated in heap, or can JVM allocate it in stack using escape analysis?

Explain your reasoning.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: JVM allocate it in stack using escape analysis

docs.title: Escape Analysis (JVM Optimization)
docs.text:
Escape Analysis is a JIT optimization technique.

It checks:

Does an object escape the method or thread?

If object does NOT escape, JVM may apply powerful optimizations.

docs.title: What Does "Escape" Mean?
docs.text:
An object escapes if it becomes accessible outside the method.

Example:

public Person create() {
    Person p = new Person();
    return p;
}

Here:

p escapes the method

Because it is returned.

So JVM must allocate it in heap.

docs.title: Example Where Object Does NOT Escape
docs.text:
public void test() {
    Person p = new Person();
}

Here:

p is used only inside method

When method ends:

object is useless

So JVM may optimize.

docs.title: Escape Analysis Optimization
docs.text: If object does not escape, JVM may do:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Stack Allocation
docs.text:
Instead of heap:

Heap allocation

JVM may allocate object in:

Stack

Stack allocation is much faster.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Scalar Replacement
docs.text:
JVM may remove the object entirely.

Example:

class Point {
    int x;
    int y;
}

Point p = new Point();
p.x = 10;
p.y = 20;

JVM may replace this with:

int x = 10
int y = 20

No object created at all.

docs.title: Your Question Code
docs.text:
public void test() {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    sb.append("Java");
}

Let's analyze.

sb:

not returned
not stored in field
not passed outside

So:

sb does NOT escape

Therefore JVM may allocate it on stack or remove object entirely.

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Most developers think:

All objects are created in heap

But with Escape Analysis:

Some objects may be optimized to stack

docs.title: JVM Optimization Chain
docs.text:
When code runs, JVM may apply:

Escape Analysis
↓
Stack Allocation
↓
Scalar Replacement
↓
Lock Elimination

These are advanced JIT optimizations.

docs.title: Lock Elimination Example
docs.text:
If object does not escape thread:

StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer();

Even though StringBuffer is synchronized, JVM may remove locking.

Because no other thread can access it.

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text:
If interviewer asks:

Are objects always allocated in heap?

Correct answer:

Usually yes,
but JVM may allocate objects on stack using Escape Analysis.

This answer shows deep JVM knowledge.

docs.title: Final JVM Architecture Summary
docs.text:
You now understand the complete JVM pipeline.

Java Source (.java)
      ↓
Compiler (javac)
      ↓
Bytecode (.class)
      ↓
ClassLoader
      ↓
Runtime Data Areas
   - Heap
   - Stack
   - Metaspace
   - PC Register
   - Native Stack
      ↓
Execution Engine
   - Interpreter
   - JIT Compiler
      ↓
Garbage Collector
      ↓
Native Machine Code

docs.title: Honest Feedback (for interviews)
docs.text:
Your JVM understanding is now good enough for most backend interviews.

You know:

✔ JVM memory ✔ Class loading ✔ Initialization traps ✔ String pool ✔ Object creation ✔ GC basics ✔ Execution engine ✔ JIT ✔ Escape analysis

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The execution engine runs Java bytecode. The JIT compiler improves performance by compiling frequently used bytecode into native machine code at runtime.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This topic explains how Java code actually runs, why Java can become faster after warm-up, and why proper benchmarking needs care.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: At first, bytecode may be interpreted. If a method runs many times, the JVM can mark it as hot code and JIT compile it into optimized native code.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Java is not only interpreted.
  • JIT compilation happens at runtime, not during javac.
  • Hot code is optimized more aggressively.
  • A small benchmark can be wrong if it ignores JVM warm-up.
  • JIT optimizations can change how code performs internally without changing behavior.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: The execution engine executes bytecode using the interpreter and JIT compiler. The interpreter starts quickly and runs bytecode line by line. The JIT compiler detects hot code and compiles it into optimized native code, which improves performance for repeated execution.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Interpreter executes bytecode.
  • JIT compiles hot code.
  • HotSpot means frequently executed code is optimized.
  • JIT runs during program execution.
  • Warm-up matters for benchmarks.
  • Common optimizations include inlining and escape analysis.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: That is another must-know interview topic.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: When an object has no references or is not reachable, it becomes eligible for GC. GC is the process of removing unreachable objects from the heap. Java can still have memory leaks when objects are not used but still reachable.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Difference Between "Eligible for GC" and "Garbage Collected"
docs.text: Answer is correct.

docs.title: Eligible for GC
docs.text:
Object has no reachable references

Example:

Person p = new Person();
p = null;

Now the object is eligible for GC.

But it still exists in heap.

docs.title: Garbage Collected
docs.text:
JVM actually removes the object from memory

Important rule:

Eligible for GC ≠ Immediately removed

Because GC runs when JVM decides.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why Java Can Still Have Memory Leaks
docs.text:
Key idea:

GC removes only unreachable objects

If an object is still reachable, GC cannot remove it.

Example:

static List<Object> cache = new ArrayList<>();

If objects are continuously added:

cache.add(new Object());

They remain reachable via the static reference.

Result:

Heap grows
Eventually → OutOfMemoryError

This is a logical memory leak.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Why Circular References Can Be Collected
docs.text:
Java GC uses:

Reachability analysis

Not:

Reference counting

Example:

class A { B b; }
class B { A a; }

A a = new A();
B b = new B();

a.b = b;
b.a = a;

a = null;
b = null;

Even though objects reference each other:

No GC root points to them

So JVM marks them unreachable and removes them.

docs.title: JVM Execution Engine (Next Topic)
docs.text:
The Execution Engine is responsible for:

Running the bytecode

Inside JVM architecture:

.class file
   ↓
ClassLoader
   ↓
Bytecode
   ↓
Execution Engine
   ↓
Machine instructions

docs.title: Components of Execution Engine
docs.text:
Execution engine mainly has:

1 Interpreter
2 JIT Compiler
3 Garbage Collector

Diagram:

Bytecode
   ↓
Execution Engine
   ├── Interpreter
   ├── JIT Compiler
   └── Garbage Collector

docs.title: 1️⃣ Interpreter
docs.text:
Interpreter reads bytecode line by line.

Example bytecode:

iload_1
iload_2
iadd

Interpreter executes instructions one at a time.

docs.title: Problem with Interpreter
docs.text:
It is slow.

Because each instruction must be interpreted every time.

Example:

loop runs 1,000,000 times

Interpreter reads bytecode again and again.

docs.title: 2️⃣ JIT Compiler (Just-In-Time)
docs.text:
To solve interpreter slowness, JVM introduced JIT Compiler.

JIT compiles frequently executed code into native machine code.

Flow:

Bytecode
   ↓
Interpreter runs initially
   ↓
Hotspot detection
   ↓
JIT compiles to machine code
   ↓
Next runs execute native code

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
for(int i=0;i<1000000;i++){
    sum += i;
}

This loop becomes hot code.

JIT compiles it to machine code.

Then execution becomes much faster.

docs.title: What is Hotspot?
docs.text:
Hotspot means:

Frequently executed code

JVM detects these methods and optimizes them.

That is why the JVM implementation is called:

HotSpot JVM

docs.title: Types of JIT Compiler
docs.text: Two types exist in modern JVM:

docs.title: C1 Compiler
docs.text:
Fast compilation
Less optimization

Used for quick startup.

docs.title: C2 Compiler
docs.text:
Slower compilation
Heavy optimization

Used for high performance.

docs.title: JVM Optimization Techniques
docs.text:
JIT performs many optimizations like:

Method inlining
Loop unrolling
Dead code elimination
Escape analysis
Constant folding

Example:

int x = 10 * 5;

JVM optimizes it to:

int x = 50;

docs.title: Method Inlining Example
docs.text:
Instead of:

sum = add(a,b);

JVM may inline the method:

sum = a + b;

This avoids method call overhead.

docs.title: Does Java compile to machine code?
docs.text:
Correct answer:

Java compiles to bytecode
JIT may later compile it to machine code

docs.title: Why Java programs become faster after some time?
docs.text:
Answer:

Because JIT compiles frequently used code

First runs slower, later runs faster.

docs.title: Interpreter vs JIT
docs.text: Feature Interpreter JIT Execution Line-by-line Native code Speed Slower Faster Compilation None Runtime

docs.title: Famous Interview Question
docs.text:
Why Java startup is slower than C++?

Answer:

Class loading
Bytecode verification
JIT compilation

But long-running programs become fast because of JIT.

docs.title: Final JVM Architecture Summary
docs.text:
Java Source (.java)
      ↓
Compiler (javac)
      ↓
Bytecode (.class)
      ↓
ClassLoader
      ↓
Runtime Data Areas
      ↓
Execution Engine
      ↓
Interpreter + JIT
      ↓
Machine Code

docs.title: Final Interview Question for You
docs.text:
Very famous JVM question.

Why does this program run faster after some time?

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        long start = System.currentTimeMillis();

        for(int i=0;i<100000000;i++){
            int x = i * 2;
        }

        long end = System.currentTimeMillis();
        System.out.println(end - start);
    }
}

If we run it multiple times in same JVM process, later runs become faster.

Why?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: Because the JIT compiler compiles this loop into native machine code.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
for(int i = 0; i < 100000000; i++){
    int x = i * 2;
}

When the program runs the first time, JVM does not immediately compile it to machine code.

docs.title: Step 1 — Interpreter Executes First
docs.text:
Initially JVM runs bytecode using the Interpreter.

Flow:

Bytecode
   ↓
Interpreter executes instruction by instruction

So execution is slower.

docs.title: Step 2 — Hotspot Detection
docs.text:
JVM monitors frequently executed methods or loops.

When code runs many times, JVM marks it as hot code.

Example:

loop executed millions of times

Now JVM decides:

This code should be optimized

docs.title: Step 3 — JIT Compilation
docs.text:
JIT compiles the hot code to native machine code.

Flow becomes:

Bytecode
   ↓
JIT Compiler
   ↓
Native Machine Code

Now the CPU executes machine code directly.

So execution becomes much faster.

docs.title: Final Flow
docs.text:
First execution:

Bytecode → Interpreter → Slow

Later execution:

Bytecode → JIT → Native Code → Fast

That is why programs become faster after some time.

docs.title: Important JVM Optimizations Done by JIT
docs.text: JIT may also perform optimizations like:

docs.title: Method Inlining
docs.text:
Instead of:

result = multiply(a, b);

JIT may inline:

result = a * b;

docs.title: Dead Code Elimination
docs.text:
If some code does nothing useful, JVM removes it.

Example:

int x = 5;
x = 10;

JVM may remove the first assignment.

docs.title: Loop Optimization
docs.text:
JIT optimizes loops heavily.

Example:

loop unrolling

docs.title: Very Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
Look at this code again:

for(int i=0;i<100000000;i++){
    int x = i * 2;
}

A very smart JVM may optimize this even further.

Because variable x is never used.

So JVM may eliminate this entire loop.

This is called:

Dead Code Elimination

That is why microbenchmarks in Java are tricky.

docs.title: Correct Way to Benchmark Java
docs.text:
Use tools like:

JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness)

Because simple timing tests can be optimized away by JVM.

docs.title: Final JVM Execution Engine Summary
docs.text:
Bytecode
   ↓
Interpreter executes
   ↓
Hotspot detection
   ↓
JIT compiler optimizes
   ↓
Native machine code

docs.title: Excellent Progress
docs.text:
You now understand most important JVM topics:

  • JVM architecture
  • Heap vs Stack
  • ClassLoader
  • Class initialization traps
  • String pool
  • Object creation
  • Garbage collection
  • Execution engine
  • JIT compiler

This is already strong JVM interview knowledge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Garbage Collection is the JVM process that removes unreachable objects from heap memory.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: GC helps you explain memory cleanup, heap usage, memory leaks, object reachability, and why Java does not require manual memory free calls.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: If Person p = new Person(); is followed by p = null;, the object may become eligible for GC if no other reference can reach it.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Eligible for GC does not mean immediately collected.
  • System.gc() does not guarantee immediate collection.
  • Circular references can be collected if they are unreachable.
  • Java can still have memory leaks when unused objects remain reachable.
  • finalize() is not a reliable cleanup mechanism.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Garbage Collection automatically clears unreachable objects from heap memory. The JVM starts from GC roots and checks which objects are reachable. Objects that cannot be reached become eligible for collection. The exact time of collection is decided by the JVM.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• GC works on heap objects.
  • Reachable objects are kept.
  • Unreachable objects are eligible for GC.
  • GC timing is not guaranteed.
  • GC roots decide reachability.
  • Memory leaks can still happen in Java.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: This is one of the most asked topics in backend interviews.

docs.title: 1. What is Garbage Collection?
docs.text:
Garbage Collection means:

JVM automatically removes unreachable objects
from heap memory.

In C/C++ developer manually frees memory.

In Java:

JVM handles memory cleanup automatically

That is why Java is easier and safer than manual-memory languages.

docs.title: 2. What is Garbage?
docs.text:
An object becomes garbage when it is no longer reachable.

Example:

Person p = new Person();
p = null;

Now the first object has no reference.

So it becomes eligible for garbage collection.

Important interview word:

Eligible for GC

Not:

Immediately removed

Because GC timing is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Does p = null destroy object immediately?
docs.text:
No.

It only makes the object eligible for GC.

Actual cleanup depends on JVM.

docs.title: 4. How JVM Knows an Object is Garbage
docs.text:
JVM starts from GC Roots.

If object is reachable from GC roots, it stays alive.

If not reachable, it can be collected.

docs.title: 5. What are GC Roots?
docs.text:
Common GC roots:

  • local variables in stack
  • active thread references
  • static references
  • JNI/native references

Example:

public static void main(String[] args) {
    Person p = new Person();
}

Here p is in stack frame, so object is reachable.

docs.title: 6. Reachability Example
docs.text:
Person p1 = new Person();
Person p2 = p1;
p1 = null;

Is object garbage?

No

Because p2 still points to it.

Another example:

Person p1 = new Person();
Person p2 = p1;
p1 = null;
p2 = null;

Now object becomes eligible for GC.

docs.title: 7. Heap Generations
docs.text:
This is very important.

Heap is divided mainly into:

Young Generation
Old Generation

Young Generation further contains:

Eden
Survivor 0
Survivor 1

Diagram:

Heap
------------------------------------------------
Young Generation
   Eden | S0 | S1

Old Generation
------------------------------------------------

docs.title: 8. Why Heap is Divided
docs.text:
Because most objects die young.

Examples:

  • temporary loop objects
  • request-scoped objects
  • short-lived StringBuilder
  • local collections

So JVM optimizes GC using this rule.

This is called:

Generational Garbage Collection

docs.title: 9. Object Life Cycle in Heap
docs.text:
When object is created:

new Person()

it usually goes to:

Eden space

If it survives a GC cycle:

Eden → Survivor

If it survives many cycles:

Survivor → Old Generation

Flow:

Eden → Survivor → Old

docs.title: Minor GC
docs.text:
Cleans Young Generation.

Usually fast.

docs.title: Major GC
docs.text:
Cleans Old Generation.

Usually slower.

docs.title: Full GC
docs.text:
Cleans whole heap.

Very expensive.

docs.title: Are Major GC and Full GC always exactly same?
docs.text:
In many interview discussions people use them loosely, but technically they are not always strictly identical depending on JVM implementation.

Safe interview answer:

Minor GC → Young generation
Major GC → Old generation
Full GC → Entire heap

docs.title: 12. Example of Minor GC Flow
docs.text:
Suppose Eden becomes full.

JVM runs Minor GC.

  • dead objects removed
  • live objects moved to Survivor
  • objects surviving multiple rounds may move to Old Gen

docs.title: 13. Example
docs.text:
for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
    String s = new String("abc");
}

Most of these objects are temporary.

They die quickly.

So they are cleaned from Young Generation.

docs.title: 14. When Does Object Move to Old Generation?
docs.text:
If object survives multiple GC cycles, JVM promotes it.

Example long-living objects:

  • cache objects
  • singleton-held objects
  • session-like long-lived structures
  • static referenced objects

These often end up in Old Generation.

docs.title: Are all objects directly created in Old Generation?
docs.text:
No.

Usually they are created in:

Young Generation → Eden

That is the expected interview answer.

docs.title: 16. Can GC Collect an Object Having Circular References?
docs.text:
Yes.

Example:

class A { B b; }
class B { A a; }

A a = new A();
B b = new B();
a.b = b;
b.a = a;

a = null;
b = null;

Now both objects reference each other.

But if no GC root points to them, JVM can still collect them.

Important point:

Java GC is based on reachability,
not simple reference counting

This is a very common interview question.

docs.title: 17. System.gc() Interview Trap
docs.text: Question:

docs.title: Does System.gc() guarantee GC?
docs.text:
No.

It is only a request/suggestion to JVM.

JVM may ignore it.

docs.title: 18. finalize() Interview Trap
docs.text:
Old interview question:

protected void finalize() throws Throwable { }

Important:

  • not guaranteed to run on time
  • not guaranteed to run at all before program exits
  • deprecated and should be avoided

So in modern interviews:

Do not rely on finalize() for cleanup

Use:

  • try-with-resources
  • AutoCloseable
  • explicit cleanup

docs.title: 19. Can an Object Be Resurrected in finalize()?
docs.text:
Theoretically yes, old-school trick:

class Test {
    static Test saved;

    protected void finalize() {
        saved = this;
    }
}

But this is bad practice and deprecated behavior territory.

Mention it only if interviewer asks deep JVM traps.

docs.title: Is an object with reference null always garbage?
docs.text:
Not necessarily.

Example:

Person p1 = new Person();
Person p2 = p1;
p1 = null;

Here p1 is null, but object is still alive because p2 points to it.

docs.title: 21. Memory Leak in Java?
docs.text:
People think Java has no memory leak because of GC.

Wrong.

Java can still have memory leaks if objects remain reachable unintentionally.

Example:

  • static collections growing forever
  • cache without eviction
  • listeners not removed
  • ThreadLocal misuse

GC removes only unreachable objects.

If your code still references them, GC cannot help.

docs.title: Q1. How does JVM decide an object is garbage?
docs.text: By checking reachability from GC roots.

docs.title: Q2. Difference between Minor GC and Full GC?
docs.text: Minor GC cleans Young Gen; Full GC cleans whole heap.

docs.title: Q3. Does setting reference to null force GC?
docs.text: No, it only makes object eligible.

docs.title: Q4. Can circularly referenced objects be garbage collected?
docs.text: Yes, if unreachable from GC roots.

docs.title: Q5. Does Java prevent memory leaks completely?
docs.text: No.

docs.title: 23. Very Important GC Trap
docs.text:
Look at this:

public class Test {
    static List<byte[]> list = new ArrayList<>();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        while (true) {
            list.add(new byte[1024 * 1024]);
        }
    }
}

What happens?

Answer:

  • objects are stored in heap
  • list is static, so reachable from GC root
  • objects cannot be collected
  • eventually OutOfMemoryError

This is a classic Java memory leak style interview example.

docs.title: Stack memory cleanup vs Heap cleanup
docs.text:
Stack variables are removed automatically when method ends.

Heap objects are removed by GC only when unreachable.

docs.title: 25. Quick Summary
docs.text:
GC removes unreachable heap objects
New objects usually start in Eden
Minor GC → Young Gen
Major GC → Old Gen
Full GC → entire heap
System.gc() is not guaranteed
Java can still have memory leaks
Circular references can still be collected

docs.title: Mini Interview Quiz
docs.text: Answer these:

What is the difference between:

  • eligible for GC
  • garbage collected
Why can Java still have memory leaks even with GC?

Why can circular references still be collected in Java?

After that I will teach the next deep topic:

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: JVM memory structure is the way the JVM divides runtime memory into areas like heap, stack, metaspace, PC register, and native method stack.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Memory structure helps you explain object creation, method calls, local variables, static data, StackOverflowError, and OutOfMemoryError.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: For Person p = new Person("Vishu");, the Person object is created in heap, the reference variable p is stored in the current stack frame, and the string literal can be stored in the string pool.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• The reference variable and object are different things.
  • Local variables are stored in stack frames.
  • Objects are usually stored in heap.
  • Static metadata is not stored in the same place as local variables.
  • Stack cleanup is automatic when a method ends.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: The JVM divides memory into multiple runtime areas. The stack stores method frames and local variables for each thread. The heap stores objects. Metaspace stores class metadata. The PC register tracks the current instruction for a thread, and the native method stack supports native calls.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Stack: method calls and local variables.
  • Heap: objects.
  • Metaspace: class metadata.
  • PC register: current instruction.
  • Native method stack: native method execution.
  • Each thread has its own stack.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
This includes:

Heap
Stack
Metaspace
PC Register
Native Method Stack

Understanding this properly will help you answer:

StackOverflowError
OutOfMemoryError
Object creation
String pool
Garbage collection

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
1️⃣ Object created in heap memory ✔ Correct.

Person object → Heap

2️⃣ Reference variable stored in function stack memory

Reference variable is stored in the stack frame
of the current method (main method here).

So more precise:

p → stored in main() stack frame

3️⃣ "Vishu" string stored in string pool which is part of heap memory ✔ Correct for Java 7+

Important interview detail:

Java Version String Pool Location Java 6 PermGen Java 7+ Heap

So today:

String Pool → inside Heap

docs.title: JVM Memory Components
docs.text:
JVM has 5 main memory areas.

JVM Memory

1 Program Counter Register (PC)

5 Native Method Stack

Diagram:

                JVM MEMORY

           +--------------------+
           |   Method Area      |

Thread 1           Thread 2
---------          ---------

PC Register        PC Register
Stack              Stack
Native Stack       Native Stack

Important rule:

Heap → shared by all threads
Stack → each thread has its own stack

docs.title: 1️⃣ JVM Stack
docs.text:
Each thread gets its own stack.

Example:

Main Thread
Worker Thread
GC Thread

Each thread has its own:

Stack

Inside stack:

Example:

Stack

| main() frame     |

Local variables

Return address

docs.text:
Q1

What causes

Too many stack frames
usually caused by recursion

Example:

docs.text:
Heap stores:

Objects
Arrays

Stores:

Example:

method bytecode
static fields

Since Java 8:

PermGen removed
Metaspace introduced

Metaspace is stored in:

Native memory (outside heap)

Method Area (Metaspace)

But many people incorrectly say heap.

docs.text:
Each thread has its own PC Register.

It stores:

Address of current instruction

Example:

Line 5 executing

docs.text:
Used for native methods.

Example:

C / C++ methods

Example:

System.arraycopy()

docs.title: Now we go deeper (Important for Senior Interviews)
docs.text:
Next topic is HEAP ARCHITECTURE.

Most people only know:

Heap → Objects

But internally JVM Heap is divided into generations.

Heap

1 Young Generation
   - Eden
   - Survivor 1
   - Survivor 2

2 Old Generation

3 (Before Java 8)
   Permanent Generation

Diagram:

Heap
------------------------------------------------

Young Generation
----------------
Eden
Survivor 0
Survivor 1

Old Generation
----------------
Long living objects

docs.title: Why JVM Divides Heap Like This
docs.text:
Because most objects die very quickly.

Example:

loop variables
temporary objects
StringBuilder
request objects

These die in seconds or milliseconds.

So JVM uses Generational Garbage Collection.

docs.title: Object Life Cycle
docs.text:
When object is created:

new Person()

Object goes to:

Eden Space

docs.title: GC Flow
docs.text:
Eden full
↓
Minor GC
↓
Objects moved to Survivor
↓
Objects survive many GC
↓
Promoted to Old Generation

docs.title: Simplified Flow
docs.text: Eden → Survivor → Old Generation

docs.title: What is Minor GC?
docs.text:
Answer:

Garbage collection in Young Generation

docs.title: What is Major GC?
docs.text: Garbage collection in Old Generation

docs.title: What is Full GC?
docs.text:
Entire heap cleanup

This is very expensive.

docs.title: Very Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
Question:

Where are new objects created?

Correct answer:

Eden space

Many candidates incorrectly say Heap.

But interviewer expects:

Young Generation → Eden

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The string pool is a JVM memory area that stores string literals for reuse. Object creation is the internal JVM process that allocates memory, initializes fields, calls constructors, and assigns references.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: String pool and object creation questions are common because they test whether you understand heap memory, references, literals, constructors, and == vs equals().

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: String s1 = "Java"; reuses a pooled literal. String s3 = new String("Java"); creates a new object, so s1 == s3 is usually false.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• == compares references, not string content.
  • String literals can be reused from the pool.
  • new String("Java") creates a separate object.
  • A constructor initializes an object; it does not allocate memory by itself.
  • Runtime string concatenation behaves differently from compile-time constants.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: String literals are stored in the string pool so the JVM can reuse them. When we use new String(...), Java creates a new object instead of reusing only the pooled literal. During object creation, the JVM loads the class if needed, allocates memory, gives default values, runs initialization logic, calls the constructor, and stores the reference.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• String literals are pooled.
  • new String() creates a new object.
  • == checks reference equality.
  • equals() checks content for strings.
  • Object creation includes allocation and initialization.
  • Constructors do not create memory; they initialize the object.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Next we will cover OBJECT CREATION INSIDE JVM.

When JVM executes:

Person p = new Person();

JVM performs 10 internal steps like:

Class loading
Memory allocation
Default initialization
Constructor call
Reference assignment

Most developers don't know these steps.

Before we go deeper, answer this interview puzzle:

String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";
String s3 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);
System.out.println(s1 == s3);

What will be the output?

Explain why. This will lead us to the String Pool deep concept, which is one of the most asked JVM interview topics.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
true
false

docs.title: Step 1 — "Java" literal
docs.text:
When JVM sees:

String s1 = "Java";

JVM checks the String Pool.

If "Java" is not present:

Create "Java" in String Pool

Memory:

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

Then

s1 → "Java"

docs.title: Step 2 — second literal
docs.text:
String s2 = "Java";

JVM again checks String Pool.

Since "Java" already exists:

No new object created

s2 → "Java"

Memory:

Stack
-----
s1 → "Java"
s2 → "Java"

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

So

s1 == s2 → true

Because == compares reference address.

docs.title: Step 3 — new String("Java")
docs.text:
String s3 = new String("Java");

Two things happen here.

docs.title: 1️⃣ JVM checks String Pool
docs.text:
If "Java" exists → reuse it.

So pool remains:

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

docs.title: 2️⃣ JVM creates a new object in Heap
docs.text:
Heap
----
String object
   value → "Java"

So memory becomes:

Stack
-----
s1 → "Java"
s2 → "Java"
s3 → Heap String object


Heap
----
String Object
   value → "Java"

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

docs.title: Why s1 == s3 is false
docs.text:
Because

s1 → pool object
s3 → heap object

Two different addresses.

So

s1 == s3 → false

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
How many objects are created?

String s = new String("Java");

Most people say 1 ❌

Correct answer:

2 objects

1️⃣ "Java" in String Pool 2️⃣ new String() object in Heap

But if "Java" already exists in pool:

Only 1 new object created

docs.title: Another Interview Trap
docs.text:
What about this?

String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1.equals(s2));

Output:

true

Because:

equals() compares content
== compares reference

docs.title: Very Important JVM Feature — intern()
docs.text:
Example:

String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = s1.intern();

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Explanation:

intern() → returns reference from String Pool

Memory:

s1 → Heap String
s2 → Pool "Java"

So

s1 == s2 → false

But:

String s3 = "Java";

System.out.println(s2 == s3);

true

Because both refer to pool object.

docs.title: Interview Level String Pool Question
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s1 = "Ja" + "va";
String s2 = "Java";

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Output:

true

Reason:

Compile-time constant folding

Compiler converts:

"Ja" + "va" → "Java"

docs.title: But This Changes Everything
docs.text:
String s1 = "Ja";
String s2 = s1 + "va";
String s3 = "Java";

System.out.println(s2 == s3);

Output:

false

Because:

s1 + "va" happens at runtime

JVM creates new object.

docs.title: This Topic Leads to Another Deep JVM Concept
docs.text: Next we should study:

docs.title: OBJECT CREATION INSIDE JVM
docs.text:
When JVM executes:

Person p = new Person();

Internally JVM performs around 8–10 steps, including:

1 Class loading
2 Memory allocation
3 Object header creation
4 Default value initialization
5 Constructor execution
6 Reference assignment

Understanding this helps in interviews about:

JVM
Memory
GC
Performance

Before we go there, answer this interview puzzle:

docs.title: What will be the output?
docs.text:
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = new String("Java").intern();

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Explain why.

Because both point to the same "Java" object in the String Pool. intern() checks whether "Java" exists in the String Pool. If it exists, it returns that reference; otherwise it creates it in the pool and returns it.

docs.title: Output:
docs.text: true

docs.title: Step 1 — "Java" literal
docs.text:
String s1 = "Java";

JVM checks the String Pool.

If "Java" is not present → it creates it.

Memory:

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

Then:

s1 → "Java" (pool object)

docs.title: Step 2 — new String("Java")
docs.text:
new String("Java")

Two things happen:

docs.title: 1️⃣ JVM checks the pool
docs.text:
"Java" already exists.

So it reuses the pool literal.

docs.title: 2️⃣ JVM creates a new String object in heap
docs.text:
Heap
-----
String object
   value -> "Java"

But at this moment:

Heap object ≠ Pool object

docs.title: Step 3 — .intern()
docs.text:
.intern()

intern() returns the reference from the String Pool.

Since "Java" already exists in the pool:

intern() → returns pool reference

So:

s2 → "Java" (pool object)

docs.title: Final Memory
docs.text:
Stack
-----
s1 → "Java"
s2 → "Java"

Heap
----
String object (unused reference)

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

docs.title: Final Comparison
docs.text:
s1 == s2

Both point to the same pool object.

true

docs.title: Important Interview Trap
docs.text: This question often comes next.

docs.title: What is the difference?
docs.text:
new String("Java")
vs
"Java"
Expression Object Created "Java" String Pool new String("Java") Heap object

docs.title: Very Famous Interview Puzzle
docs.text:
Predict output:

String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Answer:

false

Because:

Two different heap objects

docs.title: Senior Interview Level Question
docs.text:
What about this?

String s1 = new String("Java").intern();
String s2 = new String("Java").intern();

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Answer:

true

Because both refer to same pool object.

docs.title: Now we move to a very important JVM topic
docs.text: This is asked in Amazon / Flipkart / backend interviews.

docs.title: Object Creation Inside JVM
docs.text:
When JVM executes:

Person p = new Person();

Internally JVM performs 8 internal steps like:

1 Class loading
2 Class linking
3 Class initialization
4 Memory allocation
5 Object header creation
6 Default field initialization
7 Constructor execution
8 Reference assignment

Understanding this explains:

ClassLoader
Heap
Stack
Metaspace

Before I explain those internal 8 JVM steps, answer this interview trap:

docs.title: What will be the output?
docs.text:
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Ja" + new String("va");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Explain why. This tests compile-time vs runtime string creation, which is a very common JVM interview topic.

This is not a compile-time constant.

docs.title: Output:
docs.text: false

docs.title: Step 1 — "Java"
docs.text:
String s1 = "Java";

JVM checks the String Pool.

If "Java" does not exist → create it.

Memory:

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

Then:

s1 → "Java"

docs.title: Step 2 — "Ja"
docs.text:
Inside

"Ja" + new String("va")

The literal "Ja" is stored in the String Pool.

String Pool
-----------
"Java"
"Ja"

docs.title: Step 3 — new String("va")
docs.text: Two things happen.

docs.title: Pool check
docs.text:
"va"

If not present → add to pool.

docs.title: Heap object creation
docs.text:
Heap
----
String object ("va")

So now:

Stack
-----
s1 → "Java"

Heap
----
String("va")

String Pool
-----------
"Java"
"Ja"
"va"

docs.title: Step 4 — String Concatenation
docs.text:
This part is important:

"Ja" + new String("va")

Because one operand is a runtime object, the compiler cannot optimize it.

So JVM converts this internally to:

new StringBuilder()
     .append("Ja")
     .append(new String("va"))
     .toString();

So JVM creates:

StringBuilder object

Then:

new String("Java")

in Heap.

Memory becomes:

Heap
----
String("va")
StringBuilder
String("Java")

Now:

s2 → Heap "Java"

docs.title: Final Memory
docs.text:
Stack
-----
s1 → Pool "Java"
s2 → Heap "Java"

String Pool
-----------
"Java"
"Ja"
"va"

Heap
----
String("va")
StringBuilder
String("Java")

docs.title: Final Comparison
docs.text:
s1 == s2

This compares references.

Pool "Java" ≠ Heap "Java"

So

false

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
If all parts are literals:

"Ja" + "va"

Compiler optimizes at compile time.

Becomes:

"Java"

So:

String s1 = "Ja" + "va";
String s2 = "Java";

s1 == s2 → true

docs.title: But if any part is runtime
docs.text:
Example:

String a = "Ja";
String s = a + "va";

Now concatenation happens at runtime.

So:

new String object created in Heap

Thus:

s1 == s2 → false

docs.title: Quick Interview Summary
docs.text: Expression Result "Ja" + "va" Compile-time constant "a" + variable Runtime concatenation new String("Java") Heap object intern() Returns pool reference

docs.title: Next Topic: Object Creation Inside JVM
docs.text:
When JVM executes:

Person p = new Person("Vishu");

most people say only:

  • object created in heap
  • reference stored in stack

That is correct, but interviewers want deeper internal steps.

docs.title: Internal Steps of Object Creation in JVM
Code
docs.text:
Person p = new Person("Vishu");

JVM internally does roughly this sequence:

docs.title: 1. Class is loaded
docs.text:
If Person.class is not loaded yet, JVM loads it through the ClassLoader subsystem.

It loads:

  • class metadata
  • fields
  • methods
  • constructor info
  • constant pool references

docs.title: 2. Class linking happens
docs.text: Linking has 3 parts:

docs.title: a) Verification
docs.text:
JVM checks bytecode is valid or not.

Examples:

  • illegal bytecode?
  • stack usage valid?
  • type safety correct?

docs.title: b) Preparation
docs.text:
Memory is allocated for static variables and they get default values.

Example:

static int x = 10;

During preparation:

  • memory allocated for x
  • first default value becomes 0

Actual 10 comes later in initialization.

docs.title: c) Resolution
docs.text:
Symbolic references are converted to direct references.

Example: class/method/field names are resolved internally.

docs.title: 3. Class initialization happens
docs.text:
Static initializers and static variables get actual values.

Example:

static int x = 10;
static {
    System.out.println("Static block");
}

Now static block runs and x becomes 10.

docs.title: 4. JVM checks memory in heap
docs.text:
JVM now checks whether enough heap space is available for the new object.

If not, it may try GC.

If still not enough:

OutOfMemoryError

docs.title: 5. Memory is allocated for object
docs.text:
Memory is allocated in heap, usually in Eden space.

This memory includes:

  • object header
  • instance fields
  • padding if required

docs.title: Object Memory Layout
docs.text: A Java object generally contains:

docs.title: 1) Object Header
docs.text:
Contains JVM internal information such as:

  • class metadata pointer
  • hash code info
  • GC age
  • lock status

docs.title: 2) Instance Data
docs.text:
Actual fields of object.

Example:

class Person {
    int age;
    String name;
}

Instance data stores:

  • age
  • reference to name

docs.title: 3) Padding
docs.text: Extra bytes may be added for memory alignment.

docs.title: 6. Default initialization of instance fields
docs.text:
Before constructor runs, fields get default values.

Example:

class Person {
    int age;
    String name;
}

Defaults become:

age = 0
name = null

This is very important.

So before constructor code runs, object is already created with default values.

docs.title: 7. Constructor executes
docs.text:
Now constructor runs.

Person(String name) {
    this.name = name;
}

Now field values are updated.

So:

name = "Vishu"

docs.title: 8. Reference is assigned to variable
docs.text:
Now the object reference is stored in local variable p inside the current stack frame.

So final result:

  • object → heap
  • p reference → stack frame of current method

docs.title: Full Flow in One Line
docs.text: Class Load → Link → Initialize → Allocate Heap Memory → Default Values → Constructor Runs → Reference Assigned

docs.title: Does constructor create the object?
docs.text:
No.

This is a very common trap.

Correct answer:

  • JVM allocates memory and creates the object first
  • then constructor initializes it

So constructor does not create the object; it initializes the already created object.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Test {
    int x;

    Test() {
        System.out.println(x);
        x = 10;
    }
}

When object is created:

  • first x = 0
  • constructor runs
  • prints 0
  • then sets x = 10

docs.title: Why can constructor use this?
docs.text:
Because the object is already allocated before constructor body executes.

That is why this is available inside constructor.

docs.title: Where does constructor code live?
docs.text:
Constructor code is part of the class metadata / bytecode, not inside heap object.

  • constructor definition → class area / metaspace side
  • object data → heap

docs.title: Visual Memory View
docs.text:
For this code:

Person p = new Person("Vishu");

Memory looks like:

Stack (main frame)
------------------
p  -----------+

Heap
------------------
Person object
  name -------> "Vishu"

String Pool / Heap
------------------
"Vishu"

Metaspace
------------------
Person.class
constructor info
method metadata
field metadata

docs.title: 1. What happens first: constructor call or memory allocation?
docs.text: Memory allocation happens first.

docs.title: 2. Are fields initialized before constructor?
docs.text: Yes. Default values first, then constructor values.

docs.title: 3. Does new only call constructor?
docs.text: No. It also triggers object memory allocation and initialization steps.

docs.title: 4. Where is object header stored?
docs.text: Inside the object in heap memory.

docs.title: Dry Run Example
docs.text:
class Person {
    int age;
    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = 25;
    }
}

Person p = new Person("Vishu");

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text: Person.class loaded if not already loaded.

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Heap memory allocated for Person object.

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Default values assigned:

age = 0
name = null

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text:
Constructor runs:

name = "Vishu"
age = 25

docs.title: Step 5
docs.text:
Reference stored in p.

Final object:

age = 25
name = "Vishu"

docs.title: Trap 1
docs.text:
Object is created in stack. ❌ Wrong

Object is created in heap.

docs.title: Trap 2
docs.text:
Constructor creates object. ❌ Wrong

Constructor only initializes object.

docs.title: Trap 3
