docs.text:
Fields directly get assigned constructor values first. ❌ Wrong

Default initialization happens first.

docs.title: Trap 4
docs.text:
Reference variable stores full object. ❌ Wrong

Reference variable stores only address/reference.

docs.title: Mini Interview Quiz
docs.text:
Answer these:

class Demo {
    int x;
    static int y;

    Demo() {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Demo d = new Demo();

docs.title: Tell me:
docs.text:
1. Where is x stored?
  2. Where is y stored?
  3. What value is printed, and why?
  4. Does constructor create the object or initialize it?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
x is stored inside object which is stored in heap memory

✔ Correct.

Memory:

Heap
-----
Demo Object
   x = 0

Instance variables always live inside the object.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
y is stored in class metadata

✔ Correct.

More precise interview answer:

Static variables belong to the class
Stored in Method Area / Metaspace

Memory:

Metaspace
---------
Demo.class
   static int y

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
0 because default initialised before constructor call

✔ Correct.

Object creation flow:

1 Allocate memory
2 Default initialization
3 Constructor execution

So before constructor runs:

x = 0

Constructor prints:

0

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Constructor initialize the object, does not create it

✔ Correct.

Important interview statement:

Object creation = JVM responsibility
Constructor = object initialization

docs.title: Excellent Progress 👍
docs.text:
You are now covering real JVM interview topics, not just syntax.

Now we move to the next big JVM subsystem.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Multithreading means running multiple threads inside one process so different tasks can make progress independently.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This is the base for Java concurrency interviews. It explains threads, processes, lifecycle, scheduling, and why concurrent code can be difficult.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A web server can use different threads to handle multiple requests at the same time.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Calling run() does not start a new thread.
  • Calling start() asks the JVM to create a new thread.
  • Thread scheduling is controlled by the JVM and operating system.
  • Output order from multiple threads is not guaranteed.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: A thread is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process. In Java, we can create threads using Thread, Runnable, or higher-level concurrency APIs. Calling start() creates a new call stack and lets the JVM run the thread separately. Calling run() is just a normal method call.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Process owns memory and resources.
  • Thread executes code inside a process.
  • start() creates a new thread.
  • run() is a normal method call.
  • Thread output order is not guaranteed.
  • Thread lifecycle matters in interviews.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: Multithreading deep dive, end-to-end. We’ll go basic → advanced, with internals + traps + interview answers. No fluff.

docs.title: Level 1: What is a Thread? What is a Process?
docs.text:
• Process: independent program instance (separate memory space).
  • Thread: execution path inside a process (threads share heap, have separate stacks).

Key interview line

Threads share heap (objects) but each thread has its own stack (local variables, frames).

docs.title: Option A: Extend Thread
docs.text:
class T extends Thread {
  public void run() { System.out.println("run"); }
}
new T().start();

docs.title: Option B: Implement Runnable (preferred)
docs.text:
class Task implements Runnable {
  public void run() { System.out.println("run"); }
}
new Thread(new Task()).start();

Why Runnable preferred?

  • Your class can extend something else (Java single inheritance)
  • Separation of task (Runnable) from execution (Thread)

docs.title: ✅ Absolute Must-Know: start() vs run() (Top trap)
docs.text:
• start() → creates a new OS/JVM thread, then calls run() on that new thread.
  • run() → normal method call, runs on current thread, no new thread.

Interview one-liner

Calling run() doesn’t start a new thread; start() does.

docs.title: Thread Lifecycle (Interview)
docs.text:
States (simplified):

  • NEW
  • RUNNABLE (ready/running)
  • BLOCKED (waiting for monitor lock)
  • WAITING (wait/join without timeout)
  • TIMED_WAITING (sleep/join with timeout)
  • TERMINATED

docs.title: CPU Scheduling Basics (What you must accept)
docs.text:
• Thread execution order is not guaranteed
  • Prints can interleave unpredictably
  • Priority is a hint, not a guarantee (OS-dependent)

docs.title: Q1: start vs run
docs.text:
class A extends Thread {
  public void run() { System.out.print("R"); }
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    A t = new A();
    t.run();
    System.out.print("M");
  }
}

What prints?

docs.title: Q2: start order
docs.text:
class A extends Thread {
  public void run() { System.out.print("T"); }
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    new A().start();
    System.out.print("M");
  }
}

Possible outputs?

docs.title: Q3: sleep
docs.text:
public class Test {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    System.out.print("A");
    Thread.sleep(0);
    System.out.print("B");
  }
}

What prints?

Reply with:

  • Q1 output
  • Q2 possible outputs
  • Q3 output

The correct answers + why (deep, interview style).

docs.title: Q1: run() vs start()
docs.text:
Code:

t.run();
System.out.print("M");

docs.title: ✅ Output
docs.text: RM

docs.title: Why
docs.text: t.run() is just a normal method call on the main thread, so it prints R, then main prints M.

docs.title: Q2: start() scheduling
docs.text:
Code:

new A().start();
System.out.print("M");

docs.title: ✅ Possible outputs
docs.text:
TM
MT

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
start() creates a new thread, but scheduling is unpredictable:

  • Thread may run first → T then M
  • Main may print first → M then T

docs.title: Q3: Thread.sleep(0)
docs.text:
Code:

System.out.print("A");
Thread.sleep(0);
System.out.print("B");

docs.title: ✅ Output
docs.text: AB

docs.title: Why
docs.text: sleep(0) does not end the thread or switch threads reliably. It just sleeps for 0 ms (effectively no-op). So prints A then B.

docs.title: ✅ Quick Fix: Your mistakes
docs.text:
• Q1: you missed that run() prints R
  • Q3: you confused print character (B) with M

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Asynchronous execution lets work run without blocking the caller. CompletableFuture models async results, and ForkJoinPool supports divide-and-conquer parallel work.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: These tools are used in backend systems for non-blocking flows, parallel computation, and combining independent tasks.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A service can call two APIs using CompletableFuture, then combine both results when they complete.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Async code does not mean faster for every task.
  • Blocking inside async tasks can waste worker threads.
  • CompletableFuture exceptions must be handled.
  • ForkJoin works best for recursive split-and-merge tasks.
  • Parallelism has overhead.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: CompletableFuture represents a result that will be available later and supports chaining, combining, and error handling. ForkJoinPool is designed for tasks that can be split into smaller tasks and joined later. Both help with concurrency, but they should be used when the workload fits the model.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Async work does not block the caller.
  • CompletableFuture supports chaining.
  • Handle async exceptions.
  • ForkJoin uses divide and conquer.
  • Work stealing improves parallel execution.
  • Use parallelism only when it helps.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Two powerful tools remain:

ForkJoinPool
CompletableFuture

These are used in high-performance async programming.

Before moving forward, one quick check:

If we create:

Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(5);

and 10 threads call acquire(), how many threads will run immediately?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: “5 threads will acquire permits and run immediately, while the remaining 5 threads will block until permits are released.”

docs.title: Step-by-step What Happens
docs.text:
Semaphore created:

Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(5);

Meaning:

5 permits available

Now 10 threads call:

semaphore.acquire();

Execution:

Thread1 → gets permit
Thread2 → gets permit
Thread3 → gets permit
Thread4 → gets permit
Thread5 → gets permit

Permits left:

0

Now:

Thread6 → waits
Thread7 → waits
Thread8 → waits
Thread9 → waits
Thread10 → waits

When a thread finishes:

semaphore.release();

Example:

Thread1 releases permit
Thread6 acquires permit

docs.title: Visual Flow
docs.text:
Permits = 5

Running threads:
T1 T2 T3 T4 T5

Waiting threads:
T6 T7 T8 T9 T10

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: A semaphore with N permits allows at most N threads to access a resource simultaneously.

docs.title: Synchronous And Asynchronous Execution
docs.text: Synchronous execution blocks until a task completes, while asynchronous execution allows tasks to run independently without blocking the main thread.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Synchronous Execution
docs.text:
In synchronous execution, tasks run one after another.

The next task waits until the previous task finishes.

Example:

task1();
task2();
task3();

Execution:

task1 → finishes
task2 → starts
task2 → finishes
task3 → starts

Everything happens in order.

Example:

Download file
Process file
Save file

Each step waits for the previous step.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Asynchronous Execution
docs.text:
In asynchronous execution, tasks can run independently without blocking the main thread.

Example:

downloadFileAsync();
processDataAsync();
sendEmailAsync();

Execution:

Task1 starts
Task2 starts
Task3 starts

All may run at the same time.

The main thread does not wait.

docs.title: Synchronous
docs.text: Task1 → Task2 → Task3

docs.title: Asynchronous
docs.text:
Task1
   ↘
Task2
   ↘
Task3

Tasks can overlap.

docs.title: Real Backend Example
docs.text:
Imagine a web server request:

User request arrives

Synchronous flow:

Fetch user
Fetch orders
Fetch recommendations
Return response

Each step waits.

Async version:

Fetch user
Fetch orders
Fetch recommendations

All run in parallel, making response faster.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Synchronous execution blocks until a task completes, while asynchronous execution allows tasks to run independently without blocking the main thread.

docs.title: Why CompletableFuture Exists
docs.text:
Java created CompletableFuture to manage asynchronous tasks easily.

It allows:

Run tasks in background
Chain tasks
Combine results
Handle errors

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
    return fetchData();
});

This runs in another thread automatically.

docs.title: Quick Thinking Question
docs.text: Which one is asynchronous?

docs.title: A
docs.text:
int data = fetchData();
process(data);

docs.title: B
docs.text:
CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> fetchData())
    .thenApply(data -> process(data));

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
✅ — B is asynchronous.

“Option B is asynchronous because the task runs in a separate thread using CompletableFuture.”

docs.title: Option A
docs.text:
int data = fetchData();
process(data);

Execution:

fetchData() → wait until complete
process(data) → start after fetchData finishes

Everything runs in same thread sequentially.

So it is synchronous.

docs.title: Option B
docs.text:
CompletableFuture
    .supplyAsync(() -> fetchData())
    .thenApply(data -> process(data));

Execution:

Main thread continues
fetchData() runs in background thread
When result ready → process() runs

So:

No blocking
Background execution

This is asynchronous programming.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Execution
docs.text:
Main thread starts CompletableFuture
        ↓
Worker thread executes fetchData()
        ↓
Result returned
        ↓
thenApply() processes result

docs.title: Why CompletableFuture is Powerful
docs.text:
It allows:

Async execution
Task chaining
Parallel tasks
Error handling
Combining multiple tasks

Example real backend use:

Fetch user profile
Fetch orders
Fetch recommendations

All done in parallel.

docs.title: Simple Example
docs.text:
CompletableFuture<String> future =
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> "Hello");

System.out.println(future.get());

Output:

Hello

Task executed in background thread.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text:
CompletableFuture provides a powerful way to perform asynchronous computations and chain dependent tasks without blocking threads.

The last concurrency concept used in high-performance parallel algorithms:

docs.title: ForkJoinPool
docs.text:
It is used for:

Parallel recursion
Divide and conquer algorithms
Parallel streams

Before I explain it, quick question:

Which algorithm type benefits most from parallel processing?

A) Sequential algorithms
B) Divide and conquer algorithms

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
ForkJoinPool is a framework for parallel divide-and-conquer algorithms that uses work-stealing to efficiently utilize CPU cores.

“the algorithm can be divided into multiple parts and executed in parallel.”

docs.title: Why Divide and Conquer Works Well with Parallelism
docs.text:
Divide and Conquer algorithms follow this pattern:

Problem
  ↓
Divide into smaller problems
  ↓
Solve each part independently
  ↓
Combine results

Example:

Sort array
   ↓
Split array
   ↓
Sort left + sort right
   ↓
Merge results

Because sub-problems are independent, they can run in parallel threads.

docs.title: This is Exactly What ForkJoinPool Does
docs.text:
Java created ForkJoinPool to efficiently run divide-and-conquer tasks in parallel.

Flow:

Task
 ↓
Fork → split into smaller tasks
 ↓
Worker threads execute tasks
 ↓
Join → combine results

docs.title: Example Algorithm
docs.text:
Imagine summing a large array:

Sum array[0..1000]

Instead of one thread:

sum(0..1000)

ForkJoin splits it:

sum(0..500)   sum(501..1000)

Then further splits:

sum(0..250) sum(251..500) sum(501..750) sum(751..1000)

Each piece runs in parallel threads.

Finally results combine.

docs.title: Java ForkJoin Example
docs.text:
ForkJoinPool pool = new ForkJoinPool();

pool.invoke(new SumTask(array, 0, array.length));

Task structure:

class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Integer> {

    protected Integer compute() {

        if(task small enough)
            compute directly
        else {
            split task
            fork subtasks
            join results
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Important Feature: Work Stealing
docs.text:
ForkJoinPool uses a powerful technique called:

Work Stealing

Meaning:

If one thread finishes early
it steals work from other threads

This keeps CPU fully utilized.

docs.title: Where ForkJoinPool is Used
docs.text:
You actually use it without knowing.

Example:

Arrays.parallelSort()
Stream.parallel()
CompletableFuture

All internally use ForkJoinPool.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ForkJoinPool is a framework for parallel divide-and-conquer algorithms that uses work-stealing to efficiently utilize CPU cores.

docs.title: Final Concurrency Interview Question
docs.text:
Which of these is NOT thread-safe?

A) Vector
B) Hashtable
C) ArrayList
D) ConcurrentHashMap

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
✅ — ArrayList is NOT thread-safe.

“ArrayList is not thread-safe because its operations are not synchronized.”

docs.title: Thread Safety of Given Collections
docs.text:
Collection Thread Safe? Reason Vector ✔ Yes All methods are synchronized Hashtable ✔ Yes Methods are synchronized ArrayList ❌ No No synchronization ConcurrentHashMap ✔ Yes Uses fine-grained concurrency

So the correct answer is:

C) ArrayList

docs.title: Why ArrayList is Not Thread-safe
docs.text:
Example:

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> list.add(1));
Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> list.add(2));

Both threads modify the list at the same time.

Possible issues:

Race condition
Data corruption
Incorrect size
Index errors

docs.title: Option 1 — Synchronized List
docs.text:
List<Integer> list =
    Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());

docs.title: Option 2 — CopyOnWriteArrayList
docs.text:
List<Integer> list = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

Used when:

Many reads
Few writes

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ArrayList is not thread-safe because its methods are not synchronized, so concurrent modifications can cause race conditions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Concurrent collections are thread-safe collection classes designed for safe access by multiple threads.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Normal collections like HashMap and ArrayList are not safe for concurrent modification. Backend systems often need concurrent maps and queues.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap allows safe concurrent reads and updates without locking the whole map like Hashtable.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• HashMap is not thread-safe.
  • Hashtable uses broad synchronization.
  • ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values.
  • ConcurrentHashMap reads are highly optimized.
  • Thread-safe does not mean every compound workflow is automatically atomic.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Concurrent collections provide thread-safe behavior for common data structures. ConcurrentHashMap is faster than Hashtable because it avoids one global lock and allows better concurrency. It also disallows null keys and values to avoid ambiguity in concurrent reads.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Use concurrent collections for shared mutable collections.
  • HashMap is unsafe for concurrent writes.
  • ConcurrentHashMap is preferred over Hashtable.
  • No null key or value in ConcurrentHashMap.
  • Concurrent collections reduce locking problems.
  • Compound operations still need careful design.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
You now know:

Threads
Race conditions
synchronized
Locks
Deadlock
volatile
CAS
Atomic classes
Thread pools
ExecutorService
shutdown vs shutdownNow
Interrupts

You are now entering senior-level territory.

docs.title: Next Major Topic (Very Important)
docs.text: Now we should cover:

docs.title: Concurrent Collections
docs.text:
Because normal collections are not thread-safe.

Examples:

ConcurrentHashMap
CopyOnWriteArrayList
BlockingQueue

These are heavily used in backend systems and interviews.

Before we start:

docs.title: Quick question
docs.text:
Is this thread-safe?

Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();

Multiple threads doing:

map.put()
map.get()

Yes or No? And why?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
HashMap is not thread-safe because concurrent modifications can cause race conditions, visibility issues, and even internal structure corruption during resize.
Let's understand step by step

docs.title: Correct Answer
docs.text:
❌ No, HashMap is not thread-safe.

If multiple threads perform:

map.put()
map.get()

without synchronization, several problems may occur.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Race Condition
docs.text:
Two threads modifying the same bucket can overwrite each other's updates.

Example:

Thread 1 → put(A,1)
Thread 2 → put(A,2)

Final value may be unpredictable.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Internal Structure Corruption (Very Important)
docs.text:
HashMap internally uses:

Array → bucket → linked list / tree

During resize (rehashing), if two threads modify it simultaneously, the internal linked list may become corrupted.

This could lead to:

Infinite loop during traversal

This was a real issue in Java 7 HashMap.

Example symptom:

CPU 100%
Thread stuck in HashMap.get()

docs.title: 3️⃣ Visibility Problems
docs.text: Without synchronization, one thread’s updates may not be visible to others due to CPU caching.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Rehashing is Dangerous in Multithreading
docs.text:
During resize:

Old bucket → new bucket redistribution

Two threads doing this simultaneously can create cyclic linked lists.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: HashMap is not thread-safe because concurrent modifications can cause race conditions, visibility issues, and even internal structure corruption during resize.

docs.title: Correct Solutions
docs.text: Instead of HashMap, use:

docs.title: 1️⃣ ConcurrentHashMap (Best)
docs.text:
Map<String,Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

Highly scalable.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Collections.synchronizedMap
docs.text:
Map<String,Integer> map =
    Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());

Uses a single lock.

docs.title: Difference
docs.text: Map Thread Safety Performance HashMap ❌ No Fast but unsafe synchronizedMap ✔ Yes Slower (global lock) ConcurrentHashMap ✔ Yes High concurrency

docs.title: How ConcurrentHashMap Works Internally
docs.text:
This is very commonly asked in senior interviews.

It involves:

Segment locking (Java 7)
CAS + bucket locking (Java 8)
Tree bins
Lock striping

Before I explain internals, try answering:

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Why is ConcurrentHashMap faster than Hashtable?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
“locks only the affected bucket and uses CAS operations.” “multiple threads can operate on different buckets concurrently.”

Now let’s refine this answer to interview-quality depth.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Hashtable Uses Global Lock
docs.text:
Hashtable methods are synchronized:

public synchronized V put(K key, V value)

Meaning:

One thread at a time
Entire map locked

Example:

Thread1 → put()
Thread2 → get()
Thread3 → put()

All must wait for the same lock.

Result:

Low concurrency
Poor scalability

docs.title: 2️⃣ ConcurrentHashMap Uses Fine-Grained Locking
docs.text:
Instead of locking the entire map, it locks only the bucket (or node).

So:

Thread1 → bucket 3
Thread2 → bucket 10
Thread3 → bucket 15

All can run simultaneously.

docs.title: 3️⃣ CAS (Compare-And-Swap)
docs.text:
For some operations, ConcurrentHashMap avoids locking entirely and uses CAS.

Example operations:

putIfAbsent
computeIfAbsent
replace

CAS is a CPU atomic instruction, so it is lock-free.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Reads Are Lock-Free
docs.text:
One of the most powerful features:

map.get(key)

is non-blocking.

Reads do not require locks in most cases.

So many threads can read simultaneously.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Internal Structure (Java 8+)
docs.text:
ConcurrentHashMap uses:

Node[]
 ↓
bucket
 ↓
LinkedList
 ↓
Tree (if collision > 8)

Same concept as HashMap but with thread-safe mechanisms.

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature Hashtable ConcurrentHashMap Locking Whole map Bucket-level Read operations Locked Mostly lock-free Concurrency Low High Performance Slow under load Scales well

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap improves concurrency by using fine-grained locking and CAS operations instead of locking the entire map like Hashtable.

docs.title: Very Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
Can ConcurrentHashMap store:

null key
null value

Yes or No — and why?

(This question appears surprisingly often in interviews.)

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values to avoid ambiguity between a missing key and a null value in concurrent environments.

Let's understand it to the real interview explanation.

docs.title: Can ConcurrentHashMap Store null Key or Value?
docs.text:
❌ No — it does NOT allow null key or null value.

Example:

Map<String, Integer> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

map.put(null, 1);     // ❌ NullPointerException
map.put("A", null);   // ❌ NullPointerException

docs.title: Why null Is Not Allowed
docs.text:
The main reason is ambiguity in concurrent reads.

Consider this call:

map.get("A")

Possible return values:

null

But what does that mean?

Two possibilities:

1️⃣ Key does not exist
2️⃣ Key exists but value is null

In single-threaded maps like HashMap, this ambiguity is manageable.

But in ConcurrentHashMap, multiple threads may be modifying the map simultaneously.

Example scenario:

Thread1 → removing key "A"
Thread2 → calling get("A")

If null values were allowed, the map cannot safely determine:

Was the key absent?
Was the value null?
Was another thread removing it?

So Java designers forbid nulls completely.

docs.title: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap
docs.text: Feature HashMap ConcurrentHashMap Null key ✔ Allowed (1) ❌ Not allowed Null value ✔ Allowed ❌ Not allowed Thread-safe ❌ No ✔ Yes

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ConcurrentHashMap does not allow null keys or values to avoid ambiguity between a missing key and a null value in concurrent environments.

docs.title: Very Important ConcurrentHashMap Topic
docs.text: Another interview question:

docs.title: What happens when many keys collide into the same bucket?
docs.text:
Example:

hash collisions

What does Java 8 do when the linked list inside a bucket becomes too long?

Hint: This is called Treeification.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
In Java 8+, when bucket collisions exceed 8 and table size is at least 64, the linked list is converted into a Red-Black tree to improve lookup from O(n) to O(log n).

Excellent ✅ — your answer is correct.

Small English correction:

  • “if bucket size is going above 8” → “if the bucket size exceeds 8”

Now let’s explain the complete concept, because interviewers often ask follow-up traps here.

docs.title: Treeification in HashMap / ConcurrentHashMap
docs.text:
When many keys collide into the same bucket:

Initially structure is:

Array
  ↓
Bucket
  ↓
Linked List

Example:

bucket[5]
   ↓
[K1] → [K2] → [K3] → [K4] → [K5] → [K6] → [K7] → [K8]

If collisions keep increasing, searching becomes:

O(n)

Which is slow.

docs.title: Java 8 Improvement
docs.text:
If bucket size becomes greater than 8, Java converts the list to a Red-Black Tree.

This process is called:

Treeification

Structure becomes:

Array
 ↓
Bucket
 ↓
Red-Black Tree

Search complexity becomes:

O(log n)

Instead of:

O(n)

docs.title: Treeification Threshold
docs.text:
TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8

Meaning:

LinkedList → Tree
when nodes > 8

docs.title: But There Is Another Important Condition ⚠
docs.text:
Treeification happens only if the table size ≥ 64.

Constant:

MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64

If the table is smaller than 64:

Java prefers resizing instead of treeifying

docs.title: Why Java Does This
docs.text:
Because collisions often happen due to small table size, not bad hashing.

So Java first tries:

resize table

instead of converting to tree.

docs.title: Reverse Operation (Very Important)
docs.text:
If elements decrease:

UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6

Then:

Tree → Linked List

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Condition Action bucket size > 8 convert to tree table size < 64 resize instead bucket size < 6 convert back to list

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: In Java 8+, when bucket collisions exceed 8 and table size is at least 64, the linked list is converted into a Red-Black tree to improve lookup from O(n) to O(log n).

docs.title: Quick Interview Trap
docs.text:
Which map maintains insertion order?

A) HashMap B) LinkedHashMap C) TreeMap

And which map maintains sorted order?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: LinkedHashMap

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: These are Java concurrency utilities for waiting, coordination, and limiting access to a shared resource.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: They are common in interview questions because they solve different coordination problems and are easy to confuse.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Use CountDownLatch when the main thread must wait for several worker tasks to finish.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• CountDownLatch cannot be reset.
  • CyclicBarrier can be reused.
  • Semaphore controls permits, not ownership like a lock.
  • A binary semaphore is not exactly the same as a Java lock.
  • Forgetting to release a semaphore permit can block other threads.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: CountDownLatch lets one or more threads wait until a count reaches zero. CyclicBarrier lets a group of threads wait for each other at a common point and can be reused. Semaphore controls how many threads can access a resource using permits.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• CountDownLatch waits for count to reach zero.
  • CountDownLatch is one-time use.
  • CyclicBarrier waits for a group.
  • CyclicBarrier is reusable.
  • Semaphore limits concurrent access.
  • Always release semaphore permits.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
You have now covered almost the full Java concurrency foundation:

Threads
Thread lifecycle
Race conditions
synchronized
Deadlock
volatile
CAS
Atomic classes
ExecutorService
Thread pools
wait / notify
Producer–Consumer
BlockingQueue
ReentrantLock
ReadWriteLock

This is already strong interview-level knowledge.

docs.title: Remaining Advanced Concurrency Topics
docs.text:
Only a few very important tools remain:

CountDownLatch
CyclicBarrier
Semaphore
ForkJoinPool
CompletableFuture

These are used in high-performance concurrent systems.

docs.title: Next Topic (Very Easy but Very Powerful)
CountDownLatch
docs.text:
Before I explain:

Imagine 5 worker threads must finish their job before the main thread continues.

Which thread should wait?

Main thread
or
Worker threads

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
✅ — the main thread waits.

Now let’s understand CountDownLatch, one of the easiest and most useful concurrency tools.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is CountDownLatch?
docs.text:
CountDownLatch is used when:

One or more threads must wait
until other threads finish their work

Example scenario:

Main thread
   ↓
Wait for 5 worker threads
   ↓
Continue execution

docs.title: 2️⃣ Real Life Example
docs.text:
Imagine a race starting gate.

Runner1 ready
Runner2 ready
Runner3 ready
Runner4 ready
Runner5 ready

The race starts only when all runners are ready.

Latch counter:

5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1 → 0

When it reaches 0, waiting thread continues.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Basic Code Example
docs.text:
Create latch:

CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);

Meaning:

Main thread waits until 3 events happen

docs.title: Worker threads
docs.text:
latch.countDown();

Each call reduces the counter:

3 → 2 → 1 → 0

docs.title: Main thread waits
docs.text:
latch.await();

Meaning:

Wait until counter becomes 0

docs.title: Full Example
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;

public class Example {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {

        CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);

        for(int i=1;i<=3;i++){
            new Thread(() -> {
                System.out.println("Worker finished");
                latch.countDown();
            }).start();
        }

        latch.await();

        System.out.println("All workers done. Main continues.");
    }
}

Output:

Worker finished
Worker finished
Worker finished
All workers done. Main continues.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Important Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose await() wait until count reaches zero countDown() decrease counter getCount() current count

docs.title: 5️⃣ Important Property
docs.text:
CountDownLatch is one-time use only.

Once count reaches:

0

You cannot reset it.

If you need reusable synchronization → use:

CyclicBarrier

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: CountDownLatch allows one or more threads to wait until a set of operations performed by other threads completes.

docs.title: Quick Interview Question
docs.text:
Suppose:

CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);

But only 2 threads call countDown().

What happens to:

latch.await()

Will it:

A) Continue B) Wait forever C) Throw exception

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
B) Wait forever

CountDownLatch.await() blocks until the count reaches zero; if the count never reaches zero, the waiting thread will block indefinitely unless a timeout is used.
Let's understand step by step

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
CountDownLatch latch = new CountDownLatch(3);

This means the latch counter starts at:

3

Now imagine only 2 threads call:

latch.countDown();

Counter changes like this:

3 → 2 → 1

It never reaches 0.

docs.title: What happens to await()?
docs.text:
latch.await();

This method waits until the counter becomes 0.

Since the counter is still 1, the waiting thread will:

Wait forever

So the correct answer is:

B) Wait forever

docs.title: Why this is important
docs.text:
If some worker thread fails or forgets to call countDown(), the main thread can get stuck permanently.

This is a common bug in concurrent programs.

docs.title: How to avoid waiting forever
docs.text:
Java provides a safer version:

latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Meaning:

Wait up to 5 seconds
If count still not zero → continue

This prevents the program from getting stuck.

docs.title: Interview one-liner
docs.text:
CountDownLatch.await() blocks until the count reaches zero; if the count never reaches zero, the waiting thread will block indefinitely unless a timeout is used.

Great. Now we go to the next important concurrency tool.

docs.title: CyclicBarrier
docs.text: This concept is very similar to CountDownLatch, but with one big difference.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is CyclicBarrier?
docs.text:
CyclicBarrier is used when:

Multiple threads must wait for each other
before continuing execution.

Example:

Thread1
Thread2
Thread3
Thread4

All threads must reach a common barrier point before moving forward.

docs.title: Real-world Example
docs.text:
Imagine 4 friends meeting at a restaurant.

Friend1 arrives
Friend2 arrives
Friend3 arrives
Friend4 arrives

Only when all 4 arrive, they start eating.

That meeting point is the barrier.

docs.title: 2️⃣ How CyclicBarrier Works
docs.text:
Create barrier:

CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(4);

Meaning:

4 threads must reach the barrier
before any can continue.

Each thread calls:

barrier.await();

Flow:

Thread1 → wait
Thread2 → wait
Thread3 → wait
Thread4 → arrives
Barrier opens
All threads continue

docs.title: 3️⃣ Example Code
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier;

public class Example {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3);

        Runnable worker = () -> {
            try {
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " ready");
                barrier.await();
                System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " started");
            } catch(Exception e){}
        };

        new Thread(worker).start();
        new Thread(worker).start();
        new Thread(worker).start();
    }
}

Output example:

Thread1 ready
Thread2 ready
Thread3 ready
Thread3 started
Thread2 started
Thread1 started

All threads start only after all arrive.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Why it is called Cyclic
docs.text:
Because it resets automatically.

Example:

Round 1 → barrier opens
Round 2 → barrier can be used again

This is different from:

CountDownLatch (one-time use)

docs.title: 5️⃣ Barrier Action (Advanced Feature)
docs.text:
You can run a task when barrier opens.

Example:

CyclicBarrier barrier =
    new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> {
        System.out.println("All threads reached barrier");
    });

This code runs before threads continue.

docs.title: 6️⃣ CyclicBarrier vs CountDownLatch
docs.text: Feature CountDownLatch CyclicBarrier Reusable ❌ No ✔ Yes Who waits One thread waits All threads wait Counter reset ❌ No ✔ Yes

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: CyclicBarrier allows a group of threads to wait for each other at a common barrier point before continuing execution.

docs.title: Important Interview Question
docs.text:
Suppose we create:

CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(5);

But only 4 threads call await().

What happens?

A) Barrier opens B) Threads wait forever C) Exception occurs

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: B) Threads wait forever

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
CyclicBarrier(5) means:

5 threads must reach the barrier

Barrier counter:

5

Threads arrive:

Thread1 → waiting
Thread2 → waiting
Thread3 → waiting
Thread4 → waiting

But the 5th thread never arrives, so:

Barrier never opens

All 4 threads remain:

WAITING

docs.title: Important Exception Case
docs.text:
If one waiting thread is interrupted, then the barrier becomes broken and other threads get:

BrokenBarrierException

docs.title: Interview One-liner
docs.text: A CyclicBarrier opens only when the specified number of threads reach the barrier; otherwise, waiting threads remain blocked.

docs.title: Quick Comparison (Very Important)
docs.text: Tool Purpose CountDownLatch One thread waits for others to finish CyclicBarrier All threads wait for each other Semaphore Controls number of threads accessing resource

docs.title: Next Topic (Last Core Concurrency Tool)
docs.text: We should now learn Semaphore, which controls resource access.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is a Semaphore?
docs.text:
A Semaphore controls how many threads can access a resource at the same time.

Think of it like limited permits.

Example:

Database connections = 3
Threads requesting DB = 10

Only 3 threads can access the database simultaneously. Other threads must wait.

That control mechanism is Semaphore.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Real-Life Example
docs.text:
Imagine a parking lot with 3 parking spaces.

🚗 Car1 → enter
🚗 Car2 → enter
🚗 Car3 → enter
🚗 Car4 → wait
🚗 Car5 → wait

When a car leaves:

Car1 leaves → space available
Car4 enters

Semaphore works exactly like this.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Java Semaphore Example
docs.text:
Create semaphore:

Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(3);

Meaning:

3 threads allowed simultaneously

Thread enters resource:

semaphore.acquire();

Thread releases resource:

semaphore.release();

docs.title: 4️⃣ Example Code
docs.text:
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class Example {

    static Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(3);

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        for(int i=1;i<=6;i++){
            new Thread(() -> {
                try {
                    semaphore.acquire();

                    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()+" entered");

                    Thread.sleep(2000);

                    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()+" leaving");

                    semaphore.release();

                } catch(Exception e){}
            }).start();
        }
    }
}

Output example:

Thread1 entered
Thread2 entered
Thread3 entered
Thread1 leaving
Thread4 entered

Only 3 threads inside at once.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Important Methods
docs.text: Method Purpose acquire() take permit (may block) release() return permit tryAcquire() try without waiting availablePermits() check remaining permits

docs.title: 6️⃣ Binary Semaphore
docs.text:
If we create:

Semaphore semaphore = new Semaphore(1);

Then only one thread allowed.

This behaves like a mutex lock.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Semaphore vs Lock
docs.text: Feature Semaphore Lock Allows multiple threads ✔ Yes ❌ No Used for resource pool ✔ Yes ❌ No Mutual exclusion Optional Yes

docs.title: Interview One-liner
docs.text: Semaphore controls access to a limited number of resources by allowing only a fixed number of threads to acquire permits simultaneously.

docs.title: Where You Are Now
docs.text:
You have now covered almost the entire Java concurrency toolkit:

Threads
synchronized
volatile
Atomic classes
ThreadPoolExecutor
wait/notify
BlockingQueue
ReentrantLock
ReadWriteLock
CountDownLatch
CyclicBarrier
Semaphore

This is very strong concurrency knowledge.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: ExecutorService is a higher-level API for running tasks with managed threads. Future represents a result that may be available later, and Callable can return a value.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Production Java code usually uses executors instead of manually creating many threads. This is a common backend interview topic.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Submit a Callable<Integer> to an ExecutorService, then call future.get() to wait for the result.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Creating unlimited raw threads is dangerous.
  • execute() does not return a result.
  • submit() returns a Future.
  • Future.get() can block.
  • Runnable cannot directly return a value.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: ExecutorService manages a pool of worker threads and runs submitted tasks. execute() runs a task without returning a result, while submit() returns a Future. Callable is like Runnable, but it can return a value and throw checked exceptions.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Use executors instead of too many raw threads.
  • execute() returns nothing.
  • submit() returns Future.
  • Callable returns a value.
  • Future.get() blocks until result is ready.
  • Always shut down executors.

docs.title: Thread Pools & Executors
docs.text:
We should now move to Thread Pools & Executors.

Because in real backend systems:

Threads are rarely created manually.

They are managed by:

ExecutorService
ThreadPoolExecutor
ForkJoinPool

Before we start that, one quick check:

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
Why is creating too many threads dangerous?

Give two reasons.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: Creating too many threads increases memory usage, context switching overhead, and scheduler pressure, which can severely degrade performance.

docs.title: Why Creating Too Many Threads is Dangerous
1️⃣ Memory Consumption (Very Important)
docs.text:
Each thread has its own stack memory.

Typical stack size:

512 KB – 1 MB per thread

If you create:

10,000 threads

Memory usage:

~10 GB stack memory

Your JVM can crash with:

OutOfMemoryError: unable to create new native thread

docs.title: 2️⃣ Context Switching Overhead
docs.text:
CPU can run only a few threads at a time.

If you create too many threads:

CPU keeps switching between threads

This is called:

Context Switching

Switching threads costs CPU time.

So performance actually becomes worse, not better.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Thread Scheduling Overhead
docs.text:
The OS scheduler must manage all threads:

ready queue
priority
scheduling

More threads → more overhead.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Resource Contention
docs.text:
Threads compete for:

CPU
memory
locks
I/O

Too many threads increases lock contention and reduces throughput.

docs.title: Real Solution: Thread Pools
docs.text:
Instead of creating many threads:

Create limited threads
Reuse them

Example:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10);

Now only 10 threads execute tasks.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Creating too many threads increases memory usage, context switching overhead, and scheduler pressure, which can severely degrade performance.

docs.title: Now We Enter a Very Important Topic
Thread Pool & Executor Framework
docs.text: Before I explain the internals, answer this:

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
What is the difference between:

execute()

and

submit()

in ExecutorService?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
execute() runs a task without returning a result, while submit() returns a Future that allows retrieving results and exceptions.

Let’s build it step by step.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is ExecutorService?
docs.text:
Instead of creating threads like this:

new Thread(task).start();

Java recommends using a thread pool:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);

Now:

  • Only 5 threads exist
  • Tasks are queued
  • Threads reuse themselves

Example:

pool.execute(() -> {
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName());
});

docs.title: 2️⃣ execute() vs submit()
docs.text: Both are used to send tasks to a thread pool, but they behave differently.

docs.title: execute()
docs.text:
Method signature:

void execute(Runnable command)

Example:

pool.execute(() -> {
    System.out.println("Task running");
});

Characteristics:

  • Takes Runnable only
  • No return value
  • Cannot capture result
  • Cannot track completion easily

docs.title: submit()
docs.text:
Method signature:

Future<?> submit(Runnable task)
Future<T> submit(Callable<T> task)

Example:

Future<Integer> result = pool.submit(() -> {
    return 10 + 20;
});

Get result:

System.out.println(result.get());

Output:

30

docs.title: Key Difference Table
docs.text: Feature execute() submit() Return value ❌ None ✅ Future Accepts Callable ❌ No ✅ Yes Get result ❌ No ✅ Yes Exception handling Goes to thread's handler Stored in Future

docs.title: Important Interview Insight
docs.text: If a task throws exception:

docs.title: execute()
docs.text: Exception goes to thread's uncaught exception handler.

docs.title: submit()
docs.text:
Exception is stored inside Future.

You see it only when calling:

future.get();

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: execute() runs a task without returning a result, while submit() returns a Future that allows retrieving results and exceptions.

docs.title: 3️⃣ What is Future?
docs.text:
Future represents result of asynchronous computation.

Methods:

future.get()       // wait for result
future.isDone()    // task finished?
future.cancel()    // cancel task

docs.title: 4️⃣ Runnable vs Callable
docs.text:
Runnable:

void run()

Callable:

T call()

Callable can:

✔ return result ✔ throw checked exceptions

docs.title: Quick Check Question
docs.text:
What will happen here?

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> {
    int x = 10 / 0;
    return x;
});

System.out.println("Done");

Question:

Will the program crash immediately or continue printing "Done"?

Then what happens when we call:

f.get();

Answer:

  • “after f.get() it will get divide by zero exception” → “when f.get() is called, it will throw the exception.”

Now let’s explain what exactly happens internally (important for interviews).

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> {
    int x = 10 / 0;
    return x;
});

System.out.println("Done");

docs.title: 1️⃣ Task submitted to thread pool
docs.text:
submit() does not execute immediately in the main thread.

Instead:

Main thread → submit task → task goes to queue
Thread pool worker → executes task

docs.title: 2️⃣ Main thread continues
docs.text:
Main thread prints:

Done

because the task runs asynchronously.

So program does not crash here.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Worker thread executes task
docs.text:
Inside thread pool worker:

int x = 10 / 0;

Exception occurs:

ArithmeticException: / by zero

But because task was submitted using submit():

Exception is captured inside Future

It is not thrown immediately.

docs.title: 4️⃣ When f.get() is called
docs.text:
Example:

f.get();

Now Java unwraps the stored exception and throws:

ExecutionException

Inside it:

ArithmeticException: / by zero

docs.title: Important Interview Detail
docs.text:
submit() wraps exceptions in:

java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException

So actual exception is inside:

e.getCause()

Example:

try {
    f.get();
} catch (ExecutionException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getCause());
}

docs.title: Key Difference With execute()
docs.text:
If we used:

pool.execute(() -> {
    int x = 10 / 0;
});

Then:

ArithmeticException

would go to UncaughtExceptionHandler immediately.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: When using submit(), exceptions are captured inside the Future and thrown as ExecutionException when Future.get() is called.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A race condition happens when multiple threads access shared data and the final result depends on timing.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Race conditions are one of the most common concurrency bugs. sleep() and wait() are also common interview traps because they behave very differently.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: If two threads execute count++ at the same time, both can read the same old value and one update can be lost.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• count++ is not atomic.
  • sleep() does not release a lock.
  • wait() releases the object monitor.
  • wait() must be called from synchronized context.
  • Timing-based fixes are not real thread-safety fixes.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: A race condition occurs when threads modify shared state without proper coordination. For example, count++ reads, increments, and writes in separate steps, so updates can be lost. sleep() only pauses the current thread, while wait() releases the monitor and waits for notification.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Race condition depends on thread timing.
  • count++ has multiple steps.
  • Use synchronization or atomic classes for shared updates.
  • sleep() keeps the lock.
  • wait() releases the lock.
  • wait() belongs to Object.

docs.title: What is a race condition?
docs.text: When multiple threads access shared data and the result depends on timing.

docs.title: 🔥 Trap 4: Predict output (very common)
docs.text:
class Counter {
  int count = 0;
  void inc() { count++; }
}

public class Test {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    Counter c = new Counter();

    Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> { for(int i=0;i<100000;i++) c.inc(); });
    Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> { for(int i=0;i<100000;i++) c.inc(); });

    t1.start(); t2.start();
    t1.join();  t2.join();

    System.out.println(c.count);
  }
}

Question:

  1. Will it always print 200000?
  2. If not, why? (one key reason)

Answer:

count++ is not atomic. It consists of read–modify–write operations, so multiple threads may read the same value and overwrite each other's updates, causing a race condition.

Now let’s explain properly.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Will it always print 200000?
docs.text: ❌ No

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why?
docs.text:
Because of a race condition.

The operation:

count++;

is not atomic.

It actually performs three steps internally.

docs.title: Internal Working of count++
docs.text:
1️⃣ Read value from memory
2️⃣ Add 1
3️⃣ Write value back

Example scenario:

Initial value:

count = 5

Thread execution:

Step Thread 1 Thread 2 Read 5 5 Add 6 6 Write 6 6

Final value:

6

But two increments happened, so expected value should be 7.

One increment is lost.

This is called:

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: count++ is not atomic. It consists of read–modify–write operations, so multiple threads may read the same value and overwrite each other's updates, causing a race condition.

docs.title: Option 1: synchronized
docs.text:
synchronized void inc() {
    count++;
}

docs.title: Option 2: AtomicInteger (better)
docs.text:
AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

count.incrementAndGet();

This uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap).

docs.title: Next Important Topic (Very Important)
docs.text: Before moving ahead, answer this.

docs.title: Trap Question
docs.text:
What is the difference between:

Thread.sleep()

and

Object.wait()

Give 2 differences. This is a very common interview question.

docs.title: sleep()
docs.text:
• It is a static method of Thread.
  • You call it as:
Thread.sleep(1000);

docs.title: wait()
docs.text:
• It is a method of Object.
  • You call it on a lock object:
lock.wait();

docs.title: sleep()
docs.text:
❌ Does NOT release any lock.

If a thread is inside a synchronized block and calls sleep, it keeps the lock.

docs.title: wait()
docs.text:
✅ Releases the lock (monitor) immediately and goes to waiting state.

This is the biggest difference.

docs.title: sleep()
docs.text:
• Can be called anywhere.
  • No special requirement.

docs.title: wait()
docs.text:
• Must be called inside synchronized context (owning the monitor of that object).
  • Otherwise you get:
IllegalMonitorStateException

Example (wrong):

lock.wait(); // ❌ if not inside synchronized(lock)

Correct:

synchronized(lock) {
    lock.wait(); // ✅
}

docs.title: 4) How does a thread wake up?
sleep()
docs.text:
• Wakes up automatically after time ends (or interrupt).
  • No other thread needs to do anything.

docs.title: wait()
docs.text:
• Wakes up if:

  • another thread calls notify() / notifyAll() on same lock object OR

  • timeout ends (wait(ms)) OR
  • interrupted

docs.title: sleep()
docs.text:
• Pause thread for some time.
  • Rate limiting, retry delay, polling delay.

docs.title: wait()
docs.text:
• Thread coordination / communication.
  • Classic producer-consumer pattern.

docs.title: ✅ Short Interview Answer (Memorize)
docs.text: sleep() pauses the current thread without releasing any locks and can be called anywhere. wait() is used for inter-thread communication; it must be called inside a synchronized block and it releases the lock until notified or timed out.

docs.title: 🔥 Quick Trap (to confirm understanding)
docs.text:
Predict what happens (no need exact output, just behavior):

Object lock = new Object();

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
  synchronized(lock) {
    try {
      Thread.sleep(2000);
    } catch (Exception e) {}
  }
});

Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
  synchronized(lock) {
    System.out.println("t2 entered");
  }
});

t1.start();
Thread.sleep(100);
t2.start();

Question: Will t2 print immediately or after ~2 seconds? Why?

Answer: 

Thread.sleep() pauses the thread but keeps the monitor lock, while wait() releases the lock and allows other threads to acquire it.

Now let’s understand deeply.

docs.title: Correct Behavior
docs.text:
t2 will print after about 2 seconds, not immediately.

Output (after ~2s):

t2 entered

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: Look carefully.

docs.title: Thread t1
docs.text:
synchronized(lock) {
    Thread.sleep(2000);
}

Steps:

1️⃣ t1 acquires the lock 2️⃣ t1 enters synchronized block 3️⃣ t1 calls sleep(2000) 4️⃣ sleep does NOT release the lock

So t1 holds the lock for 2 seconds.

docs.title: Thread t2
docs.text:
synchronized(lock) {
    System.out.println("t2 entered");
}

But t2 needs the same lock.

Since t1 is holding the lock:

t2 → BLOCKED state

t2 must wait until t1 exits the synchronized block.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
t1 start
t1 acquires lock
t1 sleeps 2 sec (still holding lock)

t2 tries to enter synchronized(lock)
t2 BLOCKED

2 seconds later:
t1 exits block
lock released

t2 enters
print "t2 entered"

docs.title: 🔥 Important Rule
docs.text:
Method Releases Lock? sleep() ❌ No wait() ✅ Yes

This is one of the most common Java interview traps.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Thread.sleep() pauses the thread but keeps the monitor lock, while wait() releases the lock and allows other threads to acquire it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: ReentrantLock is an explicit lock with more control than synchronized. ReadWriteLock separates read locks and write locks.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: These locks help when you need timeout locking, interruptible locking, fairness, or many readers with fewer writers.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A cache can allow multiple reader threads at the same time, but only one writer thread when data is updated.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• You must call unlock() manually.
  • Use finally to release a ReentrantLock.
  • Fair locks can reduce throughput.
  • ReadWriteLock helps only when reads are much more frequent than writes.
  • A writer must wait until readers release the read lock.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: ReentrantLock provides explicit lock control with features like tryLock(), timeout, interruptible locking, and fairness. ReadWriteLock improves read-heavy workloads by allowing multiple readers at the same time while still giving exclusive access to writers.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• ReentrantLock needs manual unlock.
  • Always unlock in finally.
  • tryLock() avoids waiting forever.
  • Read lock allows multiple readers.
  • Write lock is exclusive.
  • Useful for read-heavy shared data.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
You now understand:

Threads
Race conditions
synchronized
volatile
Atomic classes
Thread pools
ExecutorService
wait/notify
Producer–Consumer
BlockingQueue

Next very powerful topic (used in high-level concurrency):

docs.title: ReentrantLock
docs.text:
It gives more control than synchronized.

Before I explain it, try answering:

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
ReentrantLock provides more flexible and powerful locking mechanisms than synchronized, including tryLock, timeout locks, interruptible locks, and fairness policies.

This is an important advanced concurrency topic. I’ll explain it clearly from basic → internal idea → interview level.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is ReentrantLock?
docs.text:
ReentrantLock is a class from:

java.util.concurrent.locks

It provides explicit locking similar to synchronized, but with more control and features.

Example:

Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();

lock.lock();
try {
    // critical section
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

This protects shared resources like synchronized.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why It Is Called “Reentrant”
docs.text:
Reentrant means:

A thread that already holds the lock
can acquire it again

Example:

lock.lock();   // first time
lock.lock();   // same thread can lock again

Java keeps a hold count.

To release:

unlock()
unlock()

This behavior is the same as synchronized.

docs.title: 3️⃣ synchronized vs ReentrantLock
docs.text: Feature synchronized ReentrantLock Lock control automatic manual Try acquiring lock ❌ No ✔ tryLock() Timeout lock ❌ No ✔ tryLock(timeout) Interruptible lock ❌ No ✔ lockInterruptibly() Fair locking ❌ No ✔ optional Multiple conditions ❌ No ✔ Condition

docs.title: 4️⃣ Important Advantage — tryLock()
docs.text:
With synchronized, if the lock is busy:

Thread waits forever

With ReentrantLock:

if(lock.tryLock()) {
   try {
      // critical section
   } finally {
      lock.unlock();
   }
} else {
   System.out.println("Lock not available");
}

Thread does not block.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Timeout Lock (Very Useful)
docs.text:
lock.tryLock(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Meaning:

Wait 5 seconds
If lock not available → give up

This helps avoid deadlocks.

docs.title: 6️⃣ Fair Locking
docs.text:
Default locks are unfair.

Meaning:

New thread may jump ahead in queue

Fair lock ensures:

First-come-first-served

Example:

Lock lock = new ReentrantLock(true);

docs.title: 7️⃣ Interruptible Lock
docs.text:
You can interrupt waiting threads.

Example:

lock.lockInterruptibly();

If thread receives interrupt:

InterruptedException thrown

synchronized cannot do this.

docs.title: 8️⃣ Condition Variables (Advanced Feature)
docs.text:
With synchronized, we use:

wait()
notify()
notifyAll()

With ReentrantLock we use:

Condition

Example:

Condition condition = lock.newCondition();

condition.await();
condition.signal();

This allows multiple wait queues, which is more powerful.

docs.title: 9️⃣ Example
docs.text:
Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();

public void increment() {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        counter++;
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

The finally block ensures the lock always releases.

docs.title: 10️⃣ Internal Concept (Interview Insight)
docs.text:
Internally ReentrantLock uses:

CAS
AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS)
FIFO wait queue

This is part of Java's high-performance concurrency framework.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ReentrantLock provides more flexible and powerful locking mechanisms than synchronized, including tryLock, timeout locks, interruptible locks, and fairness policies.

docs.title: Very Common Interview Question
docs.text:
What happens if we forget:

lock.unlock();

inside ReentrantLock code?

What problem will occur?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
If unlock() is not called, the lock remains held and other threads waiting for it may block indefinitely.

“Other threads will remain blocked because the current thread never releases the lock.”

Now let’s explain it clearly.

docs.title: What Happens If unlock() Is Not Called
docs.text:
Example:

Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();

lock.lock();
counter++;
// unlock() forgotten

Result:

Lock remains held forever

So:

Thread1 → holds lock
Thread2 → waiting for lock
Thread3 → waiting for lock
Thread4 → waiting for lock

All other threads will block indefinitely.

docs.title: This Can Cause
docs.text:
Thread starvation
Application freeze
Deadlock-like situation

Your program may appear hung.

docs.title: Why finally Is Mandatory
docs.text:
Correct pattern:

lock.lock();
try {
    // critical section
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}

Why?

Because even if an exception occurs:

lock.unlock() still executes

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: If unlock() is not called, the lock remains held and other threads waiting for it may block indefinitely.

docs.title: Important Difference From synchronized
docs.text:
With synchronized:

synchronized(obj) {
    // code
}

Lock release is automatic when the block exits.

With ReentrantLock:

Lock release is manual

So forgetting unlock() is dangerous.

docs.title: Where We Are in Multithreading
docs.text:
You now know:

Threads
Race conditions
synchronized
volatile
Atomic classes
Thread pools
ExecutorService
wait / notify
Producer–Consumer
BlockingQueue
ReentrantLock

We are now very close to complete Java concurrency fundamentals.

docs.title: Next Important Topic
docs.text:
Now we move to ReadWriteLock.

This is used when:

Many threads read data
Few threads write data

Before I explain:

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Why would allowing multiple readers but only one writer improve performance?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
ReadWriteLock improves performance in read-heavy systems by allowing concurrent reads while ensuring exclusive access for writes.

“Multiple readers do not block each other, but writers must block other threads to maintain data consistency.”

docs.title: Why Multiple Readers Improve Performance
docs.text:
In many systems:

Reads >> Writes

Example:

Database lookup
Cache reading
Configuration reading
User profile fetching

So most operations are read operations.

docs.title: Problem With Normal Lock (synchronized / ReentrantLock)
docs.text:
If we use a normal lock:

lock.lock();
readData();
lock.unlock();

Then:

Thread1 reading
Thread2 reading
Thread3 reading
Thread4 reading

All of them wait for each other, even though reading does not modify data.

So concurrency is wasted.

docs.title: ReadWriteLock Idea
docs.text:
Allow:

Multiple readers simultaneously
But only one writer at a time

Rules:

Reader + Reader  → allowed
Reader + Writer  → blocked
Writer + Writer  → blocked

docs.title: Visual Example
docs.text:
Without ReadWriteLock:

R1 → wait
R2 → wait
R3 → wait

Only one thread executes.

With ReadWriteLock:

R1 reading
R2 reading
R3 reading

All run simultaneously.

Performance improves significantly.

docs.title: When Writer Appears
docs.text:
If a writer comes:

Writer must wait until all readers finish

Because writing modifies shared data.

docs.title: Java Implementation
docs.text:
Java provides:

ReentrantReadWriteLock

Example:

ReentrantReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

Lock readLock = lock.readLock();
Lock writeLock = lock.writeLock();

docs.title: Reading
docs.text:
readLock.lock();
try {
    readData();
} finally {
    readLock.unlock();
}

Multiple threads can run this.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
writeLock.lock();
try {
    writeData();
} finally {
    writeLock.unlock();
}

Only one writer allowed.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: ReadWriteLock improves performance in read-heavy systems by allowing concurrent reads while ensuring exclusive access for writes.

docs.title: Real System Example
docs.text:
Imagine a cache system:

1000 threads reading cached data
5 threads updating cache

Using ReadWriteLock:

1000 reads can run concurrently

Huge performance improvement.

docs.title: Quick Interview Question
docs.text:
What happens if:

5 readers are reading
1 writer arrives

Will:

A) Writer run immediately B) Writer wait for readers to finish

Which one?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: Correct ✅ — Writer must wait until all readers release the read lock.

docs.title: Why Writer Must Wait
docs.text:
When threads hold the read lock:

R1 reading
R2 reading
R3 reading
R4 reading
R5 reading

A writer arrives:

W1 wants to write

But writing modifies shared data, so the writer needs exclusive access.

Rule of ReadWriteLock:

Readers + Readers → allowed
Readers + Writer  → NOT allowed
Writer + Writer   → NOT allowed

So the writer must wait until:

R1 unlock
R2 unlock
R3 unlock
R4 unlock
R5 unlock

Then the writer acquires the write lock.

docs.title: Important Interview Follow-up (Very Common)
docs.text:
What happens if:

Readers keep arriving continuously
Writer is waiting

Example:

R1 reading
R2 reading
R3 reading
Writer waiting
R4 arrives
R5 arrives
R6 arrives
...

Possible problem:

Writer may never get the lock

This is called:

Writer Starvation

docs.title: How Java Solves This
docs.text:
ReentrantReadWriteLock can use fair mode.

Example:

ReentrantReadWriteLock lock =
        new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true);

Fair lock ensures:

Threads acquire locks in arrival order

So writers are not starved.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: In ReadWriteLock, multiple readers can access simultaneously, but writers require exclusive access and must wait until all readers release the lock.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Executor shutdown stops accepting new tasks, and interruption is Java’s cooperative way to ask a thread to stop blocking or running.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Clean shutdown is important in backend services. Java does not safely kill threads by force because it can corrupt state.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: shutdown() lets submitted tasks finish. shutdownNow() tries to interrupt running tasks and returns tasks that did not start.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• shutdown() does not kill running tasks.
  • shutdownNow() is not guaranteed to stop a task immediately.
  • Interrupt works only if code checks or responds to it.
  • Forcefully killing threads can leave locks and state broken.
  • Thread-safe collections are needed when multiple threads share data.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: shutdown() stops new task submission and lets existing tasks finish. shutdownNow() attempts to stop running tasks by interrupting worker threads and returns pending tasks. Java uses cooperative interruption because forcefully killing a thread can leave shared state inconsistent.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• shutdown() is graceful.
  • shutdownNow() attempts interruption.
  • Interrupt is cooperative.
  • Blocking methods often react to interrupt.
  • Do not force-kill threads.
  • Shared data needs thread safety.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Explain what happens in each:

  1. shutdown()
  2. shutdownNow()

Let's go step-by-step.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Why ThreadPool Shutdown Is Needed
docs.text:
If you create a thread pool:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5);

and never stop it, the JVM will not exit because:

ThreadPool threads are non-daemon threads

So we must shutdown the pool.

Java provides two methods:

shutdown()
shutdownNow()

docs.title: 2️⃣ shutdown()
docs.text:
Graceful shutdown.

pool.shutdown();

What happens:

✔ Stop accepting new tasks
✔ Already submitted tasks will execute
✔ Running tasks continue
✔ Queue tasks will execute

Example timeline:

Task1 running
Task2 running
Task3 in queue
shutdown() called

Result:

Task1 finishes
Task2 finishes
Task3 executes
Pool terminates

So everything completes normally.

docs.title: 3️⃣ shutdownNow()
docs.text:
Force shutdown.

pool.shutdownNow();

What happens:

❌ Stop accepting new tasks
❌ Cancel queued tasks
⚠ Interrupt running tasks

Meaning:

Running threads receive interrupt signal
Queue tasks removed

But interruption only works if the task handles interrupts.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Example
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);

pool.submit(() -> {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(5000);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        System.out.println("Interrupted!");
    }
});

pool.shutdownNow();

Output may be:

Interrupted!

Because thread receives interrupt.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Key Difference
docs.text: Feature shutdown() shutdownNow() Accept new tasks ❌ No ❌ No Running tasks Continue Interrupted Queued tasks Execute Removed Shutdown style Graceful Force

docs.title: 6️⃣ Checking Pool State
docs.text:
Useful methods:

pool.isShutdown()
pool.isTerminated()

docs.title: 7️⃣ Waiting for Completion
docs.text:
pool.shutdown();
pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Meaning:

Wait 10 seconds for tasks to finish

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: shutdown() performs a graceful shutdown allowing existing tasks to finish, while shutdownNow() attempts to stop all running tasks immediately and clears the queue.

docs.title: Quick Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict behavior:

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();

pool.submit(() -> {
    while(true) {
    }
});

pool.shutdownNow();

Question:

Will the thread stop or keep running forever? Why?

the correct answer is:

❌ The thread will likely keep running forever.

Let’s understand why — this is a very important interview trap.

docs.title: What shutdownNow() Actually Does
docs.text:
When we call:

pool.shutdownNow();

Java does NOT forcibly kill the thread.

Instead it does:

Thread.interrupt()

It only sends an interrupt signal.

docs.title: Your Code
docs.text:
pool.submit(() -> {
    while(true) {
    }
});

This loop:

while(true)
  • never checks interrupt status
  • never blocks
  • never throws InterruptedException

So the thread ignores the interrupt.

Result:

Thread continues running forever

docs.title: When Interrupt Actually Works
docs.text:
Interrupt works when thread is doing something like:

Thread.sleep()
wait()
join()
BlockingQueue.take()

Example:

while(true) {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
}

Now shutdownNow() → interrupt → InterruptedException.

Thread stops.

docs.title: Correct Way to Write Interruptible Code
docs.text:
Good thread code checks interrupt status.

Example:

while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
    // do work
}

or

while (true) {
    if (Thread.interrupted()) break;
}

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: shutdownNow() does not forcibly kill threads; it only interrupts them, and threads must cooperatively handle the interrupt.

docs.title: Why does Java not allow killing threads forcefully?
docs.text: (Hint: It existed before — Thread.stop() — but was removed.)

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Java avoids forcefully killing threads because it can leave shared data and locks in inconsistent states; instead it uses cooperative cancellation via interrupts.

Good — this is actually a very important historical design decision in Java, and interviewers sometimes ask it.

docs.title: Why Java Does NOT Allow Forcefully Killing Threads
docs.text:
Earlier Java had a method:

Thread.stop()

It could forcefully terminate a thread.

But it was deprecated and removed from safe usage.

docs.title: The Main Problem: Inconsistent State
docs.text:
Imagine a thread is modifying shared data.

Example:

class BankAccount {
    int balance = 1000;

    void transfer() {
        balance = balance - 500;   // step 1
        // thread killed here
        balance = balance + 200;   // step 2
    }
}

If the thread is killed between step 1 and step 2:

balance = 500

System becomes corrupted.

docs.title: Another Dangerous Case: Locks
docs.text:
Example:

synchronized(account) {
    updateBalance();
}

If the thread is killed while holding the lock:

Lock is never released

Now:

Other threads block forever

Deadlock-like situation.

docs.title: Memory Consistency Problems
docs.text:
Forcefully killing threads may leave:

partially updated objects
inconsistent shared data
broken invariants

docs.title: Cooperative cancellation
docs.text:
Threads must stop themselves.

Using:

interrupt()
volatile flags
future.cancel()

Example:

volatile boolean running = true;

while(running) {
    work();
}

Another thread:

running = false;

Thread exits safely.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Java avoids forcefully killing threads because it can leave shared data and locks in inconsistent states; instead it uses cooperative cancellation via interrupts.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: synchronized is Java’s built-in locking mechanism. Deadlock happens when threads wait forever for locks held by each other.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Locks protect shared state, but wrong lock ordering can block a system. Interviewers often test both correct locking and deadlock prevention.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: If Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1, both threads are stuck.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Every object can act as a monitor lock.
  • Static synchronized methods lock the class object.
  • Instance synchronized methods lock the current object.
  • Deadlock is not solved by wait()/notify() alone.
  • Nested locks need consistent lock ordering.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: synchronized allows only one thread at a time to enter a protected block for the same lock. It is used to protect shared mutable state. Deadlock happens when two or more threads hold locks and wait for each other forever. The usual fix is to avoid nested locks, use a fixed lock order, or use timeout-based locking.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Instance method lock: current object.
  • Static method lock: class object.
  • Locks protect critical sections.
  • Deadlock requires circular waiting.
  • Use fixed lock order to prevent deadlock.
  • Keep synchronized blocks small.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: We now move to synchronized internals + monitor locks.

docs.title: 1️⃣ What is a Lock?
docs.text:
In multithreading, a lock is a mechanism that ensures:

Only one thread at a time can access a critical section of code.

Think of it like a room with one key.

Example analogy:

Room = critical code
Key = lock
Thread = person

Only the person holding the key can enter the room.

Other people must wait outside.

docs.title: 2️⃣ What is synchronized?
docs.text:
synchronized is a Java keyword used to protect critical sections.

It ensures:

Only one thread can execute that block/method at a time.

It works using monitor locks.

docs.title: A) Synchronized Block
docs.text:
You explicitly specify the lock object.

Object lock = new Object();

synchronized(lock) {
    // critical section
}

Here:

  • lock object acts as the monitor
  • Only one thread holding that lock can enter

docs.title: B) Synchronized Method
docs.text:
Example:

class Test {

    synchronized void m1() {
        // critical section
    }

}

Here Java automatically uses:

this (current object) as lock

Equivalent code:

void m1() {
    synchronized(this) {
        // critical section
    }
}

docs.title: 4️⃣ Static Synchronized Method
docs.text:
Example:

class Test {

    static synchronized void m3() {
        // critical section
    }

}

Here the lock is:

Class object

Equivalent to:

synchronized(Test.class) {
    // code
}

docs.title: 5️⃣ Summary Table
docs.text: Type Lock Used synchronized(obj) obj synchronized method this (object) static synchronized Class object

docs.title: 6️⃣ Why Locks Are Needed (Race Condition Fix)
docs.text:
Earlier problem:

count++

Two threads modify same variable → wrong result.

Solution:

synchronized void inc() {
    count++;
}

Now only one thread can execute inc() at a time.

docs.title: Now You Can Answer My Question
docs.text:
Given:

class Test {

    synchronized void m1() {}

    synchronized void m2() {}

    static synchronized void m3() {}

}

How many different locks exist here?

Hint:

  • object lock
  • class lock

✅ Answer: — two different locks exist here.

Good. Now let’s explain clearly so it becomes crystal clear for interviews.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
class Test {

    synchronized void m1() {}

    synchronized void m2() {}

    static synchronized void m3() {}

}

docs.title: 1️⃣ Lock for m1() and m2()
docs.text:
These are instance synchronized methods.

Java internally converts them to:

void m1() {
    synchronized(this) {
    }
}

void m2() {
    synchronized(this) {
    }
}

So both methods use the same lock:

this (current object)

Meaning:

If one thread executes m1(), another thread cannot execute m2() on the same object.

Because both require the same lock.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Lock for m3()
docs.text:
This is a static synchronized method.

Java internally converts it to:

synchronized(Test.class) {
}

So the lock is:

Test.class

This is a class-level lock, not object lock.

docs.title: Final Lock Summary
docs.text:
Method Lock Used m1() object lock (this) m2() object lock (this) m3() class lock (Test.class)

So:

Total locks = 2

docs.title: 🔥 Important Interview Insight
docs.text:
Object locks and class locks are independent.

So this is possible:

Thread 1:

obj.m1();

Thread 2:

Test.m3();

Both can run at the same time.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Instance synchronized methods use the object monitor (this), while static synchronized methods use the class monitor (ClassName.class).

docs.title: Next Critical Trap
docs.text:
Predict behavior:

class Test {

    synchronized void m1() {
        System.out.println("m1 start");
        try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch(Exception e) {}
        System.out.println("m1 end");
    }

    synchronized void m2() {
        System.out.println("m2");
    }

}

Test t = new Test();

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> t.m1());
Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> t.m2());

t1.start();
t2.start();

Question:

Will "m2" print immediately or after 2 seconds? Why?

ANswer: ❌ Not immediately. It will print after ~2 seconds.

docs.title: Why (very important)
docs.text:
Both m1() and m2() are instance synchronized methods, so they use the same lock:

the object lock = t (i.e., this)

docs.title: What happens:
docs.text:
• t1 enters t.m1() and acquires lock on t
  • t1 sleeps 2 seconds but still holds the lock (sleep does not release lock)
  • t2 tries to enter t.m2() but cannot, because lock is still held
  • After 2 seconds, t1 exits m1() and releases lock
  • Then t2 enters m2() and prints "m2"

So "m2" prints after "m1 end" (after ~2 seconds).

docs.title: Key interview line
docs.text: Two synchronized instance methods on the same object block each other because they use the same monitor (this).

docs.title: Quick follow-up trap
docs.text:
If t2 called new Test().m2() instead of t.m2(), would it print immediately? (Yes/No)

✅ Answer: — Yes, it would print immediately.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Because:

  • t1 is locking on object t
  • t2 would lock on a different object new Test()

Different objects → different monitors → no blocking.

Interview one-liner:

synchronized locks are per-object. Two threads only block each other if they synchronize on the same monitor object.

docs.title: Next Level: Deadlock (Most asked trap)
docs.text:
Consider:

Object A = new Object();
Object B = new Object();

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
  synchronized(A) {
    synchronized(B) {
      System.out.println("t1 done");
    }
  }
});

Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
  synchronized(B) {
    synchronized(A) {
      System.out.println("t2 done");
    }
  }
});

docs.title: Question:
docs.text:
1. What problem can happen here?
  2. How to fix it (one practical rule)?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Deadlock occurs when threads acquire locks in different order causing circular wait. The common fix is enforcing a consistent lock acquisition order.

Let’s go step by step.
