docs.title: 1️⃣ What Problem Happens Here?
docs.text:
✔ Deadlock

Deadlock means:

Two or more threads wait forever for each other’s locks.

docs.title: How Deadlock Happens Here
docs.text:
We have two locks:

Lock A
Lock B

docs.title: Thread t1
docs.text:
Lock A
then tries Lock B

docs.title: Thread t2
docs.text:
Lock B
then tries Lock A

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
t1 acquires A
t2 acquires B

t1 tries B → blocked
t2 tries A → blocked

Now:

t1 waiting for B
t2 waiting for A

Both wait forever.

This is deadlock.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why wait()/notify() is NOT the Fix
docs.text:
wait() / notify() are used for:

Thread communication

Example:

  • Producer-consumer
  • Task coordination

They do not solve deadlocks caused by lock ordering.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Correct Fix (Most Important Rule)
docs.text:
Always acquire locks in the same order.

Example fix:

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
  synchronized(A) {
    synchronized(B) {
      System.out.println("t1 done");
    }
  }
});

Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
  synchronized(A) {   // same order
    synchronized(B) {
      System.out.println("t2 done");
    }
  }
});

Now:

Both threads acquire A first
Then B

No circular wait → no deadlock.

docs.title: 🔥 Four Conditions for Deadlock (Interview Gold)
docs.text:
Deadlock happens when these 4 exist:

1️⃣ Mutual exclusion 2️⃣ Hold and wait 3️⃣ No preemption 4️⃣ Circular wait

Break any one → deadlock avoided.

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Deadlock occurs when threads acquire locks in different order causing circular wait. The common fix is enforcing a consistent lock acquisition order.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: ThreadPoolExecutor is the core Java thread pool implementation that controls worker count, task queues, and rejection behavior.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: It helps you explain how Java handles many tasks without creating unlimited threads.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A pool can start core threads first, then queue tasks, then create extra threads up to max size, then reject tasks when overloaded.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Queue type changes pool behavior.
  • Unbounded queues can hide overload and grow memory.
  • SynchronousQueue has no capacity.
  • maximumPoolSize may not matter with an unbounded queue.
  • RejectedExecutionHandler controls overload behavior.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: ThreadPoolExecutor uses core pool size, maximum pool size, keep-alive time, a work queue, and a rejection policy. When tasks arrive, the pool creates core threads, queues extra work, creates more threads if the queue cannot accept tasks, and rejects work when both queue and pool are full.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Core threads are created first.
  • Queue stores waiting tasks.
  • Max threads handle pressure after queue limits.
  • SynchronousQueue hands off directly.
  • Bounded queues help control memory.
  • Rejection policy handles overload.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Now we move to ThreadPoolExecutor Internals — this is where senior interview questions come from.

First question:

docs.title: Why does a ThreadPool need a task queue?
docs.text: What problem does the queue solve?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Thread pools reuse a limited number of threads to execute many tasks efficiently while controlling resource usage.

Perfect — this is the right time to understand ThreadPoolExecutor deeply, because many backend interviews ask internals and tuning questions.

We will go step-by-step.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Why Thread Pools Exist
docs.text:
If you create threads manually:

new Thread(task).start();

Problems:

Too many threads
Memory consumption
Context switching overhead
Thread creation cost

Solution:

Create a limited number of threads
Reuse them for multiple tasks

That is Thread Pool.

docs.title: 2️⃣ ThreadPool Basic Idea
docs.text:
Instead of:

1 thread per task

We do:

Few threads
Many tasks
Tasks wait in queue

Architecture:

        Tasks
          |
          v
      Task Queue
          |
          v
   ThreadPool Workers
   [T1] [T2] [T3]

Threads pick tasks from the queue.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Why the Task Queue Is Needed
docs.text:
Imagine 100 tasks arrive instantly but pool size is 5 threads.

Without queue:

95 tasks would be lost

Queue allows:

Tasks wait until a thread is free

So queue solves:

Load buffering
Thread reuse
Task management

docs.title: 4️⃣ ThreadPoolExecutor Internal Components
docs.text: ThreadPoolExecutor has 4 main parts.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Core Pool Size
docs.text:
Minimum number of threads always kept alive.

Example:

corePoolSize = 4

Pool always keeps 4 threads ready.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Maximum Pool Size
docs.text:
Maximum threads allowed.

Example:

maxPoolSize = 10

Pool may grow to 10 threads during heavy load.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Task Queue
docs.text:
Where tasks wait.

Common types:

LinkedBlockingQueue
ArrayBlockingQueue
SynchronousQueue

docs.title: 4️⃣ KeepAlive Time
docs.text:
Extra threads (above core size) are destroyed after inactivity.

Example:

keepAlive = 60 seconds

docs.title: 5️⃣ ThreadPool Execution Algorithm (Very Important)
docs.text: When a task arrives:

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
If active threads < corePoolSize

Create new thread

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text:
Else if queue not full

Add task to queue

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Else if threads < maxPoolSize

Create extra thread

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text:
Else

Reject task

docs.title: Visual Flow
docs.text:
Task arrives
     |
     v
Threads < corePool ? → create thread
     |
     v
Queue full ? → add to queue
     |
     v
Threads < maxPool ? → create thread
     |
     v
Reject task

docs.title: 6️⃣ Task Rejection Policies
docs.text:
If pool is full and queue is full:

Java applies RejectionPolicy.

Common ones:

docs.title: AbortPolicy (default)
docs.text: throws RejectedExecutionException

docs.title: CallerRunsPolicy
docs.text: Caller thread executes the task.

docs.title: DiscardPolicy
docs.text: Task silently discarded.

docs.title: DiscardOldestPolicy
docs.text: Oldest queued task removed.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Example ThreadPoolExecutor
docs.text:
ExecutorService pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        2,              // corePoolSize
        4,              // maximumPoolSize
        60,             // keepAliveTime
        TimeUnit.SECONDS,
        new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(10)
);

Meaning:

2 core threads
up to 4 threads under load
10 tasks in queue
extra threads die after 60 sec

docs.title: 8️⃣ Executors Utility Methods
docs.text: Java provides shortcuts:

docs.title: Fixed Thread Pool
docs.text:
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(5)

Fixed number of threads.

docs.title: Cached Thread Pool
docs.text:
Executors.newCachedThreadPool()

Creates threads dynamically.

docs.title: Single Thread Executor
docs.text:
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()

Only one worker thread.

docs.title: Important Interview Warning
docs.text:
In production systems, many engineers avoid Executors.newFixedThreadPool() because:

Queue is unbounded
Memory can explode

Instead they prefer ThreadPoolExecutor directly.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Thread pools reuse a limited number of threads to execute many tasks efficiently while controlling resource usage.

docs.title: Now a Very Important Interview Question
docs.text:
Consider this pool:

corePoolSize = 2
maxPoolSize = 4
queue capacity = 2

If 7 tasks arrive at the same time, how many:

1️⃣ Threads will be created 2️⃣ Tasks will wait in queue 3️⃣ Tasks will be rejected

Given:

  • core = 2
  • max = 4
  • queue capacity = 2
  • 7 tasks arrive

Let’s do the exact step-by-step using the real ThreadPoolExecutor algorithm.

docs.title: Task 1
docs.text: Active threads = 0 < core(2) ✅ Create thread #1 → runs Task1

docs.title: Task 2
docs.text:
Active threads = 1 < core(2) ✅ Create thread #2 → runs Task2

Now active threads = 2 (core reached)

docs.title: Task 3
docs.text: Core full → try queue ✅ Queue Task3 (queue size 1/2)

docs.title: Task 4
docs.text: ✅ Queue Task4 (queue size 2/2 full)

docs.title: Task 5
docs.text: Core full and queue full → try to expand threads up to max(4) ✅ Create thread #3 → runs Task5

docs.title: Task 6
docs.text:
✅ Create thread #4 → runs Task6

Now active threads = 4 (max reached)

docs.title: Task 7
docs.text: Core full + queue full + max threads reached ❌ Reject Task7

docs.title: ✅ Final Correct Answers
docs.text:
1️⃣ Threads created = 4 total (2 core threads + 2 extra threads)

2️⃣ Tasks waiting in queue = 2 (Task3 and Task4)

3️⃣ Tasks rejected = 1 (Task7)

docs.title: 🔥 Interview one-liner
docs.text: ThreadPoolExecutor first fills core threads, then queue, then grows up to max threads, then rejects.

docs.title: Next Tricky Question (very common)
docs.text:
If we change the queue to SynchronousQueue (capacity = 0), with same core=2, max=4, and 7 tasks arrive:

How many tasks will be rejected?

docs.title: What is SynchronousQueue?
docs.text:
It has zero capacity.

That means:

  • It cannot store tasks.
  • A task can be handed off only if a worker thread is ready to take it immediately.

So it’s like a direct hand-to-hand transfer.

docs.title: ThreadPoolExecutor behavior with SynchronousQueue
docs.text:
Given:

  • core = 2
  • max = 4
  • queue = SynchronousQueue (capacity 0)
  • 7 tasks arrive

Algorithm:

  1. Fill core threads
  2. Try to queue (but queue can’t hold anything)
  3. Create extra threads up to max
  4. Then reject

docs.title: Task 2 → create thread #2 (core)
docs.text: Now core is full (2 threads busy)

docs.title: Task 3 → try queue → cannot (capacity 0)
docs.text: So create thread #3 (extra)

docs.title: Task 4 → create thread #4 (extra)
docs.text: Now we reached max threads = 4

docs.title: Task 5 → cannot queue + cannot create more → reject
✅ Final Answer
docs.text:
• Threads created: 4
  • Queue waiting: 0
  • Tasks rejected: 3 (tasks 5, 6, 7)

docs.title: Why this matters (interview)
docs.text:
• newCachedThreadPool() uses SynchronousQueue
  • It creates threads aggressively under load
  • If max is very high, it may create too many threads

docs.title: Quick check (1 line)
docs.text:
Which queue is safer to prevent creating too many threads?

A) SynchronousQueue B) Bounded LinkedBlockingQueue(100)

Answer A or B.

No worries — I’ll explain quickly and then you’ll be able to answer confidently.

docs.title: ✅ LinkedBlockingQueue(100) (bounded)
docs.text:
• It can store up to 100 tasks
  • If all threads are busy, tasks wait in queue
  • Prevents creating too many threads quickly
  • Helps control CPU + memory

docs.title: ⚡ SynchronousQueue (0 capacity)
docs.text:
• It stores nothing

  • If a thread isn’t immediately free:

  • ThreadPool tries to create a new thread (up to max)

  • Can grow threads rapidly under load

docs.title: Which is safer to prevent creating too many threads?
docs.text:
✅ B) Bounded LinkedBlockingQueue(100)

Because tasks wait in queue instead of forcing new thread creation.

docs.title: Interview one-liner
docs.text: A bounded queue limits memory and controls thread growth; SynchronousQueue pushes the pool to create threads aggressively.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: volatile gives visibility guarantees. Atomic classes give atomic operations using low-level compare-and-swap behavior.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This topic explains memory visibility, instruction reordering, and why some thread-safe code still fails without proper happens-before relationships.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A volatile boolean ready flag lets one thread publish a change that another thread can see reliably.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• volatile does not make count++ atomic.
  • volatile is useful for visibility, not compound updates.
  • Atomic classes help with atomic counters.
  • Instruction reordering can affect unsynchronized code.
  • Happens-before is about visibility and ordering guarantees.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: volatile ensures that reads and writes go to main memory with visibility guarantees, so one thread can see another thread’s update. It does not make compound operations atomic. For atomic increments, use AtomicInteger or synchronization. Happens-before rules define when one thread’s changes are guaranteed to be visible to another thread.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• volatile gives visibility.
  • volatile prevents some reordering around the variable.
  • count++ is still not atomic.
  • Atomic classes use CAS.
  • Happens-before gives ordering and visibility.
  • Use the right tool for the shared state pattern.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: We now go to:

docs.title: volatile (Most misunderstood Java keyword)
docs.text: Before I explain it, tell me:

docs.title: Question
docs.text: What problem does volatile solve?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
volatile ensures visibility of variable updates across threads but does not guarantee atomicity.

Let’s explain from the ground up.

docs.title: 1️⃣ The Real Problem volatile Solves
docs.text:
In multithreading there are two major problems:

1️⃣ Visibility problem 2️⃣ Atomicity problem

volatile solves only the visibility problem.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why Visibility Problem Happens
docs.text:
Each thread has its own working memory (CPU cache).

Architecture simplified:

Main Memory (Heap)
      |
  ------------
  |          |
Thread 1   Thread 2
Cache      Cache

Threads do not always read directly from main memory.

They may read from their local cache.

docs.title: Example Problem
docs.text:
class Test {

    static boolean running = true;

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Thread t = new Thread(() -> {
            while(running) {
            }
            System.out.println("Stopped");
        });

        t.start();

        try { Thread.sleep(2000); } catch(Exception e){}

        running = false;
    }
}

docs.title: Expected behavior
docs.text:
After 2 seconds:

Stopped

docs.title: What may happen
docs.text:
Thread may run forever.

Why?

Thread t may cache:

running = true

It keeps reading cached value, not updated value from main memory.

So it never sees:

running = false

docs.title: 3️⃣ Solution: volatile
docs.text:
static volatile boolean running = true;

Now Java guarantees:

Read directly from main memory
Write directly to main memory

No caching issue.

docs.title: 4️⃣ What volatile Guarantees
docs.text: volatile provides:

docs.title: ✔ Visibility
docs.text: Changes made by one thread are immediately visible to other threads.

docs.title: ✔ Happens-before relationship
docs.text: Write → immediately visible to readers.

docs.title: 5️⃣ What volatile DOES NOT Solve
docs.text:
volatile does NOT make operations atomic.

Example:

volatile int count = 0;

count++;

Still unsafe.

Because count++ =

read
add
write

Multiple threads can break it.

So for increments we need:

synchronized
AtomicInteger
Lock

docs.title: 6️⃣ Interview Table
docs.text: Feature volatile Visibility ✔ Atomicity ❌ Prevent caching ✔ Locking ❌

docs.title: 🧠 Interview One-Liner
docs.text: volatile ensures visibility of variable updates across threads but does not guarantee atomicity.

docs.title: Now a Very Important Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Test {

    volatile int count = 0;

    void inc() {
        count++;
    }

}

If 10 threads run inc() 1000 times each:

Expected:

10000

Will we always get 10000?

Yes or No — and why?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
volatile ensures visibility but does not guarantee atomicity, so operations like count++ remain unsafe in multithreading.

Now let’s explanation to interview-quality clarity.

docs.title: Correct Answer
docs.text: ❌ No, we will NOT always get 10000.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because:

count++

is not atomic.

Even though count is volatile, the operation still executes as three steps:

1. Read count
2. Add 1
3. Write count

Example race condition:

Initial:

count = 5

Thread 1 reads:

5

Thread 2 reads:

5

Both increment:

6

Both write:

6

One increment is lost.

docs.title: What volatile Actually Guarantees
docs.text:
✔ Visibility ✔ Prevents CPU caching issues

But it does NOT guarantee:

❌ Atomic operations ❌ Mutual exclusion

docs.title: Option 1 — synchronized
docs.text:
synchronized void inc() {
    count++;
}

docs.title: Option 2 — AtomicInteger (best)
docs.text:
AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();

count.incrementAndGet();

Uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap).

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: volatile ensures visibility but does not guarantee atomicity, so operations like count++ remain unsafe in multithreading.

docs.title: Now a Very Important Multithreading Trap
docs.text:
Predict the output:

class Test {

    volatile boolean flag = false;

    void writer() {
        flag = true;
    }

    void reader() {
        if(flag) {
            System.out.println("Visible");
        }
    }

}

Two threads run:

Thread 1 → writer()
Thread 2 → reader()

Question:

Is it guaranteed that thread 2 sees flag = true?

Yes / No — and why?

docs.title: volatile ensures visibility of updates across threads, but it does not guarantee ordering of thread execution.
Correct Answer
docs.text:
✔ Yes — if thread 2 reads flag after thread 1 writes it, it will see true.

But we must add an important condition.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because flag is declared as:

volatile boolean flag = false;

volatile guarantees visibility between threads.

Meaning:

Write by one thread → immediately visible to other threads

So when thread 1 does:

flag = true;

the updated value is written to main memory.

When thread 2 reads:

if(flag)

it must read from main memory, not a cached copy.

docs.title: Important Detail (Interview Trap)
docs.text:
volatile does NOT guarantee execution order between threads.

So two scenarios exist:

docs.title: Scenario 1
docs.text:
Thread 1 executes first.

writer() → flag = true
reader() → sees true

Output:

Visible

docs.title: Scenario 2
docs.text:
Thread 2 executes first.

reader() → flag still false
writer() → later sets true

Output:

(no output)

docs.title: Therefore the correct statement
docs.text: volatile guarantees visibility, but not thread execution order.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: volatile ensures visibility of updates across threads, but it does not guarantee ordering of thread execution.

docs.title: Next Critical Topic (Very Important)
docs.text:
Now we move to Atomic Variables & CAS (Compare-And-Swap) — this is used inside:

  • AtomicInteger
  • ConcurrentHashMap
  • many lock-free algorithms.

First question for you:

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Why is AtomicInteger faster than synchronized in many cases?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
AtomicInteger uses lock-free CAS operations at the CPU level, avoiding blocking and context switching, which makes it faster than synchronized in many scenarios.

Now let’s explain the real reason deeply, because this is an important interview topic.

docs.title: Why AtomicInteger is Often Faster than synchronized
docs.text:
Your intuition is correct: it avoids heavy locking.

The main reason is:

AtomicInteger uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap) instead of locks.

docs.title: 1️⃣ How synchronized Works
docs.text:
When a thread enters:

synchronized void inc() {
    count++;
}

The JVM must:

1️⃣ Acquire monitor lock 2️⃣ Block other threads 3️⃣ Execute code 4️⃣ Release lock

If many threads compete:

Thread waiting
Context switching
Lock management

These operations are expensive.

docs.title: 2️⃣ How AtomicInteger Works
docs.text:
AtomicInteger uses a lock-free algorithm.

Example:

AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();

count.incrementAndGet();

Internally it uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap).

docs.title: 3️⃣ CAS (Compare-And-Swap)
docs.text:
CAS is a CPU-level atomic instruction.

It works like this:

compare current value with expected value
if equal → update
if not equal → retry

Example:

Initial:

count = 5

Thread wants to update:

expected = 5
newValue = 6

CPU instruction:

if(count == 5)
   count = 6
else
   retry

This happens without locking.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Why CAS is Faster
docs.text:
CAS:

✔ No thread blocking ✔ No OS context switching ✔ CPU-level atomic operation

So performance is usually better under moderate contention.

docs.title: Interview Comparison
docs.text: Feature synchronized AtomicInteger Locking Yes No Blocking Yes No Uses CAS No Yes Performance Slower under contention Usually faster

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: AtomicInteger uses lock-free CAS operations at the CPU level, avoiding blocking and context switching, which makes it faster than synchronized in many scenarios.

docs.title: Important Limitation
docs.text:
CAS can suffer from a problem called:

ABA problem

We’ll discuss that later.

docs.title: Next Important Trap
docs.text:
Predict the behavior:

AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> {
    for(int i=0;i<1000;i++)
        count.incrementAndGet();
});

Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> {
    for(int i=0;i<1000;i++)
        count.incrementAndGet();
});

t1.start();
t2.start();
t1.join();
t2.join();

System.out.println(count);

docs.title: Question:
docs.text: Will this always print 2000? Why?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Yes — it will always print 2000.
AtomicInteger uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap) in a retry loop to ensure atomic updates without using locks.

docs.title: Correct Answer
docs.text: ✔ Yes — it will always print 2000.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because:

count.incrementAndGet();

is an atomic operation.

Internally it uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap).

docs.title: Internal Working (Simplified)
docs.text:
Suppose:

count = 5

Thread tries to update:

expected = 5
newValue = 6

CPU executes CAS:

if(count == expected)
    count = newValue
else
    retry

If another thread changed the value meanwhile:

CAS fails → retry loop

So no updates are lost.

docs.title: Internal Loop (conceptually)
docs.text:
AtomicInteger works like this:

while(true) {
   int current = value;
   int next = current + 1;

   if(CAS(current, next))
       return next;
}

CAS success → operation done CAS failure → retry

docs.title: Important Interview Point
docs.text:
AtomicInteger guarantees:

✔ Atomicity ✔ Visibility ✔ Lock-free behavior

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: AtomicInteger uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap) in a retry loop to ensure atomic updates without using locks.

docs.title: Now a Very Important Multithreading Trap
docs.text:
Predict output possibility:

class Test {

    int x = 0;
    int y = 0;

    void writer() {
        x = 1;
        y = 1;
    }

    void reader() {
        if(y == 1) {
            System.out.println(x);
        }
    }

}

Two threads:

Thread 1 → writer()
Thread 2 → reader()

docs.title: Question:
docs.text:
Is it possible for this program to print:

0

Yes or No — and why?

This question leads to Java Memory Model & instruction reordering, one of the most important multithreading topics.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Yes — it is possible to print 0 (in some executions), because without volatile/synchronization there is no happens-before relationship between the threads.

Let me explain clearly.

docs.title: Why 0 is possible
docs.text:
You’re thinking in single-thread order:

writer sets x=1 then y=1, so if reader sees y==1 it must see x==1.

That guarantee exists only in single-thread reasoning.

In multithreading, without proper memory barriers, two things can happen:

docs.title: 1) Visibility issue
docs.text:
Thread 1 updates x and y, but thread 2 may see:

  • the update to y
  • but still see old cached value of x

So reader can observe:

y == 1
x == 0

docs.title: 2) Reordering
docs.text:
The compiler/CPU can reorder writes for performance (as long as single-thread behavior stays correct). So it’s possible that:

  • y=1 becomes visible before x=1

Again reader can see y==1 first.

docs.title: Key concept: Happens-Before
docs.text:
Because there is no synchronization:

  • writer’s actions are not guaranteed to be visible in same order to reader.

So 0 is possible.

docs.title: How to Fix It (two correct ways)
Option A: Make y volatile
docs.text:
volatile int y = 0;

If writer does:

x = 1;
y = 1;

And reader checks:

if (y == 1) System.out.println(x);

Now volatile write/read creates a happens-before:

  • If reader sees y==1, it will also see x==1.

docs.title: Option B: Use synchronized
docs.text: Put writer and reader under same lock.

docs.title: Interview one-liner
docs.text: Without a happens-before relation, reads can see stale values and writes can appear reordered, so y==1 does not guarantee x==1.

docs.title: Quick check question (yes/no)
docs.text:
If we make only x volatile (not y), is printing 0 still possible?

Let’s go step-by-step with a mental model.

We’ll answer both questions:

  1. Why volatile int y fixes the issue
  2. When this problem happens (same object vs different object)

docs.title: 1️⃣ First Understand the Problem Clearly
docs.text:
Code:

class Test {

    int x = 0;
    int y = 0;

    void writer() {
        x = 1;
        y = 1;
    }

    void reader() {
        if (y == 1) {
            System.out.println(x);
        }
    }
}

Two threads:

Thread 1 → writer()
Thread 2 → reader()

You assumed:

x = 1
y = 1

So if y == 1, then x must be 1.

But multithreading breaks that assumption.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Why 0 Can Print
docs.text:
Modern CPUs and JVM optimize execution.

Two things may happen:

docs.title: A) CPU Cache (Visibility Problem)
docs.text:
Each thread may read from its own CPU cache, not main memory.

Example:

Main memory:

x = 1
y = 1

Thread 2 cache may still have:

x = 0
y = 1

So it prints:

0

docs.title: B) Instruction Reordering
docs.text:
The JVM or CPU may reorder instructions.

Writer code:

x = 1
y = 1

May internally execute like:

y = 1
x = 1

Then reader may see:

y == 1
x == 0

Again prints:

0

docs.title: 3️⃣ How volatile Fixes It
docs.text:
If we declare:

volatile int y = 0;

Then y becomes a memory barrier.

Writer:

x = 1;
y = 1;   // volatile write

Reader:

if (y == 1) {  // volatile read
    System.out.println(x);
}

Now JVM guarantees:

All writes before volatile write
must be visible to threads reading that volatile variable

Meaning:

x = 1 happens-before y = 1

So if reader sees:

y == 1

then it must see:

x == 1

Now 0 cannot happen.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: A volatile write establishes a happens-before relationship with subsequent volatile reads, ensuring visibility of prior writes.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Your Second Question (Very Important)
docs.text:
You asked:

Does this happen when two threads operate on the same object or different objects?

docs.title: Answer
docs.text:
The problem occurs when:

Two threads access shared variables

It does NOT depend on object count, but on shared memory.

Example:

docs.title: Case A — Same Object
docs.text:
Test obj = new Test();
Thread 1 → obj.writer()
Thread 2 → obj.reader()

Shared variables:

obj.x
obj.y

Problem possible.

docs.title: Case B — Static Variables
docs.text:
static int x
static int y

All objects share them → problem possible.

docs.title: Case C — Separate Objects
docs.text:
Test obj1 = new Test();
Test obj2 = new Test();

Thread 1 uses obj1 Thread 2 uses obj2

Now variables are not shared → no issue.

docs.title: Rule to Remember
docs.text:
Multithreading problems occur when:

Shared mutable state + multiple threads

docs.title: 5️⃣ Visual Memory Model
docs.text:
Main Memory
   x=1 y=1
     |
---------------------
|                   |
Thread 1 Cache   Thread 2 Cache
 x=1 y=1         x=0 y=1

Reader prints:

0

docs.title: Quick Check (Important)
docs.text:
If we declare:

volatile int x;
volatile int y;

docs.title: Will the problem still happen?
docs.text: Yes or No — and why?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
No

Answer “No” is correct, but let’s understand why, because this touches the Java Memory Model (JMM) and the concept of happens-before.

docs.title: If both variables are volatile
docs.text:
volatile int x = 0;
volatile int y = 0;

void writer() {
    x = 1;
    y = 1;
}

void reader() {
    if (y == 1) {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Two threads:

Thread 1 → writer()
Thread 2 → reader()

docs.title: What volatile guarantees
docs.text:
A volatile write has two important guarantees:

1️⃣ Visibility The value written by one thread becomes immediately visible to other threads.

2️⃣ Ordering (memory barrier) Operations before a volatile write cannot be reordered after it.

docs.title: Execution Order With Volatile
docs.text:
Writer thread executes:

x = 1
y = 1   (volatile write)

Because y is volatile:

x = 1  happens-before  y = 1

docs.title: Reader Thread
docs.text:
Reader does:

read y (volatile read)

A volatile read guarantees that the thread sees all writes that happened before the volatile write.

So if the reader sees:

y == 1

Then the reader must see:

x == 1

docs.title: Therefore
docs.text:
Printing:

0

is not possible when y is volatile (or both are volatile).

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
A volatile write establishes a happens-before relationship with subsequent reads of that variable.

So:

write volatile → read volatile

ensures memory visibility.

docs.title: Important Detail
docs.text:
Actually only y needs to be volatile in this example. x does not have to be volatile.

Because the volatile access to y acts as the memory synchronization point.

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: A volatile write creates a happens-before relationship with subsequent volatile reads, ensuring that all previous writes become visible to other threads.

docs.title: Quick Challenge (Very Important Interview Trap)
docs.text:
Predict if this program can print 0.

class Test {

    volatile boolean ready = false;
    int number = 0;

    void writer() {
        number = 42;
        ready = true;
    }

    void reader() {
        if (ready) {
            System.out.println(number);
        }
    }
}

Two threads run writer() and reader().

Question: Can it print 0 or will it always print 42? Why?

Not this time — ✅ with ready as volatile, it should not print 0 if the reader sees ready == true.

Here’s the exact rule:

docs.title: What volatile ready guarantees
docs.text:
In writer():

number = 42;     // normal write
ready = true;    // volatile write

A volatile write (ready = true) creates a happens-before edge:

All writes before the volatile write become visible to any thread that later reads that volatile variable as true.

So in reader():

if (ready) {          // volatile read
    System.out.println(number);
}

If the reader sees ready == true, then it must see number == 42.

docs.title: What outputs are possible?
docs.text:
• If reader runs before writer sets ready=true: it prints nothing.
  • If reader runs after it sees ready=true: it prints 42.

✅ Printing 0 is not allowed in a correctly implemented JVM under the Java Memory Model, given ready is volatile.

docs.title: Interview one-liner
docs.text: Volatile is often used as a “publish” flag: writing the flag volatile safely publishes prior writes.

docs.title: Quick check (trap)
docs.text: If we remove volatile from ready, is printing 0 possible? (Yes/No)

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Yes, printing 0 becomes possible if ready is not volatile.

Let’s understand why, because this is a very important Java Memory Model concept.

docs.title: Code Without volatile
docs.text:
class Test {

    boolean ready = false;
    int number = 0;

    void writer() {
        number = 42;
        ready = true;
    }

    void reader() {
        if (ready) {
            System.out.println(number);
        }
    }
}

Two threads:

Thread 1 → writer()
Thread 2 → reader()

docs.title: Why 0 Can Print
docs.text:
Without volatile, there is no happens-before relationship between the threads.

Two issues may occur:

docs.title: 1️⃣ Visibility Problem
docs.text:
Thread 1 updates memory:

number = 42
ready = true

But Thread 2 might see:

ready = true
number = 0

Because it reads stale cached values.

So output:

0

docs.title: 2️⃣ Instruction Reordering
docs.text:
The CPU or JVM may reorder instructions.

Writer code:

number = 42
ready = true

May execute internally as:

ready = true
number = 42

Now the reader sees:

ready == true
number == 0

Again prints:

0

docs.title: Why volatile ready Fixes It
docs.text:
When ready is volatile:

number = 42
ready = true   (volatile write)

Reader:

if(ready)   (volatile read)

Java guarantees:

All writes before volatile write
are visible after volatile read

So if reader sees:

ready == true

it must see:

number == 42

docs.title: Visual Timeline
docs.text:
Without volatile:

Writer Thread          Reader Thread

number = 42
ready = true  ------->  ready == true
                        number == 0

Possible output:

0

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Without synchronization or volatile, there is no happens-before relationship, so a thread may observe writes out of order or see stale values.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: wait() and notify() coordinate threads through an object monitor. BlockingQueue provides a safer high-level way to solve producer-consumer problems.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Producer-consumer is a classic interview problem and a real backend pattern for handoff between threads.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A producer adds items to a queue, and a consumer removes them. If the queue is empty, the consumer waits. If it is full, the producer waits.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Call wait() inside synchronized code.
  • Use while, not if, when waiting on a condition.
  • notify() does not release the lock immediately.
  • Manual wait/notify code is easy to get wrong.
  • BlockingQueue handles waiting and thread safety for you.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: wait() releases the monitor and waits until another thread calls notify() or notifyAll(). Producer-consumer can be built with wait/notify, but BlockingQueue is cleaner because it handles blocking, waking, and thread safety internally.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• wait() releases the monitor.
  • notify() wakes waiting thread(s).
  • Always check condition in a loop.
  • Producer-consumer needs coordination.
  • BlockingQueue is the modern safer choice.
  • put() and take() can block.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Let’s go deeper in this order:

1️⃣ wait() / notify() / notifyAll()
2️⃣ Producer–Consumer
3️⃣ BlockingQueue
4️⃣ ReentrantLock
5️⃣ ReadWriteLock
6️⃣ CountDownLatch
7️⃣ CyclicBarrier
8️⃣ Semaphore

After that you will understand almost all Java concurrency questions.

docs.title: Let’s Start the Next Important Concept
sleep() vs wait()
docs.text:
This question appears in almost every Java interview.

First try answering:

docs.title: Question
docs.text:
What is the difference between:

Thread.sleep()

and

Object.wait()

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
sleep() pauses a thread without releasing the lock, while wait() releases the lock and waits until another thread calls notify or notifyAll.

Let’s refine it to interview-perfect clarity.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Thread.sleep()
docs.text:
Method:

Thread.sleep(1000);

Characteristics:

Static method of Thread class
Can be called anywhere
Pauses the thread for a fixed time
Does NOT release locks

Example:

synchronized(obj) {
    Thread.sleep(5000);
}

Here:

Thread sleeps
But still holds the lock
Other threads cannot enter the synchronized block

docs.title: 2️⃣ Object.wait()
docs.text:
Method:

obj.wait();

Characteristics:

Instance method of Object class
Must be called inside synchronized block
Releases the lock
Thread goes to WAITING state

Example:

synchronized(obj) {
    obj.wait();
}

What happens:

Thread releases the lock
Thread waits
Another thread calls notify()
Thread wakes up and tries to reacquire the lock

docs.title: Important Flow
docs.text:
Thread states:

RUNNING
  ↓
WAITING (wait())
  ↓
NOTIFIED
  ↓
BLOCKED (trying to acquire lock)
  ↓
RUNNING

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature sleep() wait() Class Thread Object Static Yes No Requires synchronized No Yes Releases lock ❌ No ✔ Yes Wake-up condition Timeout notify / notifyAll

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: sleep() pauses a thread without releasing the lock, while wait() releases the lock and waits until another thread calls notify or notifyAll.

docs.title: Very Important Interview Trap
docs.text:
What happens here?

Object lock = new Object();

lock.wait();

Will it:

A) Compile B) Throw exception C) Work normally

What do you think?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text: ❌ It WILL compile. ⚠ But it will throw an exception at runtime.

docs.title: What Happens Here
docs.text:
Code:

Object lock = new Object();
lock.wait();

This compiles successfully.

But when the program runs, it throws:

java.lang.IllegalMonitorStateException

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text:
Rule in Java:

wait()
notify()
notifyAll()

must be called only when the thread owns the object's monitor lock.

Meaning:

You must be inside synchronized(lock)

Correct usage:

Object lock = new Object();

synchronized(lock) {
    lock.wait();
}

Now it works.

docs.title: Why Java Enforces This
docs.text:
Because wait() must do two things safely:

1️⃣ Release the object's lock
2️⃣ Put the thread into WAITING state

If the thread doesn't own the lock, Java cannot release it.

So JVM throws:

IllegalMonitorStateException

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: wait(), notify(), and notifyAll() must be called while holding the object's monitor lock, otherwise the JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException.

docs.title: Next Important Multithreading Concept
docs.text:
Now we move to the classic Producer–Consumer problem.

This is one of the most famous concurrency problems and appears in interviews frequently.

Before I explain it, tell me:

docs.title: What do you think "Producer–Consumer" means in programming?
Answer
docs.text:
The Producer–Consumer problem coordinates threads producing and consuming data using a shared buffer while preventing race conditions and overflow/underflow.

Let's build it from intuition → code → interview level.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Real World Idea (Producer–Consumer)
docs.text:
Imagine a restaurant kitchen.

Chef (Producer) → cooks food
Waiter (Consumer) → takes food to customers

Between them there is a table where food is placed.

Chef → puts food on table
Waiter → takes food from table

Rules:

If table is full → chef must wait
If table is empty → waiter must wait

This is exactly the Producer–Consumer problem.

docs.title: 2️⃣ Programming Version
docs.text:
Producer thread → generates data
Consumer thread → processes data

Between them there is a shared buffer / queue.

Example:

Producer → add task to queue
Consumer → remove task from queue

docs.title: 3️⃣ Why It Is a Multithreading Problem
docs.text:
Because multiple threads share the same buffer.

Problems may happen:

Producer adds while consumer removes
Queue becomes empty
Queue becomes full
Race conditions

So we need thread coordination.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Classic Solution Using wait() / notify()
docs.text:
Shared buffer example:

capacity = 5

docs.title: Producer logic
docs.text:
if buffer full → wait()
else add item
notify consumer

docs.title: Consumer logic
docs.text:
if buffer empty → wait()
else remove item
notify producer

docs.title: Shared buffer
docs.text:
class Buffer {

    Queue<Integer> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    int capacity = 5;

    public synchronized void produce(int value) throws InterruptedException {

        while(queue.size() == capacity) {
            wait();
        }

        queue.add(value);
        System.out.println("Produced " + value);

        notifyAll();
    }

    public synchronized void consume() throws InterruptedException {

        while(queue.isEmpty()) {
            wait();
        }

        int value = queue.poll();
        System.out.println("Consumed " + value);

        notifyAll();
    }
}

docs.title: Producer thread
docs.text:
while(true) {
    buffer.produce(i++);
}

docs.title: Consumer thread
docs.text:
while(true) {
    buffer.consume();
}

docs.title: 6️⃣ Why We Use while, Not if
docs.text:
Interview trap ⚠

We write:

while(queue.isEmpty()) {
    wait();
}

NOT:

if(queue.isEmpty()) {
    wait();
}

Because of:

Spurious wakeups

Threads may wake up without notify().

So we re-check the condition.

docs.title: 7️⃣ Modern Java Solution (Better)
docs.text:
Instead of writing wait() / notify() manually, Java provides:

BlockingQueue

Example:

BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(5);

Producer:

queue.put(value);

Consumer:

queue.take();

Queue automatically handles:

locking
waiting
wakeup

docs.title: 8️⃣ Interview One-Liner
docs.text: The Producer–Consumer problem coordinates threads producing and consuming data using a shared buffer while preventing race conditions and overflow/underflow.

docs.title: Quick Thinking Question
docs.text:
Suppose:

Buffer capacity = 5
Producer speed = very fast
Consumer speed = very slow

What problem will happen if we do not use wait()?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
Buffer Overflow will happen.

“The producer may keep adding items faster than the consumer removes them, causing the buffer to overflow.”

Now let’s explain it clearly.

docs.title: What Happens Without wait()
docs.text:
Assume:

Buffer capacity = 5
Producer = very fast
Consumer = slow

Producer keeps executing:

queue.add(item);

Without checking capacity.

So the buffer becomes:

[1,2,3,4,5]  (full)

Producer continues:

[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9...]

Result:

Buffer overflow
Memory growth
Possible crash

docs.title: Why wait() Solves This
docs.text:
Producer logic:

while(queue.size() == capacity) {
    wait();
}

Meaning:

Buffer full → producer sleeps
Consumer removes item → notify producer
Producer wakes up

Now buffer stays controlled.

docs.title: Opposite Problem
docs.text:
If consumer is faster than producer.

Example:

Consumer tries to remove item
Buffer is empty

This causes:

Buffer Underflow

Consumer must also wait:

while(queue.isEmpty()) {
    wait();
}

docs.title: Final Flow
docs.text:
Producer
   ↓
Shared Buffer
   ↓
Consumer

Rules:

Buffer full → producer waits
Buffer empty → consumer waits

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: Producer–Consumer uses wait() and notify() to coordinate threads sharing a bounded buffer, preventing overflow and underflow.

docs.title: Where We Are Now in Multithreading
docs.text:
You now understand:

Threads
Race conditions
synchronized
Deadlock
volatile
CAS
Atomic classes
ExecutorService
Thread pools
wait/notify
Producer–Consumer

You're already covering most Java concurrency interviews.

docs.title: Next Very Important Topic
docs.text:
Now we move to BlockingQueue — which is the modern Java solution for Producer–Consumer.

Before I explain it, answer this:

docs.title: Why is BlockingQueue better than using wait() and notify() manually?
BlockingQueue simplifies concurrent producer–consumer implementations by automatically handling thread blocking and synchronization.
Why BlockingQueue Is Better Than wait()/notify()
docs.text:
Your core idea is right:

BlockingQueue automatically handles waiting and waking threads.

Let’s explain the full reasons.

docs.title: 1️⃣ Automatic Waiting (Blocking)
docs.text:
When queue is full:

queue.put(item);

Producer automatically blocks until space becomes available.

When queue is empty:

queue.take();

Consumer automatically blocks until an item appears.

So we do not need:

wait()
notify()
synchronized

docs.title: 2️⃣ Built-in Thread Safety
docs.text:
BlockingQueue internally uses:

locks
conditions
safe memory visibility

So we avoid writing complicated synchronization code.

docs.title: 3️⃣ Prevents Classic Bugs
docs.text:
Manual wait/notify code can cause:

missed notification
deadlock
spurious wakeups
incorrect synchronization

BlockingQueue handles these correctly.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Cleaner Code
docs.text:
Manual producer-consumer:

synchronized(buffer) {
   while(buffer full) wait();
   add item
   notifyAll()
}

Using BlockingQueue:

queue.put(item);

Much simpler.

docs.title: 5️⃣ Used Everywhere in Java Internals
docs.text:
Many frameworks use BlockingQueue:

ThreadPoolExecutor
ExecutorService
Task scheduling systems
Message processing systems

Example:

ThreadPoolExecutor
        ↓
   BlockingQueue
        ↓
    Worker Threads

docs.title: Common BlockingQueue Implementations
docs.text: Queue Description ArrayBlockingQueue fixed capacity queue LinkedBlockingQueue optionally bounded queue PriorityBlockingQueue priority ordering DelayQueue delayed tasks SynchronousQueue direct handoff

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: BlockingQueue simplifies concurrent producer–consumer implementations by automatically handling thread blocking and synchronization.

docs.title: Quick Interview Question
docs.text:
Which method does NOT block if the queue is full?

put()
offer()
take()

Which one?

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
The correct answer is: ✅ offer()

Let’s understand clearly.

docs.title: 1️⃣ put()
docs.text:
queue.put(item);

Behavior:

If queue is full → thread BLOCKS
Waits until space is available

So put() blocks.

docs.title: 2️⃣ take()
docs.text:
queue.take();

Behavior:

If queue is empty → thread BLOCKS
Waits until element appears

So take() also blocks.

docs.title: 3️⃣ offer()
docs.text:
queue.offer(item);

Behavior:

If queue is full → returns false
Does NOT block

Example:

boolean success = queue.offer(10);

If queue is full:

success = false

docs.title: There is Also Timed Offer
docs.text:
queue.offer(item, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Meaning:

Wait up to 5 seconds
If still full → return false

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Method Behavior put() blocks if full take() blocks if empty offer() does NOT block poll() does NOT block

docs.title: Interview One-Liner
docs.text: put() and take() are blocking operations, while offer() and poll() return immediately if the queue cannot accept or provide an element.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Object-Oriented Programming organizes code around objects that contain data and behavior.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: OOP is a core Java interview topic because Java classes, inheritance, abstraction, polymorphism, and encapsulation are used in almost every backend project.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A BankAccount class can hide its balance field and expose methods like deposit() and withdraw() to protect valid behavior.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Encapsulation is not only making fields private.
  • Abstraction and encapsulation are related but different.
  • Inheritance should not be used only for code reuse.
  • Polymorphism depends on runtime object type for overridden methods.
  • Fields are not polymorphic like methods.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: OOP is a programming style based on objects. The four main pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism. Encapsulation protects state, abstraction hides complexity, inheritance models an is-a relationship, and polymorphism allows the same reference type to call different overridden behavior at runtime.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Encapsulation protects data.
  • Abstraction hides implementation details.
  • Inheritance models is-a relationship.
  • Polymorphism allows dynamic behavior.
  • Prefer composition when inheritance is not natural.
  • Java uses classes and interfaces to model OOP.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: We will cover:

docs.title: Definition (Interview Ready)
docs.text:
Encapsulation means:

Binding data and methods together in a single unit
and restricting direct access to the data.

In Java this is achieved using:

private variables
public getter/setter methods

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class BankAccount {

    private double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) {
        balance += amount;
    }

    public double getBalance() {
        return balance;
    }
}

Usage:

BankAccount acc = new BankAccount();
acc.deposit(500);
System.out.println(acc.getBalance());

docs.title: Why Encapsulation?
docs.text:
Encapsulation provides:

Data hiding
Controlled access
Security
Maintainability

Example:

You cannot directly do:

acc.balance = -1000;

because balance is private.

docs.title: Real World Example
docs.text:
ATM machine

User cannot directly modify bank database.

They interact using:

deposit()
withdraw()

methods.

docs.title: Interview Trap
docs.text:
Question:

Is Encapsulation only about data hiding?

Answer:

No.
Encapsulation is binding data and behavior together.
Data hiding is one benefit of encapsulation.

docs.title: Notes for Interview
docs.text:
You can answer like this:

Encapsulation means wrapping data and methods together in a class and restricting direct access to the data using access modifiers like private. This helps achieve data hiding and controlled access through public methods.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Abstraction means:

Hiding implementation details
and showing only essential features.

docs.title: Real Example
docs.text:
Car driving

Driver uses:

steering
brake
accelerator

But driver doesn't know internal engine working.

That is abstraction.

docs.title: How Java Implements Abstraction
docs.text:
Java provides two ways:

Abstract class
Interface

docs.title: Abstract Class Example
docs.text:
abstract class Animal {

    abstract void sound();

    void sleep() {
        System.out.println("Animal sleeping");
    }
}

Subclass:

class Dog extends Animal {

    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barking");
    }
}

docs.title: Interface Example
docs.text:
interface Payment {
    void pay();
}

Implementation:

class UPI implements Payment {
    public void pay() {
        System.out.println("Pay using UPI");
    }
}

docs.title: Interview Trap
docs.text:
Question:

Difference between abstraction and encapsulation?

Answer:

Encapsulation → hiding data
Abstraction → hiding implementation

Example:

Encapsulation → private variables
Abstraction → abstract class / interface

docs.title: Interview Ready Answer
docs.text: Abstraction means hiding internal implementation and exposing only necessary functionality to the user. In Java, abstraction is achieved using abstract classes and interfaces.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Inheritance means:

One class acquiring properties and behavior of another class.

Example:

Parent → Child relationship

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Animal {

    void eat() {
        System.out.println("Animal eating");
    }
}

Child class:

class Dog extends Animal {

    void bark() {
        System.out.println("Dog barking");
    }
}

Usage:

Dog d = new Dog();
d.eat();
d.bark();

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
Code reuse
Hierarchy modeling
Method overriding

docs.title: Types of Inheritance in Java
docs.text:
Java supports:

Single inheritance
Multilevel inheritance
Hierarchical inheritance

Java does NOT support multiple inheritance with classes.

But supports it via:

Interfaces

docs.title: Interview Trap
docs.text:
Question:

Why Java does not support multiple inheritance?

Answer:

Diamond problem ambiguity

Example:

A
↑ ↑
B   C
↑
D

JVM would not know which method to use.

docs.title: 4️⃣ Polymorphism
docs.text:
Polymorphism means:

One interface, multiple implementations.

Two types:

Compile-time polymorphism
Runtime polymorphism

docs.title: Compile-Time Polymorphism
docs.text:
Also called:

Method Overloading

Example:

class Calculator {

    int add(int a, int b) {
        return a + b;
    }

    int add(int a, int b, int c) {
        return a + b + c;
    }
}

Method decided during compilation.

docs.title: Runtime Polymorphism
docs.text:
Also called:

Method Overriding

Example:

class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal sound");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog barking");
    }
}

Usage:

Animal a = new Dog();
a.sound();

Output:

Dog barking

Method decided during runtime.

docs.title: Interview Trap
docs.text:
Question:

Animal a = new Dog();

Which method executes?

Answer:

Method of Dog class

Because of runtime polymorphism.

docs.title: Method Dispatch Rule
docs.text:
Method call resolved at runtime
based on object type

Not reference type.

docs.title: Interview Ready OOP Summary
docs.text:
You can answer like this:

OOP in Java is based on four main principles:

Encapsulation – wrapping data and methods together and restricting direct access using access modifiers.

Abstraction – hiding implementation details and exposing only essential functionality using abstract classes and interfaces.

Inheritance – allowing one class to acquire properties and behavior of another class for code reuse.

Polymorphism – allowing one interface to have multiple implementations, achieved through method overloading and method overriding.

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text:
When interviewer asks:

"Explain OOP concepts"

Answer in this order:

Encapsulation
Inheritance
Polymorphism
Abstraction

This is the most natural explanation order.

Now we start Polymorphism Deep Dive, which is one of the most asked OOP topics in interviews.

We will cover:

1. Method Overriding rules
2. Dynamic Method Dispatch
3. Covariant Return Type
4. Method Hiding (static methods)
5. super vs this
6. Constructor chaining
7. Important interview traps

I will also give short notes you can remember for interviews.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: == checks reference identity for objects. equals() checks logical equality when properly overridden. hashCode() supports hash-based collections.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: This topic is critical for HashMap, HashSet, object comparison, and many Java interview questions.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Two different Employee objects with the same id can be logically equal if equals() compares the id.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• == and equals() are different for objects.
  • If two objects are equal, they must have the same hashCode.
  • Overriding equals without hashCode breaks hash collections.
  • Mutable fields in equals/hashCode can break HashSet and HashMap.
  • String overrides equals to compare content.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: == compares whether two object references point to the same object. equals() can be overridden to compare business equality. hashCode() must be consistent with equals() because hash-based collections use hashCode to find buckets and equals to confirm equality.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• == checks reference identity.
  • equals() checks logical equality when overridden.
  • Equal objects must have equal hash codes.
  • HashSet and HashMap depend on this contract.
  • String compares content with equals.
  • Avoid mutable equality keys.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text: Now the next most important interview area is:

docs.title: equals(), ==, hashCode(), toString()
docs.text:
This is asked very frequently because it checks whether you really understand:

  • object comparison
  • collections behavior
  • HashMap / HashSet basics
  • Object class methods

Let’s start with the most common one.

docs.title: ==
docs.text:
For objects:

Compares references (address-like identity)

Example:

String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1 == s2);

Output:

false

Because both are different objects.

docs.title: equals()
docs.text:
Compares content or logical equality

Example:

String s1 = new String("Java");
String s2 = new String("Java");

System.out.println(s1.equals(s2));

Output:

true

Because content is same.

docs.title: Important Trap
docs.text:
For custom classes:

class Person {
    String name;
}

Person p1 = new Person();
p1.name = "Vishu";

Person p2 = new Person();
p2.name = "Vishu";

System.out.println(p1.equals(p2));

What will be the output if we do not override equals()?

docs.title: Output
docs.text: false

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Because we did not override equals().

So Java uses the default implementation from:

java.lang.Object

Default equals() implementation is basically:

return (this == obj);

So it compares references, not object content.

docs.title: Memory Concept
docs.text:
Stack
-----
p1 → Person Object A
p2 → Person Object B

Heap
-----
Person Object A
   name = "Vishu"

Person Object B
   name = "Vishu"

Even though the values are same, the objects are different.

So:

p1.equals(p2) → false

docs.title: Correct Way: Override equals()
docs.text:
Example:

class Person {

    String name;

    public boolean equals(Object obj) {

        if (this == obj)
            return true;

        if (obj == null || getClass() != obj.getClass())
            return false;

        Person p = (Person) obj;

        return name.equals(p.name);
    }
}

Now:

Person p1 = new Person();
p1.name = "Vishu";

Person p2 = new Person();
p2.name = "Vishu";

System.out.println(p1.equals(p2));

Output:

true

Because now comparison is based on content.

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text:
When interviewer asks:

Why override equals()?

Answer:

To compare logical equality of objects instead of reference equality.

docs.title: Very Important Rule
docs.text:
Whenever you override:

equals()

you must also override:

hashCode()

Otherwise collections like:

HashMap
HashSet

will behave incorrectly.

We will cover this next.

docs.title: Next Famous Interview Question
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Person {
    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }
}

HashSet<Person> set = new HashSet<>();

set.add(new Person("Vishu"));
set.add(new Person("Vishu"));

System.out.println(set.size());

What will print?

1
or
2

Explain why.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
2

Because HashSet uses hashCode() and equals() to determine object uniqueness and bucket placement. Here both objects are not considered equal, so both will be stored in the set.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
We did not override:

equals()
hashCode()

So the default implementations from Object are used.

Default behavior:

equals() → reference comparison
hashCode() → memory-based hash

docs.title: What Happens Internally in HashSet
docs.text:
When you add an object:

HashSet → internally uses HashMap

Each object is stored as:

key → object
value → dummy value

docs.title: Step 1 — First Object
docs.text:
new Person("Vishu")

HashSet computes:

hashCode()

A bucket is selected.

Object stored.

docs.title: Step 2 — Second Object
docs.text:
new Person("Vishu")

Another object is created.

Even though name is same:

Different object
Different reference
Different hashCode()

So HashSet thinks:

This is a new unique element

Thus it stores it.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: set.size() → 2

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
For HashSet to detect duplicates:

hashCode() must be same
AND
equals() must return true

Both conditions must hold.

docs.title: Correct Implementation
docs.text:
class Person {

    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {

        if (this == obj) return true;
        if (!(obj instanceof Person)) return false;

        Person p = (Person) obj;
        return name.equals(p.name);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return name.hashCode();
    }
}

Now:

set.add(new Person("Vishu"));
set.add(new Person("Vishu"));

Result:

set.size() → 1

docs.title: Important Interview Contract
docs.text:
Java rule:

If two objects are equal according to equals(),
they must have the same hashCode().

But the reverse is not required.

Meaning:

Same hashCode ≠ objects must be equal

docs.title: Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
Look at this code:

class Person {
    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public boolean equals(Object obj) {
        Person p = (Person) obj;
        return name.equals(p.name);
    }
}

Here we override:

equals()

but not:

hashCode()

Now this code:

HashSet<Person> set = new HashSet<>();

set.add(new Person("Vishu"));
set.add(new Person("Vishu"));

System.out.println(set.size());

docs.title: What will print?
docs.text:
1
or
2

This is one of the most famous Java interview questions.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
2

It will print 2.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
We overrode equals(), but we did not override hashCode().

HashSet works in two steps:

Step 1 → hashCode() decides bucket
Step 2 → equals() checks duplicate inside bucket

docs.title: First Object
docs.text:
new Person("Vishu")

JVM calls:

hashCode()

Since we did not override it, Object.hashCode() is used.

A bucket is chosen.

Object is stored.

docs.title: Second Object
docs.text:
new Person("Vishu")

JVM calls:

hashCode()

Again default hashCode().

But this object is a different object, so it usually produces a different hashCode.

Therefore:

Different bucket

Because buckets are different:

equals() is never called

So HashSet stores it.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: set.size() → 2

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Always remember this:

If equals() is overridden,
hashCode() must also be overridden.

Otherwise collections like:

HashSet
HashMap
HashTable

will behave incorrectly.

docs.title: Interview Contract (Very Important)
docs.text:
Java rule:

If two objects are equal according to equals(),
they must have the same hashCode().

But the reverse is not required.

Meaning:

Same hashCode does not guarantee equality.

docs.title: Correct Implementation
docs.text:
class Person {

    String name;

    Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object obj) {

        if (this == obj) return true;

        if (!(obj instanceof Person)) return false;

        Person p = (Person) obj;

        return name.equals(p.name);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return name.hashCode();
    }
}

Now:

set.size() → 1

because both objects are considered equal.

docs.title: Interview Summary Notes (Important)
docs.text:
You can answer like this:

HashSet first uses hashCode() to determine the bucket.
If two objects fall into the same bucket, equals() is used to check logical equality.
Therefore when overriding equals(), we must also override hashCode() to maintain the contract.

docs.title: Very Famous Interview Question (Final Trap)
docs.text:
Predict output:

String a = "Java";
String b = "Java";
String c = new String("Java");

System.out.println(a == b);
System.out.println(a == c);
System.out.println(a.equals(c));

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
a == b → true a == c → false a.equals(c) → true

Now let’s explain it the way interviewers expect.

docs.title: Step 1 — "Java" literal
docs.text:
String a = "Java";

JVM checks the String Pool.

If "Java" is not present → create it.

Memory:

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

Then:

a → "Java"

docs.title: Step 2 — second literal
docs.text:
String b = "Java";

JVM checks the pool again.

Since "Java" already exists:

b → same pool object

Memory:

a → "Java"
b → "Java"

docs.title: First Output
docs.text:
a == b

== compares references.

Both references point to the same pool object.

true

docs.title: Step 3 — new String("Java")
docs.text:
String c = new String("Java");

Two things happen:

1️⃣ "Java" literal exists in the pool 2️⃣ JVM creates a new String object in heap

Memory:

Stack
-----
a → pool "Java"
b → pool "Java"
c → heap "Java"

Heap
-----
String("Java")

String Pool
-----------
"Java"

docs.title: Second Output
docs.text:
a == c

Reference comparison.

pool object ≠ heap object

So:

false

docs.title: Third Output
docs.text:
a.equals(c)

equals() compares content, not reference.

Both contain:

"Java"

So:

true

docs.title: Important Interview Summary
docs.text: Expression What it compares == reference equals() content

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Object initialization is the process where Java allocates an object, sets default values, runs field initializers and blocks, and then runs constructors.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Initialization order is a common interview trap, especially when constructors call overridden methods or parent and child classes initialize together.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: When creating a child object, Java first initializes the parent part, then the child part.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Parent constructor runs before child constructor body.
  • Overridden methods called from constructors can run before child fields are initialized.
  • Fields get default values before explicit initialization.
  • Constructor does not create the object; it initializes it.
  • Initialization order affects output questions.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: When an object is created, memory is allocated first and fields get default values. Then Java runs superclass initialization before subclass initialization. Constructor bodies run after field initialization for that class. Calling overridable methods from constructors is risky because child state may not be ready.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Memory allocation happens before constructor body.
  • Fields get default values first.
  • Parent initialization happens before child initialization.
  • Avoid calling overridable methods in constructors.
  • Constructor initializes object state.
  • Initialization order is important for output questions.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Before finishing OOP, the next deep topics are:

Object class methods
equals() vs ==
hashCode()
toString()
clone()

These appear in almost every Java interview.

docs.title: Predict output:
docs.text:
class Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Animal");
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    void sound() {
        System.out.println("Dog");
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Animal a = new Dog();
        a.sound();

        a = new Animal();
        a.sound();
    }
}

What will print? Explain why.

docs.title: Output:
docs.text:
Dog Animal

Better explanation sentence:

The output is Dog then Animal because method execution depends on the object type at runtime.

docs.title: First Line
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();

Reference type:

Animal

Object type:

Dog

Now:

a.sound();

JVM checks object type, not reference type.

Object type = Dog

So JVM calls:

Dog.sound()

Output:

Dog

docs.title: Second Line
docs.text:
a = new Animal();

Now:

Reference type:

Animal

Object type:

Animal

Now:

a.sound();

JVM calls:

Animal.sound()

Output:

Animal

docs.title: Final Output
docs.text:
Dog
Animal

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Instance methods follow:

Runtime Polymorphism

Meaning:

Method execution depends on object type

docs.title: Visual Memory
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();

Stack
-----
a  →  Dog Object

Heap
-----
Dog Object

Later:

a = new Animal();

Stack now points to new object:

a → Animal Object

docs.title: Interview Tip
docs.text:
When interviewer asks:

Animal a = new Dog();

Always explain two things:

Reference Type
Object Type

This shows strong OOP understanding.

docs.title: Very Important OOP Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Animal {
    int x = 10;
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    int x = 20;
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Animal a = new Dog();
        System.out.println(a.x);
    }
}

docs.title: What will print?
docs.text: Explain why.

docs.title: Answer:
docs.text:
10 is correct ✅.

Because variables are resolved using the reference type, not the object type.

But the reason interviewers expect is slightly more precise.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
class Animal {
    int x = 10;
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    int x = 20;
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Animal a = new Dog();
        System.out.println(a.x);
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text: 10

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
Here:

Reference type → Animal
Object type → Dog

But variables do NOT use runtime polymorphism.

Variables are resolved at compile time.

So JVM checks the reference type.

Reference type = Animal

So JVM uses:

Animal.x

Which is:

10

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
This is a very famous Java rule.

Methods → runtime polymorphism (object type)
Variables → compile-time binding (reference type)

docs.title: Visual Explanation
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();

Memory:

Stack
-----
a → Dog object

Heap
-----
Dog Object
   x = 20
   (inherits Animal.x = 10)

But compiler resolves:

a.x → Animal.x

So output:

10

docs.title: Why Java Works Like This
docs.text:
Because variables cannot be overridden, they can only be hidden.

Example:

Animal.x
Dog.x

Both variables exist separately.

This is called:

Variable Hiding

docs.title: Interview Trick
docs.text:
Look at this modified code.

Animal a = new Dog();
Dog d = new Dog();

System.out.println(a.x);
System.out.println(d.x);

Output:

10
20

Because:

a.x → Animal.x
d.x → Dog.x

docs.title: Another Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Animal {
    int x = 10;

    void show() {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    int x = 20;
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Animal a = new Dog();
        a.show();
    }
}

Will it print:

10
or
20

Explain why.

It will print 10.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
10

Now let's understand why, because the reasoning here is very important for interviews.

docs.title: Step 1 — Object creation
docs.text:
Animal a = new Dog();

Reference type:

Animal

Object type:

Dog

Memory conceptually:

Stack
-----
a → Dog Object

Heap
-----
Dog Object
   x = 20
   inherits Animal.x = 10

Both variables exist:

Animal.x
Dog.x

docs.title: Step 2 — Method call
docs.text:
a.show();

Methods follow runtime polymorphism.

So JVM checks object type.

Object type = Dog.

But Dog does not override show().

So JVM uses:

Animal.show()

docs.title: Step 3 — Inside show()
docs.text:
Inside method:

System.out.println(x);

Here x belongs to Animal class, because the method is defined in Animal.

So it accesses:

Animal.x

Value:

10

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Remember this clearly:

Method execution → object type (runtime)
Variable access → class where method is defined

Or more commonly stated:

Methods → runtime binding
Variables → compile-time binding

docs.title: What If Dog Overrides show()?
docs.text:
Example:

class Dog extends Animal {

    int x = 20;

    void show() {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

Now code:

Animal a = new Dog();
a.show();

Output becomes:

20

Because now:

Dog.show()

runs.

docs.title: Interview Summary Rule
docs.text:
Method overridden → runtime decision
Method not overridden → parent method executes
Variables never overridden → only hidden

docs.title: One More Famous Interview Trap
docs.text:
Predict the output:

class Parent {

    Parent() {
        print();
    }

    void print() {
        System.out.println("Parent");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {

    int x = 10;

    void print() {
        System.out.println(x);
    }
}

public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Child();
    }
}

Will it print:

10
0
Parent

docs.title: Output
docs.text: 0

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
This is a very famous Java interview trap.

The tricky part is:

Parent() {
    print();
}

Inside the parent constructor, JVM calls:

print();

Because print() is an overridden instance method, JVM uses runtime polymorphism.

So it calls:

Child.print()

docs.title: But Why Does It Print 0 Instead of 10?
docs.text: Because during object creation, initialization happens in this order:

docs.title: Step 1 — Memory allocated
docs.text:
Child object is created in heap.

At this moment all instance variables get default values:

x = 0

docs.title: Step 2 — Parent constructor runs first
docs.text:
Before child constructor body and child field initialization, parent constructor executes.

So this line runs:

print();

Due to overriding, it calls:

Child.print()

But x is still:

0

because child field initialization:

int x = 10;

has not happened yet.

So output is:

0

docs.title: Full Initialization Flow
docs.text:
For:

new Child();

JVM does roughly this:

1. Allocate Child object
2. Set default values
   x = 0
3. Call Parent constructor
4. Parent constructor calls print()
5. Due to polymorphism, Child.print() runs
6. Child.print() prints x → 0
7. Parent constructor finishes
8. Child field initialization happens
   x = 10
9. Child constructor body runs

docs.title: Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Never call overridable methods from constructors

Because subclass state may not be initialized yet.

This can cause:

  • unexpected values
  • bugs
  • partially initialized object behavior

docs.title: Why This Happens
docs.text:
Because:

Methods are polymorphic even inside constructors

But:

Subclass fields are initialized only after parent constructor finishes

That combination creates this trap.

docs.title: Interview-Ready Note
docs.text:
You can answer like this:

The output is 0 because during object creation the parent constructor runs before child field initialization. The parent constructor calls the overridden print() method, so Child.print() executes, but x still has its default value 0 at that time.

docs.title: Very Important OOP Trap Summary
docs.text:
Remember this order:

Default initialization
→ Parent constructor
→ Child field initialization
→ Child constructor

docs.title: One more interview question
docs.text:
Predict output:

class Parent {
    Parent() {
        show();
    }

    void show() {
        System.out.println("Parent show");
    }
}

class Child extends Parent {
    String name = "Vishu";

    void show() {
        System.out.println(name);
    }
}

public class Test {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        new Child();
    }
}

Will it print:

Vishu
null
Parent show

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
It will print null.

null

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: This is the same constructor + polymorphism trap.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
When this runs:

new Child();

JVM does:

1. Allocate Child object
2. Default initialize instance variables
   name = null
3. Call Parent constructor
4. Parent constructor calls show()
5. Due to overriding, Child.show() runs
6. name is still null
7. After parent constructor ends, child field initialization runs
   name = "Vishu"

So when show() is called from parent constructor, name has not yet been assigned "Vishu".

Therefore output is:

null

docs.title: Very Important Interview Rule
docs.text:
Do not call overridable methods from constructors

Because child state may still have:

  • default values
  • partial initialization
  • invalid state

docs.title: Notes for Interview
docs.text:
You can say:

The output is null because the parent constructor calls an overridden method. At that time the child object is created but child instance variables are only default-initialized, so name is null. Child field initialization happens after the parent constructor completes.

docs.title: Important Initialization Order
docs.text:
Remember this exact order:

1. Memory allocation
2. Default values
3. Parent constructor
4. Child instance field initialization
5. Child constructor

This order is very important for OOP interviews.

docs.title: Mini Note: constructor vs method behavior
docs.text:
Constructors are not overridden
Methods are overridden
Calling overridden methods inside constructor is dangerous

docs.title: Object Methods: toString, getClass, and clone
Definition
docs.text: Every Java class inherits common methods from Object, including toString(), getClass(), and clone().

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: These methods appear in debugging, logging, equality checks, reflection, and copy-related interview questions.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: Overriding toString() makes logs and printed objects readable instead of showing class name plus hash-like text.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Default toString() is usually not useful for business output.
  • getClass() returns the runtime class.
  • clone() is tricky and often avoided.
  • Shallow copy and deep copy are different.
  • Cloneable does not define a public clone method.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Java objects inherit methods from Object. toString() gives a string representation and is commonly overridden for readable output. getClass() returns runtime class information. clone() can copy objects but is tricky because default cloning is shallow, so many codebases prefer copy constructors or factory methods.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• All classes extend Object directly or indirectly.
  • Override toString for readable logs.
  • getClass returns runtime class.
  • clone creates shallow copy by default.
  • Deep copy must copy nested objects.
  • Prefer clear copy methods over clone in many designs.

docs.title: Deep Dive
docs.text:
Now we move to Object Class Methods.

These are extremely common interview topics:

equals()
hashCode()
toString()
clone()
getClass()

Most interview questions come from:

equals()
hashCode()
toString()

You already understand equals + hashCode, so let's finish OOP with:

docs.title: What is toString() ?
docs.text:
Every class in Java inherits from:

java.lang.Object

Inside Object class there is:

public String toString()

Default implementation looks like:

ClassName@HexHashCode

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
class Person {
    String name = "Vishu";
}

public class Test {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        Person p = new Person();
        System.out.println(p);
    }
}

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Example output:

Person@4a54c0de

Why?

Because internally Java calls:

p.toString()

docs.title: Default toString() Implementation
docs.text:
Inside Object class:

public String toString() {
    return getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(hashCode());
}

So output becomes:

ClassName@HashCode

docs.title: Overriding toString()
docs.text:
Usually we override it to print meaningful data.

Example:

class Person {

    String name;
    int age;

    Person(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String toString() {
        return name + " " + age;
    }
}

Usage:

Person p = new Person("Vishu", 30);
System.out.println(p);

Output:

Vishu 30

docs.title: Interview Question
docs.text:
Why override toString()?

Answer:

To provide a meaningful string representation of an object.

Very useful for:

logging
debugging
printing objects

docs.title: Example in Collections
docs.text:
List<Person> list = new ArrayList<>();

list.add(new Person("Vishu",30));

System.out.println(list);

If toString() is overridden:

[Vishu 30]

Otherwise:

[Person@15db9742]

docs.title: getClass()
docs.text:
Example:

Person p = new Person();

System.out.println(p.getClass());

Output:

class Person

docs.title: One More Important OOP Topic
docs.text: Before finishing OOP, we should cover:

docs.title: clone() Method
docs.text:
This is sometimes asked in interviews.

Example:

class Person implements Cloneable {

    int age = 30;

    protected Object clone() throws CloneNotSupportedException {
        return super.clone();
    }
}

Usage:

Person p1 = new Person();
Person p2 = (Person) p1.clone();

Now:

p1 ≠ p2

But they contain same data.

docs.title: Interview Trap
docs.text:
Difference between:

Shallow Copy
Deep Copy

Example:

clone() → shallow copy by default
