    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;

    private String email;
    private String name;
}

docs.title: Repository
docs.text:
public interface UserRepository extends JpaRepository<User, Long> {
    Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);
}

docs.title: Service Layer
docs.text:
@Service
public class UserService {
    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }

    public UserResponse getUser(Long id) {
        User user = userRepository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new UserNotFoundException(id));

        return UserResponse.from(user);
    }
}

docs.title: Transaction
docs.text:
@Transactional
public void transferMoney(Long fromId, Long toId, BigDecimal amount) {
    // multiple DB updates as one unit
}

docs.title: Lazy Loading
docs.text:
Lazy loading means related data is loaded only when accessed.

Trap:

LazyInitializationException

This can happen when accessing lazy relation outside transaction/session.

docs.title: N+1 Problem
docs.text:
Example:

1 query to fetch users
N queries to fetch orders for each user

Fix options:

  • fetch join
  • entity graph
  • DTO query
  • batch fetching

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Design database access around use cases. Do not expose entities as API responses. Understand when to use JPA, when to write custom queries, and when a simpler JDBC approach may be better.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Spring Security provides authentication, authorization, and protection mechanisms for Spring applications.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Security is required in most backend systems. Interviewers expect clear understanding of authentication, authorization, filters, password hashing, sessions, JWT, and role-based access.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text:
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
public void deleteUser(Long id) {
    userRepository.deleteById(id);
}

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Confusing authentication and authorization.
  • Storing plain text passwords.
  • Trusting client-provided roles.
  • Not validating JWT properly.
  • Disabling CSRF without understanding why.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Authentication checks who the user is. Authorization checks what the user is allowed to do. Spring Security uses a filter chain to process requests, establish security context, and enforce access rules.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Authentication: identity.
  • Authorization: permission.
  • Passwords must be hashed.
  • JWT is stateless token-based auth.
  • SecurityContext stores current authentication.
  • Filter chain processes requests.

docs.title: Authentication vs Authorization
docs.text:
Authentication:

Who are you?

Authorization:

What can you access?

docs.title: Password Hashing
docs.text:
Never store plain text passwords.

Use strong password hashing:

PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder();

docs.title: JWT Basic Flow
docs.text:
1. User logs in.
2. Server verifies credentials.
3. Server returns token.
4. Client sends token in Authorization header.
5. Server validates token for protected requests.

Header:

Authorization: Bearer <token>

docs.title: Role-Based Access
docs.text:
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('USER_READ')")
public UserResponse getUser(Long id) {
    return userService.getUser(id);
}

docs.title: Common Security Layers
docs.text:
• Transport security: HTTPS.
  • Authentication.
  • Authorization.
  • Input validation.
  • CSRF protection where needed.
  • Rate limiting.
  • Audit logs.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Security is not only annotations. You must think about token expiry, refresh tokens, password reset, audit logs, least privilege, secret management, and failure responses that do not leak sensitive details.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Testing Spring Boot applications means verifying business logic, web endpoints, database behavior, and integration boundaries.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Testing proves that code works and protects refactors. Strong Spring developers know when to use unit tests, slice tests, and full integration tests.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text:
@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerTest {
    @Autowired
    MockMvc mockMvc;
}

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Using full @SpringBootTest for every test.
  • Testing framework behavior instead of your logic.
  • Mocking too much in integration tests.
  • Ignoring database tests.
  • Not testing error responses.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: Spring Boot testing can be done at different levels. Unit tests test plain Java logic. Slice tests like @WebMvcTest test a layer such as controllers. @SpringBootTest loads the full context for integration tests. The right test depends on what confidence is needed.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Unit test: fast, no Spring context.
  • @WebMvcTest: controller layer.
  • @DataJpaTest: repository layer.
  • @SpringBootTest: full context.
  • Mock external dependencies.
  • Test success and failure paths.

docs.title: Unit Test
docs.text:
class PriceCalculatorTest {
    @Test
    void appliesDiscount() {
        PriceCalculator calculator = new PriceCalculator();
        BigDecimal result = calculator.applyDiscount(new BigDecimal("100"), 10);
        assertEquals(new BigDecimal("90"), result);
    }
}

No Spring needed.

docs.title: Controller Test
docs.text:
@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerTest {
    @Autowired
    MockMvc mockMvc;

    @MockBean
    UserService userService;
}

Use for:

  • request mapping
  • validation
  • status codes
  • response body

docs.title: Repository Test
docs.text:
@DataJpaTest
class UserRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired
    UserRepository userRepository;
}

Use for:

  • query methods
  • custom queries
  • entity mappings

docs.title: Full Integration Test
docs.text:
@SpringBootTest
class ApplicationIntegrationTest {
}

Use when you need full application context.

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text:
Good test strategy uses a test pyramid:

  • many unit tests
  • some slice tests
  • fewer full integration tests

For real systems, use Testcontainers or dedicated integration environments for database-dependent tests.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Production readiness means the application is observable, configurable, secure, stable, and deployable.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Building an API is not enough. Senior developers must know how the app behaves in production, how to diagnose issues, and how to operate it safely.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text:
Spring Boot Actuator can expose health information:

/actuator/health

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Logging sensitive data.
  • Not using profiles.
  • Missing health checks.
  • No timeout configuration.
  • No metrics or traceability.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: A production-ready Spring Boot application should use externalized configuration, profiles, structured logging, health checks, metrics, proper error handling, secure secrets, timeouts, and graceful shutdown. Spring Boot Actuator provides many production endpoints.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Use profiles for environments.
  • Use Actuator for health and metrics.
  • Configure logging carefully.
  • Do not expose secrets.
  • Add timeouts for external calls.
  • Monitor errors and latency.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
spring.profiles.active=dev

Common profile files:

application-dev.properties
application-prod.properties

docs.title: Actuator
docs.text:
Actuator provides endpoints for:

  • health
  • metrics
  • info
  • environment
  • loggers

Common health endpoint:

/actuator/health

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Good logs include:

  • what happened
  • request id or trace id
  • important business id
  • error code
  • exception details when safe

Do not log:

  • passwords
  • tokens
  • card details
  • private user data

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Use environment variables or secret stores for sensitive values.

Avoid committing secrets to git.

docs.title: External Calls
docs.text:
Always think about:

  • timeout
  • retry
  • circuit breaker
  • fallback
  • idempotency

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: Production readiness is about failure handling. Ask what happens when database is slow, downstream API fails, memory grows, deployment restarts, or traffic spikes.

docs.title: Phase 8: Interview and System Design Connections
Definition
docs.text: Spring Boot interview preparation connects framework features with backend design decisions.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: Interviewers often ask not only what an annotation does, but why the design is clean, scalable, testable, and production-ready.

docs.title: Core Example
docs.text: A clean Spring Boot API usually separates controller, service, repository, DTO, validation, exception handling, and configuration.

docs.title: Common Traps
docs.text:
• Explaining only annotations.
  • Not knowing request flow.
  • Not separating layers.
  • Ignoring transactions.
  • Not connecting Spring features to design principles.

docs.title: Interview Answer
docs.text: In a Spring Boot application, a request enters through the web layer, reaches the controller, passes validated data to the service layer, executes business logic, uses repositories for persistence, and returns a DTO response. Cross-cutting concerns like security, logging, transactions, and exception handling are managed separately.

docs.title: Quick Revision
docs.text:
• Controller handles HTTP.
  • Service handles business logic.
  • Repository handles persistence.
  • DTO protects API boundary.
  • @Transactional controls DB unit of work.
  • Security and exceptions are cross-cutting concerns.

docs.title: Typical Request Flow
docs.text:
Client
  -> Filter Chain
  -> DispatcherServlet
  -> Controller
  -> Service
  -> Repository
  -> Database

Response returns back through the same layers.

docs.title: Layered Design
docs.text:
Controller:

  • request and response
  • status codes
  • validation trigger

Service:

  • business rules
  • transaction boundary
  • orchestration

Repository:

  • database access
  • query methods
  • persistence abstraction

docs.title: Design Principles in Spring
docs.text:
Dependency Inversion:

Service depends on repository interface.

Single Responsibility:

Controller does not contain database logic.

Open Closed:

Add new strategy implementation instead of editing large if-else.

Proxy Pattern:

Spring AOP and @Transactional use proxy-based behavior.

Singleton:

Default Spring beans are singleton scoped inside ApplicationContext.

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
What does @SpringBootApplication do?
What is dependency injection?
Why constructor injection?
What is the difference between @Component, @Service, and @Repository?
How does @Transactional work?
How do you handle validation errors?
How do you secure REST APIs?
How do you test controller and repository layers?
How do you make a Spring Boot app production-ready?

docs.title: Senior-Level Notes
docs.text: A senior answer explains trade-offs. For example, do not just say “use cache”; explain cache invalidation, TTL, consistency, memory cost, and fallback behavior.
